b:pons_sublicius_v1.summary: The oldest bridge of Rome, built entirely of wood on piles (sublicae) and fastened without iron, the bridge Horatius Cocles held against Porsenna. It crossed the Tiber from the Forum Boarium near the Porta Trigemina just below the later Pons Aemilius; its exact position is debated (Coarelli just downstream of the Pons Aemilius; others nearer the Aventine).

phases.t: Built by Ancus Marcius according to tradition, of timber held together without iron so that it could be dismantled.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Sublicius
Coarelli, Il Foro Boario (1988)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Sublicius
Taylor, 'Tiber river bridges and the development of the ancient city of Rome', The Waters of Rome 2 (2002)
b:pons_sublicius_v1.note: Placed about 170 m below the Pons Aemilius, between the Porta Trigemina and the Salinae, crossing roughly perpendicular to the southward current. Length assumes an ancient river about 110 m wide here. Number of pile bents unknown (10 assumed).

b:pons_sublicius_v2.summary: The oldest bridge of Rome, built entirely of wood on piles (sublicae) and fastened without iron, the bridge Horatius Cocles held against Porsenna. It crossed the Tiber from the Forum Boarium near the Porta Trigemina just below the later Pons Aemilius; its exact position is debated (Coarelli just downstream of the Pons Aemilius; others nearer the Aventine).

phases.t: Cut down behind Horatius Cocles against Porsenna (508); repeatedly carried away by floods and rebuilt in timber under the care of the pontifices.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Sublicius
Coarelli, Il Foro Boario (1988)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Sublicius
Taylor, 'Tiber river bridges and the development of the ancient city of Rome', The Waters of Rome 2 (2002)
b:pons_sublicius_v2.note: Placed about 170 m below the Pons Aemilius, between the Porta Trigemina and the Salinae, crossing roughly perpendicular to the southward current. Length assumes an ancient river about 110 m wide here. Number of pile bents unknown (10 assumed).

b:pons_sublicius_v3.summary: The oldest bridge of Rome, built entirely of wood on piles (sublicae) and fastened without iron, the bridge Horatius Cocles held against Porsenna. It crossed the Tiber from the Forum Boarium near the Porta Trigemina just below the later Pons Aemilius; its exact position is debated (Coarelli just downstream of the Pons Aemilius; others nearer the Aventine).

phases.t: Swept away in the flood of 23 BC (Cassius Dio 53.33.5) and rebuilt; restored again by Antoninus Pius; still listed among the bridges in the 4th-century Notitia. Possibly given stone piers in the Empire, timber deck kept for religious reasons.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Sublicius

b:pons_sublicius_v3.note: Placed about 170 m below the Pons Aemilius, between the Porta Trigemina and the Salinae, crossing roughly perpendicular to the southward current. Length assumes an ancient river about 110 m wide here. Number of pile bents unknown (10 assumed).

b:pons_aemilius_v1.summary: The first stone bridge of Rome: in 179 BC the censors laid stone piers (pilae) across the Tiber from the Forum Boarium to Transtiberim, carrying a wooden deck.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Aemilius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Aemilius
b:pons_aemilius_v1.note: Axis from the surviving arch of the Ponte Rotto: the remnant pier block (OSM) has its short sides along about 77/257 degrees, the bridge running from the bridgehead by the Casa dei Crescenzi (left bank) obliquely WSW to Transtiberim; endpoints set at the modern embankments.
b:pons_aemilius_v1.builderName: the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior

b:pons_aemilius_v2.summary: In 142 BC the censors vaulted the piers of 179 BC with arches, making the Pons Aemilius the first fully stone bridge over the Tiber.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Aemilius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
b:pons_aemilius_v2.note: Six arches assumed (as in the medieval bridge); spans about 24 m at the centre.
b:pons_aemilius_v2.builderName: the censors P. Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus and L. Mummius

b:pons_aemilius_v3.summary: Rebuilt by Augustus (an inscription of 12 BC is attributed to it) with travertine facing and flood openings over the piers; repaired often (Probus, 280; late antiquity). It stood through our period; its last arch survives as the Ponte Rotto after the flood of 1598.

phases.t: Augustan reconstruction.
Restored under Probus (dubious).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Aemilius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Taylor, 'Tiber river bridges', The Waters of Rome 2 (2002)
b:pons_aemilius_v3.note: Ruin of one arch in mid-river at the given axis point (OSM Ponte Rotto, 41.88934 N 12.47937 E).

b:pons_fabricius.summary: The oldest Roman bridge still in use: built in 62 BC by L. Fabricius, curator viarum, from the Campus Martius (by the Theatre of Marcellus) to the Tiber Island, with two arches of about 24.5 m and a small flood arch over the central pier. Restored in 21 BC by the consuls M. Lollius and Q. Lepidus (inscriptions on both faces).

phases.t: Built by L. Fabricius (CIL VI 1305), replacing a wooden bridge of 192 BC.
Inspected and approved by the consuls M. Lollius and Q. Aemilius Lepidus after the flood of 23 BC.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Fabricius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Claridge, Rome (2010) 241
b:pons_fabricius.note: Line from the OSM deck way (Ponte Fabricio), left bank NE to the island SW; length 62-65 m, width 5.5 m. Deck elevation estimated (about 14 m above mean water).

b:pons_cestius_v1.summary: Bridge from the Tiber Island to Transtiberim, of uncertain late-Republican date (c. 46 BC), with one main arch of 23.65 m flanked by small flood arches.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Cestius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
b:pons_cestius_v1.note: Island end from the OSM deck; the Transtiberim end placed 52 m along the axis (the ancient bridge was about 48.5 m long; the 1888-92 rebuilding lengthened it to 80 m when the channel was widened).
b:pons_cestius_v1.builderName: a Cestius (perhaps L. Cestius, praetor 44 BC)

b:pons_cestius_v2.summary: Rebuilt in 365-370 by the emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, partly with travertine from the Theatre of Marcellus, and dedicated as the Pons Gratiani (inscriptions CIL VI 1175-1176).

phases.t: Dedicated as Pons Gratiani under Valentinian, Valens and Gratian.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Cestius
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Cestius

b:pons_agrippae.summary: Bridge named after Agrippa, known from a cippus of the curatores riparum of AD 147 and from piers found in the riverbed in 1887 about 120 m upstream of the Ponte Sisto; it linked the Campus Martius by the Euripus/Stagnum district with Transtiberim. It may have been replaced by the Pons Aurelius on the Ponte Sisto site.

phases.t: Repaired under Antoninus Pius (cippus CIL VI 31545).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Agrippae
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Taylor, 'Tiber river bridges', The Waters of Rome 2 (2002)
b:pons_agrippae.note: Position from the 1887 riverbed finds (about 120 m upstream of Ponte Sisto), axis parallel to Ponte Sisto. Some scholars identify it with the Pons Aurelius/Antoninus. Date of construction (Agrippa's works of c. 25 BC) and end date (not in the 4th-century list, so perhaps ruined or superseded; shown as foundations from 400) are uncertain.

b:pons_aurelius_v1.summary: The bridge on the site of the Ponte Sisto, named Aurelius (Notitia) and probably built or rebuilt by an Antonine emperor (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, i.e. Caracalla, is often preferred), carrying the Via Aurelia's city route from the Campus Martius into Transtiberim. From 271-275 it was joined to the Aurelian Wall at the Porta Aurelia/Septimiana side.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Aurelius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Aurelius
b:pons_aurelius_v1.note: Line from the OSM deck of Ponte Sisto (whose piers stand on the ancient foundations). Date of construction uncertain (Antonine; 212-215 assumed).

b:pons_aurelius_v2.summary: Rebuilt in 365-367 by Valentinian and Valens and dedicated by the prefect Symmachus with a triumphal arch at its left-bank end, whose bronze statues and inscriptions were recovered from the river in 1878-92. Below it in 537 Belisarius moored his floating mills. Damaged in 792, it was rebuilt as the Ponte Sisto in 1473-79.

phases.t: Dedication with the arch (CIL VI 31402-31412).
Belisarius' floating mills moored in the current below the bridge (Procopius 5.19.19-22).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Aurelius
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Valentiniani
b:pons_aurelius_v2.builderName: Valentinian I and Valens; the urban prefect L. Aurelius Avianius Symmachus

b:pons_neronianus.summary: Imperial bridge from the Campus Martius (end of the later Via Recta) to the Vatican plain, the Horti Agrippinae and the Circus of Gaius and Nero, built by Caligula or Nero. Missing from the 4th-century bridge list, it was probably ruined or deliberately broken by then; low-water remains of its piers lie just below the Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II near S. Spirito.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Neronianus
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Neronianus
b:pons_neronianus.note: Axis and position estimated from the low-water pier remains about 40 m downstream of Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II (OSM deck 12.4648 41.9008 to 12.4639 41.9015). Construction date (40-50) and ruin date (by 400) approximate.

b:pons_aelius.summary: Hadrian's bridge to his mausoleum, dedicated in 134: three main arches of 18.4 m over the river and sloping ramps on small arches at each end (three on the Campus side, two on the mausoleum side), faced in travertine. From 271-275 the mausoleum became a bridgehead fortress of the Aurelian Wall. The three central arches survive in the Ponte Sant'Angelo.

phases.t: Dedicated (CIL VI 973).
Integrated into the defences of the Mausoleum/Castellum under Honorius.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Aelius
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
Claridge, Rome (2010) 248
b:pons_aelius.note: Axis from the OSM deck of Ponte Sant'Angelo; total length with ramps about 135 m (the modern bridge's outer arches replaced the ramps in 1892-94).

b:pons_probi_v1.summary: Bridge built under Probus (276-282) below the Aventine, linking the Emporium and Marmorata with Transtiberim near the Porta Portuensis.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Probi
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Pons Probi
Galliazzo, I ponti romani (1994-95)
b:pons_probi_v1.note: Remains seen near the Marmorata (Via Marmorata / Arco di S. Lazzaro) and removed in 1484; crossing placed opposite them, about 180 m downstream of the modern Ponte Sublicio.

b:pons_probi_v2.summary: Restored under Theodosius (381-387) and thereafter called Pons Theodosii; Symmachus' letters complain of the slow work. It fell in the 11th century.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Pons Probi

b:horti_sallustiani_v1.summary: The gardens laid out by the historian Sallust in the valley between the Pincian and the Quirinal, on land once Caesar's, filled with pavilions, porticoes and sculpture (the Ludovisi Throne, the Dying Gaul group and the Niobids are attributed to them).
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Sallustiani
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Hartswick, The Gardens of Sallust: a changing landscape (2004)
Talamo, in Horti Romani (1998)
b:horti_sallustiani_v1.note: Extent from Piazza Sallustio (the surviving domed pavilion) between Via Veneto, the Servian Wall line and the Porta Salaria; boundaries schematic.

b:horti_sallustiani_v2.summary: Imperial park from AD 20, a favoured residence of Vespasian, Nerva (who died here), Hadrian and Aurelian, with the obelisk now at Trinita dei Monti and the domed Hadrianic pavilion still standing in Piazza Sallustio. Fighting in 69 reached them (Tacitus); in 410 Alaric's Goths, entering by the nearby Porta Salaria, set the house on fire.

phases.t: Flavian troops fight their way through the gardens (Tac. Hist. 3.82).
Hadrianic rebuilding of the main pavilion.
Burned by Alaric's Goths (Procopius 3.2.24): the half-burned house still stood in Procopius' day.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Sallustiani
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Hartswick, The Gardens of Sallust: a changing landscape (2004)
Talamo, in Horti Romani (1998)
b:horti_sallustiani_v2.note: After 410 continued as a ruinous estate (v3).

b:horti_sallustiani_v3.summary: The half-burned palace and overgrown grounds after the Gothic sack.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Sallustiani
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Hartswick, The Gardens of Sallust: a changing landscape (2004)
Talamo, in Horti Romani (1998)

b:horti_lucullani_v1.summary: Lucullus' gardens on the Pincian above the Campus Martius, the first great luxury horti of Rome: terraces stepping down the hill with a monumental exedra-nymphaeum under the Trinita dei Monti and Villa Medici, and a temple-like pavilion at the summit. Messalina coveted them and had Valerius Asiaticus driven to suicide in 47.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Luculliani
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Broise and Jolivet, in Horti Romani (1998) (excavations at Villa Medici)
b:horti_lucullani_v1.note: Terraced layout from the excavations of Broise and Jolivet; footprint from the slope between Piazza di Spagna, Via Sistina and the Villa Medici, stopping inside the later Aurelian Wall.

b:horti_lucullani_v2.summary: Imperial property after Messalina was killed here in 48. In late antiquity the Pincian estates passed to the Anicii and Pincii.

phases.t: Death of Messalina in the gardens (Tac. Ann. 11.37).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Luculliani
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Broise and Jolivet, in Horti Romani (1998) (excavations at Villa Medici)

b:horti_aciliorum_v1.summary: Gardens of the Acilii Glabriones on the northern Pincian, with terrace walls that the Aurelian Wall incorporated (the Muro Torto stretch).

Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
b:horti_aciliorum_v1.note: Northern Pincian between the Horti Lucullani and the Muro Torto; dates approximate (2nd-4th century).

b:horti_aciliorum_v2.summary: In late antiquity the Pincian estate of the Pincii became the Palatium Pincianum; Belisarius made it his headquarters in the siege of 537-538, commanding the Porta Pinciana and Salaria.

b:horti_pompeiani.summary: Pompey's gardens beside his theatre complex in the Campus Martius, seized after his death and occupied by Antony (Cicero's Second Philippic). Pompey also had 'upper gardens' elsewhere (perhaps on the Pincian or Esquiline), not drawn.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Pompeiani

b:horti_maecenatis_v1.summary: Maecenas' gardens laid over the Servian agger and the Esquiline paupers' cemetery, praised by Horace, with the high tower from which Nero watched Rome burn and the 'Auditorium' (a garden triclinium-nymphaeum) still standing on Largo Leopardi. Bequeathed to Augustus in 8 BC.

b:horti_maecenatis_v2.summary: Imperial gardens, their western edge absorbed by Trajan's baths and the Sette Sale reservoir.

b:horti_lamiani_v1.summary: Gardens of L. Aelius Lamia south of the Via Labicana around the present Piazza Vittorio, east of Maecenas'.

b:horti_lamiani_v2.summary: Imperial from 33; Caligula lived here, enlarged the pavilions and was hastily buried here after his murder. Finds include the Esquiline Venus, the bust of Commodus as Hercules and the Lancellotti Discobolus.

phases.t: Caligula receives the Alexandrian embassies while inspecting the rooms (Philo).
Caligula's body half-burned and buried here (Suet. Cal. 59).

scholarship: Haeuber, Horti Romani: die Horti Maecenatiani und die Horti Lamiani auf dem Esquilin (1991) and later work
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Barbera et al., excavations under the ENPAM building (2006-09); Museo Ninfeo
b:horti_lamiani_v2.note: Out of use by the 4th century (end date approximate).

b:horti_maiani.summary: Gardens known only from the joint procuratorship with the Horti Lamiani; location unknown, placed adjoining them to the east.
scholarship: Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Haeuber, Horti Romani: die Horti Maecenatiani und die Horti Lamiani auf dem Esquilin (1991) and later work

b:horti_tauriani_v1.summary: Gardens of the Statilii Tauri north of the Via Labicana-Praenestina, bordering the Lamiani.

b:horti_pallantiani.summary: Gardens of Claudius' powerful freedman Pallas near Spes Vetus; Frontinus places the terminal piscina of the Claudia and Anio Novus and the start of the Rivus Herculaneus 'behind' them.

Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Pallantiani

b:horti_liciniani.summary: Gallienus' gardens between the Via Labicana and Via Praenestina near the walls, where his court lived; the great domed decagonal pavilion (the so-called Temple of Minerva Medica, early 4th century) belonged to them.

Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Liciniani
b:horti_liciniani.note: Extent schematic around the Minerva Medica pavilion; the terminal castellum of the Claudia lies within this footprint.

b:horti_epaphroditiani.summary: Gardens of Nero's freedman Epaphroditus at Spes Vetus; Frontinus puts the junction of the Appia and its Augustan branch on their boundary with the Horti Torquatiani.
scholarship: Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Epaphroditiani
b:horti_epaphroditiani.note: The shared vertex with the Horti Torquatiani is the Appia junction 'ad Spem Veterem'.

b:horti_torquatiani.summary: Gardens at Spes Vetus by the later Porta Maggiore, named by Frontinus as bordering the Epaphroditiani at the Appia junction.
scholarship: Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Horti Torquatiani
b:horti_torquatiani.note: Later absorbed into the Severan Horti Spei Veteris (end date conjectural).

b:horti_spei_veteris_v2.summary: The part of the Severan estate inside the Aurelian Wall: the Palatium Sessorianum, where Helena lived; its hall became the church of S. Croce in Gerusalemme.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Agrippae, Stagnum Agrippae
Haselberger, Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)

b:horti_scipionis.summary: Gardens of the Scipios just outside the pomerium near the Campus Martius, where in 163 BC the consul Ti. Sempronius Gracchus pitched the augural tent for the elections and later found he had taken the auspices invalidly.

b:horti_caesaris_v1.summary: Caesar's gardens across the Tiber along the Via Portuensis, where Cleopatra lodged in 46-44 BC.

Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)

Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)

b:horti_domitiae_v1.summary: Imperial gardens on the right bank in the bend of the Tiber, in which Hadrian built his mausoleum.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Domitiae
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)

Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)

b:horti_agrippinae_v1.summary: Gardens of Agrippina the Elder on the Vatican plain.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Agrippinae
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Liverani, La topografia antica del Vaticano (1999)
b:horti_agrippinae_v1.note: Vatican plain around the later St Peter's.

b:horti_agrippinae_v2.summary: Caligula built his circus here and received Philo's embassy; after the fire of 64 Nero opened the gardens for the spectacle of the Christians' execution, the setting of the tradition of St Peter's martyrdom. From the 2nd century the roadside necropolis spread over the area.

phases.t: Caligula receives the Alexandrian Jewish embassy here (Philo).
Christians burned as torches in Nero's gardens (Tac. Ann. 15.44).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Agrippinae
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Liverani, La topografia antica del Vaticano (1999)

b:horti_getae.summary: Gardens of Geta in Transtiberim near the Severan baths and the Porta Septimiana (Via della Lungara).
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Horti Getae
Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
b:horti_getae.note: Location from their association with the Porta Septimiana; extent conjectural.

b:lucus_furrinae.summary: Sacred grove of the old goddess Furrina on the Janiculum slope (Villa Sciarra), with a spring; here Gaius Gracchus had his slave kill him in 121 BC. In the 2nd-4th centuries a Syrian sanctuary (Jupiter Heliopolitanus) rose inside it.

phases.t: Death of Gaius Gracchus in the grove (Plut. C. Gracch. 17).
Syrian sanctuary built (rebuilt in the 4th century).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Lucus Furrinae
Goddard, in Horti Romani (1998)
b:lucus_furrinae.note: Centred on the Syrian sanctuary in Via Dandolo / Villa Sciarra.

b:nemus_caesarum_a.summary: The grove Augustus planted around his Naumachia and dedicated to his grandsons Gaius and Lucius Caesar; Nero later held festivities in it.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Naumachia Augusti, Nemus Caesarum
Taylor, AJA 101 (1997)
b:nemus_caesarum_a.note: A 40 m band around a basin of 1800 x 1200 Roman feet (533 x 355 m) assumed centred near S. Cosimato with the long side running NNW-SSE (345/165 deg), matching the naumachia_augusti_v1 pool; split into two L-shaped halves so each footprint is a simple polygon. Position and orientation of the basin are uncertain.

b:nemus_caesarum_b.summary: The grove Augustus planted around his Naumachia and dedicated to his grandsons Gaius and Lucius Caesar; Nero later held festivities in it.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Naumachia Augusti, Nemus Caesarum
Taylor, AJA 101 (1997)

Cosimato with the long side running NNW-SSE (345/165 deg), matching the naumachia_augusti_v1 pool; split into two L-shaped halves so each footprint is a simple polygon. Position and orientation of the basin are uncertain.

b:lucus_libitinae.summary: Grove of Libitina, goddess of funerals, where the undertakers (libitinarii) kept their equipment and every death was registered with a coin; on the Esquiline by the old necropolis outside the Porta Esquilina.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Lucus Libitinae
Bodel, 'Graveyards and groves' AJAH 11 (1994)
b:lucus_libitinae.note: Exact site unknown; placed just outside the Porta Esquilina north of the Via Labicana. Its survival after the transformation of the Esquiline is uncertain.

b:lucus_fagutalis.summary: The beech grove (fagus) with the shrine of Jupiter Fagutalis that gave the Fagutal its name, on the western Oppius near S. Pietro in Vincoli.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Fagutal, Lucus Fagutalis
Haeuber, Horti Romani: die Horti Maecenatiani und die Horti Lamiani auf dem Esquilin (1991) and later work
b:lucus_fagutalis.note: Haeuber argues the name Fagutal applies to the grove, not a hilltop.

b:lucus_petelinus.summary: Grove outside the Porta Flumentana where M. Manlius Capitolinus was condemned in 384 BC out of sight of the Capitol he had saved, and where the people met in 342 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Lucus Petelinus
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Lucus Petelinus
b:lucus_petelinus.note: Placed on the river plain just north-west of the Porta Flumentana; built over by the 2nd century BC (end date conjectural).

b:adonaea_vigna_barberini_v1.summary: The great artificial terrace of the Flavian palace at the north-east corner of the Palatine (Vigna Barberini), planted as a formal garden with rows of plant beds and a surrounding portico; identified by some with the 'Adonaea' (gardens of Adonis) labelled on the Severan Marble Plan.
scholarship: Villedieu (ed.), La Vigna Barberini I-II (1997-2007)
Coarelli, Palatium (2012)
Claridge, Rome (2010) 159
b:adonaea_vigna_barberini_v1.note: Terrace about 150 x 105 m aligned with the Flavian palace (axis about 340 degrees). Identification with the Adonaea disputed. Replaced in 219-222 by Elagabalus' temple of Sol Invictus Elagabal, whose courtyard garden continued (v2).

b:adonaea_vigna_barberini_v2.summary: After Elagabalus' temple was rededicated to Jupiter Ultor by Severus Alexander, the terrace kept a planted court around the temple.
scholarship: Villedieu (ed.), La Vigna Barberini II (2007)
b:adonaea_vigna_barberini_v2.note: The temple itself belongs to the buildings collection.

b:campus_martius_meadow_v1.summary: After the expulsion of the Tarquins their land between the Capitol and the bend of the Tiber was consecrated to Mars (Livy 2.5): an open meadow for the army's musters, the centuriate assembly at the Saepta (Ovile), the Villa Publica and horse races, with the Tarentum altar by the river and only scattered temples near the Capitol.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Campus Martius

b:campus_martius_meadow_v2.summary: The Circus Flaminius (221 BC) and the triumphal temples of the Forum Holitorium, Largo Argentina and the Porticus Metelli fill the southern end; the open field still runs from there to the river bend.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Campus Martius

b:campus_martius_meadow_v3.summary: Pompey's theatre and porticus (55 BC) and Caesar's Saepta Iulia project take the central-southern plain.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Campus Martius
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio (1997)
Haselberger, Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)

b:campus_martius_meadow_v4.summary: After Agrippa's Pantheon, baths, Saepta and Stagnum and the Augustan Mausoleum, Ara Pacis and Horologium, Strabo describes the 'Campus' as a great open grass field for chariot racing, ball games and exercise ringed by porticoes and monuments: the western plain (later the Stadium of Domitian) and the north toward the Mausoleum.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Campus Martius

b:campus_martius_meadow_v5.summary: Domitian's Stadium and Odeum (c. 86) and Hadrianic and Antonine temples and columns fill the west and centre; the open ground survives in the north, by the river and the imperial ustrina.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Campus Martius

b:campus_martius_meadow_v6.summary: Only the northern margin by the Mausoleum of Augustus and the river stays open; from the 5th century the built-up Campus becomes the core of the shrinking medieval city.
scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Campus Martius

b:forum_boarium_square.summary: The cattle market by the river landing, Rome's oldest trading place, between the Palatine, the Capitol and the Tiber: a cluster of the oldest cults (Hercules, Portunus, Fortuna, Mater Matuta) around the port, where Greek and Phoenician traders met Latins and Etruscans. A bronze bull from Aegina marked it.

b:temple_portunus_v1.summary: The god of the harbour and of gates had his shrine (Portunium) by the river landing from early times; his festival, the Portunalia of 17 August, belongs to the oldest calendar.

Restored in the 1st century AD; it became a church in 872, which saved it.

Octavius Herrenus, and dedicated to Hercules Victor (Olivarius, patron of the oil trade): a cella ringed by twenty Corinthian columns on a stepped base, 14.8 m across.

b:ara_maxima_v1.summary: The Greatest Altar of Hercules Invictus, set up by Evander or by Hercules himself after killing Cacus, served until 312 BC by the Potitii and Pinarii; generals dedicated a tithe of their booty here. Coarelli identifies it with the massive tufa platform under Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

b:ara_maxima_v2.summary: Listed by Tacitus among the venerable monuments burned in 64 and restored afterwards; dedications of urban praetors continue into the 3rd century. In the late 4th century its podium was built into the hall of the Statio Annonae, and later into the crypt of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

b:temple_hercules_pompeianus.summary: Temple of Hercules near the Circus Maximus restored or rebuilt by Pompey, cited by Vitruvius with that of Ceres as an example of the widely spaced Tuscan (araeostyle) temple with terracotta and gilded bronze pediment figures.

b:temple_jupiter_om_v1.summary: The great Etruscan-plan temple of the Capitoline Triad, vowed by Tarquinius Priscus, built by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus on 13 September 509 BC. The largest temple of its age in Italy: a cappellaccio podium about 53 x 62 m carrying a deep porch of three rows of six widely spaced tufa columns, three cellae (Jupiter in the wider central one, flanked by Juno and Minerva) and a timber superstructure clad in painted terracottas by Vulca of Veii, crowned by a terracotta quadriga (bronze from 296 BC).

b:domus_publica_v2.summary: Rebuilt after 148 BC; Caesar lived here as pontifex maximus from 63 BC and left from it on the Ides of March. The Bona Dea scandal of 62 BC took place in it. Augustus gave it to the Vestals in 12 BC.

phases.t: Clodius profanes the Bona Dea rites
Caesar leaves for the Senate on 15 March

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 132
Digitales Forum Romanum (Humboldt-Universitat zu Berlin), phase reconstructions

b:temple_antoninus_faustina.summary: Built by Antoninus Pius for his deified wife Faustina in 141, and rededicated to both after his death in 161: a hexastyle porch of monolithic cipollino columns 17 m high, with a frieze of griffins and candelabra, facing the Sacra Via. Medieval rope grooves mark the columns; the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda was built into it after 641.
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 13-14
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 11

b:temple_antoninus_faustina.note: Facade on the Sacra Via (SSW, 213); centre placed between the OSM outline of the porch and that of the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda in the cella, so that the steps reach the Sacra Via.

b:temple_romulus_v1.summary: A domed brick rotunda on the Sacra Via with a concave facade and two flanking apsed halls, entered through bronze doors between porphyry columns that still turn on their ancient hinges. Traditionally Maxentius' shrine for his deified son Romulus (died 309); it may instead be the temple of the Penates or of Jupiter Stator, or a vestibule of the Urban Prefecture.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 333-334
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) IV s.v. Romulus, divus, templum (Fiore)

b:temple_romulus_v1.note: OSM outline; facade on the Sacra Via (204). Rotunda c. 15 m across.

b:temple_romulus_v2.summary: From 527 the rotunda served as the vestibule to the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano behind it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 333

b:santi_cosma_e_damiano_church.summary: Pope Felix IV, with gifts from Theodoric's daughter Amalasuntha, turned a hall of the Templum Pacis (perhaps the library or the hall of the city survey with the Marble Plan on its wall) into the first church in the Forum, with the great apse mosaic of Christ arriving on clouds between Peter, Paul and the two physician saints.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 287
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2014)
b:santi_cosma_e_damiano_church.note: OSM outline of the church (hall of the Templum Pacis); entrance originally through the rotunda on the Sacra Via.

b:basilica_nova_v1.summary: Maxentius began the largest vaulted hall in Rome about 307 on the site of the Horrea Piperataria: a central nave 80 m long and 35 m high under three groin vaults resting on eight marble columns, flanked by three huge coffered barrel-vaulted bays on each side, entered from the east end facing the Colosseum valley with an apse at the west.
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 76-78
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 51-52

b:basilica_nova_v1.note: OSM outline (c. 100 x 65 m); original entrance on the ESE short side (121). Finished by Constantine after 312.

b:basilica_nova_v2.summary: Constantine completed the hall, added a porphyry-columned entrance on the Sacra Via side and a second apse opposite it, and placed his colossal seated statue in the west apse (the head and hand are in the Capitoline Museums).
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 76-78

b:basilica_nova_v2.note: New main entrance from the Sacra Via (SSW, 211).

b:horrea_piperataria.summary: Domitian's warehouses for pepper and spices from the East on the Sacra Via, burned in 191 when Galen lost his books stored there, and demolished for the Basilica of Maxentius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 193
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Horrea Piperataria (Santangeli Valenzani)

b:domus_aurea_vestibule.summary: Nero's entrance court to the Golden House on the Velia summit, a vast colonnaded atrium approached by porticoed avenues from the Forum, with the 35 m bronze Colossus of the emperor standing in it. Hadrian cleared it for the Temple of Venus and Rome and moved the Colossus with 24 elephants.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 119-121
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) II s.v. Domus Aurea: vestibulum (Panella)

b:domus_aurea_vestibule.note: Assumed to occupy the later temple platform.

b:venus_roma_precinct.summary: The terrace 145 x 100 m raised on the Velia over the Neronian vestibule, with colonnades of grey granite along its long sides and propylaea toward the Colosseum.
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 552-554
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 409-411
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) V s.v. Venus et Roma, aedes, templum (Cassatella)

b:venus_roma_precinct.note: Footprint from the OSM outline of the archaeological area.

b:temple_venus_roma_v1.summary: Hadrian's own design, founded on the Parilia of 121 and dedicated about 135, the largest temple in Rome: a Greek-style decastyle peripteral temple 110 x 53 m on a stepped base, with two cellae back to back, Venus Felix facing the Colosseum and Roma Aeterna facing the Forum. Apollodorus' criticism of its proportions reputedly cost him his life.
scholarship: Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) 552-554
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 409-411

Cassatella and Panella, in Archeologia Laziale 10 (1990)
b:temple_venus_roma_v1.note: Bearing given for the Roma cella facing the Forum (WNW, 290); the Venus cella faced the opposite way (110). Column height c. 17.7 m (estimated from 1.8 m diameter).

b:temple_venus_roma_v2.summary: After a fire in 307 Maxentius rebuilt the cellae with back-to-back apses and coffered vaults, walls of brick faced with porphyry and other coloured marbles; the Roma apse survives in the convent of Santa Francesca Romana. Pope Honorius I removed its gilded bronze tiles for St Peter's around 630.

phases.t: fire
admired by Constantius II on his visit
bronze roof tiles removed by Honorius I

b:neronian_porticoes_sacra_via_s.summary: After the fire of 64 Nero straightened and widened the Sacra Via up the Velia as a colonnaded avenue to the vestibule of the Golden House, lined by porticoes over rows of shops; the brick piers remain along the south side.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 339
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) IV s.v. Sacra Via (Coarelli)

b:neronian_porticoes_sacra_via_n.summary: The northern portico of Nero's Sacra Via, later replaced by the Horrea Piperataria and the Basilica of Maxentius.
scholarship: Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) IV s.v. Sacra Via

b:arch_of_titus.summary: Single-bay marble arch set up by Domitian after 81 on the summit of the Sacra Via in honour of his deified brother, with the passage reliefs of the triumph of 71 showing the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple, the menorah among them, and Titus' apotheosis in the vault. The first dated use of the Composite order. Later built into the Frangipane fortress.

Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 30

Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
b:arch_of_titus.note: OSM outline; facade bearing 293 toward the Forum along the Sacra Via.

b:arch_of_septimius_severus.summary: Triple arch of Proconnesian marble dedicated in 203 to Septimius Severus and his sons for the Parthian victories, with four large panels of the campaigns and a bronze six-horse chariot on top; Geta's name was erased from the attic after his murder in 212. It stood at the head of the Sacra Via beside the Rostra.

b:arch_of_septimius_severus.note: OSM outline (pier footprint); dimensions from published survey. Facade bearing 126 toward the square.

b:arch_of_tiberius.summary: Arch voted in AD 16 for the recovery by Germanicus of the standards lost with Varus, spanning the Sacra Via between the Basilica Julia and the Rostra at the foot of the Clivus Capitolinus; a relief on the Arch of Constantine shows it behind the Rostra.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 31

b:fornix_fabianus.summary: The first honorific arch in the Forum, built in 121 BC by Q. Fabius Maximus Allobrogicus over the Sacra Via near the Regia, and restored in 57 BC by his grandson with statues of the family.

b:column_phocas_v1.summary: A fluted Corinthian column of the 2nd century, re-erected on a brick base in front of the Rostra, probably as one of the late-antique honorific columns of the square.

b:column_phocas_v2.summary: On 1 August 608 the exarch Smaragdus set a gilded statue of the emperor Phocas on the column and rebuilt its base as a stepped pyramid; the last monument erected in the Forum, put up for the emperor who had given the Pantheon to the pope.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 95
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
b:column_phocas_v2.note: Column 13.6 m on a stepped base; statue removed after Phocas fell in 610.

b:equus_domitiani.summary: The colossal gilded bronze equestrian statue of Domitian set up in 91 in the middle of the square, described at length by Statius; its concrete base 11.8 x 5.9 m with travertine foundation blocks was found by Boni. Destroyed after Domitian's murder and damnatio.

b:equus_constantini.summary: Gilded equestrian statue of Constantine dedicated in 334 near the Rostra; the Regionary catalogues list it among the sights of Region VIII.

b:decennalia_monument.summary: For the tenth anniversary of the Caesars and the twentieth of the Augusti in 303, five columns were raised on the Rostra: four carrying statues of the Tetrarchs and a taller central one with Jupiter. The 'Decennalia base' with sacrifice reliefs survives; the monument is shown on the Arch of Constantine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 95
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

b:base_constantius_ii.summary: Base of an equestrian statue of Constantius II, set up after his victory over Magnentius, beside the Arch of Septimius Severus.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

b:columna_rostrata_duilii.summary: Column hung with the bronze prows of the Carthaginian ships captured by C. Duilius at Mylae in 260 BC, Rome's first naval victory; the inscription was recut under Claudius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 95
b:columna_rostrata_duilii.note: Placed near the Rostra; exact site unknown.

b:columna_maenia.summary: Honorific column for C. Maenius, victor over the Latins in 338 BC, at the west end of the Comitium near the Carcer; petty criminals were tried in front of it by the tresviri capitales.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 96
b:columna_maenia.note: Probably removed in the Caesarian works; site approximate.

b:lacus_curtius_v1.summary: A sacred pool or pit in the middle of the square, a relic of the marsh drained by the Cloaca, explained by stories of the Sabine Mettius Curtius or of the young Marcus Curtius who leapt into a chasm in 362 BC; coins were thrown into it for the emperor's health.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 229-230
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Lacus Curtius (Giuliani)

b:lacus_curtius_v2.summary: Paved over in the Sullan and Augustan repavings as a trapezoidal enclosure with a balustrade and an altar; a relief of Curtius on horseback was found here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 230
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

b:sacellum_cloacinae.summary: The small round shrine of Venus of the Cloaca where the great drain entered the Forum, a balustraded platform with two cult statues shown on coins of 42 BC; the Romans and Sabines were said to have purified themselves here with myrtle.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 92
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) I s.v. Cloacina, sacrum
b:sacellum_cloacinae.note: OSM outline in front of the Basilica Aemilia.

b:umbilicus_urbis.summary: A round brick monument in three tiers beside the Arch of Septimius Severus, marking the notional centre of the city; it may cover the older mundus, the pit opened three days a year to the underworld.

b:miliarium_aureum.summary: The Golden Milestone set up by Augustus in 20 BC as curator of roads at the head of the Forum near the Temple of Saturn: a marble column sheathed in gilt bronze listing the distances to the main cities of the empire.

b:ianus_geminus.summary: The small bronze shrine of Janus at the entrance of the Argiletum, a double gateway whose doors stood open in war and were shut in peace: closed only twice before Augustus, who shut it three times. Procopius saw it still standing, all of bronze, in the 6th century.

Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) III s.v. Ianus Geminus, aedes (Tortorici)

b:domitianic_vestibule.summary: Domitian built a monumental entrance to the palace at the Forum level: a huge brick hall (once called the Temple of Augustus) with walls still over 20 m high, and beside it a covered ramp climbing in seven flights to the Domus Tiberiana.

b:santa_maria_antiqua_v1.summary: Part of Domitian's Forum vestibule to the palace: a quadriporticus atrium and an inner hall with rooms, perhaps a guard station.

b:oratory_forty_martyrs.summary: A room of the imperial buildings at the foot of the Palatine beside the Lacus Iuturnae turned into an oratory painted with the martyrs of Sebaste freezing in the lake.

b:oratory_forty_martyrs.note: OSM outline; conversion date in the 6th-7th century approximate.

b:horrea_agrippiana.summary: Warehouse built by Agrippa on the Vicus Tuscus between the Forum and the Velabrum: three storeys of rooms around a courtyard with a shrine to the genius of the horrea, of travertine and tufa with later brick rebuildings.

b:elagabalium_v2.summary: After Elagabalus' murder in 222 the god was sent back to Emesa and Severus Alexander rededicated the temple to Jupiter Ultor; a medieval church of San Sebastiano later rose on the site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 1

b:santa_anastasia_v1.summary: A titular church at the foot of the Palatine toward the Circus Maximus, built in the 4th century in a converted Roman building; perhaps the palace church of the Byzantine governors later.
scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2014)
Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae I (1937)
b:santa_anastasia_v1.note: OSM outline of the present church; facade WNW.

b:santa_anastasia_v2.summary: Enlarged with a transept in the later 5th century under Pope Hilarus; in the 6th and 7th centuries it was the court church of the Byzantine officials on the Palatine.
scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2014)
Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae I (1937)

b:castra_peregrina.summary: Headquarters on the Caelian of the frumentarii and other soldiers seconded from the provincial armies (peregrini), who served as couriers, police agents and spies under a princeps peregrinorum. A mithraeum of its soldiers lies under Santo Stefano Rotondo. The Alamannic king Chnodomarius was held here in 357.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:castra_peregrina.note: Location from Pleiades (Villa Celimontana, W of Santo Stefano Rotondo); plan and size reconstructed on the type of urban barracks.

b:statio_cohortis_v_vigilum.summary: The barracks of the cohort of firemen-watchmen responsible for Regions I and II, found in 1820 in Villa Mattei near Santa Maria in Domnica with dedications of 205 and 210 to Septimius Severus and Caracalla listing the whole cohort.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
b:statio_cohortis_v_vigilum.note: Located from the findspot of the inscriptions; plan reconstructed (cf. the excubitorium of Cohort VII in Trastevere).

b:macellum_magnum.summary: Nero's great provisions market on the Caelian, dedicated in 59 and shown on his coins as a two-storey colonnaded rotunda with a dome, set in a court of shops. It was still listed in the 4th century. Santo Stefano Rotondo (district D) was built on or beside it about 468-483, and its circular plan has sometimes been explained by the market.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:macellum_magnum.note: Exact site debated: under Santo Stefano Rotondo or just N of it, near the Ospedale Militare. Plan from the coin type.

b:basilica_hilariana.summary: Seat of the college of dendrophori (tree-bearers of the cult of Magna Mater), built in the mid-2nd century by the pearl merchant Manius Poblicius Hilarus, whose statue base was found in 1889; excavated again in 1987 at the Ospedale Militare. The entrance mosaic shows the evil eye attacked by animals.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:arch_of_dolabella.summary: A plain travertine arch built in AD 10 by the consuls P. Cornelius Dolabella and C. Iunius Silanus, probably replacing the Servian Porta Caelimontana; Nero used it to carry the Arcus Neroniani branch of the Aqua Claudia across the Caelian.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:arch_of_dolabella.note: Location from Pleiades. The road through it runs NW-SE (Via di S. Paolo della Croce); rot 150 faces SE toward Piazza della Navicella. The aqueduct arches are in the aqueduct collection.

b:case_romane_celio.summary: An insula of the 2nd century with shops on the Clivus Scauri, converted in the 3rd century into a wealthy house with painted rooms and a nymphaeum, and in the 4th used by Christians; the church of SS. Giovanni e Paolo (district D) was built over it about 410.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
b:case_romane_celio.note: Location from Pleiades; facade on the Clivus Scauri (SW, rot 210).

b:domus_valeriorum.summary: The palace of the Valerii, the richest senatorial family of late Rome, found under the Ospedale di San Giovanni. Valerius Pinianus and Melania the Younger tried to sell it about 404 when they gave away their wealth, but no one could afford it; it burned in Alaric's sack of 410.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:domus_symmachorum.summary: The urban residence of the Symmachi, family of the orator Q. Aurelius Symmachus, identified by inscriptions found at the former Villa Casali on the Caelian.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:domus_tetricorum.summary: The Historia Augusta says the Gallic emperors Tetricus father and son, pardoned by Aurelian, lived in a fine house on the Caelian 'between the two groves, opposite the Isium Metellinum', with a mosaic showing Aurelian investing them.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:domus_tetricorum.note: Placed on the N slope of the Caelian facing the Via Labicana; conjectural.

b:caput_africae.summary: A street and district on the Caelian named after a monument (perhaps a head of Africa) where the imperial school for page-boys (paedagogium Caput Africae) stood; many epitaphs of its paedagogi survive.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:castra_priora_equitum_singularium.summary: The first barracks of the emperor's horse guard, the equites singulares Augusti, founded by Trajan; parts with dedications were found in 1885 at Via Tasso. Constantine disbanded the unit, which had fought for Maxentius, and demolished its camps in 312.
scholarship: Speidel, Die Denkmaeler der Kaiserreiter: Equites singulares Augusti (1994)
Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:castra_priora_equitum_singularium.note: Location at Via Tasso; plan and size generic.

b:castra_nova_equitum_singularium.summary: The new camp built by Septimius Severus when he doubled the horse guard. Its barrack blocks, with painted rooms, lie under the nave of the Lateran basilica, which Constantine built on the levelled camp after 312 as a deliberate erasure of Maxentius' cavalry.
scholarship: Speidel, Die Denkmaeler der Kaiserreiter: Equites singulares Augusti (1994)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:castra_nova_equitum_singularium.note: Under the Lateran basilica (district D); the camp's grid is assumed parallel to the basilica (E-W). Size reconstructed.

b:domus_laterani_v1.summary: The mansion of the Plautii Laterani on the Caelian. Plautius Lateranus, consul designate, was executed for his part in the Pisonian conspiracy of 65 and the house was confiscated; Juvenal names the 'egregias Lateranorum aedes' besieged by soldiers.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:domus_laterani_v1.note: Remains attributed to the Laterani lie under and W of the basilica; location approximate.

b:domus_laterani_v2.summary: Septimius Severus gave the property to his friend T. Sextius Lateranus, and the house was rebuilt with a bath suite. After 312 the imperial estate 'Lateranum' passed to the bishop of Rome; the episcopium (district D) grew over it.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:domus_faustae.summary: The house of Fausta, Constantine's wife, at the Lateran, where Pope Miltiades held the synod against the Donatists in October 313. It became the core of the bishop's residence, later the Patriarchium.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:domus_faustae.note: Chains into district D's lateran_episcopium (from 313, Domus Faustae / Patriarchium) at the same position.

b:domus_anniorum_caelian.summary: Marcus Aurelius was born in 121 in the gardens of his grandfather Annius Verus on the Caelian, near the Lateran; the bronze equestrian statue of Marcus that stood at the Lateran in the Middle Ages may have come from this property.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:domus_vectiliana.summary: A suburban-style imperial residence on the Caelian to which Commodus moved, saying he could not sleep on the Palatine; he was strangled there by the athlete Narcissus on the last night of 192.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:domus_vectiliana.note: Site unknown; placed on the Caelian plateau between the Claudianum and the Lateran.

b:domus_vedii_pollionis.summary: The vast mansion of the equestrian P. Vedius Pollio, notorious for feeding slaves to his lampreys. He left it to Augustus, who in 15 BC razed it to the ground so that no one should live in such luxury, and built the Porticus Liviae on the site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
b:domus_vedii_pollionis.note: Same site as the Porticus Liviae; size and plan invented to fill the plot; from-date arbitrary.

b:porticus_liviae.summary: A colonnaded garden square about 115 x 75 m dedicated by Livia and Tiberius in 7 BC on the site of Vedius Pollio's house, on the Oppius along the Clivus Suburanus. Its double colonnade enclosed planted walks shaded by a single enormous vine; the Marble Plan shows the plan with a central shrine. A favourite place for strolling, mentioned by Pliny the Younger.

phases.t: dedicated by Livia and Tiberius

scholarship: Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:porticus_liviae.note: Marble Plan fragment 10. Placed between the Clivus Suburanus and the NE wall of the Baths of Trajan; facing NNE onto the clivus (rot 25).

b:macellum_liviae_v1.summary: A provisions market on the Esquiline just outside the Porta Esquilina, dedicated together with the Porticus Liviae; a court of shops round a central tholos on the standard macellum plan.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:macellum_liviae_v1.note: Remains reported by Lanciani near San Vito; plan reconstructed on the standard type. Faces W toward the gate.

b:macellum_liviae_v2.summary: Restored by the emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, whose inscription survives; in the 4th century the area around it, the Esquiline market district, was one of the busiest of the late city.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

b:temple_of_tellus.summary: Vowed by P. Sempronius Sophus during an earthquake in battle against the Picentes in 268 BC, on the site of the house of Sp. Cassius, razed after his execution in 485. On its walls hung a painted map of Italy (Varro). The Senate met here on 17 March 44 BC, two days after the Ides, to debate an amnesty for the assassins. Quintus Cicero restored part of the precinct in 54 BC.

phases.t: vowed and built
restoration by Quintus Cicero
Senate meeting of 17 March

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:temple_of_tellus.note: Carinae, on the W slope of the Oppius near Via del Colosseo; exact site unknown. Builder P. Sempronius Sophus has no person id.

b:temple_of_juno_lucina.summary: Temple of Juno of childbirth, dedicated on 1 March 375 BC in her ancient grove on the Cispius; the Matronalia was celebrated here, and Pliny says the lotus tree in the grove was older than the temple. A coin was paid into its treasury for every birth.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
b:temple_of_juno_lucina.note: Located only as 'on the Cispius'; placed near S. Prassede.

b:esquiline_necropolis.summary: The great cemetery outside the Porta Esquilina, used from the Iron Age: chamber tombs of the archaic and Republican aristocracy (with the famous painted 'Esquiline historical fragment' of Fannius and Fabius), and the puticuli, open pits into which the bodies of the poor, slaves and animals were thrown. Horace recalls the white bones lying about until Maecenas covered the area with 7-8 m of earth for his gardens.
scholarship: Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
b:esquiline_necropolis.note: Explored by Lanciani in 1870s-80s (around 75 pits). Tomb blocks are scattered placeholders inside the cemetery area, not mapped tombs.

b:turris_maecenatiana.summary: The tall tower of Maecenas' gardens ('molem propinquam nubibus arduis', Horace) from which, Suetonius says, Nero watched the city burn in 64 singing of the sack of Troy.
scholarship: Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:auditorium_maecenatis.summary: A half-sunken hall with a stepped exedra at one end and garden paintings in its niches, found in 1874 on the line of the Servian agger. Traditionally the hall where Maecenas' poets recited; more probably a cool garden dining hall with a water cascade over the steps.
scholarship: Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:auditorium_maecenatis.note: Location from Pleiades. The hall runs NW-SE with the exedra at the NW end; entrance ramp from the SE (rot 135). Floor about 2.5 m below the garden level.

b:nymphaeum_alexandri_v1.summary: A monumental three-storey fountain at the fork of the Via Labicana and the road to Tibur, built by Severus Alexander as the display terminal of an aqueduct branch (Aqua Iulia or Claudia), shown on his coins of 226. Water fell through basins in the central exedra; the upper arches held the two marble trophies (in fact Domitianic) that medieval Romans thought were Marius' trophies over the Cimbri, now on the Capitol balustrade.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
b:nymphaeum_alexandri_v1.note: Location from Pleiades. The facade faced W toward the Porta Esquilina and the city (rot 260), derived from the street fork.

b:nymphaeum_alexandri_v2.summary: Dry after the aqueducts were cut by the Goths in 537; the brick core still stands in Piazza Vittorio.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)

b:temple_of_minerva_medica_v1.summary: A decagonal domed hall about 24.5 m across and 32 m high, its brick walls opened by niches below and large windows above, probably a nymphaeum or dining pavilion of the Horti Liciniani built in the early 4th century. A milestone of late Roman dome construction, with brick ribs in the concrete. The name comes from a misidentified statue.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:temple_of_minerva_medica_v1.note: Location from Pleiades. The entrance side is uncertain; the vestibule is assumed on the S toward the Via Labicana (rot 160).

b:temple_of_minerva_medica_v2.summary: Soon after construction cracks led to the addition of heavy buttresses and two large apsed side halls to shore up the dome. The dome stood until 1828.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)

b:arch_of_gallienus_v1.summary: The Servian Porta Esquilina was rebuilt in Augustan times as a triple arch of travertine with Corinthian pilasters, through which the Clivus Suburanus left the city toward the Via Tiburtina and Via Praenestina.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
b:arch_of_gallienus_v1.note: Gate structure itself (Servian circuit) belongs to the walls collection; this is the arch. Road through the arch runs about WNW-ESE; outer face toward the ESE (rot 100).

b:arch_of_gallienus_v2.summary: In 262 the urban official M. Aurelius Victor re-inscribed the Augustan arch in honour of Gallienus and Salonina, 'whose invincible courage is surpassed only by his piety'. Only the central bay survives; the side bays were demolished in the 15th century.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:lacus_orphei.summary: A public fountain at the top of the Clivus Suburanus with a statue of Orpheus charming the beasts, which Martial uses as a landmark on the way to Pliny's house on the Esquiline.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:lacus_orphei.note: Near S. Lucia in Selci (S. Lucia in Orphea).

b:basilica_iunii_bassi.summary: An apsed reception hall built by Junius Bassus, consul of 331, famous for its opus sectile wall panels in coloured stone. Pope Simplicius turned it into the church of S. Andrea Catabarbara about 471 (district D).
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:basilica_iunii_bassi.note: Location from Pleiades (12.50025, 41.89731); district D places Sant'Andrea Catabarbara about 150 m NW, one of the two should be reconciled. Destroyed in 1686, known from Renaissance drawings. Orientation assumed.

b:iseum_metellinum.summary: The sanctuary of Isis that gave Regio III its name (Isis et Serapis), called Isis Metellina, probably founded in the 1st century BC by a Caecilius Metellus. The Historia Augusta places the house of the Tetrici nearby. Remains of an Isiac sanctuary were recorded around Via Labicana and Piazza Iside.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)

b:domus_pompeiana_carinae.summary: Pompey's ancestral house on the fashionable Carinae, its vestibule hung with ships' beaks from his pirate war. Mark Antony bought it at auction after Pharsalus, to Cicero's disgust; later it was imperial property, and Tiberius lived here before moving to the Horti Maecenatis.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

b:tigillum_sororium.summary: A wooden beam across a lane of the Carinae under which, by tradition, the surviving Horatius passed in expiation for killing his sister. Maintained at public expense, it still stood in Livy's day and is listed in Regio IV in the 4th century; ritual on 1 October.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:tigillum_sororium.note: Site conjectural, on the Vicus Cuprius below San Pietro in Vincoli.

b:subura_insula_a_v1.summary: Representative tenement of the Subura, the crowded, noisy valley between the Viminal, Esquiline and the fora: shops and workshops on the ground floor, rented flats above in three or more storeys, notorious for fires and collapses. Juvenal and Martial complain of its mud and din.
scholarship: Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:subura_insula_a_v1.note: Generic fabric record, not a mapped building; location chosen in the Subura valley.

b:subura_insula_a_v2.summary: After the fire of 64 Nero required brick and stone construction, height limits, setbacks and street porticoes for rebuilt insulae; this is the fabric of the imperial Subura, which stayed densely inhabited into the 5th century before thinning out.
scholarship: Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:subura_insula_b_v1.summary: Representative tenement of the Subura, the crowded, noisy valley between the Viminal, Esquiline and the fora: shops and workshops on the ground floor, rented flats above in three or more storeys, notorious for fires and collapses. scholarship: Carandini (ed.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017)

Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:turris_mamilia.summary: An old tower in the Subura belonging to the Mamilii, on which the people of the Subura fixed the head of the October Horse when they won the annual fight for it against the men of the Sacra Via.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:domus_caesaris_subura.summary: Suetonius says Caesar first lived in a modest house in the Subura, moving to the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via when he became pontifex maximus in 63 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:domus_caesaris_subura.note: Site unknown; record ends when Caesar moved (the house itself is not traced further).

b:temple_of_spes_vetus.summary: An ancient temple of Hope on the eastern Esquiline that gave the district near the later Porta Maggiore its name, 'ad Spem Veterem'; the Etruscans camped near it in 477 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coates-Stephens, Porta Maggiore: Monument and Landscape (2004)
b:temple_of_spes_vetus.note: Site conjectural, W of Porta Maggiore.

b:isis_patricia.summary: A shrine of Isis named after the Vicus Patricius on the Esquiline, listed in Regio V of the Regionary Catalogues; distinct from the Isis Metellina of Regio III, though the two are often confused.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

b:domus_plinii_esquiliae.summary: Martial sends his tenth book up the steep Clivus Suburanus past the fountain of Orpheus to the 'eloquent' Pliny's house on the Esquiline, warning it not to knock drunk at his door at the wrong hour.

b:forum_iulium_v1.summary: The first imperial forum: an enclosed rectangular piazza about 160 x 75 m on land bought from 54 BC by Cicero and Oppius for Caesar (60 million sesterces, later over 100 million). Double porticoes lined the long sides, shops of tufa ashlar opened onto the Clivus Argentarius behind the SW side, and the Temple of Venus Genetrix closed the NW end, with Caesar's equestrian statue in the middle. Caesar dedicated it unfinished on 26 September 46 BC at his quadruple triumph; Octavian completed it.

b:forum_iulium_v2.summary: Domitian began, and Trajan completed, a total reconstruction that cut back the Capitol-Quirinal saddle behind the forum, rebuilt the shops in brick on two storeys, added the Basilica Argentaria on the SW flank of the temple and a large latrine, and repaved the square in travertine. Trajan rededicated forum and temple on 12 May 113, a day after the dedication of his own Column.

b:forum_iulium_v3.summary: After the great fire of 283 under Carinus, which also gutted the Curia and Basilica Julia, Diocletian restored the forum; the Curia was rebuilt on the forum's grid at the same time. In the late 4th century a secretarium senatus was installed nearby. The square decayed from the 6th century; by the 9th it held houses and gardens.

b:temple_of_venus_genetrix_v1.summary: Vowed at Pharsalus in 48 BC and dedicated with the forum on 26 September 46 BC to Venus as ancestress of the Julii. It held Arcesilaus' cult statue, two paintings by Timomachus (Ajax and Medea) bought for 80 talents, a cuirass of British pearls, engraved gems, and a gilded statue of Cleopatra set beside the goddess.

Three Trajanic columns were re-erected in 1932. Column height estimated from the surviving order (about 1.5 m lower diameter). Faces SE down the forum axis (rot 150).

b:temple_of_venus_genetrix_v2.summary: Rebuilt from the podium up in the Domitianic-Trajanic works and rededicated on 12 May 113. The rich Trajanic entablature with Erotes pouring incense and the three standing Corinthian columns belong to this rebuilding.

b:basilica_argentaria_v1.summary: A two-storey hall of tufa piers and vaults behind the SW portico of the Forum of Caesar, beside the temple and along the Clivus Argentarius, built in the Trajanic rebuilding. Named in the Regionary Catalogues, it is usually taken as the bankers' (argentarii) exchange; the piers still carry graffiti of the 2nd century, including a line of Virgil.

b:equus_caesaris.summary: A bronze equestrian statue of Caesar stood in front of the temple: according to Statius it was Lysippus' statue of Alexander with Caesar's head substituted, and Pliny says the horse had human-like forefeet, like Caesar's own horse.

b:forica_fori_iulii.summary: A large public latrine with marble seats around a central light-well, built behind the Basilica Argentaria in the Trajanic rebuilding of the forum.

b:forum_of_augustus_v1.summary: Vowed with the temple at Philippi in 42 BC and dedicated, unfinished, in 2 BC, the year Augustus became Pater Patriae. A marble piazza flanked by raised colonnades, each opening into a great semicircular exedra beside the temple, with statues of Aeneas and the Julii on one side, Romulus and the summi viri on the other, each with an elogium. A 33 m firewall of peperino and Gabine stone shut out the Subura. Here the Senate debated war and triumphs, and young men assumed the toga virilis.

phases.t: vowed at Philippi
standards recovered from Parthia, later placed in the temple
dedicated 1 August (or 12 May)
arches of Drusus and Germanicus added beside the temple

b:forum_of_augustus_v1.note: Axis perpendicular to the Forum of Caesar: temple at the NE end against the Subura firewall, facing SW (rot 237, derived from the Pleiades centroids of temple and forum, bearing 237). The NE (rear right) corner is irregular because Augustus would not expropriate the houses there (Suet. Aug. 56.2); footprint simplified to a rectangle, with the two great exedrae as params.

b:forum_of_augustus_v2.summary: Restored by Hadrian; still in use for legal hearings in the 4th century (last mentioned 395). Excavation shows systematic dismantling of the marble in the first half of the 6th century; in the 9th century a Basilian monastery occupied the temple podium and the area became the Hortus Mirabilis.

b:temple_of_mars_ultor_v1.summary: The temple of Mars the Avenger, vowed for the vengeance on Caesar's murderers and dedicated in 2 BC. It housed the standards recovered from Parthia in 20 BC, the sword of Caesar, and the cult group of Mars, Venus and Divus Iulius in an apse. Magistrates left from here for their provinces, and the Senate met here to decide on war and triumphs.

b:temple_of_mars_ultor_v2.summary: Restored with the forum by Hadrian. Despoiled in the 6th century; three columns of the right flank and the podium survive.

b:firewall_forum_augusti.summary: The enclosure wall that separated Augustus' forum from the Subura, built of peperino with bands of travertine and Gabine stone, rising to about 33 m behind the temple and stepping down along the sides. It was both a status display and a protection against the fires of the crowded insulae. Its irregular course on the NE follows property lines Augustus could not buy.

b:hall_of_the_colossus.summary: A marble-lined hall at the north end of the NW portico, beside the exedra, which held a colossal statue (perhaps the Genius of Augustus) 11-12 m tall on a base whose footprints survive. Pliny records two paintings by Apelles displayed in the most frequented parts of the forum.

b:forum_transitorium_v1.summary: Built by Domitian in the narrow space between the Forum of Augustus and the Templum Pacis, along the old Argiletum street, which it monumentalised as a passage (hence Transitorium) from the Forum Romanum to the Subura. Domitian was murdered before its dedication, and Nerva dedicated it in 97. Severus Alexander set colossal statues of deified emperors here.

b:temple_of_minerva_forum_nerva.summary: Hexastyle prostyle Corinthian temple of Domitian's patron goddess, its rear wall bulging into the curved Porticus Absidata. It stood almost intact until Pope Paul V demolished it in 1606 for marble for the Acqua Paola fountain; Renaissance drawings (Palladio, Du Perac) record it.

b:porticus_absidata.summary: A horseshoe-shaped colonnaded court behind the Temple of Minerva, built by Domitian to articulate the junction of the Forum of Augustus, the Forum of Nerva, the Templum Pacis and the street into the Subura. Its outline is shown on the Severan Marble Plan.

b:templum_pacis_v1.summary: Vespasian's precinct of Peace, built from the spoils of the Jewish War on the site of the Republican Macellum burnt in 64 and dedicated in 75. Unlike the other fora it was a garden: porticoes of pink granite enclosed six long planted beds with water channels, around which stood Greek masterpieces by Phidias, Polyclitus, Myron and Leochares. The menorah and table of the Jerusalem Temple were displayed in the cult hall. Pliny ranked it among the three most beautiful buildings in the world.

b:templum_pacis_v2.summary: Destroyed in the fire of 192, which also burnt Galen's books in the warehouses nearby, and rebuilt by Septimius Severus with the halls repaved in opus sectile. Constantius II admired it in 357; Procopius still saw its bronze statues in the 6th century, though it was by then decaying, and the halls were never repaired after the 5th-century sacks.

b:macellum_republican.summary: Rome's central provisions market, built by the censors M. Fulvius Nobilior and M. Aemilius Lepidus in 179 BC NE of the Forum, absorbing the older fish and delicacy markets (forum piscarium, forum cuppedinis). A courtyard of shops around a central tholos, the type later copied all over Italy. Burnt in 64; Vespasian built the Templum Pacis over it.

b:argiletum_tabernae.summary: The Argiletum led from the Forum between the Curia and the Basilica Aemilia up into the Subura. Its shops were known for booksellers and cobblers; Martial sends readers here to buy his books. Domitian's Forum Transitorium swallowed its lower course.

b:forum_of_trajan_mon_v1.summary: The largest and last of the imperial fora, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and paid for with the Dacian spoils. To make room the saddle between the Capitol and Quirinal was cut away, as the Column's inscription records. A marble piazza about 118 m deep, with porticoes and two great exedrae on its sides, led to the Basilica Ulpia; beyond rose the Column between two libraries. Ammianus describes Constantius II stunned by it in 357. In the 6th century poets still recited Virgil here.
