b:equus_traiani.summary: A colossal gilt-bronze equestrian statue of Trajan stood in the piazza; when Constantius II said he would copy it, the Persian prince Hormisdas replied that he should first build a stable like this one. Its foundation was found in the centre of the square.
scholarship: Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)
Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
b:equus_traiani.note: Base foundation found in the piazza (2000s).

b:arcus_traiani_forum.summary: Coins show a single-bayed arch with six columns, statues and a six-horse chariot as the monumental entrance from the Forum of Augustus, voted by the Senate in 116. Recent excavation found a straight wall with a central passage at the SE end; some (La Rocca, Meneghini) now place the Temple of Divus Traianus here instead.
scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
La Rocca, 'Templum Traiani et columna cochlis', Roemische Mitteilungen 111 (2004)
Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)

b:basilica_ulpia.summary: The largest basilica in Rome when built: 170 m long including the two hemicycles at its ends, 60 m wide, a 25 m nave framed by a double ring of grey granite columns, with galleries above. Its long side formed the NW end of the forum, entered through three projecting columnar porches. Pausanias admired its bronze roof. It served the courts and, by tradition, ceremonies of manumission.

phases.t: dedicated 1 January

scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:basilica_ulpia.note: Long axis NE-SW; facade faces SE onto the piazza (rot 141).

b:column_of_trajan.summary: A column 100 Roman feet tall (29.78 m with base and capital) of 29 Luna marble drums, on a pedestal carved with Dacian arms, wrapped by a frieze about 200 m long in 23 turns showing the two Dacian wars. A spiral stair of 185 steps lit by slits leads to the top. Its inscription says it shows how high the hill was that the works removed. A golden urn with Trajan's ashes was placed in the pedestal in 117, the first burial inside the pomerium.

phases.t: dedicated 12 May
ashes of Trajan placed in the pedestal

scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:column_of_trajan.note: Total height including the lost statue base and bronze statue of Trajan about 38-40 m.

b:bibliotheca_ulpia_sw.summary: One of the two libraries, Greek and Latin, flanking the small court of the Column, each a rectangular hall with niches for book presses in two orders. Aulus Gellius read old praetorian edicts in the 'library of the temple of Trajan'; the Historia Augusta claims to cite its linen books.
scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:bibliotheca_ulpia_sw.note: Which hall held Greek and which Latin books is unknown. The library opens onto the column court.

b:bibliotheca_ulpia_ne.summary: One of the two libraries, Greek and Latin, flanking the small court of the Column, each a rectangular hall with niches for book presses in two orders. Aulus Gellius read old praetorian edicts in the 'library of the temple of Trajan'; the Historia Augusta claims to cite its linen books.
scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:bibliotheca_ulpia_ne.note: Which hall held Greek and which Latin books is unknown. The library opens onto the column court.

b:trajan_column_court.summary: The small paved court between the Basilica Ulpia and the libraries in which the Column stood, framed by two-storey porticoes from whose upper floors the frieze could be viewed.
scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)

b:temple_of_divus_traianus.summary: Hadrian built a temple to his deified adoptive parents, the only building in Rome on which he put his own name (an exception). Its location is debated: traditionally NW of the Column under Palazzo Valentini, where colossal grey granite shafts of 50 Roman feet and a giant capital were found; excavations there found houses and baths instead, and La Rocca and Meneghini place it at the SE end of the forum. Modelled here in the traditional position.

phases.t: dedication approximate

scholarship: Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
La Rocca, 'Templum Traiani et columna cochlis', Roemische Mitteilungen 111 (2004)
Meneghini and Santangeli Valenzani, I Fori Imperiali: gli scavi del Comune di Roma 1991-2007 (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:temple_of_divus_traianus.note: Location deliberately flagged as debated (north of the Column vs. the SE end of the forum). Columns: 50-ft grey granite shafts with white marble capitals, so colH about 17.8 m.

b:markets_of_trajan.summary: A brick-and-concrete complex of about 150 rooms terraced into the cut slope of the Quirinal behind the NE exedra of the forum, rising on six levels from the Great Hemicycle at forum level (a curved three-storey facade with arched shopfronts and pedimented windows) to the Via Biberatica and the Great Hall above. Probably offices and stores of the imperial administration as much as shops. Brick stamps date it to about 100-110, before the forum itself.

phases.t: substantially complete (brick stamps 100-110)

scholarship: Ungaro (ed.), Il Museo dei Fori Imperiali nei Mercati di Traiano (2007)
Lancaster, 'Building Trajan's Markets', AJA 102 (1998)
Meneghini, I Fori Imperiali e i Mercati di Traiano (2009)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:markets_of_trajan.note: Hemicycle centre from it.wikipedia; it faces SW (rot 231) concentric with the forum exedra. Block z values approximate the terracing of the hillside (about 25 m difference in level).

b:aula_grande_markets_of_trajan.summary: A covered hall 28 x 9.8 m roofed by six concrete cross vaults springing from travertine brackets, flanked by two storeys of shops, at the upper level of the markets near the Via Biberatica. One of the earliest surviving large cross-vaulted spaces, ancestor of the frigidaria of the great baths.
scholarship: Ungaro (ed.), Il Museo dei Fori Imperiali nei Mercati di Traiano (2007)
Lancaster, 'Building Trajan's Markets', AJA 102 (1998)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:aula_grande_markets_of_trajan.note: Placed just inside the modern museum entrance on Via IV Novembre, long axis parallel to that street (NE-SW).

b:via_biberatica_tabernae.summary: The basalt-paved street that curves through the upper markets behind the Great Hemicycle, lined with brick shopfronts on two storeys. The name (perhaps from bibere, 'to drink') is medieval.
scholarship: Ungaro (ed.), Il Museo dei Fori Imperiali nei Mercati di Traiano (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:via_biberatica_tabernae.note: Line approximates the curve concentric with the hemicycle, about 13 m above forum level.

b:atrium_libertatis_v2.summary: Rebuilt by C. Asinius Pollio from his Dalmatian spoils after 39 BC and fitted with the first public library in Rome, Greek and Latin, adorned with portraits of authors; the censors' archives stayed here. It probably disappeared when Trajan cut away the Capitol-Quirinal saddle, its functions passing to the Basilica Ulpia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Packer, The Forum of Trajan in Rome: A Study of the Monuments (1997)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:atrium_libertatis_v2.note: Location debated. District A models the Republican phase (atrium_libertatis_v1, to 55 BC) N of the Comitium following Coarelli; if Caesar's forum displaced it, Pollio's rebuilding is placed here on the saddle later removed for Trajan's forum. Size invented.

b:athenaeum_hadriani.summary: Three parallel halls with steep stepped seating found in 2008-2012 under Piazza Venezia during the Metro C works, identified with the Athenaeum that Hadrian founded for rhetoric and poetry recitals, beside the Forum of Trajan. In the 6th-7th century one hall housed a metal workshop.
scholarship: Egidi, Serlorenzi et al., excavation reports on Piazza Venezia (2010s)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:athenaeum_hadriani.note: Location from Pleiades; orientation assumed parallel to the forum grid. Boundary building between districts.

b:baths_of_diocletian_v1.summary: The largest baths ever built in Rome, begun by Maximian in 298 on his return from Africa and dedicated in the name of Diocletian between 305 and 306 on the high ground of the Viminal-Quirinal saddle, after demolishing a whole quarter of houses. A walled precinct of some 376 x 361 m enclosed gardens, libraries, round corner halls and a theatre-like exedra; the bath block repeated the Caracallan plan on a larger scale, with a 3,500 m2 open-air natatio, a vast cross-vaulted frigidarium on eight granite columns, a rotunda tepidarium and a rectangular caldarium.

phases.t: begun by Maximian
dedication inscription (between May 305 and July 306)

scholarship: Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)
DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (JRA Suppl. 25, 1997)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:baths_of_diocletian_v1.note: Main entrance on the NE, exedra on the SW now traced by Piazza della Repubblica; axis bearing 48 from the exedra centre to Santa Maria degli Angeli (the frigidarium) and the line of Via Nazionale. Precinct 376 x 361 m; core about 250 x 180 m (Wikipedia gives 280 x 160). Frigidarium = transept of S. Maria degli Angeli, columns 14.8 m granite monoliths. Centre reconstructed from the exedra and the Pleiades polygon.

b:baths_of_diocletian_v2.summary: Restored in the early 5th century and kept in use until the Gothic siege; Olympiodorus counted 3,000 seats in them.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
b:baths_of_diocletian_v2.note: Main entrance on the NE, exedra on the SW now traced by Piazza della Repubblica; axis bearing 48 from the exedra centre to Santa Maria degli Angeli (the frigidarium) and the line of Via Nazionale. Precinct 376 x 361 m; core about 250 x 180 m (Wikipedia gives 280 x 160). Frigidarium = transept of S. Maria degli Angeli, columns 14.8 m granite monoliths. Centre reconstructed from the exedra and the Pleiades polygon.

b:baths_of_diocletian_v3.summary: Out of use after Vitiges cut the aqueducts in 537; the vaults survived so well that in 1561-66 Michelangelo turned the frigidarium into Santa Maria degli Angeli.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:baths_of_diocletian_v3.note: Main entrance on the NE, exedra on the SW now traced by Piazza della Repubblica; axis bearing 48 from the exedra centre to Santa Maria degli Angeli (the frigidarium) and the line of Via Nazionale. Precinct 376 x 361 m; core about 250 x 180 m (Wikipedia gives 280 x 160). Frigidarium = transept of S. Maria degli Angeli, columns 14.8 m granite monoliths. Centre reconstructed from the exedra and the Pleiades polygon.

b:baths_of_constantine_v1.summary: The last imperial baths of Rome, smaller than their predecessors because of the cramped site on the Quirinal ridge, built for or by Constantine (Aurelius Victor) about 315, perhaps begun by Maxentius. The bronze statues of Constantine and his sons and the Horse Tamers (Dioscuri) now in Piazza del Quirinale came from here.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
b:baths_of_constantine_v1.note: Plan after Palladio and Du Perac (destroyed for Palazzo Rospigliosi-Pallavicini and the Consulta, 1605-1611). Site from Pleiades (bbox about 100 x 127 m). Orientation conjectural: caldarium projecting SW for the afternoon sun, entrance NE from the Alta Semita (rot 50). Built on a terrace over the W edge of the Quirinal.

b:baths_of_constantine_v2.summary: Badly damaged 'by the fury of the fires and the destruction of war' (the sack of 410), the baths were restored in 443 by the urban prefect Petronius Perpenna Magnus Quadratianus.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:baths_of_constantine_v2.note: Plan after Palladio and Du Perac (destroyed for Palazzo Rospigliosi-Pallavicini and the Consulta, 1605-1611). Site from Pleiades (bbox about 100 x 127 m). Orientation conjectural: caldarium projecting SW for the afternoon sun, entrance NE from the Alta Semita (rot 50). Built on a terrace over the W edge of the Quirinal.

b:baths_of_constantine_v3.summary: Dry from 537; ruins stood to the 17th century.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:baths_of_constantine_v3.note: Plan after Palladio and Du Perac (destroyed for Palazzo Rospigliosi-Pallavicini and the Consulta, 1605-1611). Site from Pleiades (bbox about 100 x 127 m). Orientation conjectural: caldarium projecting SW for the afternoon sun, entrance NE from the Alta Semita (rot 50). Built on a terrace over the W edge of the Quirinal.

b:temple_of_serapis_quirinal_v1.summary: The most colossal temple of imperial Rome after the Temple of Venus and Roma, on the W edge of the Quirinal above the Campus Martius. An inscription records that Caracalla built or rebuilt an aedes of Serapis; Lanciani's attribution to Aurelian's Temple of the Sun has been abandoned. Its court lay to the E, and great stairs descended W from behind it to the plain.
scholarship: Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:temple_of_serapis_quirinal_v1.note: Remains in the Colonna gardens SW of Piazza del Quirinale; columns about 21.2 m (lower diameter about 2 m), the cornice block 'Frontispizio di Nerone' among the largest carved blocks in Rome. The temple faced E onto its court toward the Alta Semita, the stairs being at its back (rot 70). Front of 12 columns and size of the precinct conjectural.

b:temple_of_serapis_quirinal_v2.summary: Closed with the pagan temples at the end of the 4th century and slowly despoiled; a corner of the entablature stood as the 'Frontispizio di Nerone' until the 1630s.
scholarship: Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:temple_of_serapis_quirinal_v2.note: Remains in the Colonna gardens SW of Piazza del Quirinale; columns about 21.2 m (lower diameter about 2 m), the cornice block 'Frontispizio di Nerone' among the largest carved blocks in Rome. The temple faced E onto its court toward the Alta Semita, the stairs being at its back (rot 70). Front of 12 columns and size of the precinct conjectural.

b:temple_of_quirinus_v0.summary: Before the temple of 293 Quirinus, the deified Romulus, had an old shrine on the hill that bore his name, mentioned by Varro among the archaic sacella of the Quirinal.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:temple_of_quirinus_v0.note: Form invented; position as the later temple.

b:temple_of_quirinus_v1.summary: Vowed by L. Papirius Cursor the elder and dedicated in 293 BC by his son, consul that year, after victories over the Samnites, and decorated with their spoils; before it was set up the first sundial in Rome. Two myrtles, patrician and plebeian, grew in front of it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
b:temple_of_quirinus_v1.note: Form of the first temple unknown.

b:temple_of_quirinus_ruin.summary: Struck by lightning and burnt in 49 BC, one of the omens of the civil war; it stood in ruins until Augustus rebuilt it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:temple_of_quirinus_v2.summary: Augustus rebuilt the temple in 16 BC as a Doric dipteros octastylos with 76 columns, and Dio remarks that the 76 columns matched the number of years Augustus lived. Vitruvius cites it as his example of a dipteral Doric temple. A fragment of the Marble Plan shows it within a porticus. A Flavian relief in the Museo Nazionale Romano shows its pediment with Romulus and Remus taking the auspices.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
b:temple_of_quirinus_v2.note: Located in or beside the gardens of the Quirinal Palace (conjectural within about 100 m). Orientation unknown; set facing NW (rot 315), parallel to the Alta Semita ridge. 76 columns = 8 front, 15 per side in two rings.

b:temple_of_salus_v1.summary: Vowed by C. Iunius Bubulcus in the Samnite war and dedicated as dictator in 302 BC on the Collis Salutaris. Its walls bore paintings by C. Fabius Pictor, one of the first named Roman painters, which survived until the temple burned under Claudius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:temple_of_salus_v1.note: Site on the SW spur of the Quirinal near the Quirinal palace; conjectural.

b:temple_of_salus_v2.summary: Rebuilt after the fire in the reign of Claudius that destroyed Fabius Pictor's paintings; still standing in the 4th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:temple_of_flora_quirinal.summary: An ancient shrine of Flora on the Quirinal near the Capitolium Vetus, said to go back to the Sabine king Titus Tatius; distinct from the temple of Flora by the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:capitolium_vetus.summary: The 'Old Capitol' on the Quirinal, a shrine of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva believed older than the Capitoline temple; Varro and Martial mention it as a landmark near the Clivus Proximus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

b:temple_of_fortuna_publica.summary: One of three temples of Fortuna on the Quirinal near the Porta Collina; Fortuna Primigenia was vowed in 204 BC by P. Sempronius Tuditanus and dedicated in 194, and Ovid gives 5 April for Fortuna Publica 'in colle'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

b:temple_of_semo_sancus.summary: Temple of the Sabine god of oaths on the Quirinal, dedicated on 5 June 466 BC; it kept the treaty with Gabii written on an ox-hide shield and a bronze statue of Tanaquil with her distaff. Inscribed bases were found in 1574 near San Silvestro al Quirinale.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

b:domus_flaviorum_malum_punicum.summary: The family house of the Flavii on the Quirinal at the street 'ad Malum Punicum' (by the pomegranate), where Domitian was born on 24 October 51.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
b:domus_flaviorum_malum_punicum.note: Location from Pleiades (Ad Malum Punicum); from-date arbitrary.

b:templum_gentis_flaviae.summary: Domitian turned his birthplace into a temple-mausoleum of the Flavian family, celebrated by Martial and Statius; his nurse secretly placed his ashes here with those of his niece Julia. Its form is unknown: a temple in a portico precinct is assumed. Fragments of Flavian reliefs from the Quirinal (the Hartwig-Kelsey fragments) may come from it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:templum_gentis_flaviae.note: Site debated (near Quattro Fontane or S. Susanna); form conjectural.

b:ara_incendii_neroniani_quirinal.summary: One of the altars vowed after the fire of 64 and built by Domitian in each region, on a paved travertine platform with boundary stones; the inscription found here orders annual sacrifices to Vulcan on 23 August and forbids building or trading within the boundary.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:ara_incendii_neroniani_quirinal.note: Location from Pleiades (Arae incendii Neroniani), Via del Quirinale.

b:castra_praetoria_v1.summary: The fortified camp in which Sejanus concentrated the nine (later more) praetorian cohorts on the edge of the Viminal plateau in AD 23, the first permanent military base at Rome and one of the earliest large brick-faced structures. Here Claudius was acclaimed in 41, the empire was auctioned to Didius Julianus in 193, and Elagabalus was murdered in 222; in 238 the people besieged it.

phases.t: camp built for Sejanus (Tacitus)
Claudius acclaimed
auction of the empire
siege by the populace

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:castra_praetoria_v1.note: Rectangle 440 x 380 m (sides along 340/160 and 70/250, from the Aurelian Wall which follows its N, E and S sides). rot 250 = side facing the city (WSW); the porta praetoria was in the NNW side and the porta principalis dextera in the E side (OSM nodes).

b:castra_praetoria_v2.summary: Aurelian incorporated three sides of the camp into his new city wall from 271, raising its walls (the original crenellations are visible in the masonry), and Maxentius heightened them again while the guard supported him.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:castra_praetoria_v2.note: Rectangle 440 x 380 m (sides along 340/160 and 70/250, from the Aurelian Wall which follows its N, E and S sides). rot 250 = side facing the city (WSW); the porta praetoria was in the NNW side and the porta principalis dextera in the E side (OSM nodes).

b:castra_praetoria_v3.summary: After the Milvian Bridge Constantine abolished the praetorian guard and demolished the inner (city-facing) wall of its camp, leaving the three outer sides as part of the Aurelian Wall.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:castra_praetoria_v3.note: Rectangle 440 x 380 m (sides along 340/160 and 70/250, from the Aurelian Wall which follows its N, E and S sides). rot 250 = side facing the city (WSW); the porta praetoria was in the NNW side and the porta principalis dextera in the E side (OSM nodes).

b:thermae_novati.summary: Private baths on the Vicus Patricius named after a Novatus whom the legend of Pudentiana makes her brother. A 2nd-century bath hall here was converted about 390 into the church of S. Pudenziana (district D), whose apse mosaic is the oldest in Rome.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:thermae_novati.note: Placed at district D's Santa Pudenziana (from 390) and given its monument id so the hall chains into the church; Pleiades puts the Thermae Novati 150 m SW.

b:thermae_olympiadis.summary: Baths on the Viminal near San Lorenzo in Panisperna, where tradition placed the martyrdom of St Laurence in 258.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:lavacrum_agrippinae.summary: Baths on the Viminal named after an Agrippina, known from inscriptions and the medieval topography of the Viminal.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:balneum_neratii_cerealis.summary: Public baths built on the Esquiline near Santa Maria Maggiore by Naeratius Cerealis, consul of 358 and urban prefect in 352-353, known from inscribed statue bases found there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:balneum_neratii_cerealis.note: Site approximate from the findspot; plan generic.

b:statio_cohortis_iii_vigilum.summary: Barracks of the cohort of vigiles serving Regions IV and VI, located near the later Baths of Diocletian.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:domus_attici_tamphiliana.summary: Cicero's friend Atticus lived in the house inherited from his uncle Caecilius on the Quirinal near the temple of Salus, modest outside but with a fine wooded garden.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:mithraeum_barberini.summary: A vaulted room of a 2nd-century building on the slope of the Quirinal converted into a mithraeum about 200; its back wall carries one of the best preserved painted tauroctonies, framed by the zodiac and scenes of the god's life.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

b:senaculum_mulierum.summary: The Historia Augusta claims that Elagabalus set up a 'little senate' of matrons on the Quirinal, on the spot where the conventus matronarum had met, presided over by his mother Soaemias, which legislated on women's dress and precedence.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:senaculum_mulierum.note: Site and building conjectural; the story may be invented.

b:tomb_of_the_sempronii.summary: The travertine facade of a late Republican family tomb of the Sempronii, with an arched doorway and inscribed frieze, which stood beside a road at the foot of the Quirinal before the city grew over the area; preserved at Via della Dataria.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:tomb_of_the_sempronii.note: Location from Pleiades. Facade orientation assumed (W).

b:porta_maggiore_v1.summary: The monumental double arch by which Claudius carried the Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus, one channel above the other, across the fork of the Via Praenestina and Via Labicana in 52. Built of deliberately rough-dressed (rusticated) travertine, with aediculae on the piers; the attic carries the dedications of Claudius (52) and the restorations of Vespasian (71) and Titus (81).

Vergilius Eurysaces built this eccentric tomb for himself and his wife Atistia in the fork of the Via Praenestina and Via Labicana about 30 BC, its walls pierced by rows of cylinders and topped by a frieze showing every stage of bread-making for the state. b:sessorium_v2.summary: After 312 the palace became the residence of Constantine's mother Helena, who restored the nearby baths; its great hall became, about 325, the church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme (district D) to hold the relics of the Cross. Still an imperial residence in the 5th century; Valentinian III and Theodoric's officials used it.

b:colosseum_v1.summary: Vespasian began the amphitheatre about 70-72 on the drained site of Nero's lake, paid for with the spoils of Jerusalem; it is the largest amphitheatre ever built, an ellipse 188 x 156 m on 80 radial walls. Titus inaugurated it in 80 with 100 days of games in which 9,000 animals were killed; Dio and Suetonius mention a flooded arena for a mock sea battle. At the inauguration the uppermost tier and attic were not yet finished.

b:colosseum_v2.summary: Domitian completed the attic storey 'ad clipea' and built the hypogeum, a two-level warren of corridors, cages and some 60 lifts under a timber arena floor, ending water spectacles. Seating was strictly graded: senators on the podium, equestrians above, then citizens by class, with women and slaves at the top. A tunnel led from the imperial box to the Ludus Magnus.

Gladiatorial combat lapsed in the early 5th century; beast hunts continued.

b:domus_mithraeum_san_clemente.summary: An insula or house of the late 1st century across a narrow alley from the Moneta, whose ground floor received a mithraeum about 200; the cult room with its benches and tauroctony altar survives under the apse of San Clemente.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:domus_mithraeum_san_clemente.note: Ends when the first church was built over both buildings (c. 390).

b:domus_transitoria_link.summary: Before the fire Nero linked the Palatine to the imperial Horti Maecenatis on the Esquiline with a 'house of passage'. Its Palatine parts (the nymphaeum under the Domus Flavia) survive; the connecting galleries across the valley are known only from Suetonius and Tacitus. It burned in July 64.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:domus_transitoria_link.note: Line entirely conjectural, from the NE corner of the Palatine across the valley and up the Oppius to the gardens. The Palatine part (domus_transitoria) is modelled by district A.

b:domus_aurea_oppian_wing.summary: The surviving pavilion of Nero's Golden House, built after the fire of 64 by Severus and Celer: a single-storey range about 240 m long facing south over the lake, with a portico along its front, a peristyle court on the west, the famous domed octagonal hall with radiating rooms and an oculus at the centre, and a pentagonal court on the east. Suetonius describes ceilings of ivory panels that showered flowers and a round dining room that turned day and night. The Flavians lived in it in part; after the fire of 104 its rooms were filled with earth as foundations for the Baths of Trajan.

phases.t: begun after the fire of July 64
Nero's death; 'at last I can live like a human being' (Suetonius)
fire; buried under the Baths of Trajan

scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
b:domus_aurea_oppian_wing.note: Centre between the Wikipedia and Pleiades points; facade faces S over the valley, rotated slightly west (rot 183), about 30 degrees off the grid of the Baths of Trajan.

b:domus_aurea_stagnum.summary: An artificial lake filled the valley between the Palatine, Velia, Oppius and Caelian, 'like a sea, surrounded by buildings like cities'. Vespasian drained it and built the Colosseum on its bed; its edge has been found under the Colosseum's foundations.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:domus_aurea_stagnum.note: Shape idealised as an ellipse slightly larger than the Colosseum ring.

b:nymphaeum_via_annibaldi.summary: A brick fountain facade with niches on the slope of the Oppius above the lake, part of the landscaped terraces of the Domus Aurea.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
b:nymphaeum_via_annibaldi.note: Location from Pleiades; facing SSW over the valley.

b:domus_aurea_porticus_stagni.summary: Colonnades and pavilions lined the lake of the Golden House, linking the vestibule on the Velia with the Esquiline wing; Suetonius' 'buildings like cities' round the stagnum. Swept away by the Flavian works.
scholarship: Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
b:domus_aurea_porticus_stagni.note: Line conjectural along the N edge of the lake.

b:colosseum_platea.summary: A travertine pavement about 17.5 m wide encircled the amphitheatre, bounded on the outside by a ring of large travertine cippi, five of which survive on the E side.
scholarship: Rea (ed.), Rota Colisei: la valle del Colosseo attraverso i secoli (2002)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:colosseum_platea.note: Outer ellipse = building plus 17.5 m on each side.

b:baths_of_titus_v1.summary: Built quickly for the inauguration of the Colosseum in 80, on part of the site of the Domus Aurea, on a raised platform reached from the valley by a wide stair. The first imperial baths on the symmetrical plan: a central axis of natatio, cross-vaulted frigidarium, tepidarium and domed caldarium, with mirrored palaestrae on either side, as drawn by Palladio. Largely destroyed; parts of the stair and substructures survive under Via Nicola Salvi.
scholarship: Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)
Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:baths_of_titus_v1.note: Plan after Palladio's drawing; dimensions approximate (about 110 x 120 m). Faces SSW toward the Colosseum on the Domus Aurea grid (rot 195).

b:baths_of_titus_v2.summary: Out of use once the aqueducts were cut in 537; the ruins were drawn by Palladio before being largely destroyed.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)

b:baths_of_trajan_v1.summary: The first of the colossal imperial thermae, begun after the fire of 104 that gutted the Domus Aurea and dedicated by Trajan in June 109, designed (says Dio) by Apollodorus. A bath block about 212 x 150 m stood within a walled garden precinct of some 330 x 340 m, with exedrae on the sides housing libraries or lecture halls and a great curved stand on the SW. The model for the later baths of Caracalla and Diocletian; supplied by the Sette Sale cistern. Used into the 5th century.

phases.t: fire in the Domus Aurea; works begin
dedicated 22 June (Fasti Ostienses)

scholarship: Yegul, Baths and Bathing in Classical Antiquity (1992)
Nielsen, Thermae et Balnea (1990)
DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (JRA Suppl. 25, 1997)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
b:baths_of_trajan_v1.note: Axis about 30 degrees off the Domus Aurea grid: main entrance on the NNE (rot 32), caldarium projecting SSW for the afternoon sun (Wikipedia: caldarium on the SW side). Precinct 330 x 340 m; central block placed against the NE side as in the Marble Plan fragments and Renaissance drawings. Centre between the Wikipedia and Pleiades positions.

b:baths_of_trajan_v2.summary: Out of use by the Gothic siege of 537 when the aqueducts were cut. A cemetery grew in front of the NE exedra from the 5th to the 7th century; later the ruins were quarried by the monks of San Pietro in Vincoli. The Laocoon was found nearby in 1506.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
b:baths_of_trajan_v2.note: Axis about 30 degrees off the Domus Aurea grid: main entrance on the NNE (rot 32), caldarium projecting SSW for the afternoon sun (Wikipedia: caldarium on the SW side). Precinct 330 x 340 m; central block placed against the NE side as in the Marble Plan fragments and Renaissance drawings. Centre between the Wikipedia and Pleiades positions.

b:sette_sale.summary: The cistern that fed the Baths of Trajan: nine parallel barrel-vaulted chambers (despite the name 'seven halls'), each about 29.5 x 5.3 m, with staggered openings to keep the water moving, holding up to 8 million litres. In the 4th century a house was built on its roof.
scholarship: Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:sette_sale.note: OSM outline; straight W facade with niches (rot 271), curved E side buried in the slope. Its orientation differs from the Baths of Trajan.

b:domus_sette_sale.summary: In the 4th century a wealthy house with an apsed reception hall and mosaic floors was built on the roof of the cistern, a typical late antique reuse of a public structure on the Oppius.
scholarship: Haeuber, The Eastern Part of the Mons Oppius in Rome (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:domus_sette_sale.note: Blocks sit on the cistern roof (z 10).

b:claudianum_terrace.summary: A vast artificial terrace about 180 x 200 m on the NW spur of the Caelian, begun by Agrippina for the cult of her deified husband in 54. Its west retaining wall of deliberately rough-cut travertine arcades still stands under the bell tower of SS. Giovanni e Paolo. Nero turned the east side into a fountain facade for the Domus Aurea.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
b:claudianum_terrace.note: Bounded by the Clivus Scauri (S), Via Claudia (E), Via di S. Gregorio (W) and the slope to the Colosseum (N); centre estimated from those streets. Builder field gives Claudius as the honorand; the work was Agrippina's (no person id).

b:nymphaeum_neronis_caelian.summary: Nero cut back the Claudian temple and turned the east face of its terrace into a 167 m long brick fountain wall with niches and cascades facing the Domus Aurea, fed by the Arcus Neroniani that he extended across the Caelian.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Ball, The Domus Aurea and the Roman Architectural Revolution (2003)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
b:nymphaeum_neronis_caelian.note: Wall along Via Claudia; the Arcus Neroniani themselves belong to the aqueduct collection.

b:temple_of_divus_claudius_v1.summary: Agrippina began a temple to the deified Claudius after 54; Suetonius says Nero almost entirely destroyed it. Shown as an unfinished shell.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:temple_of_divus_claudius_v1.note: Form unknown; assumed like Vespasian's temple.

b:temple_of_divus_claudius_v2.summary: Vespasian rebuilt the temple of Claudius in the centre of the terrace, surrounded by a garden precinct; the Marble Plan shows a hexastyle temple set among rows of trees. Martial notes that its portico spread wide shade.
scholarship: Colini, Storia e topografia del Celio nell'antichita (1944)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
b:temple_of_divus_claudius_v2.note: Temple faces W toward the Palatine (rot 265), following the travertine W front of the terrace. Dimensions estimated from the Marble Plan.

b:arch_of_constantine.summary: The Senate's triple arch for Constantine's victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312, dedicated for his decennalia in 315 'instinctu divinitatis'. It stands on the triumphal route between the Circus Maximus and the Colosseum and reuses sculpture from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius beside Constantinian friezes. Some argue that its lower part reuses a Hadrianic arch.

phases.t: dedicated 25 July for the decennalia

scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed., 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
b:arch_of_constantine.note: OSM outline 25.4 x 7.0 m, facade line 103/283; faces NNE toward the Meta Sudans and Colosseum (rot 13) and SSW toward Via di S. Gregorio.

b:circus_flaminius_v1.summary: Laid out by the censor Gaius Flaminius in 221 BC on the Prata Flaminia: not a racecourse with stands but a long open space used for the plebeian games, for assemblies, for triumphal musters and as the start of the triumphal procession. Victory temples and porticoes lined its edges.

phases.t: laid out by the censor C. Flaminius
triumphal games and temples begin to line it

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 83
Gatti, in Carettoni et al., La pianta marmorea di Roma antica (1960)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31ii
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
b:circus_flaminius_v1.note: Following Gatti: an open strip about 300 x 100 m between the Tiber and the joint facade of the Porticus Octaviae and Porticus Philippi, running ESE-WNW parallel to that facade, with its rounded end to the WNW under Monte dei Cenci. rot 124 = from the rounded WNW end toward the open ESE end (the schema's circus convention). Boundaries on the long sides are the Marble Plan lines (fr. 31ii, 31u, 31cc, 31z); length is reasoned from Monte dei Cenci to the Theatre of Marcellus. No seating has ever been found.

b:circus_flaminius_v2.summary: After the Augustan rebuilding of the Porticus Octaviae and Philippi and the building of the Theatre of Marcellus, which cut into its eastern end, the Circus Flaminius was a monumental paved piazza in front of the porticoes. In 2 BC it was flooded and 36 crocodiles were slaughtered in it. The Regionary Catalogues still name it in the 4th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 83
Gatti, in Carettoni et al., La pianta marmorea di Roma antica (1960)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31ii
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Circus Flaminius
b:circus_flaminius_v2.note: Gatti suggested the area was paved in the imperial period. Same footprint as v1; the Theatre of Marcellus overlaps its ESE end.

b:temple_apollo_medicus_v1.summary: Vowed in 433 BC during a plague and dedicated by the consul Gnaeus Julius in 431, the first and for centuries the only temple of Apollo in Rome, outside the pomerium in the Prata Flaminia (the Apollinar). The Senate met here when it had to receive generals and envoys outside the city.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 12
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Apollo, aedes in circo
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
b:temple_apollo_medicus_v1.note: Form unknown: a tufa podium of an earlier temple was found under the Augustan one. Modelled as a small Tuscan temple on the later footprint and orientation; dimensions are guesses.

b:temple_apollo_medicus_v2.summary: Restored in the mid-Republican building campaigns; in 179 BC the censor M. Fulvius Nobilior contracted for a porticus running from the temple toward the Tiber. A podium wall attributed by Frank to this phase survives under the Augustan temple.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 12
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Apollo, aedes in circo
b:temple_apollo_medicus_v2.note: Frank dated much of the surviving podium to 179 BC; others (Delbrueck) to the original. Form conjectural.

b:temple_apollo_sosianus_v3.summary: Rebuilt from 34 BC by Gaius Sosius, Antony's partisan, and completed after Actium as an Augustan monument, dedicated on 23 September, Augustus' birthday. Hexastyle, with Carrara marble columns along the front and pronaos and engaged columns down the cella; the pediment carried a Greek Amazonomachy of the 5th century BC and the cella held famous Greek statuary. Three columns stand re-erected beside the Theatre of Marcellus.

phases.t: Sosius begins the rebuilding
dedicated on 23 September as an Augustan monument (date approximate)

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 12-13
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Apollo, aedes in circo
La Rocca, Amazzonomachia: le sculture frontonali del tempio di Apollo Sosiano (1985)
b:temple_apollo_sosianus_v3.note: Oriented almost due south, unlike its neighbours. The frontal stair was replaced by two lateral stairs when the Theatre of Marcellus was built against its front. Column height ~14.6 m from the re-erected columns; podium ~40 x 21 m.

b:temple_bellona_v1.summary: Vowed by Appius Claudius Caecus in 296 BC during the battle against Etruscans and Samnites. Outside the pomerium, it was where the Senate received envoys and victorious generals asking for triumphs; before it stood the Columna Bellica, over which the fetial threw the spear that declared war on a distant enemy.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 57-58
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Bellona, aedes in circo
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:temple_bellona_v1.note: Identified (Coarelli) with the podium immediately east of Apollo Sosianus, which has a different orientation; rot 170 is approximate. Dedication date c. 290 BC assumed.

b:temple_bellona_v2.summary: Restored in the Augustan remodelling of the area around the Theatre of Marcellus, when Bellona, Apollo and the theatre were tied into one architectural group. Still the setting of the Senate's war ceremonies under the emperors; Marcus Aurelius threw the fetial spear from the Columna Bellica in 178.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 57-58
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
b:temple_bellona_v2.note: Augustan restoration inferred from the tight planning of the group; details conjectural.

b:temple_pietas_in_circo.summary: A small temple of Pietas that Pliny says stood on the site later taken by the Theatre of Marcellus; Caesar demolished it with other shrines when he cleared the ground for his theatre.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 290
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Pietas, aedes in circo Flaminio
b:temple_pietas_in_circo.note: Location only known as 'where the Theatre of Marcellus is'; placed under the stage area. Form invented from typical small Republican temples.

b:theatre_marcellus_v1.summary: Begun by Caesar, who demolished temples to clear the site, and finished by Augustus in the name of his dead nephew and heir Marcellus; dedicated in 13 or 11 BC. A travertine cavea about 111 m across with three tiers of arcades (Doric, Ionic and a Corinthian attic) rising 32.6 m, seating perhaps 15,000. Its stage looked toward the Tiber.

phases.t: Caesar clears the site
used, perhaps unfinished, for the scenic games of the Secular Games
dedicated in the name of Marcellus (Dio; Pliny gives 11 BC)

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 382-383
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Fidenzoni, Il teatro di Marcello (1970)
Ciancio Rossetto, in LTUR V (1999)
b:theatre_marcellus_v1.note: Centre fitted to the surviving curve of the facade (radius ~56 m). The curved facade wraps the north and east, so the audience looked WSW toward the stage on the river side; rot 258 is estimated from the arc and could be off by 10 degrees. Height 32.6 m to the top of the attic. Dio dates the dedication to 13 BC, Pliny to 11 BC.
b:theatre_marcellus_v1.builderName: begun by Julius Caesar, completed by Augustus

b:theatre_marcellus_v2.summary: Vespasian restored the stage building and Severus Alexander repaired the theatre again; it remained one of the three great stone theatres of Rome through the 4th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Theatrum Marcelli

b:theatre_marcellus_v3.summary: Travertine blocks were taken from the theatre around 370 to rebuild the Pons Cestius as the Pons Gratiani, a sign that parts of it were already derelict; yet in 421 the prefect Petronius Maximus still set up statues here. After the 6th century it decayed into a quarry and later a fortress of the Pierleoni, Savelli and Orsini.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Theatrum Marcelli
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
b:theatre_marcellus_v3.note: The Ammianus passage concerns the prefect Symmachus and the bridge; the reuse of the theatre's travertine for the Pons Gratiani is inferred by modern scholars. Statues of Petronius Maximus are known from inscriptions. Stage height reduced to show partial dismantling.

b:porticus_metelli.summary: Built by Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus after his Macedonian triumph of 146 BC around the temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno Regina. In front of the temples stood Lysippus' bronze group of Alexander's 25 horsemen at the Granicus, taken as booty from Dion in Macedonia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317

Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u
b:porticus_metelli.note: Assumed to share the later footprint (Marble Plan shows the Severan state about 119 x 132 m). Facade (and the surviving propylon) faces SW onto the Circus Flaminius; rot 214 from the alignment of the propylon and Via del Portico d'Ottavia.

b:porticus_octaviae_v1.summary: Augustus rebuilt the porticus in his sister Octavia's name, adding a library (Latin and Greek, founded by Octavia in memory of Marcellus), a curia and scholae, and filling it with Greek art: works by Praxiteles, Phidias, Apelles and others. The Senate sometimes met in its curia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317-318
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Octaviae
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
b:porticus_octaviae_v1.note: Dio (49.43.8) dates a dedication to 33 BC, perhaps confusing it with the Porticus Octavia of Cn. Octavius; work is usually placed after 27 BC (from = -23 as a mid-range date).

b:porticus_octaviae_v2.summary: The fire of AD 80 destroyed Octavia's buildings and their books (Dio). They were restored, probably under Domitian.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 318
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Octaviae
b:porticus_octaviae_v2.note: Restoration by Domitian is likely but not attested by inscription.

b:porticus_octaviae_v3.summary: After a fire (that of 191) Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored the porticus in 203, as the inscription on the surviving propylon records. The Marble Plan, made in these same years, shows it with its two temples and double colonnades.

Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u, 31bb
b:porticus_octaviae_v3.note: Propylon remains: brick-faced concrete and marble, four columns across the front; dedicatory inscription of 203 on the architrave.

b:porticus_octaviae_v4.summary: Two columns of the propylon's front, brought down by the earthquake of 442, were replaced with the brick arch still visible. The porticus became the medieval fish market and the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria was built into the propylon in 755.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)

b:porticus_octaviae_v4.note: The arch is generally attributed to the repair after the earthquake of 442.

b:temple_jupiter_stator_campus_v1.summary: The first temple in Rome built entirely of marble, designed by the Greek architect Hermodoros of Salamis for Metellus Macedonicus. Vitruvius cites it as the model peripteros, six columns by eleven.

b:temple_jupiter_stator_campus_v2.summary: Restored after the fire of 80 with the rest of the porticus.

b:temple_jupiter_stator_campus_v3.summary: Rebuilt with the porticus by Septimius Severus and Caracalla in 203; shown on the Marble Plan.

b:temple_juno_regina_campus_v1.summary: Vowed by M. Aemilius Lepidus in the Ligurian war of 187 BC and dedicated by him as censor on 23 December 179; later enclosed with Jupiter Stator in the Porticus Metelli.

b:porticus_philippi_v1.summary: L. Marcius Philippus, Augustus' stepfather, rebuilt the Temple of Hercules Musarum and enclosed it in this porticus about 29 BC, part of the Augustan transformation of the Circus Flaminius. It held paintings by Zeuxis, Antiphilus and Theon and became a haunt of Rome's poets and hairdressers alike.

To evade the old ban on permanent theatres, a temple of Venus Victrix crowned the top of the cavea so that the seats served as its steps; the temple was dedicated in 52. The cavea was about 150 m across.

Fulvius Flaccus in a cavalry battle in Spain in 180 BC and dedicated in 173; he scandalously stripped the marble roof tiles from the temple of Juno Lacinia at Croton for it and was made to return them. Vitruvius saw it 'by the stone theatre'; by AD 22 it no longer existed.

b:pantheon_v1.summary: Built by Agrippa in 27-25 BC in his third consulship as part of his monumentalisation of the Campus Martius, decorated with caryatids by Diogenes of Athens and bronze capitals of Syracusan bronze. Dio says Agrippa wanted to name it after Augustus and place his statue inside; refused, he put statues of Augustus and himself in the pronaos.

Beltrami (1892-93) found remains he read as a T-shaped temple with a transverse cella 43.76 x 19.82 m facing SOUTH; the 1996-97 excavations under the portico showed the Agrippan building also faced NORTH, with a pronaos about 21 m wide, and La Rocca argues for a circular open precinct behind. Modelled as a north-facing (rot 356) rectangular temple with transverse cella on Beltrami's dimensions; treat as one hypothesis.

b:pantheon_v2.summary: Burned in the fire of AD 80 and restored by Domitian; struck by lightning and burned again in 110 under Trajan.

b:pantheon_v3.summary: Rebuilt from scratch under Hadrian (brick stamps of c. 114-126; perhaps begun under Trajan by Apollodorus) with Agrippa's inscription repeated on the frieze. A rotunda whose concrete dome spans 43.3 m, exactly equal to its height, open to the sky through an 8.9 m oculus, fronted by a porch of sixteen monolithic granite columns in three rows and a tall intermediate block. Hadrian held court here.

b:saepta_julia_v1.summary: Caesar planned in 54 BC a marble voting enclosure a mile around; Lepidus continued it and Agrippa finished and dedicated it in 26 BC, adorned with marble tablets and paintings. A vast colonnaded court about 310 x 120 m, its long sides formed by the Porticus Argonautarum (west, by the Pantheon) and the Porticus Meleagri (east). As voting lost its meaning it served for gladiatorial shows, a naumachia under Augustus, and as a luxury market.

b:temple_minerva_chalcidica.summary: A temple of Minerva built by Domitian, Minerva being his patron goddess; the medieval name Santa Maria sopra Minerva preserves the memory of a Minerva sanctuary in the area.

b:temple_minerva_chalcidica.note: Placed east of the Iseum toward the Via Lata (Collegio Romano area). A round temple drawn in this area in the Renaissance is often identified with it; position and form conjectural.

b:hadrianeum_precinct.summary: The temple stood in a colonnaded square; reliefs of personified provinces from its attic or podium survive in the Capitoline and Naples museums.

b:hadrianeum_temple.summary: Dedicated by Antoninus Pius in 145 to his deified adoptive father. Eleven Proconnesian marble columns of the north flank, 14.8 m high, stand in the facade of the former Stock Exchange on Piazza di Pietra, with the peperino cella wall behind.

b:temple_matidia.summary: The first temple in Rome to a deified woman not of an emperor's direct blood: Hadrian's mother-in-law Matidia, consecrated in 119. Cipollino column shafts 1.7 m thick (one survives in Vicolo della Spada d'Orlando) imply a huge temple flanked by the basilicas of Matidia and Marciana.

b:basilicae_marcianae_matidiae.summary: Two halls named after Trajan's sister Marciana and her daughter Matidia flanking the temple of Matidia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 55

b:baths_nero_v1.summary: Nero's baths, the first symmetrical 'imperial' bath plan, built c. 62-64 between the Pantheon and the later Stadium of Domitian. Martial's quip: 'What is worse than Nero? What is better than Nero's baths?'

b:baths_nero_v2.summary: Rebuilt and enlarged by Severus Alexander in 227, who brought a new aqueduct (Aqua Alexandrina) to feed them; granite columns from them were used to restore the Pantheon's portico in the 17th century.

b:gymnasium_neronis.summary: Nero dedicated a Greek-style gymnasium in 60/61 with free oil for senators and knights; struck by lightning in 62, it burned down, and a bronze statue of Nero melted into a shapeless mass.

b:stadium_domitian_v1.summary: Built by Domitian for the Greek athletic contests of his Capitoline Games (first held in 86): 275 x 106 m with a travertine arcaded facade in two orders and seats for about 30,000. Its arena survives as Piazza Navona, the curved north end and straight south end still legible in the square.

b:stadium_domitian_v2.summary: Restored by Severus Alexander, who held gladiatorial games here while the fire-damaged Colosseum was being repaired. Constantius II admired it on his visit in 357. In the Middle Ages houses were built into its cavea, preserving its shape; the martyr Agnes was venerated in its arcades.

b:odeum_domitian_v1.summary: A roofed hall for musical contests of the Capitoline Games, south of the Stadium. The curved facade of Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne follows its cavea.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 276

b:odeum_domitian_v2.summary: Completed or rebuilt by Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus; Ammianus lists it with the Pantheon and the Stadium among the wonders Constantius II saw in 357.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 276

b:column_marcus_aurelius.summary: A 100-foot spiral column of Luna marble, modelled on Trajan's, whose frieze narrates Marcus Aurelius' wars against the Marcomanni and Sarmatians (172-175), including the 'rain miracle'. Begun after his death in 180, it was finished by 193, when its custodian Adrastus was granted timber from the scaffolding to build himself a house beside it.

b:temple_divus_marcus.summary: The Senate decreed a temple to the deified Marcus Aurelius with its own priesthood; it is thought to have stood west of his column.

b:column_antoninus_pius.summary: A plain monolith of red Aswan granite, 50 feet high, raised by Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus to Antoninus Pius and Faustina after his death in 161. Its marble pedestal, with the apotheosis of the imperial couple and the cavalry parade of the funeral games, was found in 1703 and is in the Vatican.

b:ustrinum_antonini_pii.summary: The cremation precinct of Antoninus Pius and Faustina: a travertine enclosure with an iron railing around a central platform for the pyre, found with the column base in 1703.

b:arch_claudius_via_lata.summary: The Senate's arch for Claudius' conquest of Britain, built in 51-52 where the Aqua Virgo crossed the Via Lata, so that the aqueduct ran through its attic. The inscription recorded the surrender of eleven British kings without loss.

b:arcus_novus.summary: A 'new arch' built by Diocletian over the Via Lata, probably for his vicennalia of 303-304, reusing Claudian reliefs (now in the Boboli Gardens and Villa Medici); demolished in 1491 when Santa Maria in Via Lata was rebuilt.

b:arco_di_portogallo_v1.summary: Two Hadrianic reliefs (an apotheosis of Sabina and an imperial address) later built into the Arco di Portogallo may come from an arch of Hadrian standing on this spot, or may have been brought from elsewhere.

b:arco_di_portogallo_v2.summary: A late antique arch over the Via Flaminia beside the later Palazzo Fiano, decorated with two Hadrianic reliefs, demolished in 1662 by Alexander VII to widen the Corso. Its modern name comes from a Portuguese cardinal's palace nearby. It is sometimes called the Arch of Marcus Aurelius, since one view dates the arch or its reliefs to him.

b:campus_agrippae.summary: The park Agrippa laid out east of the Via Lata, opened to the people by Augustus in 7 BC with the Porticus Vipsania along its edge.

Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Campus Agrippae

b:porticus_vipsania.summary: Begun by Agrippa's sister Vipsania Polla and completed by Augustus, it displayed Agrippa's great map of the world, drawn from his commentaries. Galba's soldiers were stationed in it in 69.

b:ara_providentiae.summary: An altar to the Providence of Augustus set up under Tiberius, at which the Arval Brethren sacrificed; the Arval acts locate it in the Campus Agrippae.

b:temple_sol_invictus.summary: Aurelian's temple of the Unconquered Sun, built after his victory over Palmyra and dedicated on 25 December 274, filled with Palmyrene spoils and served by a new college of pontifices Solis. Wine for the plebs was stored in its porticoes.

The preferred site is east of the Via Lata in the former Campus Agrippae around San Silvestro in Capite, where Renaissance drawings (Palladio and others) record a huge double precinct: an outer court with semicircular ends and an inner court with a round(?) temple. The older location on the Quirinal (Colonna gardens) is now assigned to Caracalla's Serapeum. Dimensions follow the drawings loosely; front toward the Via Lata (rot 266).

b:horologium_obelisk.summary: An obelisk of Psammetichus II brought from Heliopolis and set up by Augustus in 10 BC, after the conquest of Egypt, as the gnomon of a great meridian (or sundial) in the northern Campus; Pliny says its gilded ball cast the shadow, but that the readings had gone wrong for some 30 years in his day. Now in Piazza di Montecitorio.

b:horologium_pavement_v1.summary: A travertine pavement with a bronze meridian line north of the obelisk on which the noon shadow marked the seasons and zodiac signs. Buchner reconstructed a full sundial grid some 160 m across, aligned so that on Augustus' birthday the shadow pointed to the Ara Pacis; later work (Heslin, Haselberger) favours a meridian line only.

b:ara_pacis.summary: The Altar of Augustan Peace, decreed by the Senate on 4 July 13 BC on Augustus' return from Spain and Gaul and dedicated on 30 January 9 BC. A marble precinct carved with the procession of the imperial family, Aeneas, Tellus and acanthus scrolls, enclosing the altar where magistrates, priests and Vestals sacrificed yearly.

b:ara_pacis.note: Original site under Palazzo Fiano at Via in Lucina, just west of the Via Flaminia; reassembled in 1938 by the Mausoleum. Precinct 11.6 x 10.6 m, main door and stair on the west toward the Campus (rot 267), back door toward the Via Flaminia. As the ground rose, a retaining wall was built around it in the 2nd century.

b:mausoleum_augustus_v1.summary: Begun by Octavian in 28 BC, after Actium, between the Via Flaminia and the Tiber: a huge drum 87 m across faced in travertine, carrying an earthen mound planted with evergreens and topped by a bronze statue of Augustus, about 42 m high. Marcellus was the first buried (23 BC); Augustus' ashes followed in AD 14, then the Julio-Claudians to Nerva. Bronze pillars at the entrance carried the Res Gestae.

b:tomb_of_hirtius.summary: The consul Hirtius, killed at Mutina in 43 BC, was given a public burial in the Campus Martius, an exceptional honour. His travertine tomb was found in 1938-40 beneath the courtyard of the Palazzo della Cancelleria beside the Euripus.

b:tomb_of_sulla.summary: Sulla was cremated and buried in the Campus Martius with an unprecedented funeral in 78 BC; his epitaph, which he wrote himself, said no friend ever outdid him in kindness nor enemy in harm. Caracalla restored the tomb.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 357

b:tomb_of_julia.summary: When Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, died in childbirth in 54 BC, the people seized her body from the consuls and buried it in the Campus Martius. Caesar's pyre was prepared next to it in 44.
