b:sepulcrum_domitiorum.note: Tradition puts it at the site of Santa Maria del Popolo, under the Pincian slope; form conjectural.

b:horti_luculliani_terraces_v1.summary: Lucullus spent his Asian fortune on terraced gardens on the Pincian slope facing the Campus, crowned by a great exedra and nymphaeum. Later owned by Valerius Asiaticus, whom Messalina drove to suicide to seize them.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 200
Broise and Jolivet, in Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Horti Luculliani
b:horti_luculliani_terraces_v1.note: Following Broise and Jolivet's reconstruction around Trinita dei Monti and Villa Medici: stepped terraces with a hemicycle (~80 m across) facing west. Dimensions approximate.

b:horti_luculliani_terraces_v2.summary: Messalina was killed in these gardens in 48 after her mock marriage to Silius; the estate passed to the emperors and later to the Acilii Glabriones.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 200
Broise and Jolivet, in Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Horti Luculliani

b:mausoleum_hadrian_v1.summary: Hadrian's dynastic tomb across the Tiber in his family's gardens, linked to the Campus by the Pons Aelius: a square base about 89 m a side carrying a drum 64 m across and 21 m high, faced in Parian marble with statues, crowned by a smaller structure with a bronze quadriga. Completed by Antoninus Pius in 139; the emperors to Caracalla were buried in it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 249-251
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Hadriani
Pierce, 'The Mausoleum of Hadrian and the Pons Aelius', JRS 15 (1925)
b:mausoleum_hadrian_v1.note: Centre fitted to the drum on satellite imagery (Castel Sant'Angelo). Entrance toward the bridge, rot 177. Upper storey reconstruction debated; total height ~48 m.

b:mausoleum_hadrian_v2.summary: Incorporated into the defences of the city as a bridgehead, probably under Honorius around 403. In the Gothic siege of 537 the defenders, out of missiles, broke up its marble statues and hurled them down on Witiges' men. Gregory the Great's vision of the archangel in 590 later gave it the name Castel Sant'Angelo.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 249-251
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Hadriani
Pierce, 'The Mausoleum of Hadrian and the Pons Aelius', JRS 15 (1925)
b:mausoleum_hadrian_v2.note: Date of fortification (Aurelianic or Honorian) debated; 403 assumed.

b:arch_gratian_valentinian_theodosius.summary: An arch at the Campus end of the Pons Aelius built between 379 and 383 to close the 'porticus maximae', the colonnaded street leading toward St Peter's.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 24
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Gratiani, Valentiniani et Theodosii
b:arch_gratian_valentinian_theodosius.note: Near the church of SS. Celso e Giuliano; position approximate.

b:porticus_maximae.summary: Colonnades lining the street from the Theatre of Pompey and the Circus Flaminius area to the Pons Aelius, sheltering pilgrims walking to St Peter's; finished with the arch of Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 316
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Maximae
b:porticus_maximae.note: Course along Via del Pellegrino / Via dei Banchi Vecchi conjectural.

b:tarentum_altar_v1.summary: A volcanic spot by the river at the western edge of the Campus, where an altar of Dis Pater and Proserpina lay buried 20 feet underground, uncovered only for the nocturnal sacrifices of the Secular Games (249 BC, 146 BC).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 377
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Tarentum
b:tarentum_altar_v1.note: Remains of the altar found in 1886-87 under Corso Vittorio Emanuele near Chiesa Nuova; position approximate.

b:tarentum_altar_v2.summary: Restored for Augustus' Secular Games of 17 BC, for which Horace wrote the Carmen Saeculare, and used again under Claudius (47), Domitian (88), Septimius Severus (204) and Philip (248); inscribed records of the Augustan and Severan games were found nearby in 1890.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 377
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Tarentum

b:trigarium.summary: An open ground near the river in the western Campus where chariots and horses were exercised.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 400
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Trigarium
b:trigarium.note: Location near San Giovanni dei Fiorentini (Coarelli) and extent conjectural.

b:navalia.summary: The naval dockyards of the Republic, where captured warships (from Antium in 338 BC, the royal galley of Perseus in 167) were kept, and where, according to Procopius, a ship said to be Aeneas' was still shown in the 6th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 263
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Tucci, 'Navalia', Archeologia Classica 57 (2006)
b:navalia.note: Debated: Coarelli puts the Navalia on the Campus bank opposite the Prata Quinctia (followed here, near Via Giulia); Tucci and Cozza identify them with the so-called Porticus Aemilia in Testaccio. Six sheds facing the river (rot 225) are a schematic stand-in.

b:insula_san_paolo_regola_v1.summary: A commercial building near the river, probably warehouses, built in the Domitianic period and preserved under a medieval house.
scholarship: Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Horrea (Via di S. Paolo alla Regola)

b:insula_san_paolo_regola_v2.summary: Rebuilt and raised in the Severan period as a multi-storey commercial and residential block; the upper floors were converted to housing.
scholarship: Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Horrea (Via di S. Paolo alla Regola)

b:santa_maria_in_via_lata.summary: A welfare centre (diaconia) set up in the ground floor of a vast Roman porticoed warehouse on the Via Lata, with 7th-century frescoes.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae III (1967)

b:temple_neptune_in_circo_v3.summary: Dio lists a temple of Neptune among the buildings of the Campus burned in AD 80; it was restored.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 267
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)

b:temple_hercules_musarum_v3.summary: The temple as drawn on the Severan Marble Plan; a restoration after the fire of 191 is assumed with that of the neighbouring porticoes. Panegyrists of Constantius I still invoke it around 297.
scholarship: Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 187

b:baths_agrippa_v0.summary: In 25 BC Agrippa built a laconicum, a dry sweating room, the nucleus of the later baths, before his aqueduct brought abundant water.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 386
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
b:baths_agrippa_v0.note: Modelled as the central round hall alone (later Arco della Ciambella).

b:ara_pacis_v2.summary: As flood deposits raised the ground of the northern Campus, a brick retaining wall was built around the precinct in the 2nd century to keep it accessible below the new level; it was gradually buried in late antiquity.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Rossini, Ara Pacis (2006)

b:temple_venus_victrix_v1.summary: The temple of Victorious Venus at the top of the cavea, on the theatre's axis, its stairs formed by the seats below; dedicated in 52 BC, with small shrines of Honos, Virtus, Felicitas and Victoria. On Pompey's victory anniversary the official calendars recorded sacrifices here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 411
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Venus Victrix, aedes
Gagliardo and Packer, AJA 110 (2006)
b:temple_venus_victrix_v1.note: Placed at the outer edge of the cavea on its axis, facing the stage (rot 92). 'podium' here is the height of the cavea top it stands on (~34 m), so h is to its ridge.

b:temple_venus_victrix_v2.summary: Restored with the theatre after the fire of 80 and kept through the later restorations.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 411

b:statue_of_pompey_v1.summary: The statue of Pompey at whose foot Caesar fell, spattered with his blood, on the Ides of March 44 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 104
b:statue_of_pompey_v1.note: Inside the Curia at its far (east) end; position approximate.

b:ianus_pompei.summary: Augustus removed Pompey's statue from the closed Curia and set it on a marble arch (ianus) opposite the royal door of the theatre's stage.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 104
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Ianus (Pompei)
b:ianus_pompei.note: Placed on the axis in front of the scaena's central door; position approximate.

b:domus_pompei.summary: Pompey built himself a fine house next to his theatre, 'like a dinghy towed behind a ship', in addition to his house in the Carinae; it later passed to Antony and to the imperial estate.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 133
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Domus Cn. Pompeius Magnus (in campo)
b:domus_pompei.note: Exact site unknown; placed north of the cavea. Form invented.

b:crypta_balbi_exedra_v1.summary: The semicircular exedra opening off the east side of the Crypta's courtyard, an ornamental feature of Balbus' porticus.
scholarship: Manacorda, Crypta Balbi (2001)
b:crypta_balbi_exedra_v1.note: Faces back into the courtyard (west, rot 268).

b:crypta_balbi_exedra_v2.summary: In the 5th century the exedra was turned into a public latrine, then filled with rubbish and workshop debris in the 6th-7th.
scholarship: Manacorda, Crypta Balbi (2001)

b:mithraeum_crypta_balbi.summary: A small Mithraeum installed in a ground-floor room next to the Crypta, with its benches and a relief of Mithras, abandoned by the end of the 4th century.
scholarship: Manacorda, Crypta Balbi (2001)
b:mithraeum_crypta_balbi.note: Dates approximate; position approximate (south part of the block).

b:divorum_temple_vespasian.summary: One of the two small temples to the deified Flavians inside Domitian's Porticus Divorum, shown on the Marble Plan.
scholarship: Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 36-37
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 111

b:divorum_temple_titus.summary: One of the two small temples to the deified Flavians inside Domitian's Porticus Divorum, shown on the Marble Plan.
scholarship: Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 36-37
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 111

b:temple_vulcan_in_circo.summary: A temple of Vulcan in the Circus Flaminius, struck by lightning in the prodigies of 214 BC; Vulcan's festival, the Volcanalia, was celebrated here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 432
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Volcanus, aedes
b:temple_vulcan_in_circo.note: Position (on the river side of the Circus) and form conjectural; founding before 214 BC.

b:temple_diana_in_circo.summary: Vowed by M. Aemilius Lepidus in the Ligurian war and dedicated in 179 BC, the day after his temple of Juno Regina.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 109
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Diana, aedes in circo

b:porticus_fulvii_ad_tiberim.summary: A porticus contracted by the censor M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BC 'behind the shipyards and to the temple of Apollo Medicus' and toward the Tiber.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 313
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
b:porticus_fulvii_ad_tiberim.note: Line from the temple toward the river conjectural; largely absorbed by the Theatre of Marcellus later.

b:columna_bellica.summary: A small column in front of the temple of Bellona over which a fetial priest hurled a spear into a plot of ground deemed enemy territory, to declare war on distant foes (first, it was said, against Pyrrhus).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 94
b:columna_bellica.note: In front of the temple; exact spot unknown.

b:arch_of_germanicus_circus_flaminius.summary: Decreed by the Senate after Germanicus' death in AD 19: a marble arch in the Circus Flaminius near the statues of Augustus and his house set up by C. Norbanus Flaccus, with gilded statues of the nations he conquered.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 26
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Germanici in circo Flaminio
b:arch_of_germanicus_circus_flaminius.note: Text-documented; its place within the Circus is conjectural.

b:temple_fortuna_redux_domitian.summary: Martial celebrates the temple of Fortuna Redux that Domitian built where he re-entered the city in triumph in 93, beside a new arch.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 155
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
b:temple_fortuna_redux_domitian.note: Usually placed near the Porta Triumphalis at the east end of the Circus Flaminius; conjectural.

b:arch_domitian_fortuna_redux.summary: Martial's 'holy arch' crowned by two chariots drawn by elephants and a golden statue of the emperor; Domitian's arches were torn down after his murder in 96.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 26
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
b:arch_domitian_fortuna_redux.note: Position conjectural; demolition in 96 assumed from the damnatio memoriae.

b:porticus_argonautarum_v1.summary: The west portico of the Saepta, beside the Pantheon, named after its painting of the Argonauts; with the Porticus Meleagri a fashionable place to stroll and shop.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 312-313
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 37
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
b:porticus_argonautarum_v1.note: Identification of the two porticoes with the long sides of the Saepta is usual; built with the Saepta.

b:porticus_argonautarum_v2.summary: Restored after the fire of 80 and again under Hadrian with the Saepta.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 312-313

b:porticus_meleagri_v1.summary: The east portico of the Saepta, named after a painting or statue of Meleager; Martial's Mamurra shopped for luxury goods here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 312-313
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 37
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
b:porticus_meleagri_v1.note: Identification of the two porticoes with the long sides of the Saepta is usual; built with the Saepta.

b:porticus_meleagri_v2.summary: Restored after the fire of 80 and again under Hadrian with the Saepta.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 312-313

b:porticus_europae.summary: A porticus with a painting of Europa and the bull and box-hedged walks, mentioned by Martial among the haunts of the Campus near the Saepta.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 313
b:porticus_europae.note: Location unknown; placed north of the Saepta, conjectural.

b:via_lata_porticus_horrea.summary: A huge building, about 250 m long, fronting the west side of the Via Lata with a porticus, whose ground-floor halls (storerooms) survive under Santa Maria in Via Lata and Palazzo Doria; perhaps public warehouses of the 3rd century.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Saepta (?), Via Lata building
b:via_lata_porticus_horrea.note: Date and function debated; length reduced to 200 m in the model. The diaconia occupied part of it from c. 600.

b:via_lata_porticoes.summary: The Via Lata, the urban stretch of the Via Flaminia, was lined in the imperial period with porticoes in front of shops and apartment blocks.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 416
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Via Lata
b:via_lata_porticoes.note: Generic street porticoes; course follows the modern Corso.

b:obelisk_domitian_iseum.summary: An obelisk quarried at Aswan and inscribed in Rome with Domitian's hieroglyphic titles; Maxentius moved it to his circus on the Via Appia, and Bernini raised it over the Fountain of the Four Rivers in 1651.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 274
Lembke, Das Iseum Campense in Rom (1994)
b:obelisk_domitian_iseum.note: Original site debated (Iseum Campense or the Temple of the Gens Flavia); placed in the Iseum. Removal date c. 309.

b:altar_temple_c_albinus.summary: A peperino altar before Temple C bearing an inscription recording its restoration by A. Postumius Albinus (consul 180 or 151 BC) under a lex Plaetoria.
scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Coarelli et al., L'Area Sacra di Largo Argentina I (1981)
b:altar_temple_c_albinus.note: Altar of the first phase, restored in the 2nd century BC.

b:statio_aquarum_argentina.summary: A building between Temples A and B identified by some with the Statio Aquarum, the office of the water board, which is known to have been in the Porticus Minucia.
scholarship: Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 368

b:domus_pinciana.summary: A late antique palace of the Pincii family on the Pincian, later imperial property; Belisarius made it his headquarters during the Gothic siege of 537-538, and Pope Silverius was deposed there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 135
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Domus Pinciana
b:domus_pinciana.note: Near the Porta Pinciana; exact site unknown.

b:sepulcrum_claudiorum.summary: A late Republican tomb near that of Bibulus at the start of the Via Flaminia, perhaps the burial place 'below the Capitol' granted to the patrician Claudii.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 352
b:sepulcrum_claudiorum.note: Identification uncertain; small tomb remains beside the Bibulus tomb.

b:ciconiae_nixae.summary: A landing place on the Campus bank named after a monument of 'resting storks', where wine brought downriver was taxed; the Regionary Catalogues list it in Regio IX.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 87
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Ciconiae
b:ciconiae_nixae.note: Placed on the bank west of the Mausoleum of Augustus (later Ripetta port); conjectural.

b:stabula_iv_factionum.summary: The headquarters and stables of the four chariot factions (Greens, Blues, Whites, Reds), listed in Regio IX of the Regionary Catalogues; the Greens' stable was near San Lorenzo in Damaso.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 366
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Stabula IIII factionum
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
b:stabula_iv_factionum.note: Placed between Campo de' Fiori and Palazzo Farnese; extent conjectural.

b:adrastus_house.summary: The procurator of the column, the freedman Adrastus, received timber from the scaffolding to build a house next to it, as his inscription records.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 95
b:adrastus_house.note: Beside the column; exact place unknown.

b:ara_pietatis_augustae.summary: An altar to Augustan Piety vowed in AD 22 and dedicated by Claudius in 43; reliefs in the Villa Medici, once attributed to it, came from the Via Lata area.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 290
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Pietas Augusta, ara
b:ara_pietatis_augustae.note: Location unknown; the Via Lata attribution of the reliefs is disputed. Placed in the Campus Agrippae.

b:insula_sub_san_lorenzo_lucina.summary: A 2nd-century apartment building, later partly used as a Christian meeting place (the titulus Lucinae), found under the church; its walls built over the Augustan meridian level.
scholarship: Brandt, in Roma: archeologia nel centro (1985)
Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae II (1962)
b:insula_sub_san_lorenzo_lucina.note: Footprint taken as that of the later church.

b:pantheon_forecourt_arch.summary: An arch closing the porticoed approach to the Pantheon; a monument called the Arcus Pietatis by medieval guides stood in this area until the 15th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 26
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Pietatis

b:temple_of_fons.summary: A shrine of Fons, god of springs, built by C. Papirius Maso from the spoils of Corsica in 231 BC, outside the Porta Fontinalis; the Fontinalia on 13 October was celebrated here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 151
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Fons, delubrum
b:temple_of_fons.note: Placed outside the Porta Fontinalis at the north foot of the Capitol; position and form conjectural.

b:iseum_obelisk_4.summary: Another of the small Egyptian obelisks attributed to the Iseum Campense and removed in modern times (now in Florence and Urbino).
scholarship: Lembke, Das Iseum Campense in Rom (1994)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 274
b:iseum_obelisk_4.note: Attribution to the Iseum and placement conjectural.

b:iseum_obelisk_5.summary: Another of the small Egyptian obelisks attributed to the Iseum Campense and removed in modern times (now in Florence and Urbino).
scholarship: Lembke, Das Iseum Campense in Rom (1994)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 274
b:iseum_obelisk_5.note: Attribution to the Iseum and placement conjectural.

b:bibliotheca_octaviae_v1.summary: The Greek and Latin libraries founded by Octavia in memory of Marcellus and run by the grammarian C. Melissus; the fire of 80 destroyed their books.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317-318
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
b:bibliotheca_octaviae_v1.note: Placed behind the temples at the back of the porticus; arrangement conjectural.

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 318

b:curia_octaviae.summary: A meeting hall in the Porticus Octaviae where the Senate sometimes sat, adorned with a Cupid by Praxiteles (or Phidias).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 318
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Curia Octaviae

b:statues_norbanus_flaccus.summary: Statues of the deified Augustus and his house set up in the Circus Flaminius by C. Norbanus Flaccus, beside which the Senate placed the arch of Germanicus in AD 19.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 26

b:granicus_group.summary: Lysippus' bronze group of the 25 Companions of Alexander who fell at the Granicus, with Alexander himself, taken from Dion in Macedonia by Metellus and set up in front of the temples of his porticus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317
b:granicus_group.note: In front of the two temples; long base ~30 m assumed. Fate after the fires unknown.

b:apoxyomenos_agrippa.summary: Agrippa placed Lysippus' bronze athlete scraping himself in front of his baths; Tiberius moved it to his bedroom until a theatre crowd shouted for its return.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 386

b:iuppiter_pompeianus.summary: A colossal bronze Jupiter dedicated by Claudius in the Campus Martius, called 'Pompeianus' from its nearness to Pompey's theatre.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 227
b:iuppiter_pompeianus.note: Near the Theatre of Pompey; exact spot and size conjectural.

b:lateran_basilica_v1.summary: The first great church of Rome and cathedral of its bishop, built by Constantine from late 312 on the levelled barracks of the Equites Singulares, Maxentius' horse guard: a five-aisled timber-roofed basilica about 98 x 56 m with a nave 19 m wide flanked by columns of red granite and verde antico, short projecting wings at the west end and an apse to the west. Occidented: the facade faced east. Endowed with a gold and silver fastigium and seven silver altars.

phases.t: council against the Donatists in the Lateran (Domus Faustae)
probable completion and dedication to the Saviour

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) V (1977)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
b:lateran_basilica_v1.note: Centre placed 24 m east of the OSM centroid of the present basilica (the 1880s apse extension and the medieval transept lengthen it westward); axis 77.5 deg, facade ENE as today (OSM main entrance on the east front). The Council of 313 met in the adjacent Domus Faustae.

b:lateran_basilica_v2.summary: Stripped by Gaiseric's Vandals in 455, restored by Leo I and Hilarus; repaired again after damage in the Gothic war. The fabric remained Constantine's until the earthquake of 896.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) V (1977)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:lateran_basilica_v2.note: Same structure, restored furnishings; version split at the 455 sack.

b:lateran_baptistery_v1.summary: Constantine's baptistery beside the cathedral, a round or octagonal room around a sunken font where, the Liber Pontificalis says, gold and silver stags poured water; built over a bath of the Lateran villa.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) V (1977)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:lateran_baptistery_v1.note: Excavations show a first round(ed) building on the same site under the Sixtine octagon.

b:lateran_baptistery_v2.summary: Sixtus III (432-440) rebuilt it as the octagon still standing: eight porphyry columns in two orders around the font, an ambulatory, an octagonal clerestory drum, and a porch with two porphyry columns; the lintel carries his verses on rebirth through baptism. The model for baptisteries throughout the West. Hilarus added three oratories around it (461-468).

phases.t: completed by Sixtus III
oratories of Hilarus added

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) V (1977)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
Pelliccioni, Le nuove scoperte sulle origini del Battistero Lateranense (1973)
b:lateran_baptistery_v2.note: Centre from OSM. The entrance porch (later the narthex of SS. Rufina e Seconda) lies on the south side; rot 170 assumed. Octagon ~20 m across, drum ~20 m high.

b:lateran_oratory_1_v1.summary: Pope Hilarus (461-468) added three chapels to the baptistery in thanks for his escape from the 'Robber Council' of Ephesus (449): two to the two Johns, opening off the octagon, and a cross-shaped oratory of the Holy Cross behind it.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:lateran_oratory_1_v1.note: Positions relative to the baptistery approximate.

b:lateran_oratory_2_v1.summary: Pope Hilarus (461-468) added three chapels to the baptistery in thanks for his escape from the 'Robber Council' of Ephesus (449): two to the two Johns, opening off the octagon, and a cross-shaped oratory of the Holy Cross behind it.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:lateran_oratory_2_v1.note: Positions relative to the baptistery approximate.

b:lateran_oratory_3_v1.summary: Pope Hilarus (461-468) added three chapels to the baptistery in thanks for his escape from the 'Robber Council' of Ephesus (449): two to the two Johns, opening off the octagon, and a cross-shaped oratory of the Holy Cross behind it. The cross-shaped oratory was demolished in 1588.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:lateran_oratory_3_v1.note: Positions relative to the baptistery approximate.

b:san_venanzio_lateran_v1.summary: Pope John IV (640-642), a Dalmatian, built a chapel against the baptistery for the relics of martyrs of Salona brought from his homeland, with an apse mosaic finished under Theodore I.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_venanzio_lateran_v1.note: Begun 640; just inside the model's end date.

b:lateran_episcopium_v1.summary: The palace of the Laterani, later of the empress Fausta, handed to Bishop Miltiades in 313, became the residence and administration of the bishops of Rome on the north side of the cathedral.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Lauer, Le palais de Latran (1911)
b:lateran_episcopium_v1.note: Layout unknown; a courtyard house block north of the basilica facade is modelled.

b:lateran_episcopium_v2.summary: Expanded through the fifth to seventh centuries into the papal palace (patriarchium) with halls, chapels, a library and the vestiarium; Gregory the Great governed Rome from here. Medieval and Sixtine rebuilding erased it.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Lauer (1911)

b:santa_croce_in_gerusalemme_v1.summary: In the Sessorian palace of Constantine's mother Helena a large rectangular hall, about 36.5 x 21.7 m, was turned into a church to house the relic of the True Cross: an apse was added at the east and two transverse arcades divided the space. It became one of the stational churches, 'Hierusalem'.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santa_croce_in_gerusalemme_v1.note: Present church footprint from OSM; facade faces WNW toward the Lateran (OSM main entrance at 296 deg). Hall dimensions from Krautheimer.

b:basilica_liberiana_v1.summary: Pope Liberius (352-366) is said to have built a basilica 'iuxta macellum Liviae'; later legend tied it to the August snowfall that marked the site of Santa Maria Maggiore. Some identify it with the Basilica Sicinini where the rival factions of Damasus and Ursinus fought in 366, leaving 137 dead.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
De Blaauw, Cultus et decor (1994)
b:basilica_liberiana_v1.note: Its site is uncertain and excavations under S. Maria Maggiore found no church predecessor; placed on the later church site as a hypothesis.

b:santa_maria_maggiore_v1.summary: Sixtus III's church of the Mother of God, built just after the Council of Ephesus (431): a three-aisled basilica with Ionic colonnades of 36 marble columns carrying a straight entablature, a classical revival in brick and marble. Its nave mosaics of Old Testament stories and the triumphal arch with the childhood of Christ survive; the apse was moved in the 13th century.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
b:santa_maria_maggiore_v1.note: Centre and axis from OSM (the Sistine and Pauline chapels widen the modern outline). Facade faces SE (OSM entrances at 123-139 deg).

b:santo_stefano_rotondo_v1.summary: A unique round church dedicated to St Stephen by Pope Simplicius (468-483), probably inspired by the Holy Sepulchre: a tall central cylinder 22 m across on 22 Ionic columns, an ambulatory, and an outer ring cut into four arms forming a Greek cross with four lower courtyards between, 66 m across overall. Pope John I and Felix IV added marble revetments; the outer ring was demolished in the 12th century.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
Brandenburg and Pal, Santo Stefano Rotondo in Roma (2000)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santo_stefano_rotondo_v1.note: Centre from OSM. The main entrance today is on the NE (OSM main entrance at 40 deg); the original had entrances on several axes.

b:san_clemente_v1.summary: The titulus Clementis, built in the late fourth century over a Roman warehouse-like building and a house with a Mithraeum; Jerome mentions it in 392 and councils met in it in 417. A three-aisled basilica with a narthex and atrium to the east, buried in the 12th century under the present church.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Guidobaldi, San Clemente: gli edifici romani, la basilica paleocristiana (1992)
b:san_clemente_v1.note: Atrium and entrance to the east as today (OSM entrance 107 deg); centre 14 m west of the OSM centroid, which includes the atrium. Abandoned 1084-1100.

b:santi_giovanni_e_paolo_v1.summary: The senator Pammachius, Jerome's friend, built a basilica on the Clivus Scauri over Roman houses in which a domestic shrine of martyrs (later identified as John and Paul) had been venerated; its arcaded facade on the street partly survives behind the medieval portico.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santi_giovanni_e_paolo_v1.note: OSM footprint and main entrance (100 deg): facade faces east onto the piazza.

b:san_pietro_in_vincoli_v1.summary: An earlier church of the Apostles built in the later fourth century over Roman houses on the Oppian; its apse was found under the present one.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)

b:san_pietro_in_vincoli_v2.summary: Rebuilt by Sixtus III with the help of the empress Licinia Eudoxia, who gave the chains of Peter brought from Jerusalem: a broad three-aisled basilica on twenty fluted Doric columns of Greek marble, with an apse to the east and its facade facing west over the Esquiline slope.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_pietro_in_vincoli_v2.note: OSM footprint; main entrance faces WSW (OSM 248 deg).

b:santa_pudenziana_v1.summary: A second-century bath hall on the Vicus Patricius converted into a church under Pope Siricius (384-399); its apse mosaic of Christ enthroned among the apostles before the heavenly Jerusalem (c. 410) is the oldest surviving apse mosaic in Rome.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santa_pudenziana_v1.note: Conversion of a bath hall, assigned here by the brief. OSM main entrance at 117 deg: facade faces SE to Via Urbana (the Vicus Patricius).

b:santa_sabina_v1.summary: Built by the Illyrian priest Peter under Pope Celestine I (422-432) on the Aventine: the best preserved early Christian basilica in Rome, 53 x 25 m, with 24 fluted Corinthian columns of Proconnesian marble (a matched set from one second-century building), wide arcades, large clerestory windows with selenite grilles, opus sectile in the spandrels, the dedicatory mosaic inscription over the door and carved cypress doors with one of the earliest Crucifixion scenes.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
b:santa_sabina_v1.note: OSM footprint (62.5 x 35.9 incl. narthex and side chapels), axis 45 deg. The narthex and original front are at the SW end next to the convent; apse NE. rot 225.

b:santa_prisca_v1.summary: Titular church built around 400 over the house with the Mithraeum, which was smashed and filled in; legend made Prisca a convert of Peter. Rebuilt after the Norman sack of 1084 and in the 17th century, keeping the ancient columns.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Vermaseren and van Essen (1965)
b:santa_prisca_v1.note: OSM footprint 34.6 x 19.8, axis 70.5; facade faces WSW toward Piazza S. Prisca (assumed, no OSM entrance).

b:san_vitale_v1.summary: Founded by the matron Vestina and dedicated by Innocent I (401-417) to the Milanese martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, later to Vitalis: a three-aisled basilica fronted by a five-arched portico whose columns survive, in the valley between Quirinal and Viminal (now below Via Nazionale).
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_vitale_v1.note: OSM footprint; facade with portico faces NW toward Via Nazionale.

b:santa_maria_in_trastevere_v1.summary: Pope Julius I (337-352) built a basilica 'iuxta Callistum' in Trastevere, on a site the community associated with Pope Callistus (died 222) and with the miraculous fountain of oil of 38 BC. The 4th-century church lies under Innocent II's rebuilding of 1140, which probably kept its plan.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santa_maria_in_trastevere_v1.note: OSM footprint (74 x 39 includes later chapels); facade faces east onto the piazza. Dimensions of the first church approximate.

b:santa_cecilia_v1.summary: Titular church of the fifth century built over Roman houses and a tannery, venerated as the house of the martyr Cecilia; rebuilt by Paschal I in 817-824, whose basilica probably followed the earlier plan.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santa_cecilia_v1.note: OSM footprint; main entrance on the ESE (121 deg) through the forecourt.

b:domus_santa_cecilia_v1.summary: Excavations under the church found a Republican house rebuilt in the second century, an insula and a tannery with vats (coriaria), part of the industrial fabric of Trastevere.
scholarship: Parmegiani and Pronti, S. Cecilia in Trastevere: nuovi scavi e ricerche (2004)

b:san_crisogono_v1.summary: One of the oldest tituli: an early fourth-century hall church about 35 x 17 m, later given an apse and an annular crypt, excavated under the 12th-century basilica beside the Via Aurelia (Viale Trastevere).
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_crisogono_v1.note: Placed at the OSM footprint of the present church; the old hall is slightly offset beneath it. Facade east to Viale Trastevere.

b:san_marco_v1.summary: Founded by Pope Mark in 336 near the Pallacinae, at the foot of the Capitol; excavations under the present church found its apse and floors.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_marco_v1.note: OSM footprint of the present church (inside Palazzo Venezia); facade toward the SSE (OSM door at 155 deg). The first church was slightly smaller.

b:san_marco_v2.summary: A second, raised church replaced Mark's around 500, before the Carolingian rebuilding of 833.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
b:san_marco_v2.note: Date of the second phase approximate.

b:san_lorenzo_in_damaso_v1.summary: Pope Damasus (366-384) built a basilica to St Lawrence beside his family house near the Theatre of Pompey, with an archive; its remains, a three-aisled basilica with a portico, were found in 1988-1993 under the courtyard of the Palazzo della Cancelleria.
scholarship: Frommel and Pentiricci, L'antica basilica di San Lorenzo in Damaso (2009)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_lorenzo_in_damaso_v1.note: Placed under the Cancelleria courtyard (OSM palace centroid); orientation from the excavated plan roughly parallel to the palace, entrance assumed ESE.

b:santi_quattro_coronati_v1.summary: A titular church of the late fourth or early fifth century on the Caelian, recorded among the presbyters at the synod of 499 as titulus Aemilianae.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
b:santi_quattro_coronati_v1.note: First church's form unknown; placed on the later site.

b:santi_quattro_coronati_v2.summary: Pope Honorius I (625-638) built a large basilica for the four crowned martyrs, broader than the 12th-century church that later occupied only its nave; its wide apse survives. The church faces west, with the apse at the east end of the walled complex.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santi_quattro_coronati_v2.note: OSM footprint of the present church (36 x 18) is smaller than the Honorian basilica, which extended over the present inner courtyard; centre shifted 0 m, dimensions from Krautheimer. Facade bearing 275 (west).

b:san_lorenzo_basilica_maior_v1.summary: Constantine built a funerary basilica next to the catacomb of St Lawrence on the Via Tiburtina: an ambulatory (circus-shaped) basilica about 98.6 x 35.5 m whose floor was packed with graves, found in the 1950s under the Campo Verano south of the present church.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_lorenzo_basilica_maior_v1.note: Placed ~70 m SSE of the present church under the Verano; orientation parallel, entrance at the straight east end assumed; the apse ambulatory at the west.

b:san_lorenzo_fuori_le_mura_v1.summary: Pelagius II (579-590) cut away the hillside to build a basilica directly over Lawrence's tomb, with galleries over the aisles reached from the higher ground; its triumphal arch mosaic shows the pope offering the church. In the 1220s Honorius III added a nave to the west, turning this church into the raised choir.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_lorenzo_fuori_le_mura_v1.note: Occupies the eastern part of the present church (OSM); original entrance at the east end (rot 76), apse west.

b:sant_agnese_basilica_constantiniana_v1.summary: Constantina, daughter of Constantine, built a vast ambulatory basilica beside the catacomb of St Agnes on the Via Nomentana, about 98 x 40 m, its floor and surroundings packed with graves; her own mausoleum adjoined its flank. Ruined by the seventh century; the outer walls still stand.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:sant_agnese_basilica_constantiniana_v1.note: Centre and axis from the OSM outline of the ruined basilica (78 x 41 visible); entrance at the SE straight end toward the Via Nomentana.

b:sant_agnese_fuori_le_mura_v1.summary: Pope Honorius I (625-638) built a new basilica sunk into the hill directly over Agnes' tomb, with galleries opening at the level of the road and an apse mosaic of Agnes between two popes, still intact.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:sant_agnese_fuori_le_mura_v1.note: OSM footprint; apse NW, entrance SE as assumed for the older basilica.

b:santa_costanza_v1.summary: Rotunda for Constantina (died 354) and her sister Helena, wife of Julian: a domed central space on twelve pairs of granite columns, a barrel-vaulted ambulatory with vine-harvest mosaics, an outer colonnade and a narthex; her porphyry sarcophagus is in the Vatican. Later a baptistery and a church.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Stanley, 'New discoveries at Santa Costanza', DOP 48 (1994)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santa_costanza_v1.note: Centre from OSM (30 x 29 m). Narthex side assumed WNW; the original outer colonnade (diameter ~40 m) is gone.

b:memoria_apostolorum_v1.summary: From 258 Christians met on a terrace 'ad catacumbas' on the Via Appia for funerary banquets in honour of Peter and Paul, scratching hundreds of invocations on the walls of a covered loggia (triclia).

sources.w: 29 June: Petri in Catacumbas et Pauli Ostense, Tusco et Basso cons. (258)

scholarship: Styger, Die romischen Katakomben (1933)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:memoria_apostolorum_v1.note: Under the nave of S. Sebastiano.

b:basilica_apostolorum_v1.summary: An ambulatory basilica of the Constantinian period built over the memoria of the apostles on the Via Appia, about 75 x 30 m, surrounded by mausolea; from the fifth century centred on the tomb of the martyr Sebastian. The present church occupies its nave.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:basilica_apostolorum_v1.note: OSM centre and axis; entrance NE toward the Via Appia (OSM main door at 53 deg), ambulatory apse SW. Inside the model bbox (the brief suggested skipping it).

b:basilica_of_marcus_v1.summary: Funerary ambulatory basilica built by Pope Mark in 336 on the Via Ardeatina and found in 1991-1993 near the catacomb of Callixtus; Mark himself was buried in it.
scholarship: Fiocchi Nicolai, studies of the circiform basilica of the Via Ardeatina (1990s)
b:basilica_of_marcus_v1.note: OSM building centroid (excavated remains); long axis 17 deg; entrance direction assumed NNE.

b:basilica_nereo_achilleo_domitilla_v1.summary: A semi-subterranean basilica cut into the catacomb of Domitilla over the graves of the martyrs Nereus and Achilleus and of Petronilla, built under Pope Siricius (384-399).
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:basilica_nereo_achilleo_domitilla_v1.note: Centre from the OSM catacomb outline; partly underground.

b:san_valentino_v1.summary: Pope Julius I built a basilica at the second milestone of the Via Flaminia over the grave of the martyr Valentine; Honorius I rebuilt it in the seventh century. Pilgrims coming from the north passed it before the Milvian bridge.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_valentino_v1.note: Remains seen in 1888 near the catacomb (Via Flaminia/Viale Pilsudski); coordinates approximate.

b:santo_stefano_via_latina_v1.summary: Funded by the noble widow Demetrias of the Anicii and completed by Leo I, a basilica with a baptistery at the third milestone of the Via Latina; ruins survive among the tombs of the Via Latina park.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santo_stefano_via_latina_v1.note: Coordinates approximate within the Parco delle Tombe di Via Latina.

b:san_pancrazio_v1.summary: Pope Symmachus (498-514) built a basilica over the grave of the boy martyr Pancras on the Via Aurelia, outside the Porta Aurelia.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)

b:san_pancrazio_v2.summary: Honorius I rebuilt the church larger, moving the altar directly over the tomb and adding a semicircular crypt, as recorded on his dedicatory inscription.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_pancrazio_v2.note: OSM footprint 59 x 30, axis 127; facade SE.

b:sant_agata_dei_goti_v1.summary: The church of the Arian Goths, founded by the patrician Ricimer around 460-470, with an apse mosaic of Christ and the apostles bearing his dedication (lost 1589); reconsecrated to Catholic use by Gregory the Great in 592-593.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:sant_agata_dei_goti_v1.note: OSM footprint; facade WSW assumed (entrance from Via Mazzarino through a forecourt).

b:santa_balbina_v1.summary: A large single-naved hall on the Little Aventine, probably built inside a Roman mansion (perhaps the Domus Cilonis) and consecrated by Gregory the Great; listed as titulus by 595.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 595

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
b:santa_balbina_v1.note: OSM footprint; facade ENE onto the piazza.

b:santa_bibiana_v1.summary: Built by Pope Simplicius (468-483) on the Esquiline, at the palace of the Licinii, for the martyr Bibiana.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
b:santa_bibiana_v1.note: OSM footprint is the 1624 Bernini rebuilding on the same site; facade faces NNE toward Via Giolitti.

b:san_giorgio_in_velabro_v1.summary: A diaconia (welfare station) beside the Arcus Argentariorum in the Velabrum, probably of the seventh century, dedicated to St George by Leo II (682) and rebuilt in the ninth century.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
b:san_giorgio_in_velabro_v1.note: Date before 641 uncertain. OSM footprint; facade assumed to face south with the arch at its west corner.

b:santi_apostoli_v1.summary: Begun by Pelagius I and finished by John III (560-574) with Narses' support after the Gothic war, for relics of the apostles Philip and James: a broad basilica with a trefoil (triconch) sanctuary on the Byzantine model.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santi_apostoli_v1.note: OSM footprint; facade faces west onto Piazza SS. Apostoli.

b:sant_andrea_catabarbara_v1.summary: The Gothic general Flavius Valila left the hall of the Basilica of Junius Bassus to the church; Pope Simplicius dedicated it to St Andrew around 470, adding a Christian apse mosaic to the fourth-century opus sectile walls.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:sant_andrea_catabarbara_v1.note: Church installed c. 470 in the hall of the Basilica of Junius Bassus (cos. 331); placed on the basilica's Pleiades position so the two records chain on one site.

b:santa_susanna_v1.summary: A titular church on the Quirinal built into a Roman house, attested as titulus Gaii in 499, rebuilt by Leo III in 795.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
b:santa_susanna_v1.note: OSM footprint is mixed with the convent; facade assumed NW onto Via XX Settembre.

b:san_sisto_vecchio_v1.summary: Titular church on the Via Appia near the Baths of Caracalla, attested as titulus Tigridae in 499.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
b:san_sisto_vecchio_v1.note: OSM footprint; orientation of the facade uncertain.

b:santi_nereo_e_achilleo_v1.summary: The titulus Fasciolae on the Via Appia, named after the bandage Peter lost here in legend, attested by an epitaph of 377; rebuilt by Leo III around 800.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
b:santi_nereo_e_achilleo_v1.note: OSM footprint; facade NE toward the Via Appia (Viale delle Terme di Caracalla).

b:sant_eusebio_v1.summary: Titular church on the Esquiline named after a priest martyred under Constantius II, attested in 474.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
b:sant_eusebio_v1.note: OSM footprint; orientation of facade uncertain.

b:san_saba_v1.summary: Monks from the monastery of St Sabas near Jerusalem, fleeing the Persian and Arab invasions, settled on the Little Aventine in the house traditionally of St Silvia, building an oratory now under the left aisle of the church.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
b:san_saba_v1.note: Probably just after 641; included at the end of the range as conjectural.

b:san_giovanni_a_porta_latina_v1.summary: A small basilica near the Porta Latina built around 500 (Gelasius I is credited) and rebuilt in 720; its columns and apse with selenite windows are original.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) I (1937)
b:san_giovanni_a_porta_latina_v1.note: OSM footprint; facade with portico assumed WNW.

b:san_martino_ai_monti_v1.summary: A third-century Roman hall on the Esquiline, used as the meeting place of the titulus Equitii under Pope Silvester (314-335); preserved beneath the church.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
b:san_martino_ai_monti_v1.note: Conversion of an existing building; below the present church.

b:san_martino_ai_monti_v2.summary: Pope Symmachus (498-514) built a basilica dedicated to St Martin beside the old titulus; rebuilt in the ninth century.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
b:san_martino_ai_monti_v2.note: OSM footprint; facade SE (OSM main entrance 136 deg).

b:san_lorenzo_in_lucina_v1.summary: A meeting place of the community in a Roman building on the Via Lata near the Horologium of Augustus; Damasus was elected here in 366.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)

b:san_lorenzo_in_lucina_v2.summary: Sixtus III built a basilica to St Lawrence on the site; it has a baptistery recently excavated. Rebuilt in 1112-1130 on its plan.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:san_lorenzo_in_lucina_v2.note: OSM footprint; facade faces N to the piazza (OSM door at 345 deg).

b:san_marcello_v1.summary: Titular church on the Via Lata, attested in 418 when Boniface I was elected in it; remains of the early church and its baptistery were found beneath the present one.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
b:san_marcello_v1.note: OSM footprint. The present church (16th century) faces east onto Via del Corso; the early basilica was oriented the other way, so its facade is set facing west (rot 254). The early church's orientation is debated.

b:santi_marcellino_e_pietro_v1.summary: Titular church of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter inside the walls on the road to their cemetery basilica on the Via Labicana, known from the fifth century and rebuilt by Gregory III.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) II (1962)
b:santi_marcellino_e_pietro_v1.note: OSM footprint of the 1751 church; early form unknown.

b:mausoleum_of_probus_v1.summary: Sextus Petronius Probus (died c. 390), four times praetorian prefect and head of the Anicii, was buried in a small apsed basilica against the apse of St Peter's, with his sarcophagus now in the Vatican grottoes.
scholarship: Johnson, The Roman Imperial Mausoleum in Late Antiquity (2009)
Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) V (1977)
b:mausoleum_of_probus_v1.note: Behind the apse of Old St Peter's, facing west.

b:san_matteo_in_merulana_v1.summary: Titular church of St Matthew on the Via Merulana, attested at the synod of 499; demolished in 1810.

sources.a: Acts of the Roman synod of 499

scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) III (1967)
b:san_matteo_in_merulana_v1.note: Site on Via Merulana between S. Maria Maggiore and the Lateran approximate; date before 499 assumed.

b:santa_felicita_salaria_v1.summary: Funerary basilica over the grave of the martyr Felicitas in the cemetery of Maximus on the Via Salaria Nova, where Boniface I took refuge in 419 and was later buried.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:santa_felicita_salaria_v1.note: Coordinates approximate (catacomb of Maximus near Via Simeto).

b:sant_ippolito_tiburtina_v1.summary: Semi-subterranean basilica built in the catacomb of Hippolytus on the Via Tiburtina near San Lorenzo, described by Prudentius around 400.
scholarship: Brandenburg, Ancient Churches of Rome from the Fourth to the Seventh Century (2005)
b:sant_ippolito_tiburtina_v1.note: Coordinates approximate (Viale Regina Margherita / Via dei Canneti).

b:santo_stefano_maggiore_vatican_v1.summary: A small basilica of St Stephen behind the apse of St Peter's, traditionally founded by Leo I (440-461) and serving a monastery of the basilica; the present Santo Stefano degli Abissini preserves its site.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Corpus Basilicarum Christianarum Romae (1937-1977) IV (1970)
b:santo_stefano_maggiore_vatican_v1.note: Position from Santo Stefano degli Abissini behind the apse of St Peter's, approximate.

b:tomb_of_annia_regilla_v1.summary: A temple-shaped tomb of finely carved red and yellow brick in the valley of the Almo, traditionally the tomb that Herodes Atticus built for his wife Annia Regilla (died c. 160) on their estate, the Triopion; long misnamed the temple of the god Rediculus.
scholarship: Richardson (1992)
b:tomb_of_annia_regilla_v1.note: OSM footprint 9.2 x 8.7; orientation of the facade assumed.

b:temple_of_ceres_and_faustina_triopion_.summary: Brick prostyle temple on the hill of the Caffarella built by Herodes Atticus in his Triopion estate, probably for Ceres and the deified Faustina the Elder; converted into the church of Sant'Urbano in the Middle Ages, which preserved it.
scholarship: Richardson (1992)
b:temple_of_ceres_and_faustina_triopion_.note: Position from the standing church of Sant'Urbano alla Caffarella (OSM way 23956788).

b:nymphaeum_of_egeria_v1.summary: A vaulted grotto nymphaeum with a reclining river god, part of Herodes Atticus' Triopion, built over the springs of the Almo valley; Renaissance antiquarians identified it with the grove of Egeria.
scholarship: Richardson (1992)
b:nymphaeum_of_egeria_v1.note: Position from the standing nymphaeum in the Valle della Caffarella (OSM node 259671299).

b:circus_maximus_v1.summary: The long valley of the Murcia between Palatine and Aventine, used for races since the regal period. Tarquinius Priscus is said to have marked out the course and let senators and knights build wooden stands (fori) on posts 12 feet high on the slopes. The brook ran down the middle, the turning points were wooden posts, and there were no permanent starting gates.

phases.t: Ludi Romani held in the valley with temporary wooden stands

scholarship: Humphrey, Roman Circuses: Arenas for Chariot Racing (1986)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
LTUR I (1993) s.v. Circus Maximus
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007)
b:circus_maximus_v1.note: Dimensions are the natural valley floor, not a built structure; the stream channel stood in for the later spina. Axis and centre from the outline of the Circo Massimo archaeological area (OSM relation 11384819): long axis bearing 126/306 deg; rot 306 = from the curved ESE end toward the WNW carceres. Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v2.summary: In 329 BC the first starting gates (carceres) were built, of wood and painted, at the western (Forum Boarium) end. Stands were still largely private timber scaffolding on the slopes.

phases.t: carceres erected (Livy 8.20.1)

Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v3.summary: In 196 BC L. Stertinius, back from Spain, set up an arch carrying gilded statues in the Circus Maximus out of his spoils, the first monumental ornament of the course.

phases.t: Fornix of L. Stertinius erected in the circus (see fornix_stertinii_circus record)

Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v4.summary: The censors Q. Fulvius Flaccus and A. Postumius Albinus rebuilt the carceres, set up the metae and the seven wooden eggs (ova) used to count the laps. A low central barrier of separate monuments began to take shape along the old stream line.

phases.t: carceres, metae and lap-counting eggs (Livy 41.27.6)
elephant hunt at Pompey's games breaks the iron railings, prompting Caesar's euripus

b:circus_maximus_v5.summary: Julius Caesar enlarged the circus to roughly its final size, about 3.5 stades long, cut a water channel (euripus) 10 feet wide and deep around the arena to protect spectators, and gave it a lower tier of masonry seating with timber stands above. Agrippa added the bronze dolphins as a second lap counter in 33 BC.

phases.t: rebuilt and lengthened for Caesar's triumphal games
Agrippa adds dolphin lap counters (Dio 49.43.2)

b:circus_maximus_v6.summary: A fire in 31 BC burned much of the circus. Augustus restored it and built the pulvinar, the imperial box on the Palatine side opposite the finish line, from which the gods' images and the emperor watched the races.

phases.t: fire destroys part of the circus (Dio 50.10.3)
pulvinar built by Augustus (RG 19)

b:circus_maximus_v7.summary: In 10 BC Augustus set up on the spina the obelisk of Ramesses II (and Seti I) brought from Heliopolis, 23.3 m tall, dedicated to the Sun after the conquest of Egypt. Dionysius describes the circus of this date: three and a half stades long, four plethra wide, three storeys of seating, the lowest of stone, the upper of wood, holding 150,000.

phases.t: obelisk (now in Piazza del Popolo) erected on the spina (CIL VI 701)
fire on the Aventine side of the circus (Tac. Ann. 6.45)

b:circus_maximus_v8.summary: Tiberius paid for the damage of the fire of 36. Claudius replaced the tufa carceres with marble and the wooden metae with gilded bronze ones and reserved seats for senators. The Great Fire of July 64 broke out in the shops built against the circus on the Palatine side.

phases.t: Claudius: marble carceres, gilded metae, senatorial seats (Suet. Claud. 21.3)
Great Fire starts in the tabernae of the circus (Tac. Ann. 15.38)

Obelisk offsets are metres from the spina centre, positive toward the carceres (along rot).

b:circus_maximus_v9.summary: Rebuilt quickly after 64: Nero's triumph of 67-68 passed through it. In 81 the Senate set a triple arch to Titus across the entrance in the curved end. Damaged again by fire under Domitian, who began a full rebuilding.

phases.t: Arch of Titus built at the curved end (CIL VI 944)
Domitian begins rebuilding after a fire

b:circus_maximus_v10.summary: Trajan completed the rebuilding in masonry around AD 103: an arcaded three-storey facade with shops, concrete vaults carrying the cavea, some 621 x 118 m overall with an arena about 580 x 79 m, seating at least 150,000 (Pliny claims 250,000, the Regionary Catalogues 385,000 places). The spina carried the obelisk, shrines, the egg and dolphin counters and the gilded metae. Under Antoninus Pius a collapse killed 1,112 people; another collapse under Diocletian killed some 13,000.

phases.t: rebuilding finished by Trajan (Pliny Pan. 51; CIL VI 955)
partial collapse of the stands under Antoninus Pius (SHA Ant. 9.1)
collapse during Diocletian's reign (Chron. 354)

b:circus_maximus_v11.summary: In 357 Constantius II, on his only visit to Rome, raised on the spina the obelisk of Thutmose III from Karnak, 32.2 m, the tallest in the city, which Constantine had meant for Constantinople. The circus kept running through the fifth century and under Theodoric; the last races recorded were given by the Gothic king Totila in 549.

phases.t: second obelisk raised (Amm. Marc. 17.4.12-17)
last chariot races in Rome, under Totila (Procopius, Goth. 3.37.4)

b:circus_maximus_v12.summary: After 549 the circus fell out of use. The stands were quarried and the valley slowly silted up; the obelisks fell and were buried, to be dug up in 1587.
