phases.t: Porticus from the gate to the Ara Martis in the Campus (Livy 35.10.12).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Fontinalis
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_fontinalis.note: On the saddle between the Arx and the Quirinal, in front of the Museo del Risorgimento: the Clivus Argentarius led up to it and the Via Lata / Flaminia began outside, past the tomb of Bibulus. In 193 BC a porticus was built from the gate to the altar of Mars (Livy 35.10.12). Destroyed with the saddle for Trajan's Forum (end date assumed). Perhaps the Porta Ratumena of the earlier wall. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Ratumena
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 309
g:porta_ratumena.note: Gate of the Arx toward the Campus Martius, named from the Veientine charioteer Ratumenna (Plutarch, Poplicola 13; Pliny NH 8.161). Possibly the predecessor of the Porta Fontinalis. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 302
g:porta_catularia.note: Known from Festus (39 L) as a gate near the Capitol where red dogs were sacrificed; placed at the foot of the Capitol near the Carmentalis. Site wholly uncertain.

phases.t: Built with the wall: single arch between two towers.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine facing and raised towers.
Witiges tries the gate; Belisarius holds it (Procopius 5.23.3).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Flaminia
g:porta_flaminia.note: Northern gate on the Via Flaminia at the foot of the Pincian, beside the river wall. Honorian gate with a single travertine arch between two semicircular towers; the present Porta del Popolo facade is of 1562-65 and its towers of Sixtus IV (1475). Faces north.

phases.t: Postern.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): upgraded to a gate with two semicircular towers.
Belisarius holds the Pinciana and Salaria sector.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Pinciana
Cozza, BullCom 1987
g:porta_pinciana.note: Gate on the Via Salaria Vetus (Via Pinciana), originally a postern; given travertine facing and two semicircular towers by Honorius. Belisarius' command post during the siege (Procopius 5.19.14); the medieval legend of Belisarius begging here.

phases.t: Built over tombs of the Via Salaria.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): raised, travertine facing.
24 August 410: Alaric enters here.
Main Gothic assault on the north side (Procopius 5.22.1).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Salaria
g:porta_salaria.note: Gate of the Via Salaria Nova, demolished in 1871 after damage in the 1870 assault and rebuilt by Vespignani (removed 1921). Single arch between semicircular towers; tombs (Q. Sulpicius Maximus) found in the towers.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine facing and semicircular towers.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Nomentana
g:porta_nomentana.note: Gate of the Via Nomentana, 75 m east of Michelangelo's Porta Pia (1561-65), which replaced it; walled up by Pius IV in 1564. The right tower survives; the left was demolished in 1827. Single arch between semicircular towers (Honorian travertine).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:postern_montebello.note: One of the posterns near the Porta Nomentana and the camp's NW corner closed under Honorius (it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane). Position approximate.

phases.t: Camp gate.
Blocked, open no longer.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 78-79
g:castra_porta_principalis_sinistra.note: Gate of the praetorian camp in the north side, walled up when Aurelian absorbed the camp; the blocked arch is still visible. OSM labels it Porta Praetoriana. From 275 these walls form part of the aurelian_wall line.

phases.t: Camp gate.
Blocked.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 78-79
g:castra_porta_principalis_dextra.note: East gate of the camp (Porta Principalis Dextera in OSM), blocked when the camp entered the Aurelian circuit. From 275 these walls form part of the aurelian_wall line.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Possibly closed in the Honorian works.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Vicus Collis Viminalis
g:porta_chiusa.note: Gate on Viale Pretoriano south of the camp, closed already in antiquity (name medieval); single arch flanked by a square tower. Probably the end of the Vicus Collis Viminalis road.

phases.t: Augustan aqueduct arch over the road.
Aqueduct arch becomes the gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): outer gate court and facade, inscription naming Arcadius and Honorius, at the suggestion of Stilicho.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Tiburtina
g:porta_tiburtina.note: Gate of the Via Tiburtina built against the travertine arch that carried the Aquae Marcia, Tepula and Julia over the road (Augustus, 5 BC; restored by Titus and Caracalla). Honorius added an outer travertine gatehouse with a single arch and square towers and the dedication of 401-402 (CIL VI 1189). Porta S. Lorenzo in the Middle Ages.

phases.t: Claudian aqueduct crossing built.
Becomes a gate of the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): outer gate with towers over the Eurysaces tomb; inscription CIL VI 1188.
Witiges' main camp opposite; Gothic assault at the Vivarium just south (Procopius 5.22-23).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 197-199
g:porta_praenestina_labicana.note: Drawn by the building record porta_maggiore (district B), which models the aqueduct arches and the Honorian gate.

phases.t: Postern-type gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): semicircular towers added.
Belisarius enters Rome (9-10 December).
Betrayed to Totila (Procopius 7.20.14-19).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Asinaria
g:porta_asinaria.note: Gate on the Via Asinaria next to the later Porta S. Giovanni (1574). Originally a postern with a single travertine arch; Honorius added two semicircular towers and a gatehouse. Through it Belisarius entered in 536 and Totila's Goths were let in by Isaurian guards on 17 December 546.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Metrovia
Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:porta_metrovia.note: Postern at the bend of the wall below the Caelian where the Marrana stream passed under the wall; mentioned by Gregory the Great (Epist. 9.69 'porta Metrovia'). Single small arch beside a square tower.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): travertine arch, towers raised.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Latina
g:porta_latina.note: Gate of the Via Latina with a single travertine arch (keystone with chi-rho on the outer face, Honorian or later) flanked by semicircular towers; the inner face is brick. Close to the church of S. Giovanni a Porta Latina.

phases.t: Double-arched gate, semicircular towers.
Honorian rebuild: single arch, attic, square tower bases.
Greek inscription to SS Conon and George (6th-7th century).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Museo delle Mura (Porta S. Sebastiano)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Appia
g:porta_appia.note: The grandest gate, on the Via Appia. Aurelian's gate had two arches and two semicircular towers with a travertine facade; Honorius (401-402) reduced it to one arch, added a high attic with two rows of six windows and an open crenellated walkway, set the towers on square marble-faced bases, and joined them to the 'Arch of Drusus' (the arch of the Aqua Antoniniana) behind by two walls forming a courtyard. A storey was added later. Towers here estimated at about 26 m.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Ardeatina
g:porta_ardeatina.note: Minor gate on the Via Ardeatina, between the Appia and the Ostiensis; obliterated by Antonio da Sangallo's bastion (1537-42). Simple arch without towers. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

phases.t: Double outer arch.
Single outer arch, towers raised, inner double-arched court.
Opened to Totila by the Isaurians (Procopius 7.36.7).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Museo della Via Ostiense (Porta S. Paolo)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Ostiensis
g:porta_ostiensis.note: Gate of the Via Ostiensis beside the Pyramid of Cestius. Aurelian's outer facade had two arches between semicircular towers; Honorius reduced the outer face to one arch, raised the towers and added an inner court whose city face keeps two arches. Totila took Rome when Isaurian guards opened it (549/550).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:postern_pyramid.note: Postern in the stretch between the Pyramid and the Tiber, closed by Maxentius and demolished in 1888 (it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane). Position approximate. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

phases.t: Two-arched gate.
Honorian rebuilding (401-403): two arches retained, gate and towers raised.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Portuensis
g:porta_portuensis.note: Southern gate of the Trastevere salient at the start of the Via Portuensis and Via Campana, at the junction of Via Portuense and Via E. Bezzi, about 450 m south of Porta Portese (1644) which replaced it when Urban VIII demolished the Janiculum walls. Honorius kept two arches, raised gate and towers and set up an inscription like those of the Tiburtina and Praenestina (CIL VI 1190). Tower form assumed.

phases.t: Built with the wall.
Held by Paulus during the siege (Procopius 5.18.35, 5.23.12).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Aurelia
g:porta_aurelia.note: Gate on the Janiculum summit where the Via Aurelia Vetus left Trastevere, called Porta S. Pancratii from the 6th century (Procopius 5.18.35). Destroyed in the 1849 siege and rebuilt by Vespignani (1854). Tower form unknown. Facing set by hand (gate at a corner of the circuit).

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Septimiana
g:porta_septimiana.note: Northern gate of the Trastevere salient at the start of Via della Lungara; the name may recall Septimius Severus (the Horti Getae nearby). Rebuilt in 1498 by Alexander VI with Ghibelline merlons.

scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Platner-Ashby, Porta Cornelia
g:porta_aurelia_sancti_petri.note: River-wall gate at the left-bank end of the Pons Aelius, through which the road to the Vatican and the Via Cornelia passed; Procopius' 'Aurelian gate, now named after Peter' (5.19.4). Covered after 403 by the fortified Mausoleum of Hadrian across the river. Form unknown.

scholarship: it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane
Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
g:postern_tor_di_nona.note: One of the small landing-stage posterns of the Campus Martius river wall; the medieval Torre dell'Annona (Tor di Nona) stood on the wall here. Some identify a 'Porta Domitia' near it.

scholarship: it.wikipedia, Mura aureliane
g:postern_ripetta.note: Posterula in the river wall opposite the Mausoleum of Augustus, where river traffic landed (later Porto di Ripetta). Illustrative position.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Sacra Via 456-459
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 99-101
s:sacra_via_forum.note: Through the Forum from the foot of the Clivus Capitolinus (by the later Arch of Septimius Severus) along the front of the Basilica Aemilia to the Regia and the Temple of Divus Iulius, where the Velia ascent begins. Line from the excavated pavement as mapped in OpenStreetMap. The paving of city streets with basalt is first recorded for the censors of 174 BC; Sullan, Augustan and later pavements overlie each other.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Sacra Via 457-458
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 338-340
s:sacra_via_velia_republican.note: From the Regia up the Velia past the House of the Rex Sacrorum and the Fornix Fabianus (121 BC) to the summa Sacra Via by Jupiter Stator and the Porta Mugonia, then down to the valley of the later Colosseum. Augustan pavement 5 m wide, falling from 28.3 m a.s.l. east of the Arch of Titus to 12.6 m at the Temple of Divus Iulius (Platner). The pre-Neronian street curved slightly north of the later straight avenue; drawn a few metres north of the imperial line.
s:sacra_via_velia_republican.modern: under the Velia (Via Sacra path east of the Regia)

phases.t: Neronian porticoed avenue to the Domus Aurea vestibule.
Arch of Titus at the summa Sacra Via.
Realigned in front of the Temple of Venus and Roma (Hadrian).
Basilica of Maxentius replaces the north porticoes.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Sacra Via 458
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 117-119
s:sacra_via_velia_imperial.note: After the fire of 64 Nero rebuilt the ascent as a straight porticoed avenue leading to the vestibule of the Domus Aurea; after Hadrian built the Temple of Venus and Roma the street from the Regia to the Velia was an avenue about 30 m wide lined with porticoes and shops (Platner). Maxentius' basilica (308-312) swallowed the northern shops. East of the Arch of Titus it runs down past the Meta Sudans. Width 30 m applies to the Velia stretch.
s:sacra_via_velia_imperial.modern: Via Sacra (archaeological path), Regia to Meta Sudans

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Nova Via
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 269-270
s:nova_via.note: Runs along the north foot of the Palatine above the House of the Vestals, from the summa Sacra Via near the Porta Mugonia west to the north corner of the hill, then (conjecturally) down the west side to the Velabrum by the Porta Romanula and the shrine of Volupia (Varro LL 5.43, 5.164, 6.24). Excavated pavement at 23.40 m behind the Atrium Vestae and 32.30 m at the Clivus Palatinus (Platner). The central stretch is from OpenStreetMap; the western end is blocked by the Domitianic hall and its course there is conjectural.
s:nova_via.modern: excavated street on the north slope of the Palatine

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Vestae
s:vicus_vestae.note: Street of Region VIII known from an inscription (CIL VI 30960); perhaps the ramp from the Temple of Vesta past the Temple of Castor to the north-west corner of the Palatine (Theodenat), Ovid's 'qua nova Romano nunc via iuncta foro est' (Fasti 6.396).
s:vicus_vestae.modern: ramp from the Lacus Iuturnae to S. Maria Antiqua

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Tuscus 579-580
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 431
s:vicus_tuscus.note: From the Forum between the Basilica Iulia and the Temple of Castor south-west along the foot of the Palatine (Via di San Teodoro) through the Velabrum to the Circus Maximus and Forum Boarium; route of the pompa circensis. Named after Etruscans settled there after Porsenna's war (Livy 2.14.9). Shops of silk, incense (vicus turarius) and clothing; brick-cube pavement seen in 1899 between Basilica and temple.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Iugarius 574-575
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 427
s:vicus_iugarius.note: From the Forum between the Basilica Iulia and the Temple of Saturn along the southern foot of the Capitol to the Porta Carmentalis and the Forum Holitorium; part of the primeval route from the north and east to the Tiber crossing below the island (Platner). Altar of Ops and Ceres; the Lacus Servilius at its Forum end.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Argiletum
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 37-38
s:argiletum.note: Main street from the Forum between the Curia and the Basilica Aemilia north-east to the Subura; shops and booksellers (Martial 1.3.1, 1.117). Domitian and Nerva turned it into the Forum Transitorium (dedicated 97), after which the route ran through that forum. Start from the excavated stretch (OpenStreetMap).
s:argiletum.modern: under the Forum of Nerva (Via della Madonna dei Monti direction)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Clivus Capitolinus 122-123
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 89
s:clivus_capitolinus.note: From the Forum by the Arch of Tiberius past the north front and west side of the Temple of Saturn, turning sharply at the Porticus Deorum Consentium and climbing at about 1:8 to the Area Capitolina, which it entered from the south-east (Platner). The triumphal route's last stretch. Paved by the censors of 174 BC (Livy 41.27.7); Sullan and Augustan pavements survive.
s:clivus_capitolinus.modern: Via del Foro Romano / Via di Monte Tarpeo (upper part)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Clivus Capitolinus
s:clivus_capitolinus_arx_branch.note: The branch that led up to the Arx 'which was at first the more important of the two' (Platner); no trace survives. Drawn past the Asylum saddle north of the Tabularium.
s:clivus_capitolinus_arx_branch.modern: Via di S. Pietro in Carcere / steps to the Aracoeli (approx.)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Clivus Argentarius
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 166
s:clivus_argentarius.note: From the Forum by the Carcer north along the east foot of the Arx, behind the Forum of Caesar, to the Porta Fontinalis, continuing as the Via Lata. Name medieval (from the argentarii); stretch of pavement and tabernae preserved behind the Forum of Caesar (OpenStreetMap trace).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Palatinus
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 136
s:clivus_palatinus.note: Modern name for the ascent from the summa Sacra Via by the Arch of Titus to the Palatine summit and the area in front of the Domus Flavia; Sullan pavement at about 29 m, Augustan above, Neronian about 17 m wide (Platner).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Victoriae
s:clivus_victoriae.note: Ascent to the Palatine from the Velabrum, named from the Temple of Victoria. Began at the Porta Romanula a little south of S. Teodoro, skirted the cliff to the north corner of the hill and turned sharply right under the substructures of the Domus Tiberiana (Platner); a Sullan repaving is alluded to in an inscription. Path from OpenStreetMap.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Scalae Caci
s:scalae_caci.note: Stair from the Circus Maximus / Forum Boarium side up to the Germalus by the hut of Romulus (Solinus 1.18); remains of the ancient stair survive at the south-west corner.
s:scalae_caci.modern: stair at the SW corner of the Palatine

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 77
s:centum_gradus.note: The Hundred Steps leading up to the Tarpeian Rock from the Forum Holitorium side (Tacitus, Hist. 3.71).
s:centum_gradus.modern: stair from the Forum Holitorium up the Capitoline (Monte Caprino area)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Scalae Gemoniae
s:scalae_gemoniae.note: Stair from the Arx down to the Forum beside the Carcer, where bodies of the executed were exposed (first named under Tiberius; Valerius Maximus 6.3.3, 6.9.13; Suetonius, Tib. 61).
s:scalae_gemoniae.modern: stair from the Arx down to the Carcer

scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 286-289
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 312-314
s:vicus_velabri.note: Street from the Vicus Tuscus through the Velabrum past the Arcus Argentariorum (204) and the Ianus Quadrifrons to the Forum Boarium; preserved by Via del Velabro beside S. Giorgio.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Curiarum
Panella (ed.), Meta Sudans I (1996)
s:vicus_curiarum.note: Street of Region X named from the Curiae Veteres (Capitoline Base, CIL VI 975); the Curiae have been found by Panella's excavations by the Meta Sudans at the NE corner of the Palatine.
s:vicus_curiarum.modern: north end of Via di San Gregorio by the Meta Sudans

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Triumphalis (2)
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 293
s:road_palatine_east_foot.note: Valley road between the Palatine and the Caelian from the Meta Sudans to the Porta Capena and the Via Appia: route of triumphs from the Circus Maximus toward the Sacra Via, passing the Arch of Constantine (315) and the Septizodium (203). Called 'Via Triumphalis' in modern literature without ancient warrant (Platner). Modern Via di San Gregorio.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 328-333
s:circus_maximus_north_street.note: Street along the Palatine side of the Circus Maximus from the Forum Boarium to the Porta Capena, outside the circus facade arcades; the procession of the pompa circensis entered the circus at the carceres end.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 328-333
s:circus_maximus_south_street.note: Street along the Aventine side of the Circus Maximus, from the Porta Trigemina area to the Porta Capena; temples of Ceres, Mercury and Flora above.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Apollinis
s:vicus_apollinis.note: Street of Region X (Capitoline Base); drawn from the head of the Clivus Palatinus to the precinct of Apollo Palatinus.
s:vicus_apollinis.modern: Palatine summit, Area Palatina to the Temple of Apollo

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 96 (Compitum Acilium)
s:clivus_acilius.note: Lane on the Velia from the Sacra Via toward the Carinae; the Compitum Acilium (shrine of the Lares) was found in 1932 during the cutting of Via dell'Impero. Path from OpenStreetMap.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Subura
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 186
s:subura_main_street.note: Main street of the Subura from the end of the Argiletum (behind the fire wall of the Forum of Augustus) east to the fork of the Clivus Suburanus and Vicus Patricius (Piazza della Suburra). Its line is preserved by Via della Madonna dei Monti and Via Leonina.
s:subura_main_street.modern: Via della Madonna dei Monti - Via Leonina

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Suburanus
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 91
s:clivus_suburanus.note: Continuation of the Subura climbing between the Oppius and Cispius to the Porta Esquilina; ancient pavement follows the line of Via di S. Lucia in Selci, Via di S. Martino and Via di S. Vito (Platner). Shown on the Marble Plan with the Porticus Liviae on its south side.
s:clivus_suburanus.modern: Via in Selci - Via di San Martino ai Monti - Via di San Vito

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Patricius 576-577
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 429
s:vicus_patricius.note: Branched from the Subura and ran north-east between the Cispius and Viminal to the Porta Viminalis (Marble Plan frg. 9); boundary of Regions IV and VI; corresponds closely to Via Urbana (Platner). Church of S. Pudenziana on it.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Longus 575
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 428
s:vicus_longus.note: Street through the valley between the Quirinal and the Viminal; its pavement crosses Via Nazionale at about 20 degrees near the Banca d'Italia and was traced for 1 km toward the Baths of Diocletian (Platner). The lower end is taken up Via dei Serpenti from the Subura. Shrines of Pudicitia Plebeia (296 BC), Febris and Fortuna. The north-eastern stretch through the baths' site is a separate record (vicus_longus_northeast).
s:vicus_longus.modern: Via dei Serpenti, then across Via Nazionale (pavement found near the Banca d'Italia) to the Baths of Diocletian

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Longus
s:vicus_longus_northeast.note: Last stretch to the Alta Semita just inside the Porta Collina, near where Via Quintino Sella meets Via XX Settembre; destroyed by the Baths of Diocletian (298-306) (Platner).
s:vicus_longus_northeast.modern: under the Baths of Diocletian to Via XX Settembre at Via Quintino Sella

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Salutis
s:clivus_salutis.note: Connected the Alta Semita with the Vicus Longus along the line of Via della Consulta; pavement found up to 18 m below ground; vicus Salutaris inscription found at the SW end of Via del Quirinale (Platner).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Insteius
s:vicus_insteianus.note: Street on the collis Latiaris (southern Quirinal) where a great flood of water burst out in 214 BC; probably ascended near the Porta Fontinalis and Piazza Magnanapoli and was destroyed by the imperial fora (Platner).
s:vicus_insteianus.modern: destroyed by the imperial fora (Largo Magnanapoli slope)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Alta Semita
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 9
s:alta_semita.note: Ridge road of the Quirinal from near the Porta Sanqualis / Salutaris to the Porta Collina, corresponding to Via del Quirinale and Via XX Settembre; ancient pavement about 1.8 m below the present level (Platner). Temples of Salus and Quirinus, later the Baths of Constantine, Temple of Serapis and Horti Sallustiani nearby. This record covers the stretch to the Quattro Fontane.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Alta Semita
s:vicus_portae_collinae.note: North-eastern part of the Alta Semita from the Quattro Fontane past S. Susanna to the Porta Collina, probably called Vicus Portae Collinae (inscription CIL VI 450 found near S. Susanna).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Mamuri
s:clivus_mamuri.note: Named from the statue of Mamurius Veturius, maker of the ancilia, near the Temple of Quirinus and the Curia Saliorum; probably ran south-east from the Alta Semita (Platner).
s:clivus_mamuri.modern: Quirinal, from Via del Quirinale south-east (conjectural)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Collis Viminalis
s:vicus_collis_viminalis.note: Ridge road of the Viminal to the Porta Viminalis; pavement found on a line from Via Napoli to the Porta Chiusa (Platner), so the stretch beyond the Servian gate ran on to the later Aurelian gate. Inscriptions CIL VI 2227-2228.
s:vicus_collis_viminalis.modern: Via Napoli - Via del Viminale ridge, on to the Porta Chiusa

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Cuprius 572
s:vicus_cuprius.note: From the Tigillum Sororium north across the slope of the Carinae to the Subura; it crossed the Clivus Orbius at its highest point where Tullia drove over her father's body (Livy 1.48.6). Line approximately that of Via del Cardello and Via del Colosseo (Platner). Varro derives the name from Sabine 'ciprum', good.
s:vicus_cuprius.modern: Via del Cardello - Via del Colosseo

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Orbius
s:clivus_orbius.note: Ancient name of the street up the Carinae to the top of the Oppius, crossing the Vicus Cuprius; afterwards called Vicus Sceleratus. Probably corresponds in part with Via di S. Pietro in Vincoli, where ancient pavement has been found (Platner).
s:clivus_orbius.modern: Via di San Pietro in Vincoli (approx.)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Orbius
s:vicus_sceleratus.note: The 'Wicked Street' where Tullia drove her carriage over the body of Servius Tullius (Livy 1.48.7; Ovid Fasti 6.609); in fact the upper part of the Clivus Orbius. Tradition attaches it to the stepped Via di S. Francesco di Paola below S. Pietro in Vincoli.
s:vicus_sceleratus.modern: Via di San Francesco di Paola (traditional)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Pullius
s:clivus_pullius.note: Ran south from the Subura across the western end of the Oppius to the Fagutal, past the site of S. Pietro in Vincoli; inscription of the clivumpullenses (CIL VI 31893) and the church of S. Giovanni in Carapullo (Platner).
s:clivus_pullius.modern: from the Subura across the west end of the Oppius past S. Pietro in Vincoli (conjectural)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Sandaliarius
s:vicus_sandaliarius.note: Street of Region IV, probably north-east of the Templum Pacis near the Temple of Tellus, perhaps coinciding with the northern part of Via del Colosseo (Platner); the Apollo Sandaliarius of Augustus and the booksellers (Gellius 18.4.1; Galen).
s:vicus_sandaliarius.modern: north part of Via del Colosseo (conjectural)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Suburanus, n. 2
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae, frg. 10
s:street_baths_trajan_clivus.note: Street that ran northward from the west side of the Baths of Trajan to join the Clivus Suburanus, found in 1922 (Platner); bordered the Porticus Liviae on the Marble Plan.

scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 183-188
s:via_biberatica.note: Paved street winding through the upper levels of Trajan's Markets, lined with shops; the name is medieval/modern. Drawn from the published plan of the markets (approximate).
s:via_biberatica.modern: Via Biberatica (modern name, Mercati di Traiano)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Clivus Scauri
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010) 330
s:clivus_scauri.note: Climbs the Caelian from the valley of the Circus Maximus beside SS. Giovanni e Paolo, whose 2nd-3rd century houses and arcades line it; also called Vicus Trium Ararum. Medieval buttress arches span it.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Caput Africae
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 70
s:vicus_capitis_africae.note: From the Colosseum to the Macellum Magnum (S. Stefano Rotondo) along the east side of the Temple of Claudius; the Paedagogium of imperial slaves stood on it (Caput Africae). Line of Via Claudia.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 200-206
s:via_caelimontana.note: Ridge road of the Caelian from the Servian gate east past the Macellum Magnum toward the Lateran and the Porta Asinaria; houses of the senatorial aristocracy (Laterani, Valerii) on it.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Asinaria
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 200
s:via_tusculana_urban.note: Valley road from the Servian Porta Querquetulana past the Ludus Magnus and the Castra Peregrina to the Lateran and the Porta Asinaria, where it continued as the Via Asinaria; S. Clemente on it. Line of Via di S. Giovanni in Laterano.
s:via_tusculana_urban.modern: Via di San Giovanni in Laterano

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Statae Matris
s:vicus_statae_matris.note: Street on the Caelian in Region II known from an altar of Stata Mater found in 1906; drawn on Via della Navicella.
s:vicus_statae_matris.modern: Caelian, near the Via della Navicella (conjectural)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Publicius
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 90
s:clivus_publicius.note: Built and paved by the plebeian aediles L. and M. Publicius Malleolus about 238 BC, from the Forum Boarium near the west end of the Circus and the Porta Trigemina up across the Aventine past the Temple of Diana to the Vicus Piscinae Publicae (Platner). Burned in 203 BC, so thickly built up.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Armilustrium
s:vicus_armilustri.note: Street of the Armilustrium, the open area on the Aventine where the arms of the army were purified (19 October), near S. Sabina in Via di S. Sabina (Platner).
s:vicus_armilustri.modern: Via di Santa Sabina - Via di Sant'Alessio

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 341
s:clivus_rocca_savella.note: Stepped lane up the north-west cliff of the Aventine from the riverside (Porta Trigemina) to the summit, on an ancient line.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Piscina Publica
s:vicus_piscinae_publicae.note: Street named from the Piscina Publica (an old public pool south of the Circus Maximus); the Clivus Publicius ran to it (Platner). Drawn through the valley between the Aventine summits from the Porta Raudusculana to the Porta Capena.
s:vicus_piscinae_publicae.modern: Viale Aventino (valley between the two Aventine summits)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Raudusculana
s:vicus_portae_raudusculanae.note: Street from the Porta Raudusculana down to the Via Ostiensis near the later Porta Ostiensis, on the line of the southern Viale Aventino.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Porta Naevia
s:vicus_portae_naeviae.note: Street named from the Porta Naevia (Capitoline Base), leading south from the gate toward the Via Ardeatina.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Delphini
s:clivus_delphini.note: Street of Region XII in the Regionary Catalogue, probably a little north of the Baths of Caracalla, possibly connecting the Via Nova with the Via Ardeatina along Via di S. Balbina (Platner).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Honoris et Virtutis
s:vicus_honoris_et_virtutis.note: Ran from the Via Appia to the Temple of Honos and Virtus on the slope of the Caelian a short distance south of the Porta Capena (Platner).
s:vicus_honoris_et_virtutis.modern: Caelian slope south of the Porta Capena (conjectural)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Camenae
s:vicus_camenarum.note: Street of Region I named from the grove and spring of the Camenae outside the Porta Capena; drawn on Via di Valle delle Camene.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Viae: Via Nova
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 418
s:via_nova_caracalla.note: Built by Caracalla parallel to the Via Appia along the front of his baths ('viam novam munivit, quae est sub eius thermis', HA Carac. 9.9); shown on the Marble Plan about 30 m wide, three times the width of the Appia (Platner). Drawn along the west front of the bath precinct; exact line conjectural.
s:via_nova_caracalla.modern: Viale Guido Baccelli side of the Baths of Caracalla (approx.)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Sulpicius
s:vicus_sulpicius.note: Street on which the Baths of Caracalla stood (HA Elag. 17.9); most probably on their southern side, inside Region I, divided in two by the Via Appia (Platner).
s:vicus_sulpicius.modern: south side of the Baths of Caracalla (conjectural)

phases.t: C. Flaminius builds the Via Flaminia (censor 220 BC).
Augustus restores the Flaminia.
Arch of Claudius carrying the Aqua Virgo over the street.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Viae: Via Lata
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
s:via_lata.note: Urban stretch of the Via Flaminia from the Porta Fontinalis past the tomb of Bibulus along the eastern edge of the Campus Martius; name Via Lata first appears in the Notitia (Reg. VII). Arches of Claudius (51-52) and the Arcus Novus (Diocletian) spanned it; porticoes lined it; the Saepta and Iseum to the west. Line of Via del Corso, which keeps the ancient alignment (ancient level 5-8 m down).
s:via_lata.modern: Via del Corso (Piazza Venezia - Piazza Colonna)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Flaminia
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
s:via_flaminia_urban.note: Northern part of the urban Via Flaminia through the Campus Martius past the Column of Marcus Aurelius, the Ara Pacis and Horologium (to the west) and the Mausoleum of Augustus to the Porta Flaminia (from 275). Line of Via del Corso.
s:via_flaminia_urban.modern: Via del Corso (Piazza Colonna - Piazza del Popolo)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Flaminia
s:via_flaminia_extra.note: From the Porta Flaminia north between the Pincian and the river, lined with tombs, to the Pons Milvius (rebuilt 109 BC) at the edge of the model area; scene of Constantine's victory over Maxentius in 312.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Tecta (on Via Recta)
Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae, pl. 8 and 15
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
s:via_recta.note: Straight street from the river at the Tarentum / later Pons Aelius east past the north end of the Stadium of Domitian to the Via Lata near the Column of Marcus Aurelius; its line is kept by Via dei Coronari and its continuation. The name 'Via Recta' rests on a misreading of Seneca (Apoc. 13), where 'Via Tecta' is right (Platner); kept here as the conventional label.
s:via_recta.modern: Via dei Coronari - Via delle Coppelle - Via degli Uffici del Vicario

phases.t: Porticoed street (date unknown, by the early Empire).
Rebuilt as the Porticus Maximae (379-383).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Tecta
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 419
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
s:via_tecta.note: Covered street of the Campus Martius linking the Flaminian district and the Circus Flaminius with the Tarentum by the river (Seneca, Apoc. 13; Martial 3.5.5, 8.75.1-2). Ancient pavement found in Via di Pescheria, del Pianto, de' Giubbonari, de' Cappellari and del Banco di S. Spirito, on the line of the fragments of the Porticus Maximae (Platner). In 379-383 Gratian, Valentinian II and Theodosius rebuilt it as the Porticus Maximae, a colonnaded street to the Pons Aelius (CIL VI 1184). Possibly the 'Via Fornicata' of Livy 22.36.8.
s:via_tecta.modern: Via del Portico d'Ottavia - S. Maria del Pianto - Giubbonari - Cappellari - Banchi Vecchi - Banco di S. Spirito

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Pallacina
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 282
s:vicus_pallacinae.note: Street of the Pallacinae district near S. Marco (Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino 18; balneae Pallacinae); placed on the east-west line of Via delle Botteghe Oscure along the north side of the Porticus Minucia and Crypta Balbi, an ancient alignment.
s:vicus_pallacinae.modern: Via delle Botteghe Oscure - Via di San Marco

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 266-275
s:triumphal_road_forum_holitorium.note: Street from the Servian gate past the temples of Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita and the Theatre of Marcellus to the Porticus Octaviae and the Circus Flaminius; part of the triumphal route in reverse.
s:triumphal_road_forum_holitorium.modern: Via del Teatro di Marcello (west side) / Via del Portico d'Ottavia

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 314
s:via_foro_olitorio.note: Short street from the Vicus Iugarius / Porta Carmentalis toward the river along the south side of the Forum Holitorium temples.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 278-283
s:street_area_sacra_east.note: North-south street between the Area Sacra and the Porticus Minucia, on the line of Via di S. Nicola de' Cesarini.
s:street_area_sacra_east.modern: Via di San Nicola de' Cesarini

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Aesculeti
s:vicus_aesculeti.note: Known from an altar of the magistri vici Aescleti found in Via Arenula about 100 m from the Tiber; pavement in the Via di S. Bartolommeo (Platner).
s:vicus_aesculeti.modern: toward Via di S. Bartolomeo dei Vaccinari (south Campus Martius)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Caprarius
s:vicus_caprarius.note: Ran south from the Aqua Virgo and Campus Agrippae; pavement in Via dei Lucchesi and at Via delle Vergini / Via dell'Umilta (Platner); a castellum of the Aqua Virgo is now visible in the vicus (the 'Citta dell'acqua').
s:vicus_caprarius.modern: Via dei Lucchesi - Via delle Vergini line

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Pons Agrippae
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
s:street_pons_agrippae.note: From the bridgehead of the Pons Agrippae / Pons Aurelius (Ponte Sisto) north toward the Theatre of Pompey and the Via Tecta, on the line of Via dei Pettinari.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 266-271
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
s:street_circus_flaminius_north.note: Street on the northern edge of the open area of the Circus Flaminius (whose extent is debated: Gatti / Coarelli), between the porticoes and the Theatre of Balbus.
s:street_circus_flaminius_north.modern: Via dei Funari - Via di S. Maria de' Calderari (approx.)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Censori
s:vicus_censori.note: Probably the only vicus on the island (CIL VI 975); the route from the Forum Holitorium over the Pons Fabricius (62 BC), past the Temple of Aesculapius, over the Pons Cestius (rebuilt 370 as Pons Gratiani) to Trastevere.
s:vicus_censori.modern: Ponte Fabricio - Via di Ponte Quattro Capi - Piazza S. Bartolomeo - Ponte Cestio

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Pons Aemilius
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 309
s:street_pons_aemilius_forum_boarium.note: Approach from the Pons Aemilius (piers 179 BC, arches 142 BC) past the Temple of Portunus and the Porta Flumentana into the Forum Boarium and the Velabrum: the city end of the Via Aurelia.
s:street_pons_aemilius_forum_boarium.modern: Via Luigi Petroselli (south end) / Piazza della Bocca della Verita

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Pons Sublicius
s:street_pons_sublicius.note: Short approach from the wooden Pons Sublicius (whose site is debated, just below the Aventine) to the Porta Trigemina and the Forum Boarium.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Aurelia
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 377
s:via_aurelia_urban.note: From the Pons Aemilius and the island bridges west through Trastevere along Via della Lungaretta (which preserves the line) past S. Maria in Trastevere and up the Janiculum to the Porta Aurelia (from 275); built or regularised about 241 BC (C. Aurelius Cotta). Upper course on the Janiculum approximate.
s:via_aurelia_urban.modern: Via della Lungaretta - Piazza S. Maria in Trastevere - Via della Paglia - Via Garibaldi

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Aurelia
s:via_aurelia_vetus_extra.note: West from the Porta Aurelia along the north side of the later Villa Doria Pamphili toward the coast; the Aqua Traiana runs beside it. Curatores administered the Aurelia vetus and nova, Cornelia and Triumphalis together (CIL VI 1512).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Rutarius
s:clivus_rutarius.note: Known from one inscription (CIL VI 7803); either part of the Via Aurelia outside the Porta Aurelia or a street running into it (Platner). Drawn on the modern Clivo Rutario in Monteverde.
s:clivus_rutarius.modern: Clivo Rutario (modern street named after it)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Portuensis
Platner-Ashby, Via Campana
s:via_portuensis_urban.note: From the bridges at the island south along the river behind the harbour of Trastevere to the Porta Portuensis (from 275): the old salt road (Via Campana) to the Campus Salinarum at the river mouth, later also the road to Claudius' harbour (Portus).
s:via_portuensis_urban.modern: Via dei Vascellari - Via di S. Michele - Via Portuense

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Campana
s:via_campana_extra.note: Along the right bank of the Tiber toward the Campus Salinarum Romanarum; modern Via Portuense follows the valley route at first. Sanctuary of the Dea Dia (Arval Brothers) at the 5th mile, beyond the model area.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Portuensis
s:via_portuensis_extra.note: The road to Portus built after Claudius' harbour (AD 42-64), keeping to the higher ground south-west of the river valley; necropolis of Pozzo Pantaleo and Jewish catacomb of Monteverde along it. Course in the model area approximate.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 378
s:road_lungara.note: Road along the right bank between the Horti Caesaris / Agrippinae and the river from Trastevere to the Vatican plain; the medieval Via Sancta to St Peter's. Ancient date assumed.

s:street_porta_septimiana_trastevere.note: Street from the north gate of Trastevere south to S. Maria in Trastevere, on the line of Via della Scala.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Pons Aurelius
s:street_pons_aurelius_trastevere.note: From the right-bank end of the Pons Aurelius (Antonine, rebuilt by Valentinian I as Pons Valentiniani) toward S. Maria in Trastevere, on Via del Moro.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Vicus Tiberini
s:vicus_tiberini.note: Street of Region XIV on the Capitoline Base; Lanciani gave the name to a street found under Via della Lungarina between Viale del Re and Piazza del Drago (Platner).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Cornelia
Liverani and Spinola, The Vatican Necropoles (2010)
s:via_cornelia.note: From the Pons Neronianus west across the Vatican plain along the north side of the Circus of Gaius and Nero, with the Vatican necropolis (and St Peter's tomb) on its north side, then west through the later Porta Pertusa; after the Pons Aelius was built it was prolonged east to it (Platner). St Peter's (from c. 320) was built over the necropolis beside it.
s:via_cornelia.modern: under the Borgo and the nave of St Peter's, then west

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Triumphalis
Steinby (ed.), La necropoli della Via Triumphalis (2003)
s:via_triumphalis.note: From the Pons Neronianus north-west across the Vatican plain (the Santa Rosa and Autoparco sections of the Vatican necropolis lie on it) and up Monte Mario on the line of modern Via Trionfale to Veii. Southern stretch approximate.
s:via_triumphalis.modern: Borgo - Santa Rosa necropolis - Via Trionfale

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Aurelia
s:via_aurelia_nova.note: Later branch of the Aurelia (attested in curator inscriptions, CIL VI 1512) leaving the Vatican district south of the Circus of Gaius and Nero and joining the old road further west; the medieval Porta Cavalleggeri stands on it.
s:via_aurelia_nova.modern: Borgo - Via di Porta Cavalleggeri - Via Aurelia

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 316
s:porticus_sancti_petri.note: Covered colonnade along which pilgrims walked from the Pons Aelius to St Peter's, mentioned by Procopius (Wars 5.19.4 refers to the road; the portico is described in later sources). Date and line approximate.
s:porticus_sancti_petri.modern: Via della Conciliazione (line of the demolished Spina di Borgo)

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 299
s:road_pons_aelius_neronianus.note: Link along the right bank between the two bridgeheads past the Mausoleum of Hadrian.
s:road_pons_aelius_neronianus.modern: Borgo Santo Spirito (east end) / Lungotevere Vaticano

phases.t: Built by Appius Claudius.
Footway paved to the temple of Mars.
Portico (Via Tecta) to the temple of Mars.
Crossed by the Aurelian Wall at the Porta Appia.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Appia
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 344-352
s:via_appia_urban.note: Built by the censor Ap. Claudius Caecus in 312 BC from the Porta Capena. In 296 BC a footway was paved in squared stone from the gate to the temple of Mars (Livy 10.23.12) and in 293 the road itself paved with selce to Bovillae (Livy 10.47.4); in 189 BC the stretch to the temple of Mars got a portico (the 'Via Tecta' outside the Porta Capena, Ovid Fasti 6.191-192). Between the Porta Capena and Piazzale Numa Pompilio it passed east of the Baths of Caracalla (Viale delle Terme di Caracalla); the Via Latina forked off at Piazzale Numa Pompilio; Via di Porta S. Sebastiano preserves the line to the gate, past the Tomb of the Scipios.
s:via_appia_urban.modern: Viale delle Terme di Caracalla - Via di Porta San Sebastiano

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Cliva: Clivus Martis
s:clivus_martis.note: The ascent of the Via Appia to the temple of Mars (dedicated 388 BC) just before the line of the later Aurelian Wall; its grade was later lowered (CIL VI 1270) (Platner).
s:clivus_martis.modern: Via di Porta San Sebastiano (last stretch before the gate)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Appia
s:via_appia_extra.note: From the Porta Appia south-east past the Almo crossing, the catacombs (Callixtus, San Sebastiano), the villa and circus of Maxentius and the Tomb of Caecilia Metella to the edge of the model area; lined with tombs. Modern Via Appia Antica on the ancient line.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Latina
s:via_latina_urban.note: Left the Porta Capena with the Appia and forked off at Piazzale Numa Pompilio toward the Porta Latina (from 275), on the line of Via di Porta Latina; older than the Appia, the route to the Sacco valley.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Latina
s:via_latina_extra.note: South-east from the Porta Latina through the necropolis (tombs of the Valerii and Pancratii beyond the model area) toward the Alban hills; modern Via Latina for the first stretch, then extrapolated on its bearing.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Ardeatina
s:via_ardeatina_urban.note: From the Servian Porta Naevia south past the west side of the Baths of Caracalla (the Clivus Delphini linked it with the Via Nova) to the Porta Ardeatina. Exact course inside the circuit conjectural.
s:via_ardeatina_urban.modern: west and south of the Baths of Caracalla (Viale Guido Baccelli area)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Ardeatina
s:via_ardeatina_extra.note: South from the Porta Ardeatina between the Appia and the Ostiensis, past the catacombs of Domitilla and Callixtus (western side).
s:via_ardeatina_extra.modern: Via di Porta Ardeatina - Via Ardeatina

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Ostiensis
Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 352
s:via_ostiensis_urban.note: From the Porta Trigemina along the foot of the Aventine through the Emporium district (Porticus Aemilia, Horrea Galbana, Monte Testaccio to the west) to the Porta Ostiensis beside the Pyramid of Cestius; line of Via Marmorata.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Ostiensis
s:via_ostiensis_extra.note: From the Porta Ostiensis south past the tomb of St Paul (basilica of S. Paolo, rebuilt from 386) to the edge of the model area; the road to Ostia.

scholarship: Richardson, NTDAR (1992) 316
s:porticus_sancti_pauli.note: Procopius (Wars 6.4.9) says a covered portico led from the Porta Ostiensis to the church of St Paul, 14 stades away; date of construction unknown (late 4th - 5th century assumed).

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Salaria
Platner-Ashby, Porta Pinciana
s:via_salaria_vetus_urban.note: Older line of the Salaria, leaving the Porta Collina and running north-west through the valley of the Horti Sallustiani to the later Porta Pinciana, beyond which it continued as Via Pinciana. Course inside the Aurelian circuit conjectural.
s:via_salaria_vetus_urban.modern: through the Horti Sallustiani valley (Via Sallustiana - Via di Porta Pinciana direction)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Salaria
s:via_salaria_vetus_extra.note: North from the Porta Pinciana along Via Pinciana and across the Parioli heights to rejoin the Salaria before the Anio (catacombs of Pamphilus and Basilla on it). Beyond Via Pinciana extrapolated.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Salaria
s:via_salaria_urban.note: The salt road, from the Porta Collina north to the Porta Salaria between the Horti Sallustiani and the Castra Praetoria; line roughly that of Via Piave.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Salaria
s:via_salaria_extra.note: North from the Porta Salaria past the catacomb of Priscilla toward the Pons Salarius on the Anio, just beyond the model area; lined with tombs.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Nomentana
s:via_nomentana_urban.note: From the Porta Collina north-east to the Porta Nomentana, on the line of the upper Via XX Settembre toward Porta Pia.

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Nomentana
s:via_nomentana_extra.note: North-east from the Porta Nomentana past Sant'Agnese and the Mausoleum of Constantina (Santa Costanza) to the edge of the model area.

scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs (2007) 192-197
s:via_tiburtina_praenestina_urban_common.note: The roads to Tibur, Praeneste and Labici left the Porta Esquilina together and divided near the later Nymphaeum of Alexander ('Trofei di Mario', Piazza Vittorio).
s:via_tiburtina_praenestina_urban_common.modern: Via di S. Vito east end - Piazza Vittorio (north side)

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Tiburtina
s:via_tiburtina_urban.note: From the fork by the Nymphaeum of Alexander north-east to the Porta Tiburtina (from 275), passing under the Augustan aqueduct arch. Inner course approximate.
s:via_tiburtina_urban.modern: Piazza Vittorio - Via Principe Amedeo direction - Porta S. Lorenzo

scholarship: Platner-Ashby, Via Tiburtina
s:via_tiburtina_extra.note: From the Porta Tiburtina east past the tomb of St Lawrence (basilica of S. Lorenzo, Constantinian funerary basilica and Pelagius II's church of 579-590) toward Tibur.

a:aqua_appia.summary: Rome's first aqueduct, built in 312 BC by Appius Claudius Caecus. Its springs lay off the Via Praenestina between the 7th and 8th milestones; it ran underground the whole way except a short arcade of 60 passus near the Porta Capena, passed beneath the Caelian and the Aventine and began distribution at the Salinae by the Porta Trigemina, serving the low-lying Forum Boarium and river port district.

phases.t: Built by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus (with C. Plautius, who found the springs): Rome's first aqueduct, almost wholly underground (11,130 passus), with only 60 passus on substructions and arches near the Porta Capena.
Repaired by the praetor Q. Marcius Rex before building the Marcia.
Repaired by Agrippa as aedile.
Augustus repairs the channel (11-4 BC) and adds the Ramus Augusta at Spes Vetus.
Frontinus measures 1825 quinariae (about 73,000 m3 a day) and lists it as the lowest-lying supply except the Alsietina.
Cut with all the aqueducts by Witiges' Goths during the siege; never restored in our period.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Platner-Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Aqua Appia
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Aqua Appia
Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)
a:aqua_appia.note: Line inside the city is reconstructed from Frontinus' termini and the finds of 1677 and 1887 near Viale Aventino; a deep channel was also reported in 2017 Metro C works on the Caelian. Channel elevations are estimates (arrival level about 20 m asl), so most of the course lies 10-25 m below ground; only the 60-passus arcade by the Porta Capena is above ground, low (a few metres above the ancient valley floor, which lies well below the modern DEM there).

a:anio_vetus.summary: Second aqueduct of Rome (272-269 BC), drawing turbid water from the Anio above Tibur. It entered the city underground at Spes Vetus, just inside the later Porta Maggiore, and ran beneath the Esquiline to the Porta Esquilina, from where Augustan cippi and a long stretch of channel lead north. A branch, the specus Octavianus, ran toward the Via Nova near the gardens of Asinius.

phases.t: Begun by the censor M'. Curius Dentatus with the spoils of Pyrrhus; completed 270/269 BC.
Repaired by Q. Marcius Rex.
Repaired by Agrippa.
Augustus' general restoration (cippi of 11-4 BC found along the channel inside the city).
Frontinus measures 4398 quinariae at the intake and reserves the turbid water for gardens and lowly uses.
Cut by the Goths; not restored.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Anio Vetus
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Anio Vetus
a:anio_vetus.note: Extramural approach inside the model area follows the approximate OSM route for the Anio Vetus; the in-city course follows Platner-Ashby (channel found just inside the Porta Maggiore with intrados at 46.15 m asl, cippi and channel north of the Porta Esquilina). All underground, typically 5-15 m below ground.
a:anio_vetus.builderName: the censor M'. Curius Dentatus (272 BC), completed by M. Fulvius Flaccus

a:aqua_marcia.summary: The finest water of Rome, brought 91 km from the upper Anio valley by Q. Marcius Rex in 144-140 BC. Its arches, later shared with the Tepula and Julia, cross the campagna into the city just north of the Porta Maggiore, run along the line later taken by the Aurelian Wall to the Porta Tiburtina, and continue underground to the terminal castellum inside the Porta Collina. Branches fed the Capitol, the Rivus Herculaneus over the Caelian to the Porta Capena, and from 212 Caracalla's baths.

phases.t: The praetor Q. Marcius Rex is commissioned to repair the Appia and Anio Vetus and to bring a new supply; arches from the 7th mile of the Via Latina to Rome.
Water reaches the Capitol.
Repaired by Agrippa.
Augustus repairs 'rivos aquarum omnium' (11-4 BC) and adds the Aqua Augusta springs; the arch over the Via Tiburtina (5/4 BC) carries his inscription.
Titus restores the Marcia (inscription on the Porta Tiburtina).
Probable restoration by Septimius Severus.
Caracalla clears the springs, adds the fons Antoninianus and builds the branch to his baths (Porta Tiburtina inscription).
Aurelian's wall swallows the arcade between the Porta Maggiore and the Porta Tiburtina.
Diocletian increases the supply for his baths (Forma Iovia).
Cut by Witiges' Goths during the siege; Belisarius blocks the channels where they enter the walls.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Aqua Marcia
Van Deman, The Building of the Roman Aqueducts (1934)
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Aqua Marcia
Taylor, Public Needs and Private Pleasures (2000)
a:aqua_marcia.note: Extramural line inside the model area follows the Acqua Felice / Marcia line along Via del Mandrione (OSM), offset 22 m south-west of the Claudian arches as on the ground (the road runs between them); the crossing beneath the Claudia before the Porta Maggiore is schematic. Channel levels use the standard arrival figures (Marcia 59, Tepula 61, Julia 64 m asl at the Porta Maggiore, after Lanciani/Ashby); the 1917 Reina levelling gives the Julia specus 57.4 m there, so these may be up to 6 m too high.

a:aqua_tepula.summary: A small aqueduct of tepid water (125 BC) from the Alban hills whose channel rides the arches of the Marcia into Rome, above the Marcia and below the Julia, and emerges again at the Porta Viminalis.

phases.t: Built by the censors of 125 BC from warm springs near the Alban hills; channel laid on top of the Marcia's arches.
Agrippa merges it with the new Julia at the source and re-divides the water.
Augustan restoration.
Cut by the Goths.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Aqua Tepula
a:aqua_tepula.note: Shares the Marcia's line and arcade (coincident geometry). Elevation about 2 m above the Marcia.
a:aqua_tepula.builderName: the censors Cn. Servilius Caepio and L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla

a:aqua_julia.summary: Agrippa's aqueduct of 33 BC, the uppermost of the three channels on the Marcia's arches. It emerged at the Porta Viminalis; a branch at Spes Vetus served the Caelian until the Claudia arrived, and from 226 an arcade branch fed the great Nymphaeum of Alexander on the Esquiline.

phases.t: Built by Agrippa as aedile from springs near Grottaferrata, merged at the source with the Tepula and carried above it on the Marcia's arches.
Augustan restoration (11-4 BC); a cippus of AD 14 implies another.
Branch on arches to the new Nymphaeum of Alexander Severus on the Esquiline.
Cut by the Goths.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Aqua Iulia, Nymphaeum Alexandri
Richardson, NTDAR (1992)
Tedeschi Grisanti, I 'Trofei di Mario' (1977)
a:aqua_julia.note: Specus floor at the Porta Maggiore 63.74 m asl (Lanciani) or 57.38 m (1917 levelling); 64 m used here.

a:aqua_virgo.summary: Agrippa's aqueduct of 19 BC, low and gentle (it falls only a few metres over 21 km), entering the city in a tunnel beneath the Pincian at the Gardens of Lucullus, emerging at Via di Capo le Case and crossing the Campus Martius on 700 passus of arches past Via del Nazareno and over the Via Lata on the Arch of Claudius to its castellum at the front of the Saepta. Its line survives as the modern Acqua Vergine feeding the Trevi Fountain.

phases.t: Opened by Agrippa on 9 June 19 BC to supply his baths in the Campus Martius; mostly underground, ending on 700 passus of arches.
Cippi of Tiberius (AD 36-37) mark the line under the Pincian.
Claudius rebuilds the arches wrecked by Caligula's works (inscription in Via del Nazareno).
The aqueduct's crossing of the Via Lata becomes Claudius' British triumphal arch.
Constantinian restoration recorded on an inscription (CIL VI 31564).

Goths cut the line and probe its underground channel to get into the city (Procopius); Belisarius has it blocked. Its deep, low course made it the easiest to revive in the Middle Ages (Hadrian I, 8th century).

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Aqua Virgo, Arcus Claudii
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Aqua Virgo
Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901)
a:aqua_virgo.note: The extramural approach in the north-east of the model area (from Salone via Pietralata, under the Via Nomentana and Salaria and the Villa Borghese) is schematic. The in-city part follows Platner-Ashby. Channel at about 20-22 m asl: the arches stood 6-8 m above the ancient Campus ground (about 13-14 m asl) but are buried 6-8 m by modern fill, so against the modern DEM the channel is at or below street level.

a:aqua_alsietina.summary: Augustus' aqueduct of 2 BC from Lake Martignano, built to fill the Naumachia in Transtiberim. Frontinus judged its water unfit to drink and its level the lowest of all; the course near Rome is mostly unknown, a stretch having been found on the Janiculum south of and well below the Aqua Traiana.

phases.t: Augustus brings the poor water of Lake Alsietinus (Martignano) to fill his Naumachia, inaugurated with the Temple of Mars Ultor; surplus to the gardens of Transtiberim and to the bridges' fountains when the river aqueducts were under repair.
Cut by the Goths.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Taylor, 'Torrent or trickle? The Aqua Alsietina, the Naumachia Augusti, and the Transtiberim', AJA 101 (1997)
Taylor, Public Needs and Private Pleasures (2000)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Aqua Alsietina
a:aqua_alsietina.note: Entirely underground (tunnel beneath the Janiculum). Taylor argues the channel arrived higher than Frontinus' remark suggests; the 17 m terminal level used here follows the common table and is uncertain by 20 m or more.

a:aqua_claudia.summary: Begun by Caligula in 38 and dedicated by Claudius in 52, the Claudia brought clear spring water 69 km from the upper Anio valley, the Anio Novus riding above it on the same colossal arcade, which crosses the model area along Via del Mandrione to the double arch of the Porta Maggiore and a terminal castellum behind the gardens of Pallas. Nero's brick arches carried part of it across the Caelian to the Temple of Claudius; Domitian took it on to the Palatine.

phases.t: Begun by Caligula together with the Anio Novus.
Dedicated by Claudius on 1 August (Porta Maggiore inscription: 45 miles, springs Caeruleus and Curtius).
Supply fails after about ten years; out of regular use for nine years.
Nero builds the Arcus Neroniani (Caelimontani) from Spes Vetus to the Temple of Claudius for his new palace.
Vespasian restores it at his own expense (second Porta Maggiore inscription).
Titus rebuilds it 'a capite' after age had ruined it to its foundations (third inscription).
Domitian completes a tunnel under Mons Aeflanus; the arcade is extended across the valley to the Palatine for the new palace.
Septimius Severus and Caracalla restore the arcus Caelimontani 'vetustate conlapsos' (CIL VI 1259); extensive Severan brick reinforcement of the main arcade.
Aurelian incorporates the double arch over the Via Praenestina and Labicana as a gate (Porta Praenestina, later Porta Maggiore) and uses the arcade as part of the wall.
Honorius rebuilds the gate with towers and a guardhouse; the channels continue to flow above.
Theodoric's repairs of the aqueducts (Cassiodorus, Variae).
Cut by Witiges' Goths; Belisarius blocks the channels with masonry where they pass the walls. Not restored before 641 (Hadrian I in the 8th century).

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Van Deman, The Building of the Roman Aqueducts (1934)
Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Aqua Claudia, Arcus Neroniani
Radicioni, Il tratto di Aqua Claudia e Anio Novus tra Porta Furba e Via Frascati (diss. Sapienza 2018)
Baiocchi et al., 'Geomatic measurement of the Claudia and Anio Novus' (2020)
Coates-Stephens, 'The walls and aqueducts of Rome in the early Middle Ages' JRS 88 (1998)
a:aqua_claudia.note: Line inside the model area from the OSM 'Acquedotto Anio Novus' route (approximate). Channel levels use the standard arrival figures (Claudia 67, Anio Novus 70 m asl at the Porta Maggiore) with about 1.2 per mille upstream; Baiocchi et al. measured the two specus about 3 m apart. The Porta Maggiore's total height (about 24 m over the ancient pavement) supports values within 2-3 m of these.

a:anio_novus.summary: The longest and highest of Rome's aqueducts (87 km, 52 AD), drawing from the Anio itself. In the model area it is the upper channel on the Claudian arcade and on the attic of the Porta Maggiore, sharing the terminal castellum behind the gardens of Pallas.

phases.t: Begun by Caligula.
Dedicated by Claudius with the Claudia; the highest of all Rome's aqueducts, carried in a brick-faced channel above the Claudia from the 7th mile of the Via Latina.
Frontinus has Trajan's predecessor Nerva improve its intake; Trajan later moves the head to the lakes of Nero's Subiaco villa.
Cut by the Goths.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Alimonti et al., 'Roman aqueduct flow' ISPRS IJGI 10 (2021)
a:anio_novus.note: Coincident with the Claudia's arcade; 3 m higher.

a:aqua_traiana.summary: Trajan's aqueduct of 109, 58 km from the springs around Lake Bracciano, the only high-level supply for Transtiberim. It arrived underground on the crest of the Janiculum by the later Porta Aurelia, where its fall drove a chain of water-mills that in late antiquity milled the city's grain; when the Goths cut it in 537 Belisarius moved the mills onto boats in the Tiber. Paul V rebuilt it as the Acqua Paola in 1605-12.

phases.t: Trajan inaugurates the aqueduct on 24 June from springs around Lake Bracciano, 'tota urbe salientem' (Fasti Ostienses); it reaches the city on the Janiculum.
Mills on the Janiculum slope driven by its water (3rd-century phases); by late antiquity they ground the city's bread grain.
Witiges cuts the aqueducts in March; the Janiculum mills stop and Belisarius blocks the channel; floating mills on the Tiber replace them.
Pope Honorius I (625-638) is credited in the Liber Pontificalis with a mill by the city wall at the place called Traianum and its water channel, implying a partial revival (interpretation debated).

scholarship: Wilson, 'The water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Bell, 'An archaeologist's perspective on the Janiculum mills' (1993)
Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Taylor, Public Needs and Private Pleasures (2000)
a:aqua_traiana.note: Line west of the Janiculum from OSM 'Acquedotto Traiano' segments (tunnel at about lat 41.889); mills and drop toward Transtiberim reconstructed. The second flowing period (from 630) represents only the partial revival for the mill; schematic.

a:aqua_alexandrina.summary: The last aqueduct of ancient Rome (226), built by Severus Alexander from the springs of Pantano Borghese to serve his baths. Its brick arcade crosses the eastern suburbs just outside the model area; the final run to the Porta Maggiore along the Via Labicana is conjectural.

phases.t: Built by Severus Alexander from springs at Pantano Borghese (about 22 km), the last of the eleven aqueducts; brick arches through Centocelle and the Alessandrino quarter.
Cut by the Goths.

scholarship: Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Aqua Alexandrina
a:aqua_alexandrina.note: Entry point near Viale dell'Acquedotto Alessandrino (Vigne Alessandrine); arches assumed only on the first stretch inside the model area. Arrival level 48-50 m asl (estimates range 43-50).

r:reg_I.note: Hulsen: it begins at the east corner of the Palatine and, beyond the Aventine, widens to the Almo beyond the Aurelian Wall. The wedge beyond the wall here is a schematic tongue to the Almo crossing of the Via Appia. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_I.character: The south-eastern approach along the Via Appia: the narrow valley between the Palatine and the Caelian (Via di S. Gregorio), the Porta Capena with the dripping aqueduct over it, the grove of the Camenae and the shrine of Honos and Virtus, then the wedge between the Via Appia and the Via Latina with the tombs of the Scipios, the arches of Drusus, Verus and Trajan, and beyond the Aurelian Wall the Temple of Mars and the bank of the Almo. Baths of Severus and Commodus, the Mutatorium Caesaris (where emperors changed into triumphal dress) and the Area Apollinis. A road and tomb district more than a residential one, though its insulae count is high.

r:reg_II.note: Northern limit the straight street from the Colosseum to the Porta Asinaria (Via di S. Giovanni in Laterano); southern limit the foot of the Caelian toward Region I and the Aurelian Wall. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_II.character: Most of the Caelian: the Temple of Divus Claudius on its western brow, the Macellum Magnum (later S. Stefano Rotondo), the barracks of the Castra Peregrina and the 5th cohort of vigiles, the gladiator schools (Ludus Matutinus and Dacicus) and their spoliarium near the Colosseum, and great aristocratic houses (the Laterani, the domus of Philip, the Victiliana, the Valerii, later the Lateran palace and basilica). Nero's arches crossed it. A prosperous, airy hill of domus and barracks.

r:reg_III.note: Bounded by Region II, the Servian Wall, the Clivus Suburanus from the Porta Esquilina westward, and a line turning south to the Meta Sudans. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_III.character: The Colosseum valley and the Oppian: the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Ludus Magnus, the Moneta, the Baths of Titus and Trajan over the ruins of the Domus Aurea, the Porticus of Livia, the Sette Sale cistern and the sanctuary of Isis and Serapis that gave the region its name. Monumental and public in its lower part, residential on the hill.

r:reg_IV.note: Hulsen: includes the Sacra Via up to the Atrium Vestae, the Subura and the Cispius; bounded by Region III, the Servian Wall, and the Vicus Patricius from the Porta Viminalis; curves between the fora of Nerva and Vespasian. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_IV.character: From the upper Sacra Via and the Velia (Basilica of Maxentius, Temple of Venus and Roma, the Colossus) north through the Templum Pacis into the crowded Subura and up the Cispius to the Servian agger. The Subura was the classic quarter of dense insulae, shops and taverns; the Argiletum its bookselling street; the Tigillum Sororium and the Carinae's grand houses lay on its edges.

r:reg_V.note: In Augustan times it excluded the Campus Viminalis and the land between the Viae Tiburtina and Salaria; by the 4th century its outer edge followed the Aurelian Wall from south of the Via Labicana to the Castra Praetoria, which is how it is drawn here. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_V.character: The Esquiline plateau outside the Servian agger: once the paupers' necropolis and the grove of Libitina, transformed from the 30s BC into the great horti (Maecenas, Lamia, Taurus, Pallas, Epaphroditus, Licinius, Spes Vetus), with the Nymphaeum of Alexander, the so-called Temple of Minerva Medica, the Macellum Liviae, and the aqueducts converging on Spes Vetus by the Porta Maggiore.

r:reg_VI.note: 4th-century limits: the Aurelian Wall around the Castra Praetoria, the Vicus Patricius toward Region IV, and a line down the west foot of the Quirinal to Trajan's Forum. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_VI.character: The Quirinal and Viminal, named after the 'high path' along the Quirinal ridge (Via XX Settembre): the old temples of Quirinus, Salus and Semo Sancus, the Flavian Temple of the Gens Flavia, the Baths of Constantine and the vast Baths of Diocletian, the Horti Sallustiani in the valley toward the Pincian, the Castra Praetoria and many senatorial houses. Residential and grand.

r:reg_VII.note: Lay between the Via Flaminia/Lata and the western limit of Region VI. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_VII.character: East of the Via Lata (Corso) from the Capitoline foot to the Porta Flaminia, including the Pincian (Collis Hortulorum) with the gardens of Lucullus and the Acilii: the Campus Agrippae and Porticus Vipsania with Agrippa's map, the Arch of Claudius over the road, the Temple of the Sun of Aurelian and the Castra Urbana. A mixed district of porticoes, warehouses and insulae.

r:reg_VIII.note: Irregular: the Forum, the imperial fora and the Capitol; on the south a line north of the Forum Boarium through the Velabrum to the east end of the Atrium Vestae. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_VIII.character: The civic heart: the Forum Romanum, the Capitol with the temples of Jupiter and Juno Moneta, the Imperial Fora of Caesar, Augustus and Trajan, the Basilicas Aemilia and Julia, the Velabrum and Vicus Tuscus. The most monumental region, yet it counted 34 vici and 3480 insulae on its fringes.

r:reg_IX.note: All the land between the Servian Wall, the Via Flaminia and the Tiber. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_IX.character: The whole Campus Martius west of the Via Lata to the Tiber: the Circus Flaminius and the temples of the Forum Holitorium and Largo Argentina, the Theatres of Pompey, Balbus and Marcellus with their porticoes, Agrippa's Pantheon and baths, the Saepta, the Stadium and Odeum of Domitian, the Baths of Nero, the Mausoleum of Augustus, the Ara Pacis and Horologium, and the Antonine columns. Largest perimeter of the inner regions and the city's great showcase.

r:reg_X.note: Within the lines of the first pomerium described by Tacitus (Ann. 12.24). Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_X.character: The Palatine: the hut of Romulus and the archaic sanctuaries, Republican aristocratic houses, the House of Augustus and Temple of Apollo, and from Domitian the imperial palace (Domus Flavia and Augustana) with the Severan extension over the Circus, the Adonaea gardens and the Temple of Elagabalus. The palace dominated, but service quarters and insulae on the slopes give it 2642/2742 insulae.

r:reg_XI.note: Very irregular; bounded by the Tiber and Regions IX, VIII, X, XII and XIII. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_XI.character: The valley of the Circus Maximus with the Forum Boarium and the river port: the round Temple of Hercules Victor, the Temple of Portunus, the Ara Maxima, the Statio Annonae, the Arch of the Argentarii and the Janus Quadrifrons, and the quays by the Pons Aemilius. Commercial and religious, with only 15 balnea and 20 lacus.

r:reg_XII.note: Bounded by the Via Appia and Region I, the Aurelian Wall, and the vici of the Porta Raudusculana and the Piscina Publica (Viale Aventino line). Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_XII.character: The eastern Aventine (Aventinus minor, S. Saba) and the valley of the Via Appia, named after the old public swimming pool: the Baths of Caracalla, the Septem Domus Parthorum, the Cohors IV vigilum, the house of Cilo, and later the Fourth-century mansions. Aristocratic houses among horrea.

r:reg_XIII.note: Between Regions XII and XI, the Aurelian Wall and the Tiber. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_XIII.character: The Aventine and the river plain below it: the Temples of Diana, Juno Regina, Minerva and Ceres, the private baths of Sura and Decius, the Armilustrium, then the Emporium, the Porticus Aemilia, the Horrea Galbana and Lolliana and Monte Testaccio, the city's great warehouse and import district. Hence 35 horrea.

r:reg_XIV.note: Limits not precisely fixable: it extended beyond the Aurelian Wall south to the Temple of Fors Fortuna and north to take in the Vatican district.
