Drawn to the Janiculum ridge and the Vatican plain as far as the Mausoleum of Hadrian. Polygon drawn to the 4th-century limits implied by the Regionary Catalogue (Hulsen, in Platner-Ashby s.v. Regiones Quattuordecim), following streets, walls and the Tiber; adjacent regions share vertices exactly. 'catalogue' gives the Curiosum readings and 'catalogueNotitia' the Notitia where they differ (parallel edition after Nordh 1949 / Valentini-Zucchetti 1940). The perimeter figures of the catalogues are in Roman feet; compare 'measured'.
r:reg_XIV.character: Everything on the right bank, with the Tiber Island: the river port and Jewish and Syrian communities of Trastevere, the Naumachia of Augustus and its grove, the Gaianum and the Horti of Caesar, Agrippina and Domitia, the Janiculum with its mills and the Lucus Furrinae, and to the north the Vatican with the Circus of Gaius and Nero, the Phrygianum, Hadrian's Mausoleum and, from Constantine, St Peter's. The largest region by perimeter and the most populous in vici (78).

r:serv_suburana.summary: The first of the four Servian regions (Varro LL 5.46-48): the Caelian within the Servian Wall, the Ceroliensis (the low ground of the later Colosseum valley and Carinae edge) and the Subura valley between the Esquiline and the Viminal-Quirinal.
scholarship: Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
r:serv_suburana.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

r:serv_esquilina.summary: Second Servian region (Varro LL 5.49-50): the Oppius and Cispius with the Fagutal, inside the agger.
scholarship: Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
r:serv_esquilina.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

r:serv_collina.summary: Third Servian region (Varro LL 5.51-52): the Quirinal and Viminal hills (colles) inside the Servian Wall.
scholarship: Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
r:serv_collina.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

r:serv_palatina.summary: Fourth Servian region (Varro LL 5.53-54): the Palatium, Germalus and Velia.
scholarship: Platner-Ashby (1929) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Richardson, NTDAR (1992) s.v. Regiones Quattuor
Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
r:serv_palatina.note: The four tribal regions attributed to Servius Tullius; the Capitol, Forum, Aventine and Campus lay outside them. Limits are schematic (along the Servian Wall and the valley floors); Suburana and Esquilina, Suburana and Collina, and Suburana and Palatina share edges. Superseded by the 14 Augustan regions in 7 BC; the start date is the traditional Servian era.

e:execution_of_brutus_sons_comitium.summary: The consul L. Junius Brutus sat on the tribunal while his own sons, caught plotting to restore the Tarquins, were stripped, flogged and beheaded at the stake. Livy stresses that the whole people watched the father's face rather than the punishment.
e:execution_of_brutus_sons_comitium.note: Legendary tradition. Livy places the punishment at the consuls' tribunal; the Comitium is the conventional site of such public executions.
e:execution_of_brutus_sons_comitium.locName: consular tribunal in the Comitium, at the NW corner of the Forum

e:tarquin_grain_into_tiber.summary: The standing grain on the Tarquins' land between city and river was cut and tipped into the Tiber. Livy reports the tradition that the sheaves caught on the shallows and silted into the Tiber Island; the confiscated field became the Campus Martius.
e:tarquin_grain_into_tiber.note: Aetiological legend; the island is a natural rock outcrop.
e:tarquin_grain_into_tiber.locName: the Tiber Island, said to have formed from the Tarquins' grain

e:publicola_demolishes_velia_house.summary: Suspected of aiming at kingship because his house towered over the Forum from the Velia, P. Valerius had it demolished overnight and rebuilt at the foot of the slope. The people repaid him with the name Publicola.
e:publicola_demolishes_velia_house.note: Later tradition located the house near the Vica Pota shrine at the foot of the Velia.
e:publicola_demolishes_velia_house.locName: summit of the Velia overlooking the Forum, later site of the Temple of Venus and Roma

e:dedication_capitoline_temple_509.summary: The consul M. Horatius Pulvillus dedicated the Capitoline temple on the Ides of September, holding the doorpost while his enemies tried to stop him with false news of his son's death. The Ides of September remained the temple's anniversary.
e:dedication_capitoline_temple_509.note: 509 is the Varronian year of the first consuls; Polybius (3.22.1) dates them 28 years before Xerxes' crossing, i.e. 508/507 BC.
e:dedication_capitoline_temple_509.locName: doorway of the cella of the Capitoline temple

e:horatius_cocles_bridge.summary: When Porsenna's army stormed the Janiculum and drove the Romans to the river, Horatius Cocles held the far end of the wooden Pons Sublicius until it was cut down behind him, then swam back in armour. A statue of him stood in the Comitium.
e:horatius_cocles_bridge.note: Legend. The exact site of the Pons Sublicius is debated; it lay just below the Pons Aemilius near the Forum Boarium.
e:horatius_cocles_bridge.locName: the Janiculum (west) end of the Pons Sublicius

e:mucius_scaevola_janiculum.summary: C. Mucius crossed to Porsenna's camp across the Tiber, killed the king's secretary by mistake and, threatened with fire, thrust his right hand into the altar flames. The land later given to him across the river was called the Mucia Prata.
e:mucius_scaevola_janiculum.note: Legend; camp position is a guess.
e:mucius_scaevola_janiculum.locName: Etruscan camp across the Tiber below the Janiculum

e:cloelia_statue_sacra_via.summary: The hostage Cloelia led the girls held by Porsenna across the Tiber under a hail of spears. Rome honoured her with an equestrian statue, the first to a woman, set up at the summit of the Sacra Via.
e:cloelia_statue_sacra_via.locName: summit of the Sacra Via on the Velia

e:temple_saturn_dedication_497.summary: The temple at the foot of the Capitol was dedicated on 17 December, the day of the Saturnalia. It held the state treasury (aerarium) for the whole of the Republic.
e:temple_saturn_dedication_497.locName: Temple of Saturn, NW end of the Forum

e:debt_riot_forum_495.summary: An elderly veteran, enslaved for debt and covered in fresh weals, burst into the Forum and told his story; the crowd rose against the creditors and nearly lynched the senators, starting the crisis that led to the plebs' secession.

e:temple_mercury_dedication_495.summary: The consuls quarrelled over who should dedicate the new temple of Mercury, the merchants' god, facing the Circus Maximus; the people gave the honour to a senior centurion, M. Laetorius, who also founded the merchants' guild. The anniversary fell on the Ides of May.
e:temple_mercury_dedication_495.locName: Temple of Mercury on the Aventine side of the Circus Maximus valley

e:temple_ceres_liber_libera_493.summary: Sp. Cassius dedicated the temple vowed during a famine, at the foot of the Aventine above the starting gates of the Circus. Built in Tuscan style with terracottas by the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus, it became the headquarters of the plebeian aediles.
e:temple_ceres_liber_libera_493.note: Exact site not excavated; placed from the ancient descriptions near the carceres. No ancient source states the dedication day; 19 April assumes it fell on the Cerialia.
e:temple_ceres_liber_libera_493.locName: Temple of Ceres at the NW foot of the Aventine, above the Circus Maximus carceres

e:instauratio_ludi_romani_490.summary: Before the Roman Games a master had a slave driven under the yoke and flogged through the middle of the Circus. Jupiter then appeared in a dream to the plebeian T. Latinius complaining that the 'leading dancer' had displeased him, and the games were repeated.
e:instauratio_ludi_romani_490.locName: the arena of the Circus Maximus

e:spurius_cassius_house_razed.summary: Accused of aiming at kingship, the three-times consul Sp. Cassius was condemned; his house was pulled down and the open space in front of the later Temple of Tellus in the Carinae was said to mark the spot.
e:spurius_cassius_house_razed.note: The Temple of Tellus (268 BC) stood in the Carinae near the Velia; its exact plan is unknown.
e:spurius_cassius_house_razed.locName: open area in front of the Temple of Tellus, Carinae

e:temple_castor_dedication_484.summary: A. Postumius' son dedicated the temple vowed at Lake Regillus beside the spring of Juturna, where the Dioscuri had been seen watering their horses after the battle. The Ides of July and the cavalry parade (transvectio equitum) were tied to it.
e:temple_castor_dedication_484.locName: Temple of Castor beside the Lacus Iuturnae, SE side of the Forum

e:vestal_oppia_buried_483.summary: Amid prodigies during the Veientine war, the soothsayers blamed neglected rites; the Vestal Oppia was convicted of unchastity and buried alive at the Colline Gate.
e:vestal_oppia_buried_483.locName: the Campus Sceleratus inside the Colline Gate

e:temple_dius_fidius_466.summary: Sp. Postumius dedicated the temple of the oath god Semo Sancus Dius Fidius on the Quirinal, near the later Porta Sanqualis; it kept the treaty with Gabii written on an ox hide and a bronze statue said to be of Tanaquil.
e:temple_dius_fidius_466.locName: Temple of Semo Sancus on the Quirinal near the Porta Sanqualis

e:herdonius_seizes_capitol_460.summary: A Sabine adventurer with some 2500 exiles and slaves landed by night from the Tiber and seized the Capitol and Arx, calling on slaves to rise. The consul P. Valerius retook the citadel with Tusculan help and was killed in the assault.

e:cincinnatus_prata_quinctia.summary: Envoys found L. Quinctius Cincinnatus digging his four-iugera farm across the Tiber, opposite the later navalia; his wife fetched his toga from the hut and he was hailed dictator. The plot was remembered as the Prata Quinctia.
e:cincinnatus_prata_quinctia.note: Livy: 'trans Tiberim, contra eum ipsum locum ubi nunc navalia sunt'. The navalia are themselves disputed (Campus Martius bend or Testaccio); placed opposite the Campus Martius bend.
e:cincinnatus_prata_quinctia.locName: the Prata Quinctia across the Tiber, opposite the Navalia

e:twelve_tables_comitium_450.summary: The decemvirs' code, the first written Roman law, was engraved on bronze (or wooden) tablets and fixed in public view in the Comitium in front of the speakers' platform; tradition says the Gauls destroyed the originals in 390.
e:twelve_tables_comitium_450.locName: the Comitium, before the old Rostra

e:verginia_killed_cloacina.summary: When the decemvir Appius Claudius adjudged Verginia a slave so he could have her, her father seized a butcher's knife from a stall by the shrine of Venus Cloacina, at the shops later called the Tabernae Novae, and stabbed her rather than see her dishonoured. The act triggered the second secession.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
e:verginia_killed_cloacina.note: Livy names the spot precisely: 'prope Cloacinae ad tabernas, quibus nunc Novis est nomen'. The round base of the Cloacina shrine survives in front of the Basilica Aemilia.
e:verginia_killed_cloacina.locName: beside the shrine of Venus Cloacina at the Tabernae Novae, N side of the Forum in front of the later Basilica Aemilia

e:second_secession_aventine.summary: After Verginia's death the army mutinied and the plebs withdrew in arms first to the Aventine, then to the Mons Sacer, until the decemvirs resigned and the tribunate was restored. The Aventine became the plebs' hill par excellence.

e:aequimaelium_maelius_house.summary: The rich grain dealer Sp. Maelius, accused of buying popularity during famine, was cut down by the master of horse C. Servilius Ahala. His house below the Capitol was razed and the empty plot was called the Aequimaelium.
e:aequimaelium_maelius_house.note: The Aequimaelium is attested near the Vicus Iugarius at the SE foot of the Capitol (Liv 24.47.15).
e:aequimaelium_maelius_house.locName: the Aequimaelium on the Vicus Iugarius below the Capitol

e:temple_apollo_medicus_431.summary: The consul Cn. Iulius dedicated the temple vowed during the plague of 433, in the Flaminian meadows outside the Porta Carmentalis. Its later rebuilding by C. Sosius gave it the name Apollo Sosianus.
e:temple_apollo_medicus_431.locName: Temple of Apollo, Prata Flaminia beside the later Theatre of Marcellus

e:juno_veii_to_aventine.summary: After the fall of Veii young men in white asked the cult statue of Juno Regina whether she wished to go to Rome; she was said to nod assent. Camillus vowed her a temple on the Aventine, dedicated in 392.
e:juno_veii_to_aventine.locName: Temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine

e:aius_locutius_nova_via_391.summary: The plebeian M. Caedicius heard in the silence of the night, on the Nova Via above the temple of Vesta, a voice louder than human telling him to warn the magistrates that the Gauls were coming. Ignored, the warning was atoned for after the sack with an altar to Aius Locutius, 'the Speaker'.
e:aius_locutius_nova_via_391.note: Livy: 'in Nova Via, ubi nunc sacellum est supra aedem Vestae'.
e:aius_locutius_nova_via_391.locName: the Nova Via above the Temple of Vesta, below the Palatine

e:fabius_dorsuo_quirinal_sacrifice.summary: During the siege of the Capitol, C. Fabius Dorsuo came down in ritual dress carrying the sacred vessels, walked through the Gallic pickets to perform his clan's sacrifice on the Quirinal, and returned unharmed.
e:fabius_dorsuo_quirinal_sacrifice.locName: the Quirinal, at the Fabian family cult site

e:geese_of_juno_arx.summary: Gauls climbed by night up the cliff near the shrine of Carmentis. The dogs stayed silent but the sacred geese of Juno, spared despite the famine, cackled; M. Manlius woke, threw the first Gaul off the summit and saved the citadel.
e:geese_of_juno_arx.note: Legend. The climb was 'ad Carmentis', near the Porta Carmentalis on the SW side; the geese were on the Arx where Juno Moneta was later built (344).
e:geese_of_juno_arx.locName: the Arx, at the sanctuary of Juno where the sacred geese were kept (later Temple of Juno Moneta)

e:gallic_gold_vae_victis.summary: When the defenders agreed to pay a thousand pounds of gold, the Gauls used false weights and Brennus threw his sword on the scale with the words 'woe to the conquered'. Tradition says Camillus arrived at that moment and refused the payment.
e:gallic_gold_vae_victis.locName: the Comitium / Forum below the Capitol

e:busta_gallica.summary: The Gauls who died of disease in the summer of the siege were heaped up and burned in a low place in the city, which kept the name Busta Gallica, 'the Gallic pyres'.
e:busta_gallica.note: Varro lists the Busta Gallica with the Doliola and Aequimaelium; probably in the valley below the Capitol.
e:busta_gallica.locName: the Busta Gallica, a low area near the Forum (site uncertain)

e:flamen_buries_sacra_doliola.summary: Before the Gauls arrived the flamen Quirinalis and the Vestals buried those sacred objects they could not carry away in small jars beside the flamen's house near the Cloaca Maxima. The spot, the Doliola, was afterwards taboo for spitting.
e:flamen_buries_sacra_doliola.locName: the Doliola beside the Cloaca Maxima, Velabrum / Forum Boarium

e:albinius_cart_vestals.summary: Climbing the Janiculum road with the rest of the fleeing crowd, the plebeian L. Albinius saw the Vestals on foot with the sacred objects, put his wife and children out of his wagon and drove the priestesses to Caere.
e:albinius_cart_vestals.locName: the road up the Janiculum beyond the Sublician bridge

e:gallic_entry_porta_collina.summary: Shortly after the Allia (the next day in Livy, the third day in Plutarch) the Gauls found the Colline Gate open and the walls unguarded. They marched down to the Forum, where the old ex-magistrates sat waiting in their robes of office in the atria of their houses.
e:gallic_entry_porta_collina.note: Livy says the Gauls entered 'porta Collina'. The Servian wall in stone postdates the sack; gate position is that of the later Porta Collina. Year is Varronian (390); Polybius (1.6.1-2) synchronises the sack with the Peace of Antalcidas and Dionysius' siege of Rhegium, i.e. 387/386 BC, the date most historians accept.
e:gallic_entry_porta_collina.locName: the Porta Collina at the N end of the Quirinal

e:marcus_papirius_strikes_gaul.summary: A Gaul stroked the beard of the ex-consul M. Papirius, who sat motionless in his curule chair in his atrium; Papirius struck him with his ivory staff and was killed, and the massacre of the old men began.
e:marcus_papirius_strikes_gaul.locName: atria of the nobles' houses around the Forum

e:rebuilding_after_gauls_389.summary: Rejecting a move to Veii, the Romans rebuilt in a year, taking stone and timber where they liked; Livy explains the crooked streets and the sewers running under houses by this haste.
e:rebuilding_after_gauls_389.locName: the whole city around the Forum

e:manlius_lucus_petelinus_trial.summary: Prosecuted for aiming at kingship, Manlius kept pointing to the Capitol he had saved; the tribunes moved the assembly to the Petelian grove outside the Porta Flumentana, from where the Capitol could not be seen, and he was condemned.
e:manlius_lucus_petelinus_trial.note: Grove placed just outside the gate in the low ground of the Campus near the river.
e:manlius_lucus_petelinus_trial.locName: the Lucus Petelinus outside the Porta Flumentana, by the Tiber

e:manlius_thrown_tarpeian.summary: The man who had saved the Capitol from the Gauls was hurled from the cliff of the same hill. His house on the Arx was razed and the gens Manlia forbade its members the name Marcus; the Temple of Juno Moneta later rose on the site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
e:manlius_thrown_tarpeian.note: The Rock's exact location is disputed (S face above the Vicus Iugarius / Forum Holitorium vs. the SE corner above the Forum).
e:manlius_thrown_tarpeian.locName: the Tarpeian Rock, S cliff of the Capitol

e:camillus_vows_concord_367.summary: As the struggle over the Licinian-Sextian laws threatened civil war, the old dictator Camillus vowed a temple to Concord if the orders were reconciled; the first plebeian consul followed.
e:camillus_vows_concord_367.locName: the site of the Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol

e:ludi_scaenici_364.summary: With plague raging and no human remedy, Etruscan dancers were brought in to perform to the pipe; Livy dates the beginning of Roman drama to this attempt to placate the gods. The performances were held in the Circus valley.

e:nail_driven_capitol_363.summary: To end a plague the elders recalled that a nail had once been driven into the wall of Jupiter's temple, on the side of Minerva's chapel, to mark the year; L. Manlius Imperiosus was named dictator just to drive it.
e:nail_driven_capitol_363.locName: right wall of the Capitoline temple, by the cella of Minerva

e:marcus_curtius_chasm.summary: A chasm opened in the middle of the Forum and the seers said it would close only when Rome's chief strength was thrown in. The young knight M. Curtius rode in fully armed; the pit closed over him and the pool that remained was the Lacus Curtius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:marcus_curtius_chasm.note: One of three aetiologies of the Lacus Curtius (others: the Sabine Mettius Curtius; the consul C. Curtius of 445 who fenced a lightning-struck spot). The paved, fenced area survives.
e:marcus_curtius_chasm.locName: the Lacus Curtius, paved enclosure in the centre of the Forum

e:juno_moneta_dedication_344.summary: L. Furius Camillus dedicated the temple vowed against the Aurunci on the site of Manlius' razed house. Later the Roman mint worked beside it, which is why money is 'moneta'.
e:juno_moneta_dedication_344.locName: Temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx

e:rostra_beaks_antium.summary: After the capture of the Antiate fleet some ships were burned and their bronze beaks (rostra) were fixed to the platform on the edge of the Comitium, which gave the Rostra its name. C. Maenius' column stood nearby.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
e:rostra_beaks_antium.locName: the old Rostra on the S edge of the Comitium

e:appius_claudius_aqua_appia.summary: The censor Appius Claudius brought Rome's first aqueduct underground from the east, to end at the Salinae by the Porta Trigemina, and began the Via Appia from the Porta Capena.
e:appius_claudius_aqua_appia.locName: terminal of the Aqua Appia near the Porta Trigemina, Forum Boarium

e:flavius_concord_shrine_volcanal.summary: The freedman's son and aedile Cn. Flavius, who had published the legal formulas and calendar on whitened boards around the Forum, dedicated a small bronze shrine of Concord in the Graecostasis on the Volcanal against the will of the nobles.
e:flavius_concord_shrine_volcanal.locName: the Area Volcani / Graecostasis beside the Comitium

e:ogulnii_wolf_ficus_ruminalis.summary: With fines collected from moneylenders the aediles Cn. and Q. Ogulnius placed a statue group of the twins suckled by the wolf beside the Ficus Ruminalis at the Lupercal, and a bronze quadriga on the roof of Jupiter's temple.
e:ogulnii_wolf_ficus_ruminalis.locName: the Ficus Ruminalis by the Lupercal, SW foot of the Palatine

e:pudicitia_plebeia_vicus_longus.summary: Excluded from the patrician shrine of Pudicitia in the Forum Boarium because she had married a plebeian, the patrician Verginia set apart part of her house on the Vicus Longus as an altar for plebeian matrons.
e:pudicitia_plebeia_vicus_longus.locName: her house on the Vicus Longus (valley between Quirinal and Viminal)

e:first_sundial_quirinus_293.summary: L. Papirius Cursor dedicated the Temple of Quirinus vowed by his father and, according to Pliny's source, set up the first sundial in Rome there.
e:first_sundial_quirinus_293.locName: Temple of Quirinus on the Quirinal

e:aesculapius_snake_island_291.summary: Envoys brought back from Epidaurus a sacred snake embodying the healing god. As the ship came up the Tiber it slipped overboard and swam to the island, where the temple of Aesculapius was then built; the island was later dressed in travertine as a ship.
e:aesculapius_snake_island_291.locName: Temple of Aesculapius at the downstream end of the Tiber Island

e:third_secession_janiculum_287.summary: Over debts the plebs seceded for the last time, to the Janiculum; the dictator Q. Hortensius ended it with the law making the decisions of the plebeian assembly binding on all.

e:appius_caecus_curia_280.summary: When the senate was inclined to accept Pyrrhus' peace offered by his envoy Cineas, the old, blind Appius Claudius had himself carried into the senate house and shamed the senators into refusing to treat while Pyrrhus remained in Italy. Cineas reported that the senate was an assembly of kings.

e:first_gladiatorial_munus_forum_boarium.summary: Decimus and Marcus Brutus Pera honoured their dead father with three pairs of gladiators fighting in the cattle market. Gladiators would later move to the Forum and, centuries later, to the amphitheatres.

e:catana_sundial_rostra_263.summary: M'. Valerius Messalla brought a sundial from captured Catana and set it on a column beside the Rostra. Its lines, drawn for Catana, did not match the hours at Rome, but Romans told the time by it for 99 years.
e:catana_sundial_rostra_263.locName: on a column beside the old Rostra

e:columna_rostrata_duilius_260.summary: After the naval victory at Mylae, Duilius was honoured with a column decorated with ship beaks near the Rostra, and allowed a torch-bearer and piper to escort him home from dinner.
e:columna_rostrata_duilius_260.locName: Columna rostrata near the Rostra / Volcanal

e:claudia_wishes_another_fleet.summary: Jostled by the crowd as she left the games, Claudia, sister of the admiral who had thrown the sacred chickens overboard and lost the fleet at Drepana, said she wished her brother were alive to lose another fleet and thin out the mob. The aediles fined her.

e:metellus_saves_palladium_241.summary: When the temple of Vesta caught fire the pontifex maximus L. Caecilius Metellus ran into the shrine, which no man might enter, and carried out the Palladium; he lost his sight and was granted the right to ride to the senate in a carriage.

e:livius_andronicus_first_play.summary: At the Roman Games of 240 the Greek freedman Livius Andronicus staged the first scripted play in Latin, a translation from Greek. Performances were in temporary wooden stands near the Circus.
e:livius_andronicus_first_play.locName: temporary stage at the Ludi Romani, Circus Maximus valley

e:janus_closed_235.summary: After the First Punic War the consul T. Manlius Torquatus closed the doors of the Ianus Geminus at the Argiletum, the sign that Rome was at peace, for the first time since King Numa. They were open again within a few years.
e:janus_closed_235.locName: the Ianus Geminus at the Forum end of the Argiletum

e:burial_alive_forum_boarium_228.summary: On orders from the Sibylline books, a Gallic man and woman and a Greek man and woman were buried alive in a stone chamber in the cattle market, a rite repeated in 216 and 114/113.
e:burial_alive_forum_boarium_228.locName: an underground chamber in the Forum Boarium

e:circus_flaminius_built_220.summary: As censor, C. Flaminius built the Via Flaminia and laid out the Circus Flaminius in the Prata Flaminia, an open arena for assemblies, markets and the Taurian games.
e:circus_flaminius_built_220.locName: Circus Flaminius in the southern Campus Martius

e:rome_after_trasimene_217.summary: News of Trasimene brought crowds to the Comitium and the Curia; toward sunset the praetor M. Pomponius announced from the Rostra: 'pugna magna victi sumus'. Women waited at the gates for news of their men.
e:rome_after_trasimene_217.locName: Comitium before the Curia; announcement from the Rostra

e:saturnalia_reformed_217.summary: After Trasimene the Saturnalia were renewed with a sacrifice at the Temple of Saturn, a lectisternium arranged by senators and a public banquet, and the cry 'Io Saturnalia' resounded through the city day and night.

e:vestals_buried_216.summary: Amid the panic after Cannae two Vestals were convicted of unchastity: one was buried alive at the Colline Gate, the other killed herself; the scribe who had seduced one was beaten to death in the Comitium. Gauls and Greeks were again buried alive in the Forum Boarium.
e:vestals_buried_216.note: The Campus Sceleratus lay inside the Servian wall just right of the road at the Porta Collina (Liv 8.15.8).
e:vestals_buried_216.locName: the Campus Sceleratus inside the Colline Gate

e:fire_salinae_carmentalis_213.summary: A fire burned for two nights and a day, levelling everything between the salt stores and the Porta Carmentalis, including the Aequimaelium, the Vicus Iugarius and the temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta, and spread widely outside the gate, where the temple of Spes also had to be rebuilt.
e:fire_salinae_carmentalis_213.locName: between the Salinae and the Porta Carmentalis, around the twin temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta (Sant'Omobono)

e:hannibal_at_colline_gate_211.summary: Marching on Rome to draw the army from Capua, Hannibal camped by the Anio and rode with 2000 horsemen to the temple of Hercules outside the Colline Gate to inspect the walls. Romans later boasted the land of his camp sold at full price during the siege.
e:hannibal_at_colline_gate_211.locName: the Temple of Hercules outside the Porta Collina

e:fire_forum_quinquatrus_210.summary: On the night before the Quinquatrus fires broke out at several points: the Seven Shops, the fish market, the Atrium Regium and the shops around the Lautumiae burned, and the Temple of Vesta was saved by thirteen slaves, who were freed. Campanian nobles were convicted of arson.
e:fire_forum_quinquatrus_210.locName: the N side of the Forum: Septem Tabernae, Forum Piscarium, Atrium Regium

e:hymn_procession_207.summary: To expiate prodigies, a procession led by two white heifers and 27 maidens singing a hymn by Livius Andronicus went from the Temple of Apollo through the Porta Carmentalis and the Vicus Iugarius into the Forum, then by the Vicus Tuscus and the Velabrum through the Forum Boarium to the temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine.
e:hymn_procession_207.locName: route: Porta Carmentalis, Vicus Iugarius, Forum, Vicus Tuscus, Velabrum, Forum Boarium, Aventine

e:vestal_fire_out_206.summary: The eternal fire in the Temple of Vesta was found extinguished through the negligence of a Vestal; she was scourged by the pontifex maximus and a day of supplication was decreed.

e:magna_mater_arrives_204.summary: The black meteorite of Cybele from Pessinus, received at Ostia by P. Scipio Nasica, was passed hand to hand by the leading matrons to the city and placed in the Temple of Victoria on the Palatine on 12 April, a day made a festival with gifts, a lectisternium and the first games, the Megalesia.
e:magna_mater_arrives_204.locName: Temple of Victoria on the Palatine (later beside the Temple of Magna Mater)

e:triumph_scipio_africanus_201.summary: Scipio returned from Africa to the most splendid triumph yet seen, depositing 123,000 pounds of silver in the treasury in the Temple of Saturn and closing at the Capitol.
e:triumph_scipio_africanus_201.locName: the treasury in the Temple of Saturn, on the triumphal route up the Clivus Capitolinus

e:ludi_romani_pompa.summary: Before the races the pompa circensis wound from the Capitol down through the Forum, along the Vicus Tuscus and the Velabrum to the Circus Maximus: the magistrate in triumphal dress, youths on horseback, chariots, athletes, dancers in armour and satyrs, and the images of the gods.
e:ludi_romani_pompa.note: Annual; Dionysius follows Fabius Pictor's description of the 3rd-century BC procession.
e:ludi_romani_pompa.locName: the Porta Pompae of the Circus Maximus at the end of the procession

e:lex_oppia_women_protest_195.summary: When the wartime law limiting women's gold and coloured clothing came up for repeal, matrons blocked every street and approach to the Forum, besieging the doors of the tribunes who opposed it, despite Cato's speech; the law was repealed.
e:lex_oppia_women_protest_195.locName: the streets and approaches to the Forum and Capitol

e:tiber_flood_porta_flumentana_193.summary: The Tiber flooded the low-lying parts of the city and several buildings collapsed around the Porta Flumentana, the river gate between Forum Holitorium and Forum Boarium.
e:tiber_flood_porta_flumentana_193.locName: around the Porta Flumentana on the river bank

e:plautus_curculio_comitium.summary: In the Curculio the stage manager tells the audience where to find every kind of Roman: perjurers in the Comitium, liars and braggarts at the shrine of Cloacina, rich spendthrift husbands under the basilica, and solid rich citizens strolling in the lower Forum.
e:plautus_curculio_comitium.note: Play dated c. 193 BC; the year is approximate.
e:plautus_curculio_comitium.locName: the Comitium and the shrine of Cloacina

e:plautus_curculio_moneylenders.summary: The same speech sends the audience to the Tabernae Veteres for those who lend and borrow at interest, to the open drain in mid-Forum for show-offs, and behind the Temple of Castor for men 'whom you would be foolish to trust'.
e:plautus_curculio_moneylenders.locName: the Tabernae Veteres on the S side of the Forum, and behind the Temple of Castor

e:plautus_curculio_vicus_tuscus.summary: In the Etruscan street running from the Forum to the Velabrum, says the Curculio, 'are men who sell themselves', a jibe at male prostitutes in the busy commercial street.
e:plautus_curculio_vicus_tuscus.locName: the Vicus Tuscus between Forum and Velabrum

e:plautus_curculio_velabrum.summary: Plautus closes his tour in the Velabrum, the low market quarter under the Palatine, 'where you will find a baker, a butcher or a soothsayer'.

e:flood_two_bridges_192.summary: A violent flood of the Tiber destroyed two bridges and many buildings, especially around the Porta Flumentana; a rock-fall from the Capitol onto the Vicus Iugarius killed many people.
e:flood_two_bridges_192.locName: Vicus Iugarius below the Capitol, and the Porta Flumentana

e:fire_forum_boarium_192.summary: A fire broke out in the Forum Boarium and for a day and a night the buildings facing the Tiber burned, with all the shops and their costly goods.
e:fire_forum_boarium_192.locName: riverside buildings of the Forum Boarium

e:ox_climbs_roof_carinae_191.summary: Among the prodigies of 191, an ox in the Carinae climbed the stairs of a building onto its tiled roof. The haruspices ordered it burned alive and its ashes thrown into the Tiber.
e:ox_climbs_roof_carinae_191.locName: a building in the Carinae, between the Velia and the Oppian

e:bacchanalia_lucus_stimulae_186.summary: The freedwoman Hispala Faecenia told the consul Postumius of nocturnal Bacchic rites in the grove of Stimula near the Aventine and the Tiber. The senate's decree led to thousands of arrests and executions across Italy.
e:bacchanalia_lucus_stimulae_186.note: Ovid (Fasti 6.503) places the grove of Stimula near the Tiber at the Aventine.
e:bacchanalia_lucus_stimulae_186.locName: the grove of Stimula at the foot of the Aventine by the Tiber

e:basilica_porcia_184.summary: As censor, Cato bought two private houses and four shops at the Lautumiae next to the Curia and built Rome's first named basilica, a covered hall for business and the tribunes' bench.
e:basilica_porcia_184.locName: beside the Curia Hostilia at the Lautumiae, NW corner of the Forum

e:numa_books_burned_comitium.summary: Workmen digging on the Janiculum in the field of the scribe L. Petillius found two stone chests inscribed with Numa's name, one empty and one holding Greek and Latin books on religion. The praetor judged them subversive and they were burned in the Comitium by the sacrificial attendants.
e:numa_books_burned_comitium.locName: a fire in the Comitium; the chests found on the Janiculum

e:basilica_fulvia_179.summary: The censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior built a basilica behind the new shops (argentariae novae) on the north side of the Forum, the predecessor of the Basilica Aemilia.
e:basilica_fulvia_179.locName: N side of the Forum behind the Tabernae Novae

e:fulvius_marble_tiles_173.summary: Q. Fulvius Flaccus took half the marble roof tiles of the temple of Juno at Croton for his new Temple of Fortuna Equestris in Rome. The senate ordered them returned, but no workman could refit them and they lay in the temple court.
e:fulvius_marble_tiles_173.locName: Temple of Fortuna Equestris near the later Theatre of Pompey

e:gracchus_buys_scipio_house_169.summary: The censor Ti. Sempronius Gracchus bought the house of Scipio Africanus behind the Old Shops by the statue of Vortumnus, together with the butchers' stalls and shops, and built the Basilica Sempronia on the site. Caesar's Basilica Julia later replaced it.
e:gracchus_buys_scipio_house_169.locName: behind the Tabernae Veteres near the Vortumnus statue, under the later Basilica Julia

e:triumph_aemilius_paullus_167.summary: For three days spoils of Macedon passed through the decorated city: statues and paintings on 250 wagons, then gold and silver, then the captive King Perseus and his children. Paullus' two young sons had died just before and after the triumph.
e:triumph_aemilius_paullus_167.locName: the triumphal route along the Sacra Via to the Capitol

e:carneades_lectures_155.summary: On the Athenian embassy of philosophers, Carneades spoke one day in praise of justice and the next refuted it, captivating Roman youth; Cato had the senate send the envoys home quickly.
e:carneades_lectures_155.locName: the Graecostasis by the Comitium, where envoys waited (lectures at unknown places)

e:theatre_demolished_lupercal_154.summary: A permanent theatre begun by the censors on the slope from the Lupercal toward the Palatine was torn down on the motion of Scipio Nasica Corculum as harmful to public morals; spectators were made to stand.
e:theatre_demolished_lupercal_154.locName: slope from the Lupercal up the Palatine

e:porticus_metelli_146.summary: Q. Caecilius Metellus surrounded the temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno Regina in the Campus with a portico and set in front the bronze equestrian group of Alexander's companions at the Granicus by Lysippus; Jupiter Stator was the first marble temple in Rome.
e:porticus_metelli_146.locName: Porticus Metelli (later Porticus Octaviae), southern Campus Martius

e:crassus_turns_to_forum_145.summary: The tribune C. Licinius Crassus, speaking from the Rostra, broke with custom by turning to face the open Forum and the people rather than the Comitium and the senate house, a gesture remembered as transferring power to the people.
e:crassus_turns_to_forum_145.note: Plutarch (CG 5) attributes the same gesture to Gaius Gracchus.
e:crassus_turns_to_forum_145.locName: the old Rostra, between Comitium and Forum

e:aqua_marcia_to_capitol_140.summary: The praetor Q. Marcius Rex built the high-level Aqua Marcia and, against the objection of the decemvirs who consulted the Sibylline books, carried its water up to the Capitol.
e:aqua_marcia_to_capitol_140.locName: the Capitol, terminus of the Aqua Marcia

e:octavius_deposed_133.summary: When his colleague M. Octavius vetoed the land bill, Tiberius Gracchus had the tribes vote him out of office; Octavius was hauled from the Rostra by Gracchus' freedmen, an unprecedented step.
e:octavius_deposed_133.locName: the Rostra and the voting space of the Forum

e:nasica_leads_senators_fides.summary: The senate met in the Temple of Fides on the Capitol while Gracchus' assembly gathered outside. When the consul refused to act, the pontifex maximus Scipio Nasica pulled his toga over his head and led senators and their clients out, armed with broken benches.
e:nasica_leads_senators_fides.note: Fides stood near the Area Capitolina; its plan has not been securely identified.
e:nasica_leads_senators_fides.locName: Temple of Fides beside the Capitoline temple precinct

e:tiberius_gracchus_killed_capitol.summary: Tiberius tripped over bodies as he fled toward the doors of Jupiter's temple and was beaten to death with a bench leg near the statues of the kings; some 300 supporters died. The bodies were thrown into the Tiber by night, the first political bloodshed in the city since the kings.
e:tiberius_gracchus_killed_capitol.locName: Area Capitolina, before the doors of the Temple of Jupiter by the statues of the kings

e:gaius_gracchus_moves_below_forum.summary: To show his sympathy with the people, Gaius Gracchus left his house on the Palatine and moved to the district below the Forum where the poor and humble lived.
e:gaius_gracchus_moves_below_forum.note: Plutarch's phrase 'the area below the agora' probably means the low quarters toward the Velabrum.
e:gaius_gracchus_moves_below_forum.locName: the crowded district below the Forum

e:gracchus_tears_down_stands.summary: Magistrates had built stands around the Forum to rent seats for a gladiatorial show; when they refused to remove them, Gracchus had his workmen tear them down in the night so the poor could watch free.
e:gracchus_tears_down_stands.locName: temporary stands around the Forum square

e:antyllus_killed_capitol_121.summary: While the consul Opimius sacrificed on the Capitol, his attendant Antyllus insulted Gracchus' supporters and was stabbed to death with writing styluses. Opimius displayed the body in the Forum and obtained the senate's emergency decree.
e:antyllus_killed_capitol_121.locName: the Capitol, at the consul's morning sacrifice

e:gracchans_occupy_aventine.summary: Fulvius Flaccus armed his men with Gallic spoils from his house and occupied the Aventine around the Temple of Diana; Opimius attacked up the hill with infantry and Cretan archers and the Gracchans broke.
e:gracchans_occupy_aventine.locName: the Temple of Diana on the Aventine

e:pomponius_laetorius_hold_bridge.summary: As Gaius fled downhill, his friend Pomponius held his pursuers at the Porta Trigemina and Laetorius at the Pons Sublicius, both fighting until killed, so that Gaius could cross the river.
e:pomponius_laetorius_hold_bridge.locName: the Porta Trigemina and the Pons Sublicius

e:gaius_gracchus_dies_furrina.summary: Gaius reached the sacred grove of Furrina on the Janiculum with one slave, Philocrates, who killed him and then himself. His head was cut off and brought to Opimius, who had promised its weight in gold; 3000 of his followers were later executed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
e:gaius_gracchus_dies_furrina.locName: the Lucus Furrinae on the Janiculum slope (site of the later Syrian sanctuary at Villa Sciarra)

e:vecordiae_opus_concord_121.summary: Opimius restored the Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol to celebrate the restoration of order. One night someone carved beneath its inscription: 'A work of madness makes a temple of Concord'.
e:vecordiae_opus_concord_121.locName: Temple of Concord below the Tabularium

e:temple_castor_rebuilt_117.summary: L. Caecilius Metellus Dalmaticus rebuilt the Temple of Castor on a high podium with a speakers' platform at its front, used thereafter for public meetings and legislative assemblies.

e:vestal_trial_burial_114.summary: After the Vestal Helvia was killed by lightning, three Vestals were tried for unchastity with knights; two were condemned. The Sibylline books again required a Gallic and a Greek couple to be buried alive in the Forum Boarium, and the temple of Venus Verticordia was founded.
e:vestal_trial_burial_114.locName: Forum Boarium, and the Atrium Vestae

e:jugurtha_contio_111.summary: Brought to Rome under safe-conduct to testify, Jugurtha was presented to a contio in the Forum; when the tribune Memmius questioned him, the bribed tribune Baebius ordered him to keep silent. Leaving Rome, he is said to have called it 'a city for sale'.

e:jugurtha_tullianum_104.summary: After walking in Marius' triumph Jugurtha was stripped, his earrings torn off with the lobes, and lowered into the underground cell of the Carcer. 'Hercules, how cold your bath is!' he said; he starved to death six days later.
e:jugurtha_tullianum_104.locName: the Tullianum, lower chamber of the Carcer below the Capitol

e:memmius_killed_comitia_100.summary: During the voting for the consuls of 99, Saturninus' and Glaucia's men clubbed to death the candidate C. Memmius in front of the assembly, turning opinion and the senate against them.
e:memmius_killed_comitia_100.note: Appian places the murder 'in the midst of the voting'; consular elections were held in the Campus Martius.
e:memmius_killed_comitia_100.locName: the voting enclosure (Ovile/Saepta) of the Campus Martius

e:triumphal_route_porta_triumphalis.summary: Triumphs mustered in the Campus Martius near the Villa Publica and entered the city by the Porta Triumphalis by the Circus Flaminius, then passed through the Forum Boarium and the Circus Maximus, around the Palatine and down the Sacra Via to climb the Capitol.
scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
e:triumphal_route_porta_triumphalis.note: Representative; the gate's position is disputed (near S. Omobono or the Circus Flaminius).
e:triumphal_route_porta_triumphalis.locName: the Porta Triumphalis (placed as in the gates layer, near the Porta Carmentalis; its position is disputed)

e:saturninus_stoned_curia_100.summary: Besieged on the Capitol after the senate's emergency decree, Saturninus, Glaucia and their followers surrendered to Marius, who shut them in the Curia Hostilia for safety. A mob climbed onto the roof, tore off the tiles and stoned them to death.
e:saturninus_stoned_curia_100.locName: inside the Curia Hostilia, struck through its roof

e:drusus_stabbed_atrium_91.summary: Returning home from the Forum with a crowd of clients, the tribune M. Livius Drusus was stabbed with a cobbler's knife in the dark atrium of his house on the Palatine; he died saying the state would not soon find another like him. His death sparked the Social War.
e:drusus_stabbed_atrium_91.note: Velleius tells how Drusus wanted the house open to every eye; it passed to Crassus and then Cicero. Site on the Palatine slope above the Forum, exact plot unknown.
e:drusus_stabbed_atrium_91.locName: atrium of Drusus' house on the N slope of the Palatine (later Cicero's house)

e:asellio_killed_castor_89.summary: The praetor A. Sempronius Asellio, who had ruled in favour of debtors, was attacked by moneylenders while offering sacrifice before the Temple of Castor; he fled toward the Temple of Vesta and was killed in a nearby tavern.
e:asellio_killed_castor_89.note: Valerius Maximus (9.7.4) places the sacrifice before the Temple of Concord; Appian (BC 1.54) says he was sacrificing to Castor and Pollux in the Forum.
e:asellio_killed_castor_89.locName: in front of the Temple of Castor

e:riot_castor_sulla_hides_88.summary: Sulpicius' armed men broke up a meeting of the consuls by the Temple of Castor and killed the son of the consul Pompeius Rufus; Sulla escaped by taking refuge in the house of his enemy Marius before leaving for his army.
e:riot_castor_sulla_hides_88.locName: the Forum by the Temple of Castor

e:sulla_forum_esquilinum_88.summary: Sulla's legions entered by the Esquiline Gate; met by a hail of tiles from the rooftops and Marius' improvised force at the Forum Esquilinum, Sulla seized a torch, ordered the houses burned and drove the Marians back toward the Temple of Tellus.
e:sulla_forum_esquilinum_88.locName: the Forum Esquilinum inside the Porta Esquilina

e:sulpicius_head_rostra_88.summary: Betrayed by a slave, the tribune Sulpicius was killed and his head was set up on the Rostra, the first time a magistrate's head was displayed there.

e:octavius_killed_janiculum_87.summary: When Cinna and Marius took Rome, the consul Cn. Octavius refused to flee and sat in his robes on his curule chair on the Janiculum; Censorinus' horsemen cut off his head, the first consul's head to be hung on the Rostra.
e:octavius_killed_janiculum_87.locName: the Janiculum, where Octavius waited on his curule chair

e:merula_suicide_capitol_87.summary: Summoned to trial by the Marians, L. Cornelius Merula, priest of Jupiter, took off his priestly cap, cut his veins in the Capitoline temple and spattered the god's altar with his blood, cursing his killers.
e:merula_suicide_capitol_87.locName: inside the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

e:marian_heads_rostra_87.summary: For five days Marius' slave bodyguard, the Bardyaei, killed whomever he did not greet; the heads of the orator M. Antonius and others were set on the Rostra.

e:gratidianus_edict_rostra_85.summary: The praetor Marius Gratidianus hurried from the tribunes' bench to the Rostra to publish alone the edict on the testing of debased coin; the grateful people set up his statues in every vicus with candles and incense.
e:gratidianus_edict_rostra_85.locName: the Rostra; statues at the compita of every vicus

e:capitol_burns_83.summary: On 6 July 83 the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus burned to the ground, perhaps by accident, destroying the Sibylline books and the treasures of four centuries.

e:gratidianus_killed_trans_tiberim_82.summary: In Sulla's proscriptions Catiline dragged Marius Gratidianus through the streets to the tomb of the Lutatii across the Tiber and there, at the grave of Catulus' father, broke his limbs and cut off his head.
e:gratidianus_killed_trans_tiberim_82.note: The tomb lay 'trans Tiberim'; site unknown.
e:gratidianus_killed_trans_tiberim_82.locName: the tomb of the Lutatii across the Tiber

e:proscription_lists_forum_82.summary: Sulla posted lists of the outlawed on whitened boards in the Forum; anyone could kill those named for a reward. The heads of the proscribed were piled at the Lacus Servilius at the head of the Vicus Iugarius.
e:proscription_lists_forum_82.locName: the Forum by the Rostra; heads at the Lacus Servilius

e:heads_lacus_servilius_82.summary: Seneca recalls the fountain basin at the head of the Vicus Iugarius as 'the spoliarium of Sulla's proscriptions', where the severed heads of senators were displayed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
e:heads_lacus_servilius_82.locName: the Lacus Servilius at the Forum end of the Vicus Iugarius, by the W corner of the later Basilica Julia

e:battle_colline_gate_82.summary: Pontius Telesinus' Samnites, marching to destroy Rome, fought Sulla's army under the walls at the Colline Gate from late afternoon into the night. Sulla's left wing was driven against the gate, but Crassus won on the right and the Samnites were annihilated.

e:massacre_villa_publica_82.summary: Sulla addressed the senate in the Temple of Bellona while some 6000 Samnite prisoners penned in the nearby Villa Publica were butchered. As the senators started at the screams, Sulla told them to pay attention: some criminals were being punished on his orders.
e:massacre_villa_publica_82.locName: the Villa Publica, with Sulla speaking in the Temple of Bellona nearby

e:sulla_triumph_81.summary: Sulla celebrated a two-day triumph with treasure from the East; returning exiles of the nobility followed his chariot calling him saviour and father.
e:sulla_triumph_81.locName: triumphal route along the Sacra Via

e:curia_cornelia_80.summary: To seat his enlarged senate of 600, Sulla rebuilt and enlarged the Curia; the statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades that had stood at the corners of the Comitium since the Samnite wars were removed.
e:curia_cornelia_80.locName: the Curia Hostilia / Cornelia and the corners of the Comitium

e:sulla_abdicates_79.summary: Sulla dismissed his lictors and bodyguard in the Forum and offered to account for his acts to anyone who asked; then he walked home through the crowd with his friends.

e:sulla_funeral_78.summary: Sulla's body was carried in a golden litter from Puteoli; matrons' spices filled 210 litters and formed an effigy of him in frankincense. After the laudation from the Rostra, knights and senators bore him to the Campus Martius, where he was the first Cornelius to be cremated.
e:sulla_funeral_78.note: The tomb was in the Campus Martius among the kings' burial places; exact site unknown.
e:sulla_funeral_78.locName: pyre and tomb in the Campus Martius

e:tabularium_built_78.summary: Q. Lutatius Catulus built the great substructure and record office closing the Forum's west end beneath the Capitol, recording it in an inscription that still survives.
e:tabularium_built_78.locName: the Tabularium on the E face of the Capitol

e:lepidus_defeated_milvian_77.summary: M. Aemilius Lepidus marched on the city at the head of disaffected Etruscans; Catulus and Pompey routed him at the Milvian Bridge and on the Janiculum outside the walls.
e:lepidus_defeated_milvian_77.locName: the Milvian Bridge on the Via Flaminia

e:pompey_leads_horse_censors_70.summary: During the review of the knights, the consul Pompey came down the Forum with his lictors leading his horse, and before the censors seated by the Temple of Castor declared that he had served all his campaigns under himself as general.
e:pompey_leads_horse_censors_70.locName: censors' tribunal in the Forum near the Temple of Castor

e:crow_falls_lex_gabinia_67.summary: When the law giving Pompey command against the pirates was debated, the shout of the crowd in the Forum was so great that a crow flying over it fell stunned among them.

e:caesar_restores_marius_trophies_65.summary: As aedile, Caesar had gilded statues and Victories commemorating Marius' victories secretly made and set up on the Capitol overnight; at dawn veterans wept at the sight, while Catulus denounced him in the senate.
e:caesar_restores_marius_trophies_65.locName: the Capitol, at the site of Marius' trophies

e:lightning_capitol_wolf_65.summary: Lightning struck statues on the Capitol, including the gilded she-wolf with the twins, the bronze tablets of the laws and an old statue of Jupiter; the haruspices foretold slaughter and civil strife, and a new statue of Jupiter was ordered facing east.

e:caesar_moves_domus_publica_63.summary: Elected pontifex maximus, Caesar left his modest house in the Subura for the official residence on the Sacra Via beside the Regia and the House of the Vestals.
e:caesar_moves_domus_publica_63.locName: the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

e:octavian_born_capita_bubula.summary: The future Augustus was born before sunrise on 23 September in a house on the Palatine at the place called Ad Capita Bubula, 'the Oxheads'; a shrine was later made there.
e:octavian_born_capita_bubula.note: Location of the Oxheads uncertain; usually placed on the NE side of the Palatine above the Sacra Via.
e:octavian_born_capita_bubula.locName: Ad Capita Bubula on the Palatine (NE slope toward the Sacra Via)

e:first_catilinarian_stator.summary: Cicero convened the senate in the fortified Temple of Jupiter Stator at the foot of the Palatine and attacked Catiline face to face: 'How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?' The senators left the benches around Catiline empty; he left Rome that night.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
e:first_catilinarian_stator.note: The temple's site near the Arch of Titus is accepted but its remains are not securely identified.
e:first_catilinarian_stator.locName: Temple of Jupiter Stator by the Porta Mugonia, at the top of the Sacra Via

e:allobroges_arrested_milvian_63.summary: In the small hours of 3 December the praetors Flaccus and Pomptinus, posted at either end of the Milvian Bridge, ambushed the Allobrogian envoys and Volturcius leaving Rome with the conspirators' letters.
e:allobroges_arrested_milvian_63.locName: both ends of the Milvian Bridge

e:senate_concord_conspirators_63.summary: Cicero led Lentulus by the hand from the Palatine to the Temple of Concord, where the senate heard the envoys and opened the sealed letters; Lentulus was made to resign his praetorship.

e:caesar_cato_debate_concord_63.summary: In the Temple of Concord, ringed by armed knights, Caesar argued for life imprisonment in Italian towns; Cato's speech for death carried the house.

e:catilinarians_strangled_tullianum.summary: Cicero led Lentulus down from the Palatine through the Forum to the Carcer, and the executioners strangled him, Cethegus, Statilius, Gabinius and Caeparius in the Tullianum, a cell twelve feet underground. Cicero announced to the crowd: 'They have lived.'
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:catilinarians_strangled_tullianum.locName: the Tullianum, lower chamber of the Carcer

e:cicero_buys_palatine_house_62.summary: Cicero borrowed to buy for 3.5 million sesterces the house of M. Crassus on the Palatine, formerly the house of Livius Drusus, overlooking the Forum, and joked that he was now so deep in debt he would join a conspiracy if anyone would have him.
e:cicero_buys_palatine_house_62.locName: Cicero's house on the N slope of the Palatine above the Forum

e:bona_dea_scandal_62.summary: During the women-only rites of the Good Goddess in Caesar's official house, P. Clodius slipped in disguised as a lute girl; recognised by his voice, he was chased out and the rites were profaned. Caesar divorced his wife: 'Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.'
e:bona_dea_scandal_62.locName: the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

e:pompey_triumph_61.summary: On his 45th birthday Pompey triumphed over fourteen nations, with placards recording 900 cities taken and an image of himself in pearls; he spent two days in the procession and did not need to kill the captive kings.
e:pompey_triumph_61.locName: triumphal route via the Sacra Via to the Capitol

e:bibulus_dung_castor_59.summary: When Bibulus tried to block Caesar's agrarian law from the steps of the Temple of Castor, a basket of dung was emptied over his head, his fasces were smashed and two tribunes wounded. He shut himself in his house for the rest of the year.
e:bibulus_dung_castor_59.locName: steps and speakers' platform of the Temple of Castor

e:clodius_fortifies_castor_58.summary: Clodius' gangs used the Temple of Castor as their stronghold in the Forum, storing arms there and tearing away its steps so it could not be stormed.
e:clodius_fortifies_castor_58.locName: Temple of Castor, its steps removed

e:cicero_house_demolished_58.summary: The day Cicero left for exile his Palatine house was plundered and burned; Clodius had the site consecrated to Libertas with a statue of a Greek courtesan from Tanagra and annexed part of it to his own neighbouring property.

e:catullus_salax_taberna.summary: Catullus attacks the regulars of 'the lusty tavern, the ninth pillar from the felt-capped brothers', the Temple of Castor and Pollux, where his girl now sits among them.
e:catullus_salax_taberna.note: 'a pileatis nona fratribus pila'; the pillars were probably those of the porticoes along the Vicus Tuscus or the Basilica Sempronia.
e:catullus_salax_taberna.locName: a tavern under the colonnade nine pillars from the Temple of Castor (toward the Vicus Tuscus)

e:forum_battle_quintus_left_dead_57.summary: When the bill to recall Cicero came before the assembly, Clodius' gladiators seized the Forum before dawn; the Tiber and the sewers were full of bodies and Quintus Cicero survived only by hiding under the corpses.

e:cicero_returns_porta_capena_57.summary: Returning from exile, Cicero found the steps of the temples at the Porta Capena crowded with the plebs; he walked through applauding crowds through the Forum to the Capitol.
e:cicero_returns_porta_capena_57.locName: the Porta Capena and the temple steps around it

e:clodius_attacks_workmen_57.summary: On 3 November armed men drove the workmen off the site of Cicero's house, threw stones at the house of Quintus nearby and set it on fire; a week later Cicero himself was attacked on the Sacra Via and took refuge in a doorway.
e:clodius_attacks_workmen_57.locName: the building site of Cicero's house on the Palatine, and the Sacra Via

e:megalesia_riot_56.summary: During the plays of the Megalesia, held before the Temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine, the aedile Clodius let a mob of slaves burst into the audience, which Cicero denounced as a sacrilege.
e:megalesia_riot_56.locName: the theatre space before the Temple of Magna Mater, Palatine

e:elephants_circus_55.summary: Twenty elephants were matched against Gaetulian hunters in the Circus Maximus; wounded and terrified, they tried to break through the iron railings and trumpeted so piteously that the crowd rose in tears and cursed Pompey.

e:catullus_searches_camerius.summary: Looking for his friend, Catullus tries the Campus Minor, the Circus, all the bookshops, the temple of great Jupiter and Pompey's new portico, where he accosts the girls.
e:catullus_searches_camerius.locName: the Porticus of Pompey (and the Campus, Circus, bookshops, Capitol)

e:theatre_pompey_dedication_55.summary: Pompey opened Rome's first permanent theatre, crowned by a temple of Venus Victrix so that the seats could pass as the temple's steps, with lavish games including plays, athletes and five days of beast hunts.
e:theatre_pompey_dedication_55.locName: Theatre of Pompey and the Temple of Venus Victrix on top of its cavea

e:tiber_flood_54.summary: The Tiber flooded the low city, soaking the brick-built houses, many of which collapsed; Dio says it was taken as a sign from the gods over the restoration of Ptolemy.
e:tiber_flood_54.locName: the low-lying Campus Martius and riverside

e:forum_iulium_land_54.summary: Through Cicero and Oppius, Caesar paid 60 million sesterces for private houses NW of the Forum to clear the site of the Forum Iulium; at the same time Aemilius Paullus rebuilt the Basilica Aemilia.
e:forum_iulium_land_54.locName: site of the Forum Iulium behind the Curia

e:julia_buried_campus_54.summary: When Pompey's wife and Caesar's daughter died in childbirth, the crowd seized her body from the funeral at the Alban villa and buried it in the Campus Martius, a rare honour, against the consul's objection.
e:julia_buried_campus_54.locName: tomb of Julia in the Campus Martius

e:clodius_body_burns_curia_52.summary: The day after Clodius was killed at Bovillae, his body was taken from his house on the Palatine to the Rostra; led by Sex. Cloelius the crowd carried it into the Curia Hostilia, built a pyre from benches, tables and the clerks' records, and burned it. The Curia and the adjoining Basilica Porcia were destroyed.
e:clodius_body_burns_curia_52.locName: inside the Curia Hostilia on the Comitium

e:milo_trial_52.summary: Milo was tried in the Forum ringed by Pompey's troops, while Pompey sat watching from the treasury by the Temple of Saturn. Unnerved by the soldiers and the Clodian crowd, Cicero spoke badly and Milo was condemned; the polished Pro Milone was written later.
e:milo_trial_52.locName: the Forum, with Pompey seated at the aerarium in the Temple of Saturn

e:isis_temple_axe_50.summary: When the senate ordered the shrines of Isis and Serapis demolished and no workman dared touch them, the consul L. Aemilius Paullus took off his toga, seized an axe and struck the doors himself.
e:isis_temple_axe_50.note: Valerius does not locate the shrine; Isis altars on the Capitol are attested in the 50s BC (Varro in Tertullian, Ad nat. 1.10).
e:isis_temple_axe_50.locName: an Isis shrine (probably on the Capitol)

e:caesar_seizes_aerarium_49.summary: When the tribune L. Metellus blocked the doors of the aerarium, Caesar told him it was harder for him to say than to do, and that he would kill him; the doors were forced and Caesar took the reserve, including the gold set aside against a Gallic invasion.
e:caesar_seizes_aerarium_49.locName: the aerarium in the Temple of Saturn

e:dolabella_riots_forum_47.summary: The tribune Dolabella barricaded the Forum to force through debt cancellation; Antony sent soldiers down from the Capitol, smashed the tablets of the law and some 800 people were killed, some thrown from the Tarpeian rock.
e:dolabella_riots_forum_47.locName: the Forum, entered from the Capitol

e:naumachia_codeta_46.summary: For his triumphal games Caesar had a lake dug in the lesser Codeta for a sea battle between Tyrian and Egyptian fleets with thousands of rowers; it was filled in after a plague in 43.
e:naumachia_codeta_46.note: The Codeta lay by the Tiber; whether the minor Codeta was in the Campus Martius or across the river is disputed.
e:naumachia_codeta_46.locName: basin in the Codeta Minor, NW Campus Martius

e:cleopatra_horti_caesaris_46.summary: Cleopatra stayed in Caesar's villa and gardens on the right bank of the Tiber, where Cicero visited and resented her arrogance; she left after the Ides of 44.
e:cleopatra_horti_caesaris_46.locName: Horti Caesaris on the right bank by the Via Portuensis

e:caesar_games_crush_46.summary: During Caesar's naval battle in the Codeta, crowds from all over Italy camped in tents in the streets and along the roads, and many people, including two senators, were crushed to death in the press.

e:caesar_axle_breaks_velabrum_46.summary: On the first day of his Gallic triumph, Caesar was nearly thrown out of his chariot when the axle broke in the Velabrum before the temple of Felicitas; he later climbed the steps of the Capitol on his knees, with forty elephants carrying torches on either side.
e:caesar_axle_breaks_velabrum_46.note: Dio names the temple of Tyche (Felicitas) built by Lucullus; the triumphal route passed through the Velabrum toward the Forum.
e:caesar_axle_breaks_velabrum_46.locName: the Velabrum, in front of the temple of Felicitas

e:vercingetorix_executed_46.summary: Held for six years since Alesia, the Gallic leader walked in Caesar's triumph and was then put to death, by tradition in the Carcer.

e:forum_iulium_dedication_46.summary: On the last day of his triumphs Caesar dedicated the Forum Iulium and the temple of his ancestress Venus Genetrix, with a gilded statue of Cleopatra beside the goddess, still unfinished.
e:forum_iulium_dedication_46.locName: Temple of Venus Genetrix at the head of the Forum Iulium

e:october_horse_46.summary: At the October festival the right-hand horse of the winning chariot was killed by the altar of Mars in the Campus Martius and the men of the Sacra Via and the Subura fought for its head, to nail it to the Regia or the Turris Mamilia. In 46 two rioting soldiers of Caesar were sacrificed in the same way and their heads hung on the Regia.
e:october_horse_46.note: Dio does not say the soldiers were killed at the October Horse festival, only that they were sacrificed in the Campus Martius by the pontiffs and the flamen of Mars during Caesar's triumphal celebrations; the link and the 15 October date are modern inferences.
e:october_horse_46.locName: the altar of Mars in the Campus Martius; heads to the Regia or the Turris Mamilia

e:caesar_statue_quirinus_45.summary: The senate voted a statue of Caesar inscribed 'to the unconquered god' in the Temple of Quirinus, the deified Romulus, prompting Cicero's quip that he preferred Caesar to share a temple with Quirinus rather than with Salus.
e:caesar_statue_quirinus_45.locName: Temple of Quirinus on the Quirinal

e:lupercalia_diadem_44.summary: Caesar sat on a golden chair on the Rostra watching the Lupercalia; Antony, naked but for the goatskin of a Lupercus, ran up and offered him a diadem wreathed with laurel. Caesar refused it to cheers and had it sent to Jupiter on the Capitol.
e:lupercalia_diadem_44.locName: the new Rostra at the NW end of the Forum

e:calpurnia_dream_44.summary: On the night before the Ides the doors and windows of Caesar's bedroom burst open; Calpurnia dreamed the gable ornament of the house fell and she held her murdered husband in her arms, and begged him not to go to the senate.
e:calpurnia_dream_44.locName: the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

e:murder_of_caesar_curia_pompeia.summary: At a meeting of the senate in the Curia of Pompey at the east end of Pompey's portico, the conspirators surrounded Caesar at his chair; stabbed 23 times, he covered his face with his toga and fell at the base of Pompey's statue, which ran with his blood.
scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:murder_of_caesar_curia_pompeia.note: The concrete foundation at the W edge of the Largo Argentina is identified as the Curia; Augustus later walled it up as a place of ill omen.
e:murder_of_caesar_curia_pompeia.locName: at the foot of Pompey's statue in the Curia of Pompey, behind Temples B and C at Largo Argentina

e:conspirators_seize_capitol_44.summary: With the senate fled and the people silent, Brutus and the conspirators, with gladiators of Decimus Brutus, marched to the Capitol proclaiming liberty and barricaded themselves there.

e:caesar_body_carried_home.summary: Caesar lay where he fell until three slaves put him on a litter and carried him home to the Domus Publica, one arm hanging down.
e:caesar_body_carried_home.locName: from the Curia Pompeia to the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

e:spurinna_ides_44.summary: At the entrance to the meeting, after unfavourable sacrifices, Caesar mocked the haruspex Spurinna, who had warned him of danger until the Ides; Spurinna replied that the Ides had come but not gone.
e:spurinna_ides_44.locName: the entrance of the Curia of Pompey

e:amnesty_temple_tellus_44.summary: Two days after the murder Antony convened the senate in the Temple of Tellus near his house in the Carinae; on Cicero's motion an amnesty was voted while Caesar's acts were confirmed.

e:caesar_funeral_rostra.summary: Caesar's body lay on an ivory couch in a gilded shrine modelled on the Temple of Venus Genetrix in front of the Rostra. Antony read the decrees of honours and the oaths of the senators to protect him, then held up the bloodstained toga; the crowd erupted.
e:caesar_funeral_rostra.locName: in front of the Rostra in the Forum

e:caesar_cremated_forum.summary: Instead of letting the body go to the pyre built in the Campus Martius, the crowd heaped benches, tribunals and shop tables on the spot in the Forum and burned it there; veterans threw in their arms, women their jewels. The Temple of Divus Julius later rose where the pyre stood.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:caesar_cremated_forum.locName: the pyre site at the E end of the Forum, marked by the round altar in front of the Temple of Divus Julius

e:helvius_cinna_lynched_44.summary: Leaving Caesar's funeral, the poet Helvius Cinna was mistaken for the conspirator L. Cornelius Cinna; the crowd tore him to pieces and carried his head around on a spear.

e:column_parenti_patriae_44.summary: Caesarians led by the false Marius (Amatius) raised a column of Numidian marble and an altar at the cremation site inscribed 'Parenti Patriae'; the consul Dolabella had it demolished and the leaders thrown from the Tarpeian rock or crucified.
e:column_parenti_patriae_44.locName: the cremation site in the Forum

e:antony_treasury_ops_44.summary: Antony took the 700 million sesterces Caesar had deposited in the Temple of Ops on the Capitol, using it to pay his debts and buy support.
e:antony_treasury_ops_44.locName: Temple of Ops on the Capitol

e:comet_caesar_star_44.summary: During Octavian's games in honour of Caesar's victories a comet blazed for seven days; the people took it for Caesar's soul received among the gods, and Octavian set a star on the head of Caesar's statue in the Temple of Venus Genetrix.
e:comet_caesar_star_44.locName: statue of Caesar in the Temple of Venus Genetrix

e:proscription_lists_43.summary: Antony, Octavian and Lepidus posted lists of the proscribed in the Forum, beginning with seventeen names and growing to some 300 senators and 2000 knights; heads were brought to the Rostra for the reward.

e:cicero_head_hands_rostra_43.summary: Antony ordered the head and the right hand that had written the Philippics nailed to the Rostra from which Cicero had spoken; Fulvia is said to have pierced the tongue with a hairpin. The crowd wept at the sight.

e:caesar_deified_42.summary: On 1 January 42 the triumvirs had the senate swear to uphold Caesar's acts and recognise him as Divus Iulius, with a temple to be built at the place in the Forum where he had been cremated.
e:caesar_deified_42.locName: the cremation site in the E Forum

e:oil_spring_trastevere.summary: At the Taberna Meritoria, a hostel for veteran soldiers across the Tiber, oil was said to have welled from the ground and flowed all day. Christian writers later read it as a sign of Christ's coming, and the site was claimed by Santa Maria in Trastevere.
e:oil_spring_trastevere.note: Date varies in the sources between 41 and 38 BC; association with S. Maria in Trastevere is medieval tradition.
e:oil_spring_trastevere.locName: the Taberna Meritoria across the Tiber (tradition: Santa Maria in Trastevere)

e:octavian_palatine_lightning_36.summary: Octavian bought the house of the orator Hortensius and neighbouring plots on the Palatine; when lightning struck part of the site the haruspices declared that the god wanted it, and Octavian vowed there the Temple of Apollo.
e:octavian_palatine_lightning_36.locName: the house of Augustus beside the Temple of Apollo, SW Palatine

e:horace_bore_sacra_via.summary: 'I was strolling by chance along the Sacra Via, as I do', when a man known only by name seized his hand. Horace could not shake him off past the Temple of Vesta, where the bore was due in court, until his opponent appeared and dragged him off: 'So Apollo saved me.'
e:horace_bore_sacra_via.locName: the Sacra Via by the Temple of Vesta

e:horace_evening_forum_marsyas.summary: Horace describes his carefree life: wandering around the swindling Circus and the evening Forum, stopping by the fortune-tellers, then home to a supper of leeks and chickpeas, and in the morning not having to face the statue of Marsyas, who cannot bear the face of the moneylender Novius.
e:horace_evening_forum_marsyas.locName: the Circus and the evening Forum by the statue of Marsyas

e:horace_witches_esquiline.summary: A wooden Priapus in Maecenas' new gardens on the Esquiline, laid over the old paupers' cemetery, tells how he scared off the witches Canidia and Sagana, digging up bones by night, with a loud crack of his fig-wood buttocks.
e:horace_witches_esquiline.locName: the Horti Maecenatis over the old Esquiline cemetery

e:agrippa_sails_cloaca_33.summary: As aedile Agrippa repaired the water system, built 700 basins and 500 fountains, and had himself rowed through the cleaned sewers to the Tiber as a public demonstration.
e:agrippa_sails_cloaca_33.locName: the Cloaca Maxima, outlet by the Pons Aemilius

e:war_spear_bellona_32.summary: Declaring war on Cleopatra rather than Antony, Octavian as fetial priest cast a bloodied spear from the column of war in front of the Temple of Bellona into a patch of ground treated as enemy territory.
e:war_spear_bellona_32.locName: the Columna Bellica before the Temple of Bellona

e:antony_will_read_senate_32.summary: Octavian seized Antony's will from the Vestals and read out to the senate its provisions: legacies to Cleopatra's children and burial beside her in Alexandria. Outrage swung opinion behind war.
e:antony_will_read_senate_32.locName: taken from the Vestals' keeping; read in the senate

e:horace_puteal_libonis.summary: Errands pursue Horace through Rome: 'Roscius begs you to be at the Puteal tomorrow before eight', the moneylenders' meeting place by the Temple of Castor and the Arch of Augustus in the Forum.
e:horace_puteal_libonis.locName: the Puteal Libonis, SE end of the Forum

e:janus_closed_29.summary: The senate decreed that the doors of the Ianus Geminus be closed, for only the third time in Roman history, to mark the end of the civil wars.

e:triple_triumph_29.summary: For three days Octavian triumphed over Illyricum, Actium and Egypt; on the third an effigy of Cleopatra with the asp was carried, with her children Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene walking behind.
e:triple_triumph_29.locName: triumphal route along the Sacra Via

e:temple_divus_iulius_dedication_29.summary: Octavian dedicated the temple of his deified father on the cremation site, its platform decorated with the beaks of ships from Actium, and held lavish games.
e:temple_divus_iulius_dedication_29.locName: Temple of Divus Iulius, E end of the Forum

e:curia_iulia_victory_29.summary: Octavian dedicated Caesar's new senate house and set inside it the statue of Victory from Tarentum on a globe, with an altar where senators offered incense before sessions; the altar would be fought over four centuries later.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:curia_iulia_victory_29.locName: the Curia Iulia, NW side of the Forum

e:apollo_palatinus_dedication_28.summary: Octavian dedicated the gleaming Luna-marble temple of Apollo next to his house, with the portico of the Danaids and the Greek and Latin libraries; Propertius describes the doors of ivory and the chariot of the Sun on the roof.

e:corona_civica_door_27.summary: The senate named Octavian Augustus and decreed that the doorposts of his Palatine house be wreathed with laurel and an oak wreath, the civic crown for saving citizens, be fixed above the door.
e:corona_civica_door_27.locName: the entrance of Augustus' house on the Palatine

e:marcellus_first_in_mausoleum_23.summary: Augustus' nephew and heir Marcellus died at 19 and was the first buried in the new Mausoleum in the Campus Martius; Virgil's lament in Aeneid 6 made Octavia faint when he read it to her.

e:tiber_flood_sublicius_23.summary: In the year of Augustus' illness the Tiber rose, swept away the wooden bridge and made the city navigable by boat for three days.

e:famine_riot_curia_22.summary: During plague and famine the people shut the senators in the Curia and threatened to burn them alive unless they voted Augustus the dictatorship; Augustus refused on his knees, baring his breast, and took the grain supply instead.

e:miliarium_aureum_20.summary: As curator of the roads, Augustus set up a gilded bronze column at the head of the Forum near the Temple of Saturn, listing the distances to the main cities of the empire.
e:miliarium_aureum_20.locName: Miliarium Aureum at the S end of the Rostra by the Temple of Saturn

e:horace_sosii_bookshop.summary: Horace teases his first book of Epistles, polished with the pumice of the Sosii, the booksellers, for eyeing 'Vertumnus and Janus' where it hopes to be put on sale, and predicts it will end up in the provinces as a schoolbook.
e:horace_sosii_bookshop.locName: the Sosii brothers' shop by the statue of Vertumnus and the arches of Janus

e:fortuna_redux_altar_19.summary: For Augustus' return from the East the senate consecrated an altar of Fortune the Home-bringer by the Porta Capena, beside the temples of Honos and Virtus; the day became the Augustalia.
e:fortuna_redux_altar_19.note: 12 October 19 BC is the day of Augustus' return, when the altar was voted (constituta) and the feriae created; the altar was dedicated on 15 December 19 BC (Fasti Amiternini).
e:fortuna_redux_altar_19.locName: beside the Porta Capena, by the Temple of Honos and Virtus

e:secular_games_tarentum_17.summary: On the night of 31 May Augustus sacrificed nine ewes and nine she-goats to the Moirai on altars by the Tiber at the Tarentum, followed by stage plays on a stage with no theatre and no seats; Augustus alone made the night sacrifices, while Agrippa joined him for the daytime sacrifices on the Capitol.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
e:secular_games_tarentum_17.note: The inscribed Acta were found in 1890 near the Tiber by Corso Vittorio Emanuele, close to the Tarentum. Marker on the underground altar of Dis and Proserpina found in 1886-87.
e:secular_games_tarentum_17.locName: the Tarentum by the Tiber in the NW Campus Martius
