e:carmen_saeculare_17.summary: On the last day 27 boys and 27 girls sang Horace's hymn before the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine and again on the Capitol. 'Carmen composuit Q. Horatius Flaccus', records the inscription.
e:carmen_saeculare_17.locName: before the Temple of Apollo Palatinus, then on the Capitol

e:propertius_vertumnus.summary: In Propertius' elegy the bronze statue of the Etruscan god Vertumnus, standing at the Forum end of the Vicus Tuscus, tells passers-by how he can be any shape and how he once was carved of maple.
e:propertius_vertumnus.locName: the signum Vortumni at the Forum end of the Vicus Tuscus

e:theatre_marcellus_dedication_13.summary: Augustus dedicated the theatre named for his nephew; during the games a tame tiger was shown for the first time and Augustus' curule chair collapsed beneath him.
e:theatre_marcellus_dedication_13.note: Dio puts the dedication in 13 BC; Pliny (NH 8.65) dates it, with the tame tiger, to 4 May 11 BC (consuls Tubero and Fabius Maximus).

e:vicus_tuscus_perfume_horace.summary: Horace imagines his bad poems used as wrapping paper in 'the street that sells incense, perfumes and pepper', the Vicus Tuscus.

e:agrippa_funeral_12.summary: Augustus delivered the funeral oration over his friend and son-in-law with a curtain hung between himself and the body, then placed his remains in his own Mausoleum.

e:augustus_pontifex_house_vesta_12.summary: Elected chief priest by a crowd from all Italy, Augustus did not move into the Domus Publica but gave it to the Vestals, made part of his own house public property and set up a shrine of Vesta beside it.
e:augustus_pontifex_house_vesta_12.locName: Augustus' Palatine house, with the new shrine of Vesta

e:obelisk_circus_maximus_10.summary: Augustus brought an obelisk from Heliopolis and set it up on the dividing barrier of the Circus Maximus, dedicated to the Sun, to mark the conquest of Egypt.
e:obelisk_circus_maximus_10.note: Now in Piazza del Popolo (Flaminio obelisk).
e:obelisk_circus_maximus_10.locName: the spina of the Circus Maximus

e:horologium_obelisk_10.summary: A second Egyptian obelisk became the gnomon of a huge meridian laid out in bronze letters on the pavement of the northern Campus Martius, near the Ara Pacis.
e:horologium_obelisk_10.locName: the meridian of Augustus, N Campus Martius

e:drusus_funeral_circus_flaminius_9.summary: The body of Drusus, dead in Germany, was escorted to Rome by Tiberius on foot. Tiberius spoke the laudation in the Forum and Augustus, who could not enter the city in mourning while holding command, spoke in the Circus Flaminius; the ashes went into the Mausoleum.
e:drusus_funeral_circus_flaminius_9.locName: the Circus Flaminius, outside the pomerium

e:ara_pacis_dedication_9.summary: The Altar of Augustan Peace, voted on his return from Spain and Gaul in 13 BC, was dedicated beside the Via Flaminia on Livia's birthday.
e:ara_pacis_dedication_9.locName: original site of the Ara Pacis by the Via Flaminia (under Palazzo Fiano)

e:porticus_liviae_7.summary: Augustus razed the extravagant house on the Oppian left to him by Vedius Pollio, who fed slaves to his lampreys, and built there a public portico in Livia's name with a shrine of Concord.
e:porticus_liviae_7.locName: Porticus Liviae on the Oppian (Esquiline) near the Clivus Suburanus

e:vici_lares_augusti_7.summary: After a fire around the Forum, Augustus reorganised the city into regions and neighbourhoods, each with elected vicomagistri who tended the Lares Augusti at the crossroads shrines. The altar of the Vicus Sandalarius (2 BC) shows Augustus with Livia and Gaius.
e:vici_lares_augusti_7.locName: compitum of the Vicus Sandalarius near the Templum Pacis (example)

e:compitalia_crossroads.summary: At the winter Compitalia every neighbourhood decorated its crossroads shrine, hung woollen dolls and balls for each free person and slave, and the vicomagistri in purple-bordered togas offered to the Lares; Augustus' reform tied the cult to his genius.
e:compitalia_crossroads.note: Annual; marker at a representative Subura crossroads.

e:naumachia_augusti_2.summary: Augustus dug a basin 1800 by 1200 Roman feet across the Tiber for a mock sea battle of Athenians and Persians with 30 warships and 3000 fighters; Ovid recommends the crowds as good hunting for lovers.

e:julia_revels_rostra_marsyas_2.summary: Augustus learned that his daughter Julia had held drunken revels in the Forum by night, on the very Rostra from which he had proposed his laws on adultery, and had crowned the statue of Marsyas. He exiled her to Pandateria.
e:julia_revels_rostra_marsyas_2.note: The Marsyas statue stood by the tribunal of the praetor near the Comitium; marker placed between the Rostra and the Lacus Curtius.
e:julia_revels_rostra_marsyas_2.locName: the Rostra and the statue of Marsyas in the Forum

e:ovid_ars_porticus_pompei.summary: The Ars Amatoria sends the would-be lover to saunter in the shade of Pompey's portico in summer, then to the porticoes of Octavia and Livia and the colonnade of the Danaids.
e:ovid_ars_porticus_pompei.locName: the Porticus of Pompey behind the theatre

e:ovid_ars_appiades.summary: Even the courts are good hunting: at the fountain of the Appiades by the Temple of Venus in Caesar's forum, Ovid jokes, the advocate is caught by love and can no longer argue his own case.
e:ovid_ars_appiades.locName: the Appiades fountain before the Temple of Venus Genetrix

e:ovid_ars_circus_seats.summary: In the Circus Maximus, says Ovid, no one stops you sitting thigh to thigh with a girl; ask whose horses are coming, brush dust from her dress, and back her favourite.
e:ovid_ars_circus_seats.locName: the seating of the Circus Maximus

e:ovid_ars_isis.summary: Ovid warns that the temple of Isis in the Campus Martius makes many girls what Io was to Jupiter, a place of assignations.

e:pater_patriae_curia_2.summary: After the plebs had acclaimed him at the theatre, Messalla spoke for the senate in the Curia, naming Augustus Pater Patriae; with tears in his eyes he replied that he had attained his highest hopes.

e:forum_augustus_dedication_2.summary: Forty years after the vow at Philippi, Augustus dedicated the temple of Mars the Avenger in his new forum, with the recovered Parthian standards inside and statues of the great men of Rome in the porticoes.
e:forum_augustus_dedication_2.note: The day is disputed: Ovid (Fasti 5.545-598) gives 12 May, Dio (60.5.3) has the games of Mars Ultor on 1 August; 1 August follows the latter view.
e:forum_augustus_dedication_2.locName: Temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus

e:ovid_last_night_capitol_8.summary: Ordered into exile, Ovid spent his last night in his house beside the Capitol, looking up at the temples 'joined in vain to my household' and praying to their gods before leaving at dawn.
e:ovid_last_night_capitol_8.note: Ovid says his house adjoined the Capitol; exact site unknown.

e:lupercalia_run_palatine.summary: Goats and a dog were sacrificed in the Lupercal cave; youths smeared with blood and laughing, naked but for goatskins, ran around the Palatine striking women with thongs of hide to make them fertile.
e:lupercalia_run_palatine.note: Annual rite on 15 February, celebrated until the 490s.
e:lupercalia_run_palatine.locName: from the Lupercal around the foot of the Palatine

e:megalesia_galli_palatine.summary: At the April games of Cybele the eunuch Galli paraded the goddess with drums, cymbals and pipes, and plays were staged before her temple on the Palatine.
e:megalesia_galli_palatine.locName: before the Temple of Magna Mater on the Palatine

e:parilia_bonfires_palatine.summary: On the birthday of the city shepherds and citizens purified themselves with ash and bean stalks from the Vestals and leapt over bonfires of straw; Ovid says he did so himself.
e:parilia_bonfires_palatine.locName: the Palatine, by the hut of Romulus

e:argei_pons_sublicius.summary: In mid-May (14 May in Ovid's calendar, the Ides in Dionysius) the Vestals threw 27 rush puppets in human shape from the wooden Pons Sublicius into the Tiber, a rite whose meaning puzzled Ovid and his contemporaries.
e:argei_pons_sublicius.note: Annual rite; Ovid's account dated to the Fasti (c. AD 8).

e:ovid_vestalia_barefoot.summary: Returning from the Vestalia, Ovid met a barefoot matron coming down the Nova Via where it joins the Forum; an old woman explained that the place was once a marsh, before the Velabrum was drained.
e:ovid_vestalia_barefoot.locName: the Nova Via where it joins the Forum

e:augustus_varus_doors_9.summary: At the news of the loss of three legions in Germany, Augustus did not shave for months and at times beat his head against the doors of his house crying out to Varus to return the legions.

e:ovid_book_sacra_via_10.summary: In Tristia 3.1 Ovid's book arrives in Rome and is led from the Forum of Caesar along the Sacra Via, past the Temple of Vesta and the Regia, to the old Porta Palatii and the Temple of Jupiter Stator.
e:ovid_book_sacra_via_10.locName: the Sacra Via past the Temple of Vesta and the Regia

e:ovid_book_augustus_door_10.summary: The book stares at the doorposts of Augustus' house, decked with arms and laurel and the oak crown, and wonders whether this is the house of Jupiter.
e:ovid_book_augustus_door_10.locName: doorway of Augustus' house on the Palatine

e:ovid_book_rejected_libraries_10.summary: The book climbs to the Palatine library by the Temple of Apollo and is refused, then tries the library in the Porticus Octaviae and the Atrium Libertatis, the first public library, and is refused again.
e:ovid_book_rejected_libraries_10.locName: the Palatine library at the Temple of Apollo; also the Porticus Octaviae and Atrium Libertatis

e:concord_rededicated_10.summary: Tiberius rebuilt the Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol from his German spoils, filling it with Greek masterpieces, and dedicated it in his own and his dead brother Drusus' names.

e:flood_ludi_forum_augusti_12.summary: The Tiber flooded the Circus Maximus so badly that the horse races of the Ludi Martiales were held in the Forum of Augustus instead.
e:flood_ludi_forum_augusti_12.locName: the Forum of Augustus, used as a racetrack

e:augustus_funeral_laudations_14.summary: Augustus' wax image lay on a gold and ivory couch; Drusus read a eulogy from the old Rostra and Tiberius the main laudation from the Rostra of the Temple of Divus Iulius.
e:augustus_funeral_laudations_14.locName: the Rostra of the Temple of Divus Iulius and the Rostra Vetera

e:augustus_cremation_campus_14.summary: Senators carried the body through the Porta Triumphalis to the pyre in the Campus Martius; an eagle was released from the flames and the ex-praetor Numerius Atticus swore he saw Augustus ascend. Livia gathered the bones for five days and laid them in the Mausoleum.
e:augustus_cremation_campus_14.note: Strabo describes the ustrinum of white marble with an iron railing near the Mausoleum.
e:augustus_cremation_campus_14.locName: the ustrinum of Augustus near the Mausoleum, N Campus Martius

e:tiber_flood_15.summary: Continuous rain raised the Tiber over the low parts of the city, wrecking houses and drowning people; the senate debated diverting its tributaries, and Tiberius created a board to manage the river.

e:germanicus_triumph_arch_17.summary: Germanicus triumphed over the Germans with the recovered standards of Varus; an arch near the Temple of Saturn commemorated their recovery.
e:germanicus_triumph_arch_17.locName: the Arch of Tiberius beside the Temple of Saturn

e:isis_scandal_paulina_19.summary: The knight Mundus bribed priests of Isis to tell the noble matron Paulina that the god Anubis desired her; she spent the night in the temple with Mundus. Tiberius crucified the priests, razed the temple and threw the statue of Isis into the Tiber.
e:isis_scandal_paulina_19.locName: the temple of Isis in the Campus Martius

e:germanicus_ashes_mausoleum_20.summary: Agrippina carried the urn from Brundisium; on the day it was placed in the Mausoleum the Campus Martius blazed with torches and crowds cried that the state had fallen.
e:germanicus_ashes_mausoleum_20.locName: the Mausoleum of Augustus and the Campus Martius

e:piso_statues_gemoniae_20.summary: During the trial of Cn. Piso for the death of Germanicus, the crowd outside the Curia dragged his statues to the Gemonian Stairs and was about to smash them. Piso's house, decorated for a banquet, looked down on the Forum.
e:piso_statues_gemoniae_20.locName: the Scalae Gemoniae below the Capitol

e:pompey_theatre_fire_22.summary: The scaena of Pompey's theatre burned; Tiberius promised to rebuild it under Pompey's name, and a statue of Sejanus was set up there for his part in saving the rest of the building.
e:pompey_theatre_fire_22.locName: the stage building of the Theatre of Pompey

e:castra_praetoria_built_23.summary: Sejanus gathered the nine praetorian cohorts, until then billeted around the city and Italy, into one fortified camp on the NE edge of Rome, a base that would make and unmake emperors.
e:castra_praetoria_built_23.locName: the Castra Praetoria beyond the Viminal

e:caelian_fire_27.summary: A fire devastated the Caelian. Only a statue of Tiberius in the house of the senator Junius was untouched, and the senate proposed renaming the hill Mons Augustus.

e:crowd_images_agrippina_curia_29.summary: When Tiberius' letter against Agrippina and her son Nero was read, the people gathered around the senate house carrying their portraits and shouting that the letter was forged.

e:sejanus_letter_apollo_31.summary: Sejanus came to the senate meeting in the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine expecting the tribunician power. The long letter from Capri ended by ordering his arrest; Macro had already replaced his guards with the vigiles.

e:sejanus_condemned_concord_31.summary: Led to the prison, Sejanus was condemned to death the same day by the senate meeting in the Temple of Concord next to the Carcer, while the crowd smashed his statues.
e:sejanus_condemned_concord_31.locName: the Temple of Concord next to the Carcer

e:sejanus_body_gemonian_stairs_31.summary: Sejanus was strangled in the Carcer and his body thrown down the Gemonian Stairs, where the mob abused it for three days before it was dragged with a hook into the Tiber; his children were later killed too.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
e:sejanus_body_gemonian_stairs_31.locName: the Scalae Gemoniae from the Carcer toward the Capitol

e:credit_crisis_33.summary: Enforcement of the old usury laws forced creditors to call in loans; land prices collapsed and debtors were ruined until Tiberius put up 100 million sesterces of interest-free loans through banks.
e:credit_crisis_33.locName: the bankers around the Ianus Medius and the Basilica Aemilia

e:drusus_caesar_starved_palace_33.summary: Germanicus' son Drusus, held in an underground room of the Palatine, died of hunger after chewing the stuffing of his mattress; Tiberius had the record of his last words read to the senate.
e:drusus_caesar_starved_palace_33.locName: a basement room of the Palatine palace

e:fire_aventine_circus_36.summary: A fire burned the part of the Circus Maximus next to the Aventine and the Aventine itself; Tiberius paid out 100 million sesterces in compensation.
e:fire_aventine_circus_36.locName: the Aventine and the adjacent side of the Circus Maximus

e:tiberius_funeral_37.summary: At the news of Tiberius' death the crowd shouted that his body should be thrown in the Tiber. It was brought to Rome, cremated in the Campus Martius with a eulogy by Caligula, and laid in the Mausoleum.
e:tiberius_funeral_37.locName: the Campus Martius and the Mausoleum of Augustus

e:caligula_bridge_capitol_39.summary: Caligula extended the palace down to the Forum, making the Temple of Castor its vestibule, where he would sit between the twin gods to be worshipped, and built a bridge over the Temple of Divus Augustus to link the Palatine with the Capitol.
e:caligula_bridge_capitol_39.locName: the Temple of Castor used as palace vestibule; bridge to the Capitol

e:caligula_money_basilica_iulia.summary: For several days Caligula threw large sums of coins down to the crowd from the roof of the Basilica Julia.
e:caligula_money_basilica_iulia.locName: the roof of the Basilica Julia

e:caligula_body_horti_lamiani_41.summary: Caligula's corpse was carried secretly to the Horti Lamiani on the Esquiline, half-burned and lightly buried; his ghost was said to haunt the place until his sisters reburied him.
e:caligula_body_horti_lamiani_41.locName: the Horti Lamiani on the Esquiline

e:caligula_murdered_cryptoporticus_41.summary: Leaving the Palatine games at midday, Caligula took a covered passage (crypta) toward the palace to see some boys from Asia rehearsing; the tribunes Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus struck him down with thirty wounds.
scholarship: Tomei, Il Palatino (1998)
e:caligula_murdered_cryptoporticus_41.note: Often linked to the surviving cryptoporticus under the Domus Tiberiana, which is in part later (Neronian).
e:caligula_murdered_cryptoporticus_41.locName: a covered passage (crypta) of the Palatine palace near the temporary theatre

e:claudius_behind_curtain_41.summary: Terrified, Claudius hid behind a curtain in a room of the palace called the Hermaeum; a soldier saw his feet, hailed him emperor and he was carried in a litter to the Castra Praetoria, where he promised each soldier 15,000 sesterces.
e:claudius_behind_curtain_41.locName: from the Hermaeum in the palace to the Castra Praetoria

e:claudius_knees_capitol_44.summary: Celebrating his British triumph, Claudius climbed the steps to the Capitoline temple on his knees, supported by his sons-in-law.
e:claudius_knees_capitol_44.locName: the steps up to the Capitoline temple

e:claudius_sick_slaves_island_47.summary: Owners abandoned sick and worn-out slaves on the island of Aesculapius to avoid the cost of care; Claudius decreed that any such slave who recovered was free.
e:claudius_sick_slaves_island_47.locName: the sanctuary of Aesculapius on the Tiber Island

e:messalina_killed_horti_lucullani_48.summary: After her bigamous marriage to C. Silius, Messalina fled to the Horti Lucullani on the Pincian, the gardens she had coveted from Valerius Asiaticus; a tribune sent by Narcissus ran her through as her mother Lepida urged her to die with dignity.
e:messalina_killed_horti_lucullani_48.locName: the Horti Lucullani on the Pincian

e:jews_expelled_trastevere_49.summary: Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were constantly rioting at the instigation of 'Chrestus', probably disputes over Jesus in the synagogues; Aquila and Priscilla left for Corinth. The Jewish community lived mainly across the Tiber.

e:claudius_pelted_crusts_51.summary: With only fifteen days' grain left, a mob caught Claudius in the middle of the Forum and pelted him with abuse and crusts, until he escaped through a back door into the palace.

e:caratacus_castra_51.summary: The captured British king was paraded with his family before the praetorians drawn up on the field in front of their camp; his speech to Claudius won pardon for him and his family.
e:caratacus_castra_51.locName: the parade ground before the Castra Praetoria

e:aqua_claudia_opened_52.summary: Claudius opened the two highest aqueducts of Rome on 1 August; their arcades crossed the Via Praenestina and Labicana in a monumental double gate, later part of the Aurelian Wall as Porta Maggiore.
e:aqua_claudia_opened_52.locName: the double arch of the aqueducts (Porta Maggiore)

e:nero_to_camp_54.summary: At noon on the day Claudius' death was announced, the doors of the palace opened and Nero went out with the prefect Burrus to the cohort on guard, was put in a litter and taken to the camp to be hailed emperor.
e:nero_to_camp_54.locName: from the palace steps to the Castra Praetoria

e:seneca_slave_dealers_castor.summary: Seneca, discussing insults, describes the slave dealers whose 'cages' of wretched slaves stood by the Temple of Castor; Plautus already placed shady dealers behind it.

e:britannicus_poisoned_55.summary: At dinner in the palace a cold-water chaser carried poison to Britannicus, who collapsed; Nero said it was epilepsy. He was buried in the Campus Martius that same night in a torrential downpour.
e:britannicus_poisoned_55.locName: the dining room of the palace on the Palatine

e:nero_wooden_amphitheatre_57.summary: Nero built a huge timber amphitheatre in the Campus Martius in a year, where he gave shows in which no one, not even a criminal, was killed.
e:nero_wooden_amphitheatre_57.locName: Nero's amphitheatre in the Campus Martius (site unknown)

e:juvenalia_nemus_caesarum_59.summary: To celebrate his first shave Nero held private games, the Juvenalia, in the grove by Augustus' naval basin across the Tiber, with booths selling luxuries; senators and old matrons were made to perform, and Nero sang to the lyre.
e:juvenalia_nemus_caesarum_59.locName: the Nemus Caesarum by the Naumachia Augusti, Trastevere

e:poppaea_statues_capitol_62.summary: At a rumour that Nero had recalled his divorced wife Octavia, the people climbed the Capitol, threw down the statues of Poppaea and carried Octavia's garlanded statues into the Forum and the temples.

e:tigellinus_banquet_stagnum_64.summary: Tigellinus gave Nero a feast on a raft towed by gilded boats on the Stagnum Agrippae, with brothels on the banks; days later Nero went through a mock wedding with the freedman Pythagoras.
e:tigellinus_banquet_stagnum_64.locName: the Stagnum Agrippae by the Baths of Agrippa

e:christians_nero_gardens_64.summary: To divert blame Nero punished the Christians: some were dressed in animal skins and torn by dogs, others crucified or set alight as night lamps in his gardens across the Tiber, while Nero mingled with the crowd dressed as a charioteer.
e:christians_nero_gardens_64.locName: Nero's gardens and circus in the Ager Vaticanus

e:peter_crucified_vatican.summary: Tradition places Peter's martyrdom in Nero's circus on the Vatican, 'between the two turning posts' near the obelisk, and his burial in the cemetery on the slope beside it, where the 'trophy' was shown by c. 200.
e:peter_crucified_vatican.locName: the spina of the Circus of Gaius and Nero by the obelisk

e:domus_aurea_begun_64.summary: On land cleared by the fire Nero built the Domus Aurea, a country estate in the city with a lake where the Colosseum now stands, a 120-foot colossus of himself in the vestibule and a revolving dining room: 'At last I can live like a human being.'
e:domus_aurea_begun_64.locName: the Esquiline (Oppian) pavilion of the Domus Aurea

e:nero_sings_tower_maecenas_64.summary: Suetonius says Nero watched the blaze from the tower in the gardens of Maecenas and, delighted by 'the beauty of the flames', sang the sack of Troy in stage costume; Tacitus reports it as a rumour that he sang on his private stage.
e:nero_sings_tower_maecenas_64.locName: the tower in the Horti Maecenatis on the Esquiline

e:refugees_campus_martius_64.summary: Nero opened the Campus Martius, the buildings of Agrippa and his own gardens to the homeless, put up temporary shelters, and cut the price of grain.
e:refugees_campus_martius_64.locName: the Campus Martius and the buildings of Agrippa

e:great_fire_starts_circus_64.summary: On the night of 19 July fire broke out in the shops full of flammable goods along the Circus Maximus where it adjoins the Palatine and Caelian; driven by wind it raced along the length of the Circus and up into the hills.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:great_fire_starts_circus_64.note: Tacitus: 'in ea parte circi ortum quae Palatino Caelioque montibus contigua est'.
e:great_fire_starts_circus_64.locName: the tabernae at the E (curved) end of the Circus Maximus, under the Palatine and Caelian

e:fire_stops_esquiline_64.summary: On the sixth day the fire was halted at the foot of the Esquiline by demolishing buildings to leave bare ground; it then broke out again in Tigellinus' Aemilian estate and burned three more days. Of fourteen regions only four were intact.
e:fire_stops_esquiline_64.note: The firebreak's exact line is unknown; marker at the foot of the Esquiline slopes on the side facing the burned districts (Subura).
e:fire_stops_esquiline_64.locName: the foot of the Esquiline, where a firebreak was cleared

e:fire_restarts_aemiliana_64.summary: The fire flared up again in the Aemilian property of Tigellinus in the Campus Martius, feeding the rumour that Nero wanted to found a new city named after himself.
e:fire_restarts_aemiliana_64.locName: the praedia Aemiliana of Tigellinus, Campus Martius

e:paul_tomb_ostiensis.summary: Paul, beheaded under Nero, was buried by tradition beside the Via Ostiensis, where the presbyter Gaius pointed to his 'trophy' c. 200; Constantine and then the three emperors of 386 built his basilica over it.
e:paul_tomb_ostiensis.locName: the tomb under the altar of San Paolo fuori le mura

e:lateranus_executed_esquiline_65.summary: Plautius Lateranus was dragged to the place reserved for the punishment of slaves and beheaded by a tribune, without even being allowed to embrace his children.
e:lateranus_executed_esquiline_65.note: The 'locus servilibus poenis sepositus' is usually placed in the Esquiline field outside the gate.
e:lateranus_executed_esquiline_65.locName: the execution ground outside the Porta Esquilina

e:poppaea_funeral_65.summary: Poppaea died from a kick by Nero while pregnant. Instead of cremation her body was embalmed with spices in the manner of foreign kings and placed in the Mausoleum of Augustus; Nero praised her beauty from the Rostra.
e:poppaea_funeral_65.locName: the Mausoleum of Augustus; eulogy on the Rostra

e:pisonian_plot_circus_65.summary: The conspirators planned to kill Nero at the Ludi Ceriales in the Circus, near the Temple of Ceres; the plot was betrayed the day before by the freedman Milichus.
e:pisonian_plot_circus_65.locName: the Circus Maximus near the Temple of Ceres

e:tiridates_crowned_rostra_66.summary: At dawn, before praetorians drawn up around the temples of the Forum, the Armenian king climbed the Rostra, knelt to Nero seated in triumphal dress, and received the diadem; Janus was closed.

e:golden_day_pompey_66.summary: For Tiridates, Nero had the whole interior of Pompey's theatre gilded in a day, with purple awnings embroidered with Nero driving a chariot among stars.

e:nero_ashes_domitii_tomb_68.summary: His nurses and Acte placed his remains in the family tomb of the Domitii on the Hill of Gardens, visible from the Campus Martius, in a porphyry sarcophagus; for years flowers appeared there.
e:nero_ashes_domitii_tomb_68.locName: tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian slope (near S. Maria del Popolo)

e:nero_flight_past_camp_68.summary: Barefoot and in a cloak, Nero rode out with four companions toward his freedman Phaon's villa between the Via Salaria and Nomentana; passing near the camp he heard the soldiers cheering Galba. He died at the villa that night.
e:nero_flight_past_camp_68.note: The Aurelian Porta Nomentana did not yet exist; marker on the line of the road just beyond the camp.
e:nero_flight_past_camp_68.locName: from the palace past the Castra Praetoria to the Nomentan road

e:otho_hailed_miliarium_69.summary: Otho slipped away from Galba's sacrifice at the Temple of Apollo and met 23 soldiers at the Golden Milestone below the Temple of Saturn, who hailed him and carried him in a litter to the camp.
e:otho_hailed_miliarium_69.locName: the Miliarium Aureum below the Temple of Saturn

e:galba_killed_lacus_curtius_69.summary: Carried in his chair into the crowded Forum, Galba was thrown out by his panicking bearers beside the Lacus Curtius. Otho's cavalry cut him down, offering his neck; his head was carried on a pole around the camp.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
e:galba_killed_lacus_curtius_69.locName: beside the Lacus Curtius in the centre of the Forum

e:piso_killed_vesta_69.summary: Galba's adopted heir took refuge in the Temple of Vesta, sheltered by a slave; he was dragged out and killed at the temple door.
e:piso_killed_vesta_69.locName: doorway of the Temple of Vesta

e:tiber_flood_otho_69.summary: A sudden flood broke the Pons Sublicius, flooded the low city and the Campus Martius and blocked the Via Flaminia, taken as an omen against Otho's campaign.
e:tiber_flood_otho_69.locName: the Pons Sublicius and the Campus Martius

e:vitellius_enters_rome_69.summary: Vitellius set out from the Milvian Bridge on horseback in uniform, ready to enter the city as a conqueror; his friends persuaded him to change into the toga, and his army filled the city.
e:vitellius_enters_rome_69.locName: from the Milvian Bridge to the Capitol

e:vitellius_abdication_rostra_69.summary: Dressed in black, Vitellius came down from the palace and offered his dagger to the consul before the Rostra; the crowd blocked the way to the Temple of Concord, where he meant to lay down his insignia, and forced him back to the palace.
e:vitellius_abdication_rostra_69.locName: the Rostra; the crowd blocked the road to the Temple of Concord

e:capitol_burns_flavian_69.summary: Vitellian troops stormed the Capitol where Flavius Sabinus held out, attacking up the Clivus Capitolinus and the Hundred Steps; fire spread from the houses to the porticoes and the Temple of Jupiter burned to the ground.
e:capitol_burns_flavian_69.locName: the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and the Clivus Capitolinus

e:domitian_escapes_isiac_69.summary: Hidden in the temple keeper's quarters, the young Domitian slipped out in linen as a devotee of Isis and hid with a client, Cornelius Primus, near the Velabrum.

e:sabinus_body_gemoniae_69.summary: Vespasian's brother was dragged in chains before Vitellius at the palace and hacked to death by the crowd; his head was cut off and his body thrown down the Gemonian Stairs.

e:flavian_fighting_campus_sallust_69.summary: The Flavian army attacked in three columns down the Via Flaminia, along the river and the Via Salaria; there was fighting in the Gardens of Sallust and the Campus Martius while the populace watched and cheered as at the games.
e:flavian_fighting_campus_sallust_69.locName: the Horti Sallustiani and the Campus Martius

e:castra_praetoria_stormed_69.summary: The last Vitellians fought from the walls and towers of the Castra Praetoria; the attackers battered the gates with siege methods and the defenders died to the last man.

e:vitellius_gemoniae_69.summary: Found hiding in a doorkeeper's lodge in the deserted palace, Vitellius was led half-naked with a noose round his neck through the Forum, forced to watch his statues fall, tortured and killed at the Gemonian Stairs; his body was dragged into the Tiber.
e:vitellius_gemoniae_69.locName: the Scalae Gemoniae, reached from the palace through the Forum

e:capitol_restoration_ceremony_70.summary: The area of the burned temple was purified with water from springs and rivers; the praetor Helvidius Priscus dedicated the site and magistrates, priests and people hauled the first stone with ropes. Vespasian later carried rubble on his own head.
e:capitol_restoration_ceremony_70.locName: the site of the Capitoline temple

e:flavian_triumph_porticus_octaviae_71.summary: After spending the night near the temple of Isis, Vespasian and Titus came at dawn, crowned with laurel, to the Porticus Octaviae where the senate waited; they offered prayers, breakfasted and set off through the Porta Triumphalis.
e:flavian_triumph_porticus_octaviae_71.locName: the Porticus Octaviae (start of the procession)

e:simon_bar_giora_executed_71.summary: As the triumph reached the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, the procession halted until news came that Simon son of Giora, led in the triumph with a noose around his neck, had been put to death in the Forum.
e:simon_bar_giora_executed_71.locName: the Forum / Carcer below the Capitol

e:jerusalem_spoils_templum_pacis_75.summary: Vespasian dedicated his Temple of Peace with a garden court and galleries of famous Greek works; the golden vessels of the Jerusalem Temple were displayed there, while the Law and purple veils were kept in the palace.

e:colossus_rededicated_sol_75.summary: Vespasian had Nero's 120-foot bronze statue in the vestibule of the Golden House given the rays of the Sun god and rewarded the engineer who proposed moving columns to the Capitol cheaply.
e:colossus_rededicated_sol_75.locName: the vestibule of the Domus Aurea on the Velia (later site of the Temple of Venus and Roma)

e:fire_campus_capitol_80.summary: While Titus was in Campania, a fire burned the Temple of Serapis and Isis, the Saepta, the Temple of Neptune, the Baths of Agrippa, the Pantheon, the Diribitorium, the Theatre of Balbus, Pompey's stage, the Porticus Octaviae and the newly rebuilt Capitoline temple.
e:fire_campus_capitol_80.locName: the central Campus Martius (Saepta, Pantheon, Iseum) and the Capitol

e:colosseum_inaugural_games_80.summary: Titus opened the Flavian Amphitheatre with a hundred days of games: 9000 animals killed in one day, women fighting beasts, cranes and elephants, and the arena flooded for a sea battle. Martial's Book of Spectacles celebrates the shows.
e:colosseum_inaugural_games_80.locName: the arena of the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:selius_dinner_hunt.summary: Martial follows the parasite Selius as he tries every haunt: the portico of Europa, the Saepta, the temples of Isis and Serapis, the Hecatostylon and Pompey's portico, then the baths of Fortunatus, Faustus, Gryllus and Lupus.
e:selius_dinner_hunt.locName: the Saepta and porticoes of the Campus Martius

e:capitoline_agon_stadium_86.summary: Domitian founded the four-yearly Capitoline contest in music, athletics and horsemanship, presiding in Greek dress with a crown bearing the Capitoline triad; the athletic events were held in his stadium in the Campus Martius.

e:martial_pear_tree_flat.summary: Martial tells an acquaintance not to send his slave all the way to his lodgings 'ad Pirum' on the Quirinal, up three high flights of stairs; better to buy his book at Atrectus' shop opposite Caesar's forum.
e:martial_pear_tree_flat.note: 'Ad Pirum' was a locality on the Quirinal; Martial later had a small house there (Mart 9.18, 10.58).
e:martial_pear_tree_flat.locName: Martial's flat at the Pear Tree on the Quirinal, third floor

e:atrectus_bookshop_argiletum.summary: 'Opposite Caesar's forum there is a shop with its doorposts covered with titles'; there Atrectus will hand over Martial's first book polished with pumice and purple for five denarii.
e:atrectus_bookshop_argiletum.locName: a bookshop in the Argiletum opposite the Forum of Caesar

e:secundus_bookshop_pacis.summary: Martial advertises a portable parchment edition of his poems sold by Secundus, freedman of Lucensis, 'behind the threshold of Peace and the Forum of Pallas', a rare early mention of the codex.
e:secundus_bookshop_pacis.locName: behind the Templum Pacis and the Forum of Nerva

e:secular_games_88.summary: Domitian held the Secular Games, reckoning from Augustus' rather than Claudius' celebration, with nocturnal rites by the Tiber at the Tarentum; Tacitus took part as one of the Fifteen.
e:secular_games_88.locName: the Tarentum in the NW Campus Martius

e:domitian_black_banquet.summary: Domitian invited senators and knights to a room painted entirely black, with tombstone-shaped place cards and boys painted black as ghosts; the terrified guests were sent home and then showered with gifts.
e:domitian_black_banquet.note: Dio places it after the Dacian war, c. 89.
e:domitian_black_banquet.locName: a dining room of the Domus Flavia

e:saturnalia_feast_amphitheatre.summary: Statius describes the Kalends of December when Domitian feasted the entire city in the amphitheatre: fruit and pastries rained from ropes, servers carried food to every row, and there were shows of women and dwarfs fighting by torchlight.

e:neronian_fire_altars_domitian.summary: In fulfilment of a vow made after the fire of 64, Domitian set up altars in every region to avert fires, with annual sacrifices on the Volcanalia; one survives on the Quirinal.
e:neronian_fire_altars_domitian.locName: altar of the Neronian fire on the Quirinal (Via del Quirinale)

e:vestal_cornelia_buried_91.summary: Domitian, as pontifex maximus, condemned the Chief Vestal Cornelia for unchastity without hearing her; protesting her innocence, she was led to the underground chamber at the Colline Gate and entombed. Her alleged lover Celer was beaten to death with rods in the Comitium.
e:vestal_cornelia_buried_91.note: Date given as 89-91; Celer's beating took place in the Comitium (Suet. Dom. 8.4).
e:vestal_cornelia_buried_91.locName: the Campus Sceleratus inside the Porta Collina

e:equus_domitiani_91.summary: A colossal bronze of Domitian on horseback was set up in the middle of the Forum, its forefoot on the head of the Rhine; Statius wrote a poem for its dedication. Its concrete foundation still lies in the square.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:equus_domitiani_91.locName: centre of the Forum Romanum, by the Lacus Curtius

e:domitian_edict_streets_92.summary: Martial celebrates an edict banning shopkeepers from encroaching on the streets: no more chained wine flasks on pillars, barbers shaving in the crowd, or cooks blocking the way. 'Now it is Rome; recently it was one big shop.'
e:domitian_edict_streets_92.locName: the shop-lined streets of the centre (Argiletum, Subura)

e:mamurra_shopping_saepta.summary: Martial's Mamurra spends a whole day in the luxury shops of the Saepta Julia, fingering slaves, tortoiseshell couches, Corinthian bronzes and crystal cups, and finally buys two cheap cups for an as.
e:mamurra_shopping_saepta.locName: the luxury shops of the Saepta Julia

e:martial_book_to_pliny_esquiline.summary: Martial sends his tenth book to Pliny on the Esquiline: up the steep path from the Subura, where it will see Orpheus dripping on top of his watery theatre and the animals around him, and Pliny's house just beyond.
e:martial_book_to_pliny_esquiline.locName: the Lacus Orphei at the top of the Clivus Suburanus, Esquiline

e:phyllis_ashes_gens_flavia_96.summary: His nurse Phyllis cremated him at her villa on the Via Latina and secretly mixed his ashes with those of his niece Julia in the Temple of the Flavian family on the Quirinal, built on the site of his birthplace.
e:phyllis_ashes_gens_flavia_96.locName: the Templum Gentis Flaviae on the Quirinal (site of Domitian's birthplace 'ad Malum Punicum')

e:domitian_shields_torn_curia_96.summary: The senate packed into the Curia abused the dead emperor, had ladders brought to wrench down his shields and portraits, and decreed that his inscriptions be erased everywhere.

e:domitian_murdered_bedroom_96.summary: The steward Stephanus, his arm bandaged to hide a dagger, handed Domitian a list of conspirators in his bedroom and stabbed him in the groin; others joined in, and the emperor died with seven wounds fighting for the sword under his pillow.
e:domitian_murdered_bedroom_96.locName: Domitian's bedroom in the residential wing of the palace

e:nerva_adopts_trajan_capitol_97.summary: Humiliated by the praetorians' mutiny, the old emperor climbed the Capitol with news of a victory in Pannonia and, before the altar of Jupiter, announced the adoption of Trajan, then governor of Upper Germany.
e:nerva_adopts_trajan_capitol_97.locName: before the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

e:trajan_enters_on_foot_99.summary: Returning from the frontier as emperor, Trajan entered the city walking among the senators, while the roofs groaned under spectators and the old and sick were carried out to see him.
e:trajan_enters_on_foot_99.locName: along the Via Lata / Flaminia into the city

e:marius_priscus_trial_100.summary: In January 100 the senate, with Trajan presiding as consul, heard the extortion case of the proconsul of Africa; Pliny spoke for nearly five hours by lamplight and Tacitus replied 'eloquently and with majesty'.

e:pliny_panegyricus_100.summary: On taking up his suffect consulship, Pliny thanked Trajan in the senate with the speech later expanded into the Panegyricus, a portrait of the ideal emperor set against Domitian.

e:juvenal_subura_martial.summary: From his farm in Spain Martial pictures his friend Juvenal wandering restlessly through the noisy Subura, climbing the Caelian, and sweating in his toga on the thresholds of the great.
e:juvenal_subura_martial.locName: the Subura and the slopes of the Caelian

e:pliny_centumviral_basilica_iulia.summary: Defending Attia Viriola, disinherited by her old father, Pliny spoke before all four panels of the Centumviral court sitting together in the Basilica Julia; the galleries were packed with men and women leaning over to listen.
e:pliny_centumviral_basilica_iulia.note: Pliny Ep. 2.14 complains of hired claques in the same court.
e:pliny_centumviral_basilica_iulia.locName: the Centumviral court in the Basilica Julia

e:dacian_triumph_games_107.summary: To celebrate the conquest of Dacia Trajan gave games lasting 123 days in which 11,000 animals were killed and 10,000 gladiators fought.

e:baths_trajan_opened_109.summary: Trajan dedicated his vast baths on the Oppian, built over the buried wing of Nero's Golden House; two days later the Aqua Traiana began to flow across the Tiber.
e:baths_trajan_opened_109.locName: the Baths of Trajan on the Oppian

e:juvenal_porta_capena.summary: In Juvenal's third satire Umbricius loads his household onto a single cart at 'the old arch and damp Capena', where the aqueduct drips, and rails against Rome's fires, collapsing tenements, night traffic and Greeks, while the grove of Egeria is rented to Jews.
e:juvenal_porta_capena.locName: the Porta Capena under the dripping arches of the Aqua Marcia

e:juvenal_night_streets.summary: The same satire describes Rome at night: carts jammed in the narrow lanes keep the sick awake, pots thrown from high windows crack the pavement, and drunken bullies pick fights with the poor man walking home by moonlight.
e:juvenal_night_streets.locName: the narrow streets of the Subura

e:forum_trajan_dedicated_112.summary: Trajan dedicated his forum, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus, with the Basilica Ulpia and the gilded equestrian statue; the Fasti Ostienses record the date.

e:trajan_column_hill_inscription.summary: The column's inscription states it was set up to show how high a hill had been removed for the great works of the forum, the saddle that joined the Capitol to the Quirinal; its spiral relief of 155 scenes was viewed from the terraces of the libraries on either side.
e:trajan_column_hill_inscription.locName: the library terraces beside Trajan's Column

e:trajan_column_dedicated_113.summary: The 100-foot column with its spiral frieze of the Dacian wars was dedicated; its inscription claims to show how high the hillside removed for the forum had been.

e:trajan_ashes_column_117.summary: Trajan died in Cilicia; his ashes in a golden urn were placed in the chamber in the base of his column, the only emperor buried inside the pomerium.
e:trajan_ashes_column_117.locName: burial chamber in the pedestal of Trajan's Column

e:hadrian_burns_debts_118.summary: To win popularity Hadrian cancelled 900 million sesterces owed to the treasury and had the records burned publicly in the Forum of Trajan.

e:venus_roma_founded_parilia_121.summary: Hadrian founded the largest temple in Rome on the Velia on the Parilia, the city's birthday, renaming the festival the Romaea.
e:venus_roma_founded_parilia_121.locName: Temple of Venus and Roma on the Velia

e:pantheon_hadrian_dedicated.summary: Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon with its unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 m across, but modestly kept Agrippa's original inscription on the porch, and sometimes held court there.
e:pantheon_hadrian_dedicated.locName: the Pantheon in the Campus Martius

e:colossus_moved_elephants.summary: To clear the site of his temple, Hadrian had the architect Decrianus move the Colossus upright, still standing, to a new base beside the Flavian Amphitheatre using 24 elephants.
e:colossus_moved_elephants.note: The base survived until 1936; date between 121 and 135.
e:colossus_moved_elephants.locName: the new base of the Colossus NW of the Colosseum

e:apollodorus_criticises_temple.summary: Shown the plans of the Temple of Venus and Roma, Apollodorus said the seated goddesses were too big for their cellas: if they wished to stand up and go out, they could not. Dio says Hadrian banished and then killed him.

e:athenaeum_hadrian.summary: Hadrian founded a school 'which they call the Athenaeum' for the liberal arts; tiered lecture halls found under Piazza Venezia in 2008 are identified with it.

e:hadrian_ashes_mausoleum_139.summary: Hadrian died at Baiae in 138; Antoninus Pius, who had to force the senate to deify him, laid his ashes in the new Mausoleum across the Tiber, reached by the Pons Aelius, the following year.

e:faustina_temple_141.summary: Antoninus Pius built a temple to his deified wife Faustina facing the Sacra Via; after his own death in 161 the senate added his name to the inscription, and its columns later fronted the church of S. Lorenzo in Miranda.
e:faustina_temple_141.locName: Temple of Antoninus and Faustina on the Sacra Via

e:hadrianeum_dedicated_145.summary: Antoninus dedicated the temple of his deified father in the Campus Martius, its podium decorated with personified provinces; eleven columns stand in the facade of the Piazza di Pietra stock exchange.

e:rome_900th_anniversary_148.summary: Antoninus Pius celebrated the ninth centenary of the city with games and animals from all over the world, and coins showing Romulus, the wolf and twins, and Aeneas.
e:rome_900th_anniversary_148.locName: the Circus Maximus and the amphitheatre

e:gellius_library_tiberiana.summary: Aulus Gellius sat with Sulpicius Apollinaris and other friends in the library of the palace of Tiberius when a book of 'M. Cato Nepos' was brought out; elsewhere he reads old praetors' edicts in the library of the Temple of Trajan.
e:gellius_library_tiberiana.locName: the library of the Domus Tiberiana

e:gellius_library_pacis.summary: Gellius tells how he searched for Aelius Stilo's commentary in the library of the Temple of Peace, one of Rome's great public collections until the fire of 192.
e:gellius_library_pacis.locName: the library of the Templum Pacis

e:fire_340_insulae_antoninus.summary: Under Antoninus Pius a fire consumed 340 tenements and houses in one blaze; the emperor paid for rebuilding.
e:fire_340_insulae_antoninus.note: District not stated; placed in the Subura as a representative dense quarter.

e:circus_collapse_antoninus.summary: Under Antoninus Pius part of the stands of the Circus Maximus collapsed during the games; the Chronograph of 354 records 1112 people killed.
e:circus_collapse_antoninus.locName: the seating of the Circus Maximus

e:monte_testaccio_amphorae.summary: Behind the river warehouses, broken olive-oil jars from Spain and Africa were stacked in terraces into an artificial hill; painted labels date most of its 50 million sherds to AD 140-250.

e:trajan_library_edicts_gellius.summary: Gellius reports sitting with a friend in the library of the Temple of Trajan and finding there the edicts of ancient praetors.
e:trajan_library_edicts_gellius.locName: the libraries of the Forum of Trajan

e:antoninus_funeral_column_161.summary: Antoninus was cremated in the northern Campus Martius; his adopted sons set up a column of red granite on a carved base showing his apotheosis with Faustina beside the ustrinum.
e:antoninus_funeral_column_161.locName: column base of Antoninus Pius by the Antonine ustrinum

e:tiber_flood_162.summary: Early in the joint reign a great flood of the Tiber destroyed many buildings in the city, drowned animals and caused a severe famine, which the emperors relieved personally.
e:tiber_flood_162.locName: the low city along the Tiber

e:galen_dissection_templum_pacis.summary: Newly arrived from Pergamum, Galen gave public demonstrations, cutting the nerves of a squealing pig to silence it, before an audience of senators and philosophers; the learned met daily at the Temple of Peace.
e:galen_dissection_templum_pacis.locName: the Templum Pacis, meeting place of physicians and philosophers

e:justin_martyr_trial_165.summary: Asked where Christians met, Justin told the prefect Rusticus he lived 'above the bath of Myrtinus' and taught anyone who came there; he and six companions were scourged and beheaded.
e:justin_martyr_trial_165.note: The bath's site is unknown; a medieval tradition linked it with the baths of Novatus at S. Pudenziana.
e:justin_martyr_trial_165.locName: Justin's lodging 'above the bath of Myrtinus' (perhaps on the Viminal)

e:plague_carts_166.summary: The army returning from the East brought the plague; so many died that corpses were taken from the city in carts and wagons, and Marcus paid for the funerals of the poor.
e:plague_carts_166.locName: the Esquiline burial grounds outside the city

e:triumph_column_marcus_176.summary: Marcus and his son Commodus triumphed over the Germans and Sarmatians; a spiral column modelled on Trajan's was later raised beside the Via Flaminia to commemorate the wars.
e:triumph_column_marcus_176.locName: the Column of Marcus Aurelius on the Via Lata

e:galen_forged_book_sandalarius.summary: In the Vicus Sandalarius, where most of Rome's bookshops were, Galen watched a man buy a book labelled 'Galen the doctor' and a scholar read two lines and tear off the title, declaring it was not his style, which moved him to list his genuine works.
e:galen_forged_book_sandalarius.locName: the bookshops of the Vicus Sandalarius near the Templum Pacis

e:quintianus_dagger_amphitheatre_182.summary: In the dark passage into the amphitheatre Claudius Pompeianus Quintianus drew a dagger on Commodus crying 'The senate sends you this!' and was seized before he struck. Lucilla, who had planned the plot, was exiled and killed.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:quintianus_dagger_amphitheatre_182.locName: the entrance passage of the amphitheatre

e:plague_189.summary: Dio, then in Rome, records the greatest plague he had known, killing often 2000 people a day; Commodus withdrew to Laurentum on his doctors' advice.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:cleander_riot_circus_190.summary: During a famine a strange tall woman with children led the crowd at the races in the Circus in shouts against the prefect Cleander; the crowd marched to Commodus' villa, was charged by cavalry, and fought back from the rooftops in the streets. Commodus surrendered Cleander's head.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:cleander_riot_circus_190.locName: the Circus Maximus during the races

e:colossus_commodus_hercules_192.summary: Commodus renamed Rome Colonia Commodiana and had the head of the Colossus replaced with his own portrait, adding a club and a lion at its feet and an inscription boasting of his victories as a gladiator.
e:colossus_commodus_hercules_192.locName: the Colossus beside the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:fire_192_templum_pacis.summary: After an earth tremor, a fire started at night and burned the Temple of Peace with its treasures and libraries, the warehouses of Egyptian and Arabian goods, and spread to the palace and the Temple of Vesta.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:fire_192_templum_pacis.locName: the Templum Pacis and the Sacra Via warehouses

e:galen_storerooms_burned_192.summary: Galen lost his rare drugs, instruments, and books, including his own unpublished works, stored in the warehouses on the Sacra Via, and the Palatine libraries burned too; he wrote 'On the Avoidance of Grief' about his losses.
e:galen_storerooms_burned_192.locName: the Horrea Piperataria on the Sacra Via (under the later Basilica of Maxentius)

e:palladium_carried_192.summary: When the Temple of Vesta caught fire, the Vestals carried the Palladium, brought from Troy and never before seen in public, along the Sacra Via to the palace.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:palladium_carried_192.locName: the Sacra Via from the Temple of Vesta to the palace

e:commodus_arena_ostrich_192.summary: At the Plebeian Games Commodus shot beasts from a raised gallery and fought as a secutor; he cut off an ostrich's head and came toward the senators waving it. Dio and his neighbours chewed laurel leaves from their garlands to keep from laughing.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:commodus_arena_ostrich_192.locName: the arena and senatorial seats of the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:commodus_strangled_192.summary: On the eve of the new year, after Marcia's poison failed, the athlete Narcissus strangled Commodus in his bath. The Historia Augusta places the murder in the Vectilian House on the Caelian, to which he had moved from the palace.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:commodus_strangled_192.note: The Vectilian House is unlocated; marker on the Caelian near the Ludus Magnus.
e:commodus_strangled_192.locName: the Domus Vectiliana on the Caelian (HA); Dio and Herodian imply the palace

e:crowd_occupies_circus_193.summary: Crowds jeered the new emperor in the Forum and then occupied the Circus Maximus, where they stayed a day and a night without food or water, calling on Niger in the East to come and save them.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:pertinax_killed_palace_193.summary: Two or three hundred praetorians marched on the palace; Pertinax met them in the halls and began to reason with them until a Tungrian soldier struck him. His head was carried on a spear back to the camp.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:pertinax_killed_palace_193.locName: the public halls of the Palatine palace

e:empire_auctioned_castra_193.summary: Sulpicianus bid from inside the camp and Didius Julianus from outside the wall, shouting his offers and holding up his fingers; Julianus won at 25,000 sesterces a soldier and was led to the Forum and the Curia under guard.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:empire_auctioned_castra_193.locName: the walls of the Castra Praetoria

e:pertinax_funeral_forum_193.summary: Dio watched as a wax effigy of Pertinax lay on a platform built next to the marble Rostra under a canopy of gold and ivory; Severus read the eulogy and the effigy was carried to a three-storey pyre tower in the Campus Martius, from which an eagle flew up.
e:pertinax_funeral_forum_193.locName: a wooden platform beside the Rostra; pyre in the Campus Martius

e:didius_julianus_killed_193.summary: Deserted as Severus approached, Julianus was killed by a soldier in the palace after 66 days; his last words were 'What wrong have I done? Whom have I killed?'

e:severus_enters_rome_193.summary: Severus came to the gates in armour, then changed into civilian dress and walked to the Capitol with his army; the city was garlanded and the people in white, but Dio found the soldiers' billeting in temples and porticoes frightening.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:severus_enters_rome_193.locName: from the gates to the Capitol

e:alexamenos_graffito.summary: On a wall of the imperial pages' building on the Palatine someone scratched a man raising his hand to a crucified figure with a donkey's head, captioned 'Alexamenos worships his god', the earliest known image of the crucifixion.
e:alexamenos_graffito.note: Date c. 200, from the context; Tertullian mentions the donkey-headed slander.
e:alexamenos_graffito.locName: the Paedagogium (Domus Gelotiana) on the SW Palatine above the Circus

e:statio_annonae_grain.summary: Holders of bronze grain tickets collected their monthly ration of free grain at one of the 45 arches of the Porticus Minucia Frumentaria, each assigned to a group of recipients on fixed days.
e:statio_annonae_grain.note: Distribution system attested from Claudius into the 3rd century; year representative.

e:san_clemente_mithraeum.summary: In the courtyard of an insula beneath the later church of S. Clemente a mithraeum with benches and a bull-slaying altar was installed around 200, next to a house believed to be the titulus of Clement.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Clauss, The Roman Cult of Mithras (2000)

e:consualia_buried_altar.summary: The altar of Consus, kept underground near the first turning post of the Circus Maximus, was uncovered only on his festival days, when horses and mules were crowned and raced; Tertullian notes its inscription.
e:consualia_buried_altar.locName: the underground altar of Consus at the first metae of the Circus Maximus

e:santa_prisca_mithraeum_202.summary: A painted inscription in the mithraeum beneath S. Prisca records a birth into the mysteries 'at first light' on 20 November in the consulship of the two Augusti, Severus and Antoninus, i.e. 202.
scholarship: Vermaseren and van Essen, The Excavations in the Mithraeum of the Church of Santa Prisca in Rome (1965)
e:santa_prisca_mithraeum_202.locName: the Mithraeum under S. Prisca on the Aventine

e:arch_septimius_severus_203.summary: The senate and people dedicated a triple arch at the NW end of the Forum to Severus and his sons for the Parthian victories; after 212 Geta's name was erased from the attic inscription.
e:arch_septimius_severus_203.locName: the Arch of Septimius Severus beside the Rostra

e:septizodium_203.summary: Severus built a three-storey colonnaded facade at the SE corner of the Palatine facing the Via Appia, so that travellers arriving from Africa would see his works first.
e:septizodium_203.locName: the Septizodium at the SE corner of the Palatine

e:arcus_argentariorum_204.summary: The argentarii and negotiantes boarii of the cattle market built a gate of marble at the entrance to the Forum Boarium beside S. Giorgio in Velabro, carving the imperial family; Geta, Plautianus and Plautilla were later chiselled out.
e:arcus_argentariorum_204.locName: the Arcus Argentariorum by S. Giorgio in Velabro

e:secular_games_tarentum_204.summary: Severus and Caracalla celebrated the Secular Games; the inscribed Acta, found by the Tiber, record the nocturnal sacrifices at the Tarentum and a hymn sung on the Palatine and Capitol by choirs of children.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:plautianus_killed_palace_205.summary: Accused of plotting, the all-powerful prefect Plautianus was summoned to the palace and cut down in the presence of Severus and Julia Domna on Caracalla's orders; a hair from his beard was carried to Plautilla. His body was thrown into the street.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:plautianus_killed_palace_205.locName: a room of the Palatine palace

e:severus_ashes_hadrian_211.summary: Severus died at York; his sons carried his ashes in a porphyry urn back to Rome, where they were placed in the Mausoleum of Hadrian after a funeral with an effigy.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:geta_killed_mothers_arms_211.summary: Caracalla persuaded their mother Julia Domna to summon both sons to her rooms for a reconciliation; centurions burst in and killed Geta as he clung to her, her hand wounded. Caracalla rushed to the camp claiming he had escaped a plot.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:geta_killed_mothers_arms_211.note: Date given as 26 December 211 (some reconstructions 19 December).
e:geta_killed_mothers_arms_211.locName: Julia Domna's apartments in the palace

e:vigiles_graffiti_trastevere.summary: In the excubitorium of the Seventh Cohort of vigiles in Trastevere, firemen scratched over a hundred dated graffiti between 215 and 245, thanking the genius of the post after their monthly sebaciaria duty of lighting the streets.
e:vigiles_graffiti_trastevere.locName: the Excubitorium of the VII Cohort, Via della VII Coorte, Trastevere

e:elagabalus_violates_vesta.summary: Elagabalus married the Vestal Aquilia Severa and, says the Historia Augusta, forced his way into the penus of Vesta, which only the Vestals and the chief priest might enter, to carry off what he thought was the Palladium to his own temple.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:elagabalus_violates_vesta.locName: the penus of the Temple of Vesta

e:elagabalium_procession_220.summary: Each midsummer the conical stone of the sun god of Emesa rode in a gilded chariot from the Palatine temple to his suburban temple at Spes Vetus, the emperor running backward before it holding the reins, the road strewn with gold dust.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:elagabalium_procession_220.locName: from the Elagabalium on the Palatine (to the temple at Spes Vetus)

e:elagabalus_killed_castra_222.summary: Mutinous praetorians killed Elagabalus and his mother Julia Soaemias in the camp, the emperor hiding in a latrine. Their heads were cut off and the bodies stripped and dragged through the city.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:elagabalus_body_pons_aemilius_222.summary: The body was dragged through the streets and around the Circus, pushed into a sewer which proved too small, and finally thrown into the Tiber from the Pons Aemilius with a weight attached so it would never be buried. He was nicknamed 'the dragged one'.
e:elagabalus_body_pons_aemilius_222.locName: the Pons Aemilius, after being dragged around the Circus Maximus

e:callistus_trastevere_222.summary: The former slave and banker Callistus, who had run the Christian cemetery on the Via Appia, died in a riot in Trastevere; legend says he was thrown into a well. The church of S. Callisto marks the site.
e:callistus_trastevere_222.note: The Passio is late; the historical death in a riot is plausible but unverified.
e:callistus_trastevere_222.locName: the well of S. Callisto near S. Maria in Trastevere

e:ulpian_killed_palace_223.summary: After three days of street fighting between the people and the praetorians, who set houses on fire, the soldiers killed the jurist and prefect Ulpian at night in the palace, before the young emperor and his mother.

e:tavern_keepers_vs_christians.summary: When the Christians occupied a public place and the tavern-keepers claimed it, Alexander ruled that it was better for a god to be worshipped there in any fashion than for it to go to tavern-keepers. Tradition identified the site with S. Maria in Trastevere.
e:tavern_keepers_vs_christians.locName: a public plot in Trastevere (tradition: S. Maria in Trastevere)

e:africanus_library_pantheon.summary: The Christian scholar Julius Africanus wrote that he had designed the beautiful library in the Pantheon by the Baths of Alexander for the emperor.
e:africanus_library_pantheon.locName: library at the Pantheon, beside the Baths of Nero/Alexander

e:gallicanus_kills_praetorians_curia_238.summary: When two or three praetorians came to the door of the senate house to listen, the senator Gallicanus and his friend Maecenas stabbed them at the altar of Victory. The people then besieged the praetorians in their camp.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:gallicanus_kills_praetorians_curia_238.locName: at the altar of Victory inside the Curia Iulia

e:gordian_iii_capitol_238.summary: As Pupienus and Balbinus went up to the Capitol, the people blocked their way demanding an emperor from Gordian's family; the 13-year-old grandson was fetched and named Caesar.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:praetorian_siege_fire_238.summary: The people attacked the Castra Praetoria and cut its water pipes; the praetorians sallied out, the people fought back from the rooftops and the soldiers set fire to the houses, burning a great part of the city.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:praetorian_siege_fire_238.locName: around the Castra Praetoria and the neighbouring streets

e:pupienus_balbinus_dragged_238.summary: During the Capitoline games, while the people were at the shows, praetorians burst into the palace, stripped the two quarrelling emperors, dragged them through the streets toward the camp and killed them.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

e:pupienus_balbinus_dragged_238.locName: from the palace through the streets toward the camp

e:plotinus_school_gemina.summary: Plotinus came to Rome at 40 and taught for 26 years in the house of the widow Gemina, where Porphyry, senators, physicians and women of the nobility attended; guardians left orphans and their property in his care.
e:plotinus_school_gemina.note: Porphyry gives no location. Marker placed by convention with the cityPlace school_plotinus; treat as unlocated.

e:millennium_games_248.summary: Philip the Arab celebrated the millennium of the city with games in the Circus Maximus, using the elephants, elk, tigers, hippopotami and other animals gathered by Gordian III, and with theatrical shows in the Campus Martius.

e:mithraeum_circus_maximus.summary: In the 3rd century the ground floor of a public building beside the Circus Maximus was turned into a mithraeum with a great relief of Mithras slaying the bull.
e:mithraeum_circus_maximus.locName: the Mithraeum of the Circus Maximus (Via dell'Ara Massima di Ercole)

e:fabian_buried_callixtus_250.summary: Fabian was among the first victims of Decius' edict; his Greek epitaph, 'Fabian, bishop, martyr', survives in the Crypt of the Popes in the cemetery of Callixtus.
e:fabian_buried_callixtus_250.locName: the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus

e:sixtus_ii_catacomb_258.summary: Under Valerian's edict soldiers surprised Bishop Sixtus II preaching seated in the cemetery of Callixtus and beheaded him with four deacons; Damasus later wrote verses for his tomb in the Crypt of the Popes.
e:sixtus_ii_catacomb_258.locName: the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus

e:lawrence_buried_verano_258.summary: Four days after Sixtus, the deacon Lawrence was executed; legend says he presented the poor as the church's treasure and was roasted on a gridiron. He was buried on the Via Tiburtina, where Constantine built a basilica.
e:lawrence_buried_verano_258.note: The gridiron legend is attested from Ambrose and Prudentius; the place of execution was later claimed by S. Lorenzo in Panisperna on the Viminal.
e:lawrence_buried_verano_258.locName: his tomb in the Ager Veranus on the Via Tiburtina (S. Lorenzo fuori le mura)

e:arch_gallienus_262.summary: The equestrian Aurelius Victor, vir egregius, rededicated the Augustan arch of the Porta Esquilina to Gallienus and Salonina, 'whose unconquered courage is surpassed only by his piety'.

e:plague_cyprian_rome_262.summary: In the worst year of the 'plague of Cyprian', the Historia Augusta claims 5000 people died in a single day in Rome, together with an earthquake and darkness over the city.

e:aurelian_walls_begun_271.summary: After the Juthungi reached Italy, Aurelian ordered a brick wall 19 km long around the city, the first new circuit since the Republic, built largely by the city guilds and completed under Probus.
e:aurelian_walls_begun_271.locName: the Aurelian Wall (Porta Appia section shown)

e:mint_workers_revolt_271.summary: Led by the official Felicissimus, the workers of the Rome mint, accused of debasing the coinage, rose in revolt and fought Aurelian's troops on the Caelian; 7000 soldiers are said to have died.
e:mint_workers_revolt_271.locName: the imperial mint (Moneta) on the Caelian near S. Clemente

e:aurelian_triumph_zenobia_274.summary: Aurelian triumphed over Palmyra and the Gallic empire; Zenobia walked weighed down by jewels and gold chains carried by a jester, and the Gallic emperor Tetricus in trousers. The procession reached the Capitol only in the evening.

e:temple_sol_dedicated_274.summary: With Palmyrene spoils Aurelian built a great temple to the Unconquered Sun in the Campus Agrippae and created a new college of pontiffs of Sol; the god's festival fell on 25 December.
e:temple_sol_dedicated_274.note: Site disputed (under S. Silvestro in Capite or the Quirinal); placed in the Campus Agrippae.
e:temple_sol_dedicated_274.locName: the Temple of Sol in the Campus Agrippae (E Campus Martius)

e:probus_forest_circus_281.summary: For his triumph Probus had soldiers uproot trees and replant them in the Circus Maximus, then released a thousand ostriches, deer, wild boars and sheep for the people to seize; lions and leopards were killed in the amphitheatre.
e:probus_forest_circus_281.locName: the arena of the Circus Maximus, turned into a forest

e:fire_of_carinus_283.summary: A fire under Carinus burned the senate house, the Forum of Caesar, the Basilica Julia and the Graecostadium; Diocletian rebuilt the Curia in the form that survives.
e:fire_of_carinus_283.locName: the Curia, Forum Iulium and Basilica Julia

e:circus_collapse_diocletian.summary: The Chronograph of 354 records that under Diocletian the upper seating of the Circus Maximus collapsed and crushed 13,000 people.
e:circus_collapse_diocletian.note: Year within Diocletian's reign unknown; the figure may be corrupt.
e:circus_collapse_diocletian.locName: the seating of the Circus Maximus

e:vicennalia_forum_303.summary: Diocletian and Maximian celebrated twenty years of rule with a triumph in Rome; five honorific columns were set up behind the Rostra, the base of one carved with a sacrifice. Diocletian, irritated by the Roman crowd's liberties, left on 20 December.
e:vicennalia_forum_303.locName: the Decennalia monument behind the Rostra

e:agnes_stadium_304.summary: The young Agnes refused marriage and sacrifice; by tradition she was exposed in a brothel under the arches of Domitian's stadium, where her hair grew to cover her, and then killed. She was buried on the Via Nomentana.
e:agnes_stadium_304.note: The brothel story is in the Passio and Prudentius; the stadium location is tradition.
e:agnes_stadium_304.locName: the arcades of the Stadium of Domitian (S. Agnese in Agone)

e:baths_diocletian_dedicated_306.summary: Maximian, returning from Africa, began the largest baths of Rome on the Viminal in Diocletian's name, clearing a whole neighbourhood; they were dedicated after the abdication of 305.
e:baths_diocletian_dedicated_306.locName: the Baths of Diocletian on the Viminal

e:maxentius_proclaimed_castra_306.summary: Angered by Galerius' plan to tax Rome and abolish the guard, the praetorians and people proclaimed Maximian's son Maxentius emperor in Rome.

e:temple_fortuna_fire_massacre.summary: When a temple of Fortuna caught fire and a soldier mocked the goddess, the crowd killed him; the soldiers rioted and massacred the people until Maxentius stopped them. The Temple of Venus and Roma was rebuilt by Maxentius after a fire.
e:temple_fortuna_fire_massacre.locName: the Temple of Venus and Roma (probably the 'temple of Fortuna' of Zosimus)

e:basilica_nova_begun_308.summary: On the site of the burned Sacra Via warehouses Maxentius began a vaulted basilica on the scale of the imperial baths; Constantine finished it and set his colossal statue in the apse.
e:basilica_nova_begun_308.locName: the Basilica of Maxentius on the Velia

e:circus_maxentius_romulus_309.summary: Maxentius built a palace, a circus with an obelisk of Domitian, and a dynastic mausoleum for his son Romulus, who died in 309, on the Via Appia.
e:circus_maxentius_romulus_309.locName: the Circus of Maxentius on the Via Appia

e:constantine_colossal_statue_312.summary: Eusebius says Constantine had a statue of himself holding the saving sign set up 'in the most public place in Rome'; the colossal marble head and hand found in 1486 in the apse of the Basilica Nova come from his giant seated statue.
e:constantine_colossal_statue_312.locName: the W apse of the Basilica Nova

e:circus_riot_constantine_312.summary: At the races for Maxentius' anniversary the crowd shouted that Constantine could not be beaten; alarmed, Maxentius consulted the Sibylline books, which foretold that 'the enemy of the Romans' would die, and marched out.

e:maxentius_drowns_milvian_312.summary: Routed at Saxa Rubra, Maxentius' army fled back across the Tiber; the pontoon bridge beside the stone Milvian Bridge collapsed and Maxentius, weighed down by armour, drowned. His body was recovered from the mud the next day.
e:maxentius_drowns_milvian_312.locName: the Milvian Bridge and the pontoon bridge beside it

e:constantine_entry_312.summary: Constantine entered by the Via Flaminia with Maxentius' head carried on a spear; the senate and people met him with joy, and he went to the palace on the Palatine.
e:constantine_entry_312.note: Whether he climbed to the Capitol to sacrifice is debated; the panegyrist is silent.
e:constantine_entry_312.locName: entry by the Porta Flaminia along the Via Lata

e:praetorians_disbanded_312.summary: Constantine dissolved the praetorians, who had fought for Maxentius, and dismantled the inner wall of their camp, ending three centuries of emperor-making from the Castra Praetoria.

e:lateran_basilica_founded_312.summary: On the site of the razed barracks of the imperial horse guard, Constantine built the Basilica Constantiniana, Rome's cathedral, and gave the bishop the adjacent Lateran palace.
e:lateran_basilica_founded_312.locName: the Lateran basilica on the barracks of the Equites Singulares

e:council_domus_faustae_313.summary: Pope Miltiades with eighteen other bishops, three from Gaul and fifteen from Italy, met in the house of Fausta on the Lateran to judge the Donatist dispute from Africa, the first church council held in an imperial residence.
e:council_domus_faustae_313.locName: the Domus Faustae on the Lateran

e:arch_constantine_dedicated_315.summary: The senate dedicated a triple arch beside the Colosseum to Constantine, who had freed the state from a tyrant 'by divine inspiration'; much of its sculpture was taken from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus.
e:arch_constantine_dedicated_315.locName: the Arch of Constantine on the triumphal route by the Meta Sudans

e:old_st_peters_begun.summary: Constantine levelled the Vatican hillside and buried a cemetery to build a five-aisled basilica with its apse over the 'trophy' of Peter; it was finished under his sons.
e:old_st_peters_begun.locName: Old St Peter's on the Vatican

e:constantine_refuses_capitol_326.summary: On his last visit, for his vicennalia, Constantine declined to join the traditional procession up to the Capitol; Zosimus says the senate and people were enraged by the insult.
e:constantine_refuses_capitol_326.locName: the processional route up the Capitol

e:constantine_baptism_legend.summary: Later legend (the Actus Silvestri) held that Pope Silvester cured Constantine of leprosy and baptised him in the Lateran baptistery; in fact he was baptised on his deathbed near Nicomedia in 337.

e:constantina_mausoleum_354.summary: Constantine's daughter Constantina, who had founded the basilica of S. Agnese beside the martyr's tomb, was buried in the domed mausoleum next to it, with its vine-harvest mosaics and porphyry sarcophagus.
e:constantina_mausoleum_354.locName: the Mausoleum of Constantina (S. Costanza) on the Via Nomentana

e:leontius_septizodium_355.summary: The city prefect Leontius had the popular charioteer Philoromus arrested and the rioters punished; when the plebs gathered again at the Septizodium, a much-frequented place, complaining of a wine shortage, Leontius went there in person, picked out the ringleader Peter Valvomeres, had him strung up and flogged, and the crowd melted away.
e:leontius_septizodium_355.locName: the Septizodium at the SE corner of the Palatine

e:obelisk_circus_constantius_357.summary: Constantine's obelisk from Karnak, the tallest in the world, arrived by river barge and was hauled on rollers through the Porta Ostiensis to the Circus, where thousands of men raised it with a forest of masts and ropes on the spina.
e:obelisk_circus_constantius_357.locName: the spina of the Circus Maximus (obelisk now at the Lateran)

e:constantius_curia_rostra_357.summary: Constantius spoke to the nobility in the Curia and to the people from the tribunal, was received in the palace and gave games, enjoying the banter of the plebs.

e:altar_victory_removed_357.summary: During his visit Constantius had the altar of Victory taken out of the senate house, though he left the statue and the privileges of the priesthoods; Julian restored it.
e:altar_victory_removed_357.locName: the altar of Victory in the Curia

e:constantius_entry_357.summary: Constantius rode in a golden carriage glittering with gems, surrounded by dragon standards and armoured cavalry, looking straight ahead without moving his head, bending only to pass under gates, as Ammianus describes in a famous scene.
e:constantius_entry_357.locName: the triumphal entry along the Via Flaminia/Lata

e:constantius_forum_trajan_357.summary: Touring the city, the emperor admired the Capitol, the baths, the Colosseum, the Pantheon, the Temple of Venus and Roma, the Temple of Peace, Pompey's theatre, the Odeum and the Stadium, but stood speechless in the Forum of Trajan. He said he would copy only the equestrian statue; the Persian prince Hormisdas replied: first build a stable like this one.
e:constantius_forum_trajan_357.locName: the equestrian statue of Trajan in the Forum of Trajan

e:liberius_snow_legend_358.summary: A medieval legend says the Virgin showed Pope Liberius and a patrician the site of her church by a summer snowfall on the Esquiline on 5 August; the Liberian basilica preceded S. Maria Maggiore.
e:liberius_snow_legend_358.note: Legend first attested in the Middle Ages.

e:junius_bassus_sarcophagus_359.summary: The city prefect Junius Bassus died in office, 'newly baptised', and was buried near Peter's tomb in a carved sarcophagus whose biblical scenes are a masterpiece of early Christian sculpture.
e:junius_bassus_sarcophagus_359.locName: near the confession of Old St Peter's

e:lampadius_house_365.summary: The vain prefect Lampadius, who requisitioned materials for his buildings without paying, so enraged the poor that they tried to burn his house near the Baths of Constantine with torches; he fled to the Milvian Bridge.
e:lampadius_house_365.locName: Lampadius' house near the Baths of Constantine on the Quirinal

e:lavatio_almo.summary: On 27 March the silver image of Cybele was carried in a cart out of the Porta Capena to the brook Almo, where its priest, robed in purple, washed it and its sacred objects; Ammianus records the rite still in the 4th century.
e:lavatio_almo.locName: the brook Almo where it crosses the Via Appia outside the Porta Appia (Ovid places the washing where the Almo flows into the Tiber)

e:damasus_ursinus_julian_basilica_366.summary: On Liberius' death the deacon Ursinus was consecrated in the Julian basilica in Trastevere and Damasus at S. Lorenzo in Lucina; Damasus' partisans attacked the Julian basilica and fought in the streets for three days.
e:damasus_ursinus_julian_basilica_366.locName: the Julian basilica in Trastevere (S. Maria in Trastevere)

e:massacre_basilica_sicinini_366.summary: Damasus' supporters stormed the Basilica of Sicininus, where the Ursinians had taken refuge, breaking in through the roof; Ammianus records 137 corpses found in a single day and drily notes the wealth of the Roman see.
e:massacre_basilica_sicinini_366.note: Usually identified with the Liberian basilica on the Esquiline, predecessor of S. Maria Maggiore.
e:massacre_basilica_sicinini_366.locName: the Basilica of Sicininus on the Esquiline (Liberian basilica, near S. Maria Maggiore)
