e:praetextatus_dii_consentes_367.summary: The pagan city prefect Vettius Agorius Praetextatus restored the statues of the Dei Consentes in their portico below the Tabularium and demolished private buildings stuck onto temples.
e:praetextatus_dii_consentes_367.locName: the Porticus Deorum Consentium on the Clivus Capitolinus

e:damasus_crypt_epigrams.summary: Pope Damasus restored the martyrs' tombs in the catacombs and placed verse inscriptions carved by Filocalus; in the Crypt of the Popes he declared he would have liked to be buried there but feared to disturb the saints.
e:damasus_crypt_epigrams.locName: the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus

e:symmachus_house_trastevere_burned.summary: The elder Symmachus, once city prefect, was rumoured to have said he would rather use his wine to slake lime than sell it cheap; the plebs burned his fine house in Trastevere and he left the city for a time.
e:symmachus_house_trastevere_burned.note: Ammianus dates it 'some time' after his prefecture (364-365); year approximate. The orator Symmachus was his son.
e:symmachus_house_trastevere_burned.locName: the house of L. Aurelius Avianius Symmachus in Trastevere

e:taurobolium_phrygianum.summary: In the sanctuary of the Great Mother beside the Vatican circus, pagan aristocrats were drenched in the blood of a bull in the taurobolium and recorded it on altars dated between 295 and 390; they were found under St Peter's square.
e:taurobolium_phrygianum.note: Year representative of the dated altars of the 370s.
e:taurobolium_phrygianum.locName: the Phrygianum near the Vatican circus (under Piazza S. Pietro)

e:jerome_marcella_aventine.summary: Marcella's palace on the Aventine became a circle of ascetic noblewomen, Paula, Asella and others, who studied Hebrew and scripture with Jerome while he served Pope Damasus.
e:jerome_marcella_aventine.note: The house is unlocated on the Aventine.
e:jerome_marcella_aventine.locName: the house of Marcella on the Aventine

e:augustine_teaches_rome_383.summary: Augustine came from Carthage because Roman students were said to be orderly, fell ill in the house of a Manichaean, and found that his pupils cheated him by moving en masse to another teacher before paying fees. In 384 he left for the chair in Milan.
e:augustine_teaches_rome_383.note: No location given. Marker in the Forum of Trajan, where public recitation and teaching are attested in late antiquity (Venantius Fortunatus, Carm. 3.18, 7.8).
e:augustine_teaches_rome_383.locName: a rhetoric school in Rome (site unknown)

e:symmachus_relatio_victory_384.summary: As city prefect, Symmachus asked Valentinian II to restore the altar of Victory to the senate house: 'We cannot attain to so great a mystery by one road.' Ambrose of Milan's replies prevailed.
e:symmachus_relatio_victory_384.locName: the altar of Victory in the Curia

e:pacatus_panegyric_389.summary: Theodosius entered Rome after defeating Magnus Maximus, walked through the city as a private citizen visiting the houses of senators, and heard the Gallic orator Pacatus praise him in the senate house.

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

e:serena_necklace_magna_mater.summary: Visiting the temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine after Theodosius' victory, Stilicho's wife Serena took the necklace from the goddess's statue and put it on; an old Vestal cursed her, and Zosimus saw her strangling in 408 as the curse fulfilled.
e:serena_necklace_magna_mater.locName: the Temple of Magna Mater on the Palatine

e:pammachius_feast_st_peters_397.summary: In memory of his dead wife Paulina, the senator Pammachius gave a great banquet for the poor of Rome in the courtyard of St Peter's, a scene Paulinus of Nola describes with the crowds filling the atrium.
e:pammachius_feast_st_peters_397.locName: the atrium of Old St Peter's

e:honorian_walls_401.summary: Under the threat of Alaric's invasion, Stilicho had the Aurelian Wall raised to nearly twice its height and the gates rebuilt with towers, recorded in inscriptions over the Porta Tiburtina and Porta Praenestina.

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

e:honorian_walls_401.locName: the Porta Tiburtina with its Honorian inscription

e:prudentius_hippolytus_shrine.summary: The Spanish poet Prudentius describes the crowds pouring out of the city on 13 August to the underground shrine of the martyr Hippolytus by the Via Tiburtina, its walls painted with his martyrdom.
e:prudentius_hippolytus_shrine.locName: the catacomb of S. Ippolito on the Via Tiburtina

e:peter_paul_feast_crowds.summary: On 29 June, Prudentius writes, the whole city streams across the Tiber to Peter's basilica on the Vatican and along the road to Paul's on the Via Ostiensis, the pope celebrating at both in one day.
e:peter_paul_feast_crowds.locName: the Pons Aelius on the way to St Peter's

e:telemachus_arena_404.summary: Theodoret says the eastern monk Telemachus leapt into the arena to separate fighting gladiators and was stoned to death by the angry spectators; Honorius then ended gladiatorial combat.
e:telemachus_arena_404.note: Date c. 404; Theodoret does not name the building.
e:telemachus_arena_404.locName: the arena of the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:melania_house_unsold.summary: Melania the Younger and Pinianus, giving away their vast fortune, could find no buyer rich enough for their house on the Caelian; after the sack of 410 it sold for a trifle, part of it burned.
e:melania_house_unsold.locName: the Domus Valeriorum on the Caelian (by the Lateran)

e:honorius_triumph_404.summary: For his sixth consulship Honorius entered Rome with Stilicho after the victories over Alaric; Claudian describes the crowds on the Pincian and the Milvian Bridge and the young emperor received on the Palatine.

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

e:honorius_triumph_404.locName: the entry by the Via Flaminia to the Palatine

e:arch_honorius_pons_aelius_405.summary: The senate dedicated an arch at the Campus Martius end of the Pons Aelius to the three emperors for the defeat of the Goths at Pollentia and Verona.
e:arch_honorius_pons_aelius_405.locName: the arch at the left-bank end of the Pons Aelius

e:ransom_statues_melted_408.summary: To pay Alaric 5000 pounds of gold and 30,000 of silver, the senate stripped temple statues of their ornaments and melted some down, among them Virtus; Zosimus says courage died in Rome with it.

e:basilica_aemilia_burned_410.summary: The basilica on the Forum was burned in the sack; bronze coins dropped by money-changers melted into its marble pavement, where green stains still show, and the hall was never rebuilt.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
e:basilica_aemilia_burned_410.note: Evidence archaeological (fused coins of the early 5th century); the 410 date is the accepted interpretation.
e:basilica_aemilia_burned_410.locName: the pavement of the Basilica Aemilia

e:marcella_beaten_aventine_410.summary: Goths burst into Marcella's house on the Aventine demanding gold; she showed her coarse tunic, was beaten, and begged only that her ward Principia be spared. They escorted both to the basilica of St Paul, where she died soon after.

e:vessels_procession_st_peters_410.summary: A Goth found an elderly virgin guarding gold vessels belonging to St Peter; Alaric ordered them carried to the basilica, and Romans and Goths together sang hymns along the route under drawn swords.
e:vessels_procession_st_peters_410.locName: the procession to Old St Peter's

e:alaric_porta_salaria_410.summary: On the night of 24 August Alaric's Goths entered Rome through the Porta Salaria, opened, as later told, by treachery or by the slaves of Proba; for three days they sacked the city, the first time in 800 years an enemy had taken it.
e:alaric_porta_salaria_410.locName: the Porta Salaria in the Aurelian Wall

e:horti_sallustiani_burned_410.summary: Procopius says the Goths burned the houses next to the gate, including the house of Sallust in the gardens near the Porta Salaria, which was still standing half-burned in his own day.
e:horti_sallustiani_burned_410.locName: the palace in the Horti Sallustiani by the Porta Salaria

e:eulalius_boniface_lateran_419.summary: After the double election of December 418, Eulalius seized the Lateran to celebrate Easter, against the emperor's order; troops expelled him and Boniface was recognised.

e:santa_sabina_built.summary: Under Celestine I the Illyrian priest Peter built the basilica of S. Sabina, recorded in its mosaic dedication; its cypress doors carry one of the earliest crucifixion images.

e:santa_maria_maggiore_sixtus_432.summary: After the Council of Ephesus, Pope Sixtus III built the great basilica of the Mother of God on the Esquiline, its arch inscribed 'Xystus episcopus plebi Dei'.
e:santa_maria_maggiore_sixtus_432.locName: S. Maria Maggiore on the Esquiline

e:earthquake_443.summary: An earthquake struck Rome, bringing down statues and porticoes; the Colosseum was damaged in this or later quakes.
e:earthquake_443.note: Date and attribution uncertain; damage to the Colosseum at this time is linked by geologists to the Monte Vettore fault (Galli et al., 2019). Marker at the Colosseum as the best-attested damaged building.
e:earthquake_443.locName: the city (damage to statues and porticoes)

e:leo_sermon_sun_steps.summary: Preaching at Christmas, Pope Leo complained that some Christians, after climbing the steps of St Peter's, turned round and bowed to the rising sun before entering.
e:leo_sermon_sun_steps.note: Sermon datable to Leo's pontificate (440-461); year representative.
e:leo_sermon_sun_steps.locName: the steps of Old St Peter's

e:valentinian_iii_killed_campus_455.summary: Watching athletes in the Campus Martius, Valentinian was struck down by Optila and Thraustila, guardsmen of the murdered Aetius, at the instigation of Petronius Maximus. The western Theodosian dynasty ended.
e:valentinian_iii_killed_campus_455.locName: the Campus Martius (some sources: 'ad duas lauros' on the Via Labicana)

e:vandals_strip_capitol_455.summary: In fourteen days of methodical plunder the Vandals loaded their ships with the palace treasures and took half the gilded bronze roof tiles of the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus.
e:vandals_strip_capitol_455.locName: the roof of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

e:vandals_take_temple_treasure_455.summary: Among the loot were the vessels of the Jerusalem Temple displayed by Vespasian in the Temple of Peace and kept in the palace; Belisarius brought them back from Carthage in 534.

e:leo_meets_gaiseric_455.summary: Three days after Petronius Maximus was stoned to death fleeing the city, the Vandals arrived; Leo went out to Gaiseric and obtained that there would be no burning, killing or torture, only plunder.
e:leo_meets_gaiseric_455.note: The meeting place is not given; the Vandals came from Portus.
e:leo_meets_gaiseric_455.locName: outside the gates (traditionally the Porta Portuensis, on the road from Portus)

e:sidonius_prays_apostles_467.summary: Arriving from Gaul in 467, Sidonius went first to the threshold of the apostles before entering the city, which he found in carnival mood for Ricimer's wedding to the emperor's daughter.
e:sidonius_prays_apostles_467.locName: the tomb of Peter at the Vatican

e:sidonius_panegyric_468.summary: The Gallic aristocrat Sidonius Apollinaris delivered a verse panegyric for Anthemius' consulship before the senate and was rewarded with the prefecture of the city, from which he had to manage a grain crisis.

e:arvandus_tiber_island_469.summary: The disgraced prefect of Gaul Arvandus, convicted of treasonable letters to the Visigoths, was held on 'the island of the Epidaurian serpent' to await execution, later commuted to exile.
e:arvandus_tiber_island_469.locName: the Tiber Island (former sanctuary of Aesculapius)

e:sant_agata_goti_ricimer.summary: Ricimer decorated the church of the Goths on the Quirinal slope with an apse mosaic recording his gift; it served the Arian Goths until it was reconsecrated to Catholic use by Gregory the Great in 592.
e:sant_agata_goti_ricimer.locName: S. Agata dei Goti on the Quirinal slope

e:bilimer_killed_pons_aelius_472.summary: During Ricimer's siege of Anthemius, the general Bilimer came from Gaul to help the emperor and was killed fighting Ricimer's troops at the bridge by Hadrian's Mausoleum.
e:bilimer_killed_pons_aelius_472.locName: the Pons Aelius before the Mausoleum of Hadrian

e:anthemius_killed_chrysogonus_472.summary: After five months of siege and famine Ricimer's men broke in; Anthemius hid among the beggars at the church of the martyr Chrysogonus in Trastevere, where Gundobad found and beheaded him. Malalas instead places the killing at St Peter's.
e:anthemius_killed_chrysogonus_472.locName: the church of S. Crisogono in Trastevere

e:senators_names_colosseum_seats.summary: Under Odoacer, the reserved seats of the amphitheatre's lower tiers were inscribed with the names of senatorial families; erased and recarved names show how the places changed hands.
e:senators_names_colosseum_seats.note: Inscriptions mostly of the later 5th century; year representative.
e:senators_names_colosseum_seats.locName: the podium seats of the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:basilius_restores_colosseum.summary: The prefect Decius Marius Venantius Basilius restored at his own expense the arena and podium of the amphitheatre ruined by an 'abominable earthquake'.
e:basilius_restores_colosseum.note: Earthquake of 484 or 508 (consul of 484 or 508 of the same name).
e:basilius_restores_colosseum.locName: the arena and podium of the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:gelasius_ends_lupercalia.summary: In a letter to the senator Andromachus, Gelasius attacked Christians who still kept the Lupercalia, the naked run around the Palatine, as a guarantee of fertility and health; it is the last record of the festival.
e:gelasius_ends_lupercalia.locName: the Lupercal and the course around the Palatine

e:double_election_498.summary: Symmachus was consecrated in the Lateran basilica and the archpriest Laurentius, backed by the pro-Byzantine senators, in S. Maria Maggiore; Theodoric decided for Symmachus.
e:double_election_498.locName: the Lateran (Symmachus) and S. Maria Maggiore (Laurentius)

e:theodoric_met_st_peters_500.summary: On his only visit to Rome, Theodoric went first to St Peter's 'as devoutly as a Catholic', where Pope Symmachus, the senate and the people met him with rejoicing outside the city.
e:theodoric_met_st_peters_500.locName: Old St Peter's on the Vatican

e:theodoric_ad_palmam_500.summary: Entering the city, Theodoric came to the senate and addressed the people at the place called Ad Palmam, between the Curia and the Arch of Severus, promising to keep everything the emperors had decreed.
e:theodoric_ad_palmam_500.note: The Palma was probably the open area by the Curia (also called Palma Aurea).
e:theodoric_ad_palmam_500.locName: Ad Palmam, between the Curia and the Arch of Septimius Severus

e:theodoric_games_palace_walls_500.summary: Theodoric entered the palace in triumph, gave games in the Circus and a distribution of grain, and assigned 200 pounds of gold a year from the wine tax for repairs to the palace and the city walls.
e:theodoric_games_palace_walls_500.locName: the Circus Maximus and the Palatine palace

e:odoin_beheaded_sessorium_500.summary: The Gothic count Odoin, accused of plotting against Theodoric, was beheaded in the palace called the Sessorium by S. Croce.
e:odoin_beheaded_sessorium_500.locName: the Sessorian palace (S. Croce in Gerusalemme)

e:laurentian_schism_street_fighting.summary: For four years partisans of Laurentius held the Lateran and churches of the city while Symmachus was confined to St Peter's; clergy were killed in the streets and nuns dragged from convents.
e:laurentian_schism_street_fighting.locName: St Peter's (Symmachus' refuge) and the streets of Rome

e:symmachus_restores_pompey.summary: Theodoric asked the senator Symmachus to repair the huge, crumbling Theatre of Pompey, whose vaults, he wrote, seemed to be caves hollowed in a mountain, offering state funds.
e:symmachus_restores_pompey.note: Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, father-in-law of Boethius; c. 507-511.

e:theodoric_cloacae_bronze.summary: Cassiodorus' letters order the repair of the great sewers, 'so wonderful that they surpass the wonders of other cities', and the punishment of those stealing bronze and lead from monuments and aqueducts.
e:theodoric_cloacae_bronze.locName: the Cloaca Maxima and public monuments

e:eutharic_games_519.summary: For the consulship of Theodoric's son-in-law Eutharic, Rome saw beasts never seen before, sent from Africa, displayed in the amphitheatre; Cassiodorus says the people wondered at them.

e:boethius_sons_consuls_522.summary: Boethius watched his two young sons led as consuls from their house to the senate house by the senators and people; he gave the panegyric of Theodoric in the Curia and then distributed largesse to the crowd in the Circus. He recalled it in prison as the summit of his fortune.
e:boethius_sons_consuls_522.locName: the Curia and then the Circus Maximus

e:last_venatio_523.summary: Theodoric wrote to the consul Maximus approving the expense of venationes in the amphitheatre while deploring the cruelty of the beast fighters, who leapt over and dodged the animals; it is the last attested hunt.
e:last_venatio_523.locName: the arena of the Flavian Amphitheatre

e:cosma_damiano_mosaics_527.summary: With Theodoric's and Amalasuntha's gift, Pope Felix IV made the hall of the Templum Pacis behind the 'Temple of Romulus' into a church of the doctor saints, the first church in the Forum, with the apse mosaic of Christ on clouds.
e:cosma_damiano_mosaics_527.locName: SS. Cosma e Damiano in the former hall of the Templum Pacis

e:agapetus_library_caelian_535.summary: Pope Agapetus and Cassiodorus planned a Christian school in Rome like those of Alexandria; a library was built at Agapetus' family house on the Clivus Scauri, where an inscription 'Bibliotheca Agapeti' was found.
e:agapetus_library_caelian_535.locName: the library of Agapetus on the Clivus Scauri (by S. Gregorio)

e:belisarius_enters_asinaria_536.summary: Invited by Pope Silverius and the people, Belisarius marched in through the Asinarian Gate on 9 December while the Gothic garrison left by the Flaminian Gate; he sent the keys of the city to Justinian.
e:belisarius_enters_asinaria_536.locName: the Porta Asinaria (Goths leaving by the Porta Flaminia)

e:janus_doors_opened_537.summary: During the siege, Procopius reports, some Romans secretly tried to force open the bronze doors of the little temple of Janus in the Forum before the Curia, closed in time of peace, in the old belief that it would bring war's luck; they did not quite succeed.
e:janus_doors_opened_537.locName: the bronze shrine of Janus in front of the Curia

e:neronian_plain_battle_537.summary: A great sortie from the Pincian and Salarian gates and across the Tiber to the Plain of Nero routed part of the Gothic army, but the Roman citizen volunteers broke and the attack ended in retreat to the walls.
e:neronian_plain_battle_537.locName: the Campus Neronis by the Vatican

e:belisarius_shut_out_salaria_537.summary: After fighting all day at the bridge on the Via Salaria, Belisarius rode back at nightfall to the Salarian gate covered in blood and dust; the defenders, told he was dead, would not open, and he led a last charge under the walls before being let in.
e:belisarius_shut_out_salaria_537.note: The battle itself was at the Pons Salarius over the Anio, just N of the model area.

e:gothic_camps_neronian_field_537.summary: Witiges built six fortified camps on the left bank from the Flaminian to the Praenestine Gate and a seventh across the Tiber in the Plain of Nero by the Vatican, closing the Milvian bridge.
e:gothic_camps_neronian_field_537.locName: the Gothic camp in the Campus Neronis by the Vatican

e:aqueducts_cut_537.summary: The Goths broke all fourteen aqueducts so no water reached the city; Belisarius sealed their channels with masonry lest the enemy creep in through them. The baths of Rome fell silent and most never worked again.
e:aqueducts_cut_537.locName: where the aqueducts enter the city at the Porta Maggiore

e:floating_mills_tiber_537.summary: With the Janiculum mills dry, Belisarius moored boats in the Tiber below the bridge and hung millwheels between them in the current; when the Goths sent logs and corpses downstream to wreck them, he stretched chains across the river.
e:floating_mills_tiber_537.locName: the Tiber below the bridge at the foot of the Janiculum

e:belisarius_shoots_goth_salaria_537.summary: As the Goths' siege towers drawn by oxen approached the Salarian gate on the day of the great assault, Belisarius laughed, shot an armoured Gothic leader through the neck, and had his archers shoot only the oxen, stranding the towers.
e:belisarius_shoots_goth_salaria_537.locName: the battlements of the Porta Salaria

e:statues_hurled_hadrians_tomb_537.summary: Attacked at close quarters at the Mausoleum of Hadrian, which formed a bastion of the wall by the Aurelian (St Peter's) gate, the defenders broke up the marble statues on its summit and threw the pieces down on the Goths.
scholarship: Lanciani, The Destruction of Ancient Rome (1899)
e:statues_hurled_hadrians_tomb_537.locName: the summit of the Mausoleum of Hadrian

e:vivarium_fight_537.summary: At the weakest point of the wall, the Vivarium where animals for the shows had been kept, the Goths broke through the outer enclosure; Belisarius let them in and then sallied out, trapping and slaughtering them and burning their engines.
e:vivarium_fight_537.locName: the Vivarium between the outer and inner walls near the Porta Praenestina

e:broken_wall_st_peter_537.summary: Near the Flaminian and Pincian gates a stretch of wall had long been split and leaning outward; Belisarius wished to rebuild it, but the Romans said St Peter had promised to guard it, and indeed the Goths never attacked there.
e:broken_wall_st_peter_537.locName: the Muro Torto on the Pincian

e:silverius_deposed_pincian_537.summary: Accused of corresponding with the Goths, Pope Silverius was summoned to Belisarius' headquarters in the Pincian palace, stripped of his pallium in Antonina's presence and sent into exile; Vigilius was made pope.
e:silverius_deposed_pincian_537.locName: the Domus Pinciana near the Porta Pinciana, Belisarius' headquarters

e:goths_aqueduct_attempt_538.summary: During the truce the Goths crept along the dry channel of the Aqua Virgo under the Pincian, intending to come up inside the city; a guard saw a torch light and Belisarius blocked the passage.
e:goths_aqueduct_attempt_538.locName: the channel of the Aqua Virgo under the Pincian

e:campus_barbaricus_538.summary: To blockade the Via Latina and Appia, the Goths walled up the arches where two aqueducts cross twice, near the later Tor Fiscale, and held it with 7000 men; the place was afterwards called the Campus Barbaricus.
e:campus_barbaricus_538.locName: the crossing of the Aqua Claudia and Aqua Marcia arcades (Tor Fiscale)

e:goths_lift_siege_milvian_538.summary: After a year and nine days the Goths burned their camps and withdrew across the Milvian Bridge; Belisarius attacked as they crossed and many were killed or drowned.

e:vigilius_seized_santa_cecilia_545.summary: While celebrating the feast of St Cecilia in her church in Trastevere, Vigilius was arrested by the imperial agent Anthemius and taken to a ship on the Tiber for Constantinople; the crowd threw stones after him.

e:famine_father_tiber_546.summary: During Totila's blockade the Romans ate nettles, dogs and mice while Bessas sold grain at extortionate prices; one father of five, unable to feed his children, covered his face and leapt from a bridge into the Tiber before their eyes.
e:famine_father_tiber_546.note: Procopius does not name the bridge.

e:totila_enters_asinaria_546.summary: Four Isaurian guards let the Goths in by night through the Asinarian gate, lowering them on ropes to open it; the garrison and Bessas fled, and Totila entered a nearly empty, starving city.

e:pelagius_pleads_totila_546.summary: Totila went to pray at St Peter's; the deacon Pelagius met him with the Gospels and begged him to spare the Romans, and Totila stopped the killing. Rusticiana, Boethius' widow, who had overthrown Theodoric's statues, was protected.

e:rome_emptied_547.summary: Totila tore down about a third of the walls and thought of razing the city; dissuaded by Belisarius' letter, he left with the senators and removed the whole population, so that, says Procopius, no human being was left in Rome.

e:belisarius_rebuilds_walls_547.summary: Belisarius marched into the empty city and in 25 days refilled the breaches with loose stones without mortar, planting stakes in the ditches; Totila's attacks on the half-built walls failed.

e:last_races_circus_maximus_550.summary: Determined to treat Rome as his own, Totila brought back senators and citizens and held horse races in the Circus Maximus, the last recorded there.

e:garrison_hadrians_tomb_550.summary: Four hundred cavalrymen under Paulus took refuge in the Mausoleum of Hadrian and the bridge before it; without food, they prepared a last charge but accepted Totila's terms, most joining his army.
e:garrison_hadrians_tomb_550.locName: the Mausoleum of Hadrian and the Pons Aelius

e:totila_enters_ostiensis_550.summary: Isaurian guards, unpaid for years, opened the Porta Ostiensis to the Goths at night while trumpeters made a diversion on the river side; the Byzantine garrison fled toward Centumcellae and was cut down.

e:narses_retakes_rome_552.summary: After Busta Gallorum, Narses attacked Rome on several sides; Dagisthaeus scaled an undefended part of the wall, the Goths in Hadrian's tomb surrendered, and the keys of the city were sent to Justinian, the fifth capture of Rome in his reign.
e:narses_retakes_rome_552.locName: the walls and the Mausoleum of Hadrian

e:pelagius_oath_st_peters_556.summary: Suspected of complicity in Vigilius' death, Pelagius walked with Narses in procession from S. Pancrazio to St Peter's and, holding the Gospels and the cross over his head, swore from the ambo that he had done Vigilius no harm.
e:pelagius_oath_st_peters_556.locName: the ambo of Old St Peter's

e:santa_maria_antiqua_palace.summary: A hall at the foot of the Palatine, once part of the imperial entrance from the Forum, was turned into the church of S. Maria Antiqua, perhaps for the Byzantine governor's court; its frescoes accumulate through the 7th and 8th centuries.
e:santa_maria_antiqua_palace.locName: S. Maria Antiqua at the NW foot of the Palatine

e:fortunatus_virgil_forum_trajan.summary: Venantius Fortunatus, writing in Gaul after leaving Italy in 565/566, imagines his poems being recited 'in the Forum of Trajan', where Rome still listened to Virgil being read in public.

e:narses_bridge_salaria_565.summary: After the Gothic wars Narses restored bridges around Rome destroyed by Totila; the inscription of the Pons Salarius records his victory over the Goths.
e:narses_bridge_salaria_565.locName: the Via Salaria out of the Porta Salaria (bridge just beyond the model area)

e:san_lorenzo_pelagius_579.summary: During the Lombard siege of Rome Pope Pelagius II rebuilt the shrine of St Lawrence on the Via Tiburtina, cutting it into the hillside; he appears in the arch mosaic offering the church.

e:tiber_flood_589.summary: In November 589 the Tiber overflowed the walls and flooded much of the city, ruining churches and the papal granaries; Gregory of Tours' deacon saw a multitude of snakes and a great dragon carried down to the sea. Plague followed.
e:tiber_flood_589.locName: the low city and the walls along the Tiber

e:litany_clergy_cosma_590.summary: Gregory ordered a sevenfold procession for three days; the clergy were to set out from the church of SS. Cosma e Damiano in the Forum, chanting, toward S. Maria Maggiore.
e:litany_clergy_cosma_590.locName: SS. Cosma e Damiano in the Forum

e:litany_abbots_gervasius_590.summary: The abbots and their monks gathered at the church of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, the titulus of Vestina (S. Vitale), at the foot of the Quirinal.
e:litany_abbots_gervasius_590.locName: SS. Gervasio e Protasio (S. Vitale) in the valley below the Quirinal

e:litany_abbesses_marcellinus_590.summary: The abbesses with their nuns set out from the church of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter near the Lateran.
e:litany_abbesses_marcellinus_590.locName: SS. Marcellino e Pietro on the Via Labicana by the Lateran

e:litany_children_giovanni_paolo_590.summary: The children of Rome were assembled at the church of John and Paul on the Caelian.
e:litany_children_giovanni_paolo_590.locName: SS. Giovanni e Paolo on the Clivus Scauri, Caelian

e:litany_laymen_stephen_590.summary: The laymen gathered at the church of the protomartyr Stephen, usually identified with S. Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian.
e:litany_laymen_stephen_590.locName: S. Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian

e:litany_widows_euphemia_590.summary: The widows gathered at the church of St Euphemia on the Vicus Patricius below the Esquiline.
e:litany_widows_euphemia_590.locName: S. Eufemia on the Vicus Patricius (destroyed)

e:litany_wives_clemente_590.summary: The married women gathered at the church of St Clement in the valley between the Caelian and the Esquiline.

e:litany_eighty_die_590.summary: As the seven processions converged on S. Maria Maggiore, chanting Kyrie eleison, eighty people collapsed and died within an hour, yet Gregory continued preaching and the procession went on.
e:litany_eighty_die_590.locName: the converging processions at S. Maria Maggiore

e:angel_hadrians_tomb_legend_590.summary: Later legend says that as Gregory's procession crossed toward St Peter's, he saw the archangel Michael on top of Hadrian's Mausoleum sheathing a bloody sword, a sign that the plague had ended; the monument has been Castel Sant'Angelo since.
e:angel_hadrians_tomb_legend_590.note: The vision is first recorded in the 13th century; contemporary sources do not mention it.
e:angel_hadrians_tomb_legend_590.locName: the summit of the Mausoleum of Hadrian

e:pelagius_ii_dies_plague_590.summary: The plague that followed the flood struck the clergy first; Pelagius II died among the first victims in February 590 and the deacon Gregory was chosen to succeed him.

e:gregory_consecrated_590.summary: After trying to flee, Gregory was consecrated pope at St Peter's on 3 September 590, once the emperor Maurice's confirmation arrived.

e:agilulf_captives_walls_593.summary: With the Lombard king Agilulf before the walls, Gregory broke off his sermons on Ezekiel: from the walls he had seen Romans led away with ropes round their necks like dogs to be sold in Gaul.
e:agilulf_captives_walls_593.locName: the Aurelian Wall (Agilulf's army before the city)

e:mission_from_st_andrew_597.summary: Gregory sent Augustine, prior of his own monastery of St Andrew on the Clivus Scauri, his family's house, with about forty monks to convert the English.
e:mission_from_st_andrew_597.locName: the monastery of St Andrew on the Clivus Scauri (S. Gregorio al Celio)

e:phocas_icons_lateran_603.summary: The portraits of the new emperor Phocas and his wife arrived in Rome and were acclaimed by clergy and senate in the Lateran basilica: 'Hear us, Christ! Long life to Phocas Augustus!'; Gregory had them placed in the oratory of St Caesarius in the Palatine palace.
e:phocas_icons_lateran_603.locName: the Lateran basilica, then the oratory of St Caesarius on the Palatine

e:gregory_buried_st_peters_604.summary: Gregory died after years of illness and was buried in the portico of St Peter's, where his epitaph called him 'God's consul'. A famine followed and the people turned against his memory.
e:gregory_buried_st_peters_604.locName: the portico of Old St Peter's

e:column_phocas_608.summary: The exarch Smaragdus set a gilded statue of the emperor Phocas on a reused fluted column in front of the Rostra, 'for the innumerable benefits of his piety and the peace procured for Italy'; Phocas was overthrown two years later.
e:column_phocas_608.locName: in front of the Rostra in the Forum

e:pantheon_consecrated_609.summary: With Phocas' permission Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as a church of the Virgin and all martyrs, bringing in bones from the catacombs; it became the first pagan temple in Rome turned into a church, which saved it.
e:pantheon_consecrated_609.note: The traditional date of 13 May 609 (possibly 610 or 613).

e:earthquake_scabies_618.summary: Under Pope Deusdedit a great earthquake struck in August, followed by an epidemic of 'scabies' so disfiguring that the dead could not be recognised.

e:deusdedit_dies_618.summary: Deusdedit, who had personally cared for the sick in the epidemic after the earthquake, died and was buried in St Peter's, leaving a bequest of a full year's stipend to all his clergy.

e:honorius_venus_roma_tiles.summary: With the emperor Heraclius' consent, Pope Honorius I stripped the gilded bronze tiles from 'the temple called of Rome', the Temple of Venus and Roma, to roof St Peter's.
e:honorius_venus_roma_tiles.locName: the Temple of Venus and Roma

e:curia_becomes_sant_adriano_630.summary: Honorius I turned the Curia Iulia, the senate house rebuilt by Diocletian, into the church of S. Adriano 'in Tribus Fatis', which preserved its walls and bronze doors.

e:sant_agnese_honorius_rebuilt.summary: Honorius built a new galleried basilica on the Via Nomentana sunk to the level of St Agnes' tomb in the catacomb, with the apse mosaic showing the saint between two popes.
e:sant_agnese_honorius_rebuilt.locName: S. Agnese fuori le mura on the Via Nomentana

e:san_pancrazio_honorius.summary: Honorius I rebuilt the basilica over the tomb of the boy martyr Pancras on the Via Aurelia outside the Porta Aurelia, where oaths were sworn on the saint's relics.
e:san_pancrazio_honorius.locName: S. Pancrazio on the Via Aurelia

e:honorius_curia_rostra_630.summary: When the Curia became the church of S. Adriano, its Diocletianic bronze doors were left in place; they were moved to the Lateran in the 17th century, where they still hang.
e:honorius_curia_rostra_630.locName: the bronze doors of the Curia Iulia

e:lateran_plundered_640.summary: With the see vacant, the chartularius Maurice incited the unpaid army to besiege the Lateran for three days, then sealed its treasure, and the exarch Isaac came from Ravenna to seize it and send part to Heraclius.
e:lateran_plundered_640.note: Event of 640, before Severinus' consecration (28 May 640).

e:san_venanzio_lateran_641.summary: The Dalmatian pope John IV built an oratory beside the Lateran baptistery for relics of martyrs brought from Dalmatia and Istria, ravaged by the Avars and Slavs; its mosaic survives.
e:san_venanzio_lateran_641.locName: the oratory of S. Venanzio by the Lateran baptistery

p:statio_cohors_i_vigilum.summary: Barracks of the cohort covering Regions VII (Via Lata) and IX (Circus Flaminius). Remains seen in the 17th century between San Marcello al Corso and Santi Apostoli included large halls and statues, among them a Genius of the cohort, and many dedications to emperors by the cohort come from the same spot.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901) pl. 22
p:statio_cohors_i_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Position from the 1644 discoveries reported by Lanciani; the barracks probably filled a whole block west of Piazza Santi Apostoli.

p:statio_cohors_ii_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions III and V, on the Esquiline plateau near the later church of Santa Bibiana, inside the Aurelian circuit and just behind the line of the Servian agger. Vigiles inscriptions found here and Pirro Ligorio's note of a large building destroyed in the 16th century fix the area.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_ii_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Exact footprint unknown; placed on Via Giolitti by Santa Bibiana.

p:statio_cohors_iii_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions IV and VI, listed by the Regionary Catalogues in Region VI (Alta Semita). Vigiles inscriptions south of the Baths of Diocletian suggest it stood on the Viminal ridge between the baths and the Vicus Patricius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_iii_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Only the general area is known.

p:statio_cohors_iv_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions XII and XIII, on the Piccolo Aventino by the church of San Saba. Inscriptions naming the cohort, including dedications by its officers, were found around San Saba and fix the barracks there, controlling the Aventine and the Emporium below.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_iv_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:statio_cohors_v_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions I and II, on the Caelian beside and below Santa Maria in Domnica (the Navicella). Two large marble rosters of the cohort dated AD 205 and 210 (CIL VI 1057-1058) and altars to the Genius of its centuries were found here in the 19th century, with a courtyard and portico.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_v_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. The rosters list over 1,000 men, showing the cohort's strength after Septimius Severus.

p:statio_cohors_vi_vigilum.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions VIII and X, placed by the Regionary Catalogues in Region VIII near the imperial fora. Its site has not been found; it probably lay on the slope between the Forum of Caesar and the Capitol along the Clivus Argentarius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_vi_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Location is a guess within Region VIII.

p:statio_cohors_vii_vigilum.summary: Main barracks of the cohort for Regions XI and XIV (Transtiberim). Unlike its excavated guardhouse by San Crisogono, the station itself is unlocated; it probably stood in the dense lowland of Trastevere between Santa Maria in Trastevere and the river crossing at the Pons Aemilius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_cohors_vii_vigilum.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_cohors_vii.summary: Guardhouse of the seventh cohort excavated in 1866-1867 about 20 m south of San Crisogono, at the corner of Via di Monte Fiore and Via della VII Coorte. A Hadrianic house with a hexagonal basin in its court and a shrine (lararium) was converted into a post; more than 100 graffiti of the vigiles, dated AD 215-245 and invoking the 'Genius excubitori', cover its walls. The upper part stands about 8 m above the ancient floor.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Mols, 'L'excubitorium della VII coorte a Trastevere', Mededelingen Rome (2002)
p:excubitorium_cohors_vii.note: Reburied in 1966. Built as a house under Hadrian (brick stamps), used by the vigiles in the early 3rd century; the aedicula paintings are Severan.

p:excubitorium_regio_i.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region I had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort V, probably stood beside the Via Appia south of the Porta Capena, between the Baths of Caracalla and the Caelian.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_i.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_iii.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region III had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort I, probably stood in the Oppian valley along the Via Labicana near the Ludus Magnus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_iii.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_iv.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region IV had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort III, probably stood in the Subura near the Vicus Patricius and the Clivus Suburanus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_iv.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_ix.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region IX had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort I, probably stood in the central Campus Martius between the Theatre of Pompey and the Pantheon.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes

Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_x.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region X had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort VI, probably stood on the Clivus Victoriae at the north-west corner of the Palatine.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes

Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_xi.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region XI had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort VII, probably stood in the Forum Boarium and Velabrum by the starting gates of the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_xi.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:excubitorium_regio_xiii.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region XIII had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort IV, probably stood on the river slope of the Aventine above the Emporium.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:excubitorium_regio_xiii.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

p:statio_praefecti_vigilum.summary: Office of the equestrian prefect commanding the 3,500 to 7,000 vigiles, with judicial powers over arson, burglary and theft. Its site is unknown; scholars have suggested the area of the Crypta Balbi or the station of the first cohort by Santi Apostoli.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
p:statio_praefecti_vigilum.note: Placed at the Crypta Balbi hypothesis; the alternative is the First Cohort's station.

p:castra_praetoria_institution.summary: Sejanus concentrated the nine (later more) praetorian cohorts, until then billeted around Rome and Italy, in a single camp on the Viminal plateau in AD 23; the urban cohorts shared it. It became the arena of imperial politics: Claudius was proclaimed here in 41, the empire auctioned here in 193. Constantine abolished the guard after the Milvian Bridge in 312 and demolished the inner wall.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Praetoria
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Praetoria
p:castra_praetoria_institution.note: The physical camp is in the buildings collection (castra_praetoria_mon); this record carries the institution.

p:castra_urbana.summary: The urban cohorts, the city police under the praefectus urbi, lived in the Castra Praetoria until Aurelian gave them their own camp 'in campo Agrippae' in the 270s. It lay in Region VII east of the Via Lata, near the Forum Suarium whose pork distribution the cohorts supervised.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Urbana
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Urbana
p:castra_urbana.note: Exact site unknown; placed in the Campus Agrippae between Via del Corso and Via del Tritone.

p:castra_peregrina.summary: Camp on the Caelian of the frumentarii and other soldiers seconded from the provincial armies, who acted as couriers, supply officers and secret police. Remains, dedications to the Genius castrorum peregrinorum and a mithraeum were found under and north of Santo Stefano Rotondo.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Peregrina
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Peregrina

p:castra_priora_equitum_singularium.summary: First barracks of the emperor's horse guard, the equites singulares Augusti, founded under Trajan. Remains with many altars of the guardsmen came to light in 1885-1886 on Via Tasso, north of the Lateran.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Equitum Singularium
Speidel, Riding for Caesar (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
p:castra_priora_equitum_singularium.note: Disbanded by Constantine in 312 for supporting Maxentius.

p:castra_nova_equitum_singularium.summary: Second barracks of the imperial horse guard, built under Septimius Severus when he doubled the unit. Constantine razed it after 312 and built the Lateran basilica on top; its walls and painted rooms survive beneath the nave of San Giovanni in Laterano.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Speidel, Riding for Caesar (1994)

p:castra_misenatium.summary: Quarters of the detachment of sailors from the fleet at Misenum, who worked the great awnings (velaria) of the Colosseum and staged naval shows. The Regionary Catalogues place it in Region III, near the amphitheatre along the Via Labicana.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Misenatium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
p:castra_misenatium.note: Exact site uncertain; placed east of the Ludus Magnus.

p:castra_ravennatium.summary: Quarters in Trastevere of the sailors of the Ravenna fleet, probably connected with the naumachiae on the right bank. Listed in Region XIV by the Regionary Catalogues; often placed near San Callisto.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Ravennatium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:castra_lecticariorum.summary: Barracks of the litter-bearers' guild in Region XIV, listed in the Regionary Catalogues. The litter carriers of the wealthy were organised as a corporation and lodged together in Trastevere.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Lecticariorum
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:statio_urbana_templum_pacis.summary: The hall on the south-east side of Vespasian's Templum Pacis, whose wall carried the Severan Marble Plan (203-211), is widely taken to have housed the records of the urban prefecture and the city survey. The plan's 150 marble slabs, 18 by 13 m, show every building at 1:240.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Tucci, The Temple of Peace in Rome (2017)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
p:statio_urbana_templum_pacis.note: The hall survives as the rear wall of Santi Cosma e Damiano (527). Function as prefecture office is inferred.

p:secretarium_tellurense.summary: In late antiquity the urban prefect heard cases at the secretarium by the Temple of Tellus on the Carinae; the acts of the martyrs and the Theodosian Code place trials 'in Tellure'. The temple had been built in 268 BC on the site of Spurius Cassius' razed house.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tellus, Aedes
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Secretarium Tellurense
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:secretarium_tellurense.note: Near San Pietro in Vincoli and Via del Colosseo.

p:statio_annonae.summary: Late 4th-century arcaded hall of the grain office by the Forum Boarium, whose columns are still embedded in the walls of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. It administered the annona, the free and subsidised food supply of the city; by the late 6th century it had become a diaconia distributing church relief.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Annonae
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:statio_annonae.note: Earlier offices of the praefectus annonae stood nearby around the Ara Maxima.

p:statio_aquarum.summary: Office of the curator aquarum, moved in the early 4th century to rooms beside the spring of Juturna in the Forum. Inscriptions of the curators of 328 and later were found in the rooms; the water board controlled the aqueducts until their cutting by the Goths in 537.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Aquarum
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

p:mensa_ponderaria_castoris.summary: The Temple of Castor in the Forum served as the bureau of weights and measures: official bronze and stone weights are inscribed as checked 'ad Castoris', and the podium chambers held deposits and bankers' strongboxes. Here traders had scales and measures tested against the public standards.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castor, Aedes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Nielsen and Poulsen, The Temple of Castor and Pollux I (1992)
p:mensa_ponderaria_castoris.note: Mensa ponderaria is the generic term for a standard-measure table; the Roman one sat at this temple.

p:lautumiae.summary: Old quarry-prison on the north-west side of the Forum, below the Arx, next to the Carcer. Livy names it in the fire of 210 BC with the Forum Piscarium, and Carthaginian hostages were kept here; the area was cleared for the Forum of Caesar.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lautumiae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:curia_hostilia_senate.summary: The traditional Senate house at the north side of the Comitium, facing south. The Senate met here through the Republic; it was burned by Clodius' supporters who cremated his body inside in January 52 BC, rebuilt by Faustus Sulla and cleared by Caesar for the Curia Iulia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:curia_iulia_senate.summary: Caesar's new Senate house, dedicated by Augustus in 29 BC and rebuilt by Diocletian after the fire of 283. The last recorded act of the Senate is the reception of Phocas' images in 603; Honorius I turned the hall into the church of Sant'Adriano in 630.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:curia_pompeia_senate.summary: Hall at the east end of Pompey's portico, used by the Senate while the Curia Hostilia lay in ruins. Caesar was murdered here at the foot of Pompey's statue on 15 March 44 BC; Augustus walled it up as an accursed place.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_concord_senate.summary: A frequent meeting place of the Senate: Cicero's fourth Catilinarian (63 BC) and the condemnation of Sejanus (AD 31) were delivered here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_jupiter_senate.summary: The new consuls convened the Senate in the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the first day of their year, after their sacrifice.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_bellona_senate.summary: Because it stood outside the pomerium, the Senate met here to receive generals still holding imperium and foreign embassies not admitted to the city. Sulla had 6,000 prisoners massacred in the Villa Publica within earshot of a meeting here in 82 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_apollo_medicus_senate.summary: Next to the Temple of Bellona in the Prata Flaminia, also used for Senate meetings outside the pomerium, especially to debate triumphs.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_jupiter_stator_senate.summary: Here, on 8 November 63 BC, Cicero delivered the First Catilinarian to a Senate guarded by armed men, with Catiline present.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_fides_senate.summary: On the Capitol near the Temple of Jupiter. The Senate was meeting here in 133 BC when Scipio Nasica led the senators out to kill Tiberius Gracchus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_tellus_senate.summary: On the Carinae near Antony's house. Two days after Caesar's murder the Senate met here and, on Cicero's motion, voted an amnesty for the assassins while confirming Caesar's acts.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_castor_senate.summary: The Senate occasionally met in the temple, whose high podium also served as a speakers' platform for assemblies in the Forum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:library_apollo_senate.summary: In his old age Augustus often held Senate meetings in the Latin library hall of the Palatine Temple of Apollo, and revised the senatorial lists there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:temple_mars_ultor_senate.summary: Augustus decreed that the Senate should deliberate here on wars and triumphs, and that victorious generals should dedicate their sceptres and crowns to Mars.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:senaculum.summary: Open waiting place of the senators between the Comitium and the Temple of Concord, where they assembled before meetings in the Curia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:secretarium_senatus.summary: Late-antique court room behind the Curia, where the Senate tried senators. It was restored by the urban prefect Epiphanius in 412 after the Gothic sack; the church of Santa Martina later occupied it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

p:macellum_republican.summary: The general provisions market behind the Basilica Aemilia, built by the censor M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BC by surrounding the older fish and delicacy markets with shops. Varro describes it as the union of the specialised fora. It burned in 64 and Vespasian's Templum Pacis was built over its site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
p:macellum_republican.note: Position under the north-west part of the Templum Pacis, reached from the Argiletum.

p:forum_piscarium.summary: The fish market north of the Forum, where Plautus' characters bargain for fish. It burned with the Lautumiae and the Atrium Regium in the arson of 210 BC and was rebuilt, then absorbed in 179 BC into Fulvius' Macellum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Piscarium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_cuppedinis.summary: Market for luxury foods and dainties (cuppedia) near the Sacra Via, north-east of the Forum. Varro derives its name from the dainties or from a knight Cuppes whose house stood there; it became part of the Macellum complex.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Cuppedinis
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:macellum_liviae.summary: Provisions market on the Esquiline just outside the Porta Esquilina, dedicated by Tiberius in 7 BC in Livia's name. It served the new Esquiline quarter; Valentinian, Valens and Gratian restored it in 364-367.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum Liviae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
p:macellum_liviae.note: Placed between the Arch of Gallienus and Santa Maria Maggiore's eastern slope, near San Vito; site not excavated.

p:macellum_magnum.summary: Great market on the Caelian dedicated by Nero in 59 and shown on his coins as a two-storey building with a domed central pavilion. Santo Stefano Rotondo (c. 470) is commonly thought to stand on its site and perhaps to echo its round plan.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum Magnum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
p:macellum_magnum.note: Identification with the site of Santo Stefano Rotondo is debated.

p:forum_esquilinum.summary: Market square just inside the Porta Esquilina. In 88 BC Sulla's troops entering the city fought Marius' supporters here; it later appears among the sights of Region V.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Esquilinum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_suarium.summary: Pork market in the Campus Agrippae, Region VII, under a tribunus fori suarii and the guild of the suarii. Aurelian added free pork to the dole in the 270s and the distribution was run from here; Valentinian III still regulated it in 452.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Suarium
Barnish, 'Pigs, plebeians and potentes', PBSR 55 (1987)
p:forum_suarium.note: Site not found; placed by the Castra Urbana whose soldiers supervised it.

p:forum_vinarium.summary: Wholesale wine market known from inscriptions of merchants 'a foro vinario'. It lay near the river where wine arrived by barge, probably by the Emporium below the Aventine or across the river at Ripa.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Vinarium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:forum_vinarium.note: Location unknown; placed at the north end of the Emporium quays.

p:ciconiae_nixae.summary: Landing place in the north-west Campus Martius, named after a monument of 'leaning storks', where wine shipments were taxed. Aurelian's subsidised wine was stored in the porticoes of the Temple of Sol and distributed through this office.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ciconiae Nixae
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
p:ciconiae_nixae.note: Coarelli places it near San Salvatore in Lauro.

p:forum_pistorum.summary: Bakers' market listed in Region XIII (Aventinus), presumably near the mills and grain warehouses of the Emporium.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Pistorum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:forum_boarium_market.summary: The cattle market by the river harbour, the oldest trading place of the city, where the Etruscan and Greek traders met the Latins at the ford below the Tiber Island. It stayed a market square through antiquity.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Boarium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:forum_holitorium_market.summary: Vegetable and herb market outside the Porta Carmentalis, between the Capitol and the river, with the temples of Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita along its west side.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Holitorium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

p:porticus_minucia_frumentaria.summary: The distribution centre of the frumentationes, the free monthly grain ration (5 modii) for some 200,000 registered citizens. Recipients carried tesserae naming a day and one of 45 numbered doors (ostia) of the portico. Aurelian replaced grain with daily bread handed out from steps (gradus) across the city.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Porticus Minucia
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Virlouvet, Tessera frumentaria (1995)
p:porticus_minucia_frumentaria.note: Coarelli identifies the Frumentaria with the large portico east of Largo Argentina along Via delle Botteghe Oscure; Manacorda prefers the Crypta Balbi area. Distribution there probably began under Claudius.

p:bakery_eurysaces.summary: The freedman baker and contractor for public bread built his tomb (c. 30 BC) at the fork of the Via Praenestina and Labicana, its frieze showing grain weighed, milled by donkeys, kneaded, baked and delivered to officials. His bakery probably stood nearby at the city edge.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Sepulcrum Eurysacis
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Petersen, The Freedman in Roman Art and Art History (2006)
p:bakery_eurysaces.note: Bakery site inferred from the tomb; the tomb itself is in buildings (tomb_of_eurysaces). Regionary Catalogues count 254 bakeries (pistrina) in the city.

p:molae_ianiculi.summary: Water-mills driven by the Aqua Traiana on the Janiculum slope, partly excavated under the American Academy and along Via Garibaldi. In 537 the Goths cut the aqueducts and Belisarius kept the city fed by mounting mills on boats moored in the Tiber.
scholarship: Wilson, 'Water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:floating_mills_537.summary: When the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537, Belisarius moored boats below the bridge at the Janiculum and hung mill-wheels between them in the current; the Goths sent logs and corpses downstream to break them, and he answered with chains across the river.
scholarship: Wilson, 'Water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
p:floating_mills_537.note: Near the Pons Aurelius (Ponte Sisto). Ship-mills remained typical of medieval Rome.

p:mill_baths_caracalla.summary: A water-mill driven by the outflow of the baths was installed in the underground service galleries of the Baths of Caracalla, one of the few urban mills known in Rome.
scholarship: Schiøler and Wikander, 'A Roman water-mill in the Baths of Caracalla', Opuscula Romana 14 (1983)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:horrea_agrippiana.summary: Warehouse of three storeys around a courtyard at the foot of the Palatine on the Vicus Tuscus, built by Agrippa and rebuilt under Domitian. A shrine in the court held a statue base to the Genius horreorum Agrippianorum. Excavated in 1902-1904 by Boni beside San Teodoro.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Agrippiana
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Astolfi, Guidobaldi and Pronti, 'Horrea Agrippiana', ArchCl 30 (1978)

p:horrea_germaniciana.summary: Listed with the Horrea Agrippiana in Region VIII; presumably named after Germanicus and standing beside them along the Vicus Tuscus towards the Velabrum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Germaniciana
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_piperataria.summary: Spice warehouses built by Domitian on the Sacra Via for pepper and eastern spices. Their burning in the fire of 192 destroyed the stock of many merchants and the books Galen kept there. Maxentius levelled them for his Basilica Nova; their rooms lie under it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Piperataria
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

p:horrea_vespasiani.summary: Warehouses attributed to Vespasian in the Chronographer of 354, probably near the Sacra Via close to the Horrea Piperataria, serving the luxury trade of the Velia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Vespasiani
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_galbana.summary: The largest warehouse complex of Rome, about 167 by 146 m around three long courtyards behind the Emporium, with some 140 rooms per floor for grain, oil and wine. Built around 100 BC on land of the Sulpicii Galbae, perhaps by Ser. Sulpicius Galba (cos. 108 BC), and enlarged under the emperor Galba. Shown on the Marble Plan.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Galbana
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project

p:horrea_lolliana.summary: Warehouse with two courtyards on the Tiber quay of the Emporium, named on fragment 25 of the Marble Plan, between the Porticus Aemilia and the river.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Lolliana
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
p:horrea_lolliana.note: Builder perhaps a Lollius of the Augustan period.

p:horrea_seiana.summary: Warehouse known from inscriptions to the Genius of the horrea Seiana found near Testaccio; it probably stood south of the Horrea Galbana, perhaps named after Seius Strabo, father of Sejanus.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Seiana

p:horrea_aniciana.summary: Warehouse named after the Anicii (or Anicetus), known from inscriptions found in the Testaccio district.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:horrea_candelaria.summary: Store for candles and tallow, shown on fragment 44 of the Marble Plan as a building around a large open area. Its location in the city has not been fixed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Candelaria
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (fragment 44)
p:horrea_candelaria.note: Placed provisionally in the Velabrum; the true position is unknown.

p:horrea_chartaria.summary: Warehouse for papyrus and writing material listed in Region IV (Templum Pacis), conveniently near the booksellers of the Argiletum and the Vicus Sandaliarius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Chartaria
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
p:horrea_chartaria.note: Exact site unknown within Region IV.

p:horrea_tinei_sacerdotis.summary: Private warehouse of the senator Q. Tineius Sacerdos (cos. 158 or his homonymous son, cos. 192), known from an inscription; likely in the Emporium district.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:horrea_ummidiana.summary: Warehouse named after the Ummidii, a senatorial family, known from inscriptions and the Marble Plan tradition; probably on the Aventine side of the city.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
p:horrea_ummidiana.note: Location unknown; placed on the lower Aventine towards the Porta Raudusculana.

p:horrea_sempronia.summary: Public granaries built under Gaius Gracchus' grain law of 123 BC to store the grain sold at a fixed low price to citizens. Their site is unknown; most scholars look to the river below the Aventine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Sempronia
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_volusiana.summary: Warehouse of the Volusii Saturnini, a great senatorial family of the early empire with a household of many hundreds of slaves, known from inscriptions; probably on the right bank near the Via Portuensis landing.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

p:horrea_via_lata.summary: A large arcaded building of the late empire on the Via Lata, interpreted as a public warehouse or porticus; its ground floor later housed the diaconia of Santa Maria in Via Lata.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
p:horrea_via_lata.note: Possibly part of the Saepta or the Porticus of the Via Lata complex.

p:latrina_via_garibaldi.summary: Public latrine on the Janiculum found in 1963 under the terrace in front of San Pietro in Montorio. A channel 0.4 m wide ran round three sides; the seats were probably wooden boards on supports. Frescoes and a geometric mosaic date it to the late 2nd or early 3rd century.
scholarship: Turismo Roma, Latrina romana di via Garibaldi
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
p:latrina_via_garibaldi.note: Turismo Roma gives 41.8934 N, which falls on lower Via Garibaldi; placed here by the church terrace described in the excavation reports.

p:latrina_forum_caesaris.summary: Public latrine installed in the Trajanic rebuilding of the Forum of Caesar, in a room at its western corner by the Basilica Argentaria and the Clivus Argentarius, with marble seats along the walls over a flushing channel.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

p:latrina_largo_argentina.summary: Public latrine of the imperial period behind Temples A and B at Largo Argentina, beside the remains of the Curia of Pompey, serving the crowds of the Porticus Minucia and the theatres.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
p:latrina_largo_argentina.note: The Regionary Catalogues count 144 public latrines (foricae) in the city.

p:lacus_orphei.summary: Public fountain on the Esquiline at the top of the Clivus Suburanus, decorated with a figure of Orpheus surrounded by enchanted beasts and birds. Martial tells his book to climb past it to reach Pliny the Younger's house.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Orphei
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:lacus_orphei.note: Near Santa Lucia in Selci and San Martino ai Monti.

p:lacus_promethei.summary: Fountain with a statue group of Prometheus, listed in Region I (Porta Capena), probably on the Via Appia between the Porta Capena and the Baths of Caracalla.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Promethei
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:lacus_pastoris.summary: Fountain 'of the Shepherd' listed in Region III (Isis et Serapis), in the valley east of the Colosseum near the gladiatorial schools.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Pastoris
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

p:lacus_fundani.summary: Fountain on the lower Quirinal, possibly named after a Fundanius; it gave its name to the area where, in 63 BC, Catilinarian conspirators were said to have met.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Fundani
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
p:lacus_fundani.note: Tacitus places Flavian fighting near it in AD 69.

p:lacus_servilius.summary: Fountain basin at the west corner of the Basilica Iulia where the Vicus Iugarius entered the Forum. Sulla displayed the heads of the proscribed senators here in 82 BC; Agrippa adorned it with a hydra statue.
